Increased RGG repeats enhance phase separation when spacings are ≤63aa (PubMed:39222785).
Extrinsic Partners & Regulations: Ded1 co-phase separates with Pab1 in stress granules (PubMed:26777405, 32359423) and G3BP1 via RG/RGG interactions (PubMed:39222785). mRNA promotes condensation, lowers saturation concentration, and enables reversibility (PubMed:32359423), while G-quadruplex DNA enhances large granule formation (PubMed:34232232). eIF4G dissolves condensates via its C-terminus (PubMed:31435012). Environmental regulators include heat (T>39°C) (PubMed:32359423, 26359986), low pH (PubMed:32359423), shear stress inducing liquid-to-solid transitions (PubMed:32661370), and ATP/RNA enabling droplet formation (PubMed:31435012). Phen-DC3 (G4 stabilizer) triggers cytoplasmic foci (PubMed:34232232).

Overall Phase Separation Overview: Synapsin 1 (P17600) undergoes self-driven liquid-liquid phase separation (LLPS) forming liquid-like condensates primarily in the cytoplasm (PubMed:37862690, 38270681, 39223639, 38693139, 29976799, 39947282, 33774037). These condensates associate with synaptic vesicle clusters and recruit vesicular components, exhibiting dynamic properties including fusion competence and rapid fluorescence recovery after photobleaching (FRAP) (PubMed:37862690, 29976799, 33774037). The intrinsically disordered region (IDR; aa 416-705) is sufficient to drive phase separation and mediate charge-dependent wetting at membrane interfaces (PubMed:37862690, 29976799). No material state transitions (e.g., liquid-to-solid) are reported for synapsin itself in the provided data.
Functional Summary: Synapsin condensates cluster synaptic vesicles to form reserve pools for neurotransmitter release during sustained neuronal activity (PubMed:38270681, 29976799, 39947282, 33774037). They generate interphase pH gradients proposed to regulate vesicular ATPase activity and neurotransmitter loading (PubMed:39947282). Phosphorylation-triggered disassembly mobilizes vesicles during synaptic activation (PubMed:29976799). SCR mutations cause gain-of-function cytoskeletal mislocalization (PubMed:39947282), while alpha-synuclein imbalance disrupts condensate kinetics and links to synucleinopathy pathogenesis (PubMed:33774037, 38693139).
Intrinsic Determinants & Regulations: Phase separation is intrinsically driven by synapsin's C-terminal intrinsically disordered region (IDR; aa 416-705) through multivalent, charge-dependent interactions (PubMed:37862690, 29976799, 39947282, 33774037). Key molecular grammars include conserved segregation of polar/proline residues and arginine preference: scrambling polar/proline blocks (SCR) weakens phase separation but preserves subsaturated clustering, while arginine-to-lysine substitution (RtoK) abolishes condensation entirely (PubMed:39947282). Phosphorylation at CaMKII sites triggers rapid condensate disassembly (PubMed:29976799). Oligomerization via the central ATP-binding domain may contribute to phase separation initiation (PubMed:29976799).
Extrinsic Partners & Regulations: Synapsin phase separation requires lipid vesicles with anionic lipids (e.g., DOPS) for vesicle sequestration and condensate formation (PubMed:37862690, 38270681, 29976799, 33774037). Essential protein partners include synaptophysin (SYP), which enables cellular condensation (PubMed:39223639, 39947282, 33774037), and SH3-domain proteins (e.g., Grb2, intersectin) that co-phase separate via multivalent interactions (PubMed:29976799). Alpha-synuclein is recruited into synapsin condensates but disrupts kinetics at high ratios (PubMed:33774037, 38693139), while N-WASP modulates alpha-synuclein recruitment through mutual exclusion (PubMed:38693139). Salt concentration regulates interfacial wetting behavior (PubMed:37862690).

Overall Phase Separation Overview: ANXA11 undergoes self-driven phase separation (PS-self) via its low-complexity domain, forming dynamic liquid-like condensates in vitro and in vivo (PubMed:40118863, 37433222, 31539493, 36651622, 33087501, 32661370, 33597515). It localizes to the cytoplasm and nucleus, associating primarily with stress granules and lysosomes where it tethers RNA granules to membranes (PubMed:31539493, 36651622, 33087501). The condensates exhibit liquid-like properties (spherical droplets, fusion, rapid FRAP recovery) but undergo pathological liquid-to-solid transitions to hydrogels, amyloid fibrils, or irreversible aggregates, accelerated by disease-associated mutations or shear stress (PubMed:37433222, 36651622, 31539493, 33087501, 32661370). Reentrant phase separation occurs at both low and high salt concentrations (PubMed:33597515).
Functional Summary: Physiologically, ANXA11 phase separation enables mRNA regulation by tethering RNA granules to lysosomes for co-trafficking during cellular stress, with mechanical properties modulated by ALG2 (stiffening) and S100A6 (fluidizing) (PubMed:40118863, 31539493). Pathologically, mutations cause irreversible liquid-to-solid transitions, impairing stress granule disassembly and mRNA delivery, which underlies amyotrophic lateral sclerosis (ALS) and oculopharyngeal muscular dystrophy (PubMed:37433222, 36651622, 33087501, 31539493). These transitions produce cytotoxic aggregates that sequester RNA-binding proteins (e.g., FUS, hnRNPA1), disrupt calcium homeostasis, induce ER stress, and trigger neuronal apoptosis (PubMed:33087501). Impaired S100A6-mediated dissolution in mutants exacerbates inclusion persistence (PubMed:37433222).
Intrinsic Determinants & Regulations: Phase separation is intrinsically driven by the N-terminal low-complexity domain (LCD; residues 1-185), which is necessary and sufficient for condensation, while the C-terminal annexin repeat domain (ARD; residues 186-502) facilitates membrane binding but not phase separation itself (PubMed:40118863, 31539493). Disease-associated mutations within the LCD (e.g., G38R, D40G, D40I, G175R, G189E) reduce dynamics, promote irreversible aggregation, and delay fibrillization, whereas mutations in the ARD (e.g., H390P, R456H, R235Q, R346C) alter calcium responsiveness and condensate reversibility (PubMed:37433222, 36651622, 31539493, 33087501). The full proline-rich domain (PRD; residues 2-196) is required for phase behavior in specific contexts (PubMed:37433222).
Extrinsic Partners & Regulations: ANXA11 phase separation is modulated by key partners: ALG2 promotes condensation and gel-like states by reducing mobility and increasing lipid order, while S100A6 (CALC) inhibits condensation, maintains fluidity, and dissolves pre-formed condensates/fibrils (PubMed:40118863, 37433222). RNA enables RNA granule tethering to lysosomes, and co-scaffolding occurs with G3BP1, TDP-43, CAPRIN1, FUS, hnRNPA1, and EWSR1 in stress granules (PubMed:31539493, 33087501). Calcium ions (Ca²⁺) are essential for membrane binding (via PI(3)P interaction) and RBP partnerships (PubMed:40118863, 31539493, 33087501). Chemical regulators include dextran (induces phase separation) and NaCl (mediates reentrant behavior), while shear stress triggers liquid-to-solid transitions (PubMed:32661370, 33597515).

Overall Phase Separation Overview: YBX1 undergoes self-driven liquid-liquid phase separation (LLPS) in vitro and in cells, forming dynamic liquid-like condensates in both the nucleus and cytoplasm (PubMed:35508543, 37459535, 34766549, 38424195, 38253057, 38436697). It associates with Stress Granules (PubMed:38253057, 38436697), P-bodies (PubMed:34766549), and nuclear condensates (PubMed:37459535). The condensates exhibit liquid material properties characterized by rapid fluorescence recovery, droplet fusion, and sensitivity to 1,6-hexanediol (PubMed:35508543, 37459535, 34766549, 38436697). No material state transitions (e.g., liquid-to-solid) are reported under physiological conditions.
Functional Summary: YBX1 phase separation regulates mRNA processing during cellular stress by facilitating recruitment into stress granules (PubMed:38253057, 38436697) and enables selective sorting of miR-223 into exosomes for intercellular communication (PubMed:34766549). Pathologically, it drives tumor progression by activating ANXA8 transcription in non-small cell lung cancer (PubMed:35508543), suppressing TPM4 expression in hepatocellular carcinoma (PubMed:37459535), and stabilizing E2F1 mRNA in ovarian cancer (PubMed:38424195). Stress granule formation confers radioresistance (PubMed:38253057) and chemoresistance by promoting cell survival under oxidative stress (PubMed:38436697).
Intrinsic Determinants & Regulations: Phase separation is intrinsically driven by the C-terminal intrinsically disordered region (CTD, residues ~129-324), where aromatic tyrosine and basic arginine/lysine residues are critical for LLPS (PubMed:34766549, 37459535, 38424195, 38253057). Deletion of the CTD (Δ128-324) abolishes phase separation (PubMed:37459535, 38424195), while point mutations (tyrosine-to-serine or arginine/lysine-to-glycine substitutions) impair condensate formation (PubMed:34766549, 38424195). Phosphorylation at S174/S176 by PLK1 enhances phase separation and stress granule recruitment (PubMed:38436697).
Extrinsic Partners & Regulations: RNA partners including lncRNA MELTF-AS1 (PubMed:35508543), circASH2 (PubMed:37459535), and m5C-modified RNA (PubMed:38424195) significantly enhance droplet formation, while miR-223 is selectively recruited into condensates (PubMed:34766549). Protein partners include ATXN2L, which facilitates stress granule recruitment (PubMed:38253057); SYNCRIP and DDX6, which co-assemble in condensates (PubMed:34766549); and APE1, which promotes PLK1-mediated phosphorylation to enhance phase separation (PubMed:38436697).

Protein Name: Cleavage and polyadenylation specificity factor subunit 6
Overall Phase Separation Overview: CPSF6 undergoes self-driven phase separation (PS-self) to form dynamic, liquid-like condensates primarily in the nucleus (PubMed:36314049, 37414787, 37777964, 39258548, 39623137). These condensates associate with nuclear speckles under basal conditions and reorganize into HIV-1-induced membraneless organelles (HIV-1 MLOs) during viral infection, exhibiting spherical morphology, fusion events, and rapid fluorescence recovery (PubMed:36314049, 37414787, 39258548, 39623137). Material state remains liquid-like without reported transitions, though phosphorylation can disrupt phase separation (PubMed:37777964, 39258548).
Functional Summary: Physiologically, CPSF6 condensates regulate alternative polyadenylation by promoting distal poly(A) site usage and longer 3' UTRs for cell-cycle genes; disrupted phase separation in cancer correlates with shortened UTRs and accelerated proliferation (PubMed:37777964). During HIV-1 infection, HIV-1 MLOs serve as hubs for nuclear reverse transcription, concentrate viral/host factors, and shield viral DNA from cGAS-mediated innate immune detection (PubMed:36314049, 37414787, 39258548, 39623137). Condensate dissolution via PF74 or CPSF6 knockout exposes viral DNA, triggering cGAS-STING activation and interferon responses (PubMed:39623137). Hyperosmotic stress induces condensation that sequesters cleavage factors, impairing transcription termination (PubMed:32857953).
Intrinsic Determinants & Regulations: Phase separation is intrinsically driven by the arginine/serine-like domain (RSLD, aa 399-551), where arginine-rich motifs mediate multivalent interactions (PubMed:37777964). The C-terminal mixed-charge domain (MCD) and prion-like domain (PrLD) also contribute to condensation, while the RRM domain stabilizes but does not initiate droplets (PubMed:39258548). Phosphorylation at specific residues (S494, S500, S506, S511, S513, S525 by CLK2 in RSLD; MCD sites by CLK1) inhibits phase separation (PubMed:37777964, 39258548). Mutations disrupting arginine residues (e.g., CPSF6-15RA) or domain deletions (ΔMCD/ΔPrLD) impair condensation (PubMed:37777964, 39258548).
Extrinsic Partners & Regulations: HIV-1 capsid (CA) acts as a primary scaffold, triggering CPSF6 condensation through direct binding and enabling higher-order co-aggregation (PubMed:36314049, 39258548, 39623137). CPSF5 co-assembles as a client protein within CPSF6 condensates without autonomous phase separation capacity (PubMed:37414787, 37777964, 38762180). Small molecules modulate dynamics: PF74 dissolves condensates by disrupting CA binding, while nevirapine stabilizes them during reverse transcription inhibition (PubMed:37414787, 39623137). CPSF6 also partitions into SNRNP70 condensates via RSLD-LC1 domain interactions and colocalizes with SC35 in nuclear speckles (PubMed:36073763, 36314049, 37414787).

Overall Phase Separation Overview: YTHDF1 undergoes self-driven liquid-liquid phase separation (LLPS) both in vitro and in vivo (PubMed:31388144, 31292544). It forms liquid-like condensates primarily in the cytoplasm and associates with stress granules under diverse stress conditions including oxidative stress, heat shock, arsenite exposure, and cellular senescence (PubMed:32451507, 31292544, 38926365). In unstressed cells, it exists in a super-saturated state forming small clusters that promote stress granule nucleation by reducing the activation energy barrier for condensation (PubMed:32451507).
Functional Summary: YTHDF1 phase separation is critical for stress granule formation under diverse stresses, enabling sequestration of m⁶A-modified mRNAs during stress response (PubMed:32451507, 31292544). Peripheral localization in stress granules may poise mRNAs for translation re-initiation post-stress (PubMed:32451507). During cellular senescence, it sequesters polymethylated mRNAs of cell-cycle regulators (e.g., SMC2, CENPE) in stress granules, repressing their translation to maintain growth arrest (PubMed:38926365). This compartmentalization facilitates mRNA fate determination through spatial regulation in membraneless organelles (PubMed:31292544).
Intrinsic Determinants & Regulations: Phase separation is intrinsically driven by YTHDF1's low-complexity domain (LCD), which autonomously undergoes concentration-dependent LLPS in vitro (PubMed:31388144, 31292544). Both the N-terminal intrinsically disordered region (N-IDR) and the YTH domain are essential for stress granule formation, with the YTH domain enabling m⁶A-RNA binding that facilitates multivalent interactions (PubMed:32451507). The D401N mutation in the YTH domain impairs m⁶A binding and disrupts stress granule formation even when oligomerized, demonstrating the functional interdependence of these domains (PubMed:32451507).
Extrinsic Partners & Regulations: Polymethylated mRNAs containing multiple m⁶A residues act as essential multivalent scaffolds that dramatically enhance LLPS by juxtaposing YTH domains and facilitating LCD interactions (PubMed:31388144, 31292544). Specific RNA motifs like AUGG(m⁶A)CUCC significantly lower the saturation concentration for phase separation (PubMed:31388144). YTHDF1 co-phase separates with paralogs YTHDF2 and YTHDF3 to form heterotypic condensates (PubMed:31292544). It spatially coordinates with G3BP1 at stress granule periphery/junctions, promoting cluster growth and stress granule assembly (PubMed:32451507).

Overall Phase Separation Overview: IGF2BP1 undergoes both self-driven (PubMed:37036576, 38525957, 36214649) and partner-induced phase separation (PubMed:36288717, 29463567, 32668274, 39891203), forming condensates primarily in the cytoplasm and nucleus during heat stress (PubMed:36288717, 29463567, 32668274, 36214649, 39891203). It associates with Stress Granules as a core component (PubMed:29463567, 32668274) and forms heat-induced m6A E7 mRNA-IGF2BP1 granules (PubMed:36288717). Condensates exhibit liquid-like properties including fusion, fission, and rapid mobility (PubMed:36288717, 37036576, 36214649, 39891203), but undergo pathological liquid-to-solid transitions during prolonged heat stress (PubMed:36288717) and partition into solid-like nanocores within Stress Granules (PubMed:29463567).
Functional Summary: Phase separation regulates mRNA during cellular stress by enabling Stress Granule assembly and mRNA sorting (PubMed:29463567, 32668274). Pathologically, it promotes tumorigenesis by stabilizing oncogenic mRNAs: GPX4 stabilization inhibits ferroptosis in breast cancer (PubMed:37036576); c-Myc/E2F1 stabilization accelerates cell-cycle progression in lung cancer via a positive feedback loop (PubMed:36214649); and ITGB1 stabilization enhances proliferation, migration, and cisplatin resistance in oral cancer (PubMed:39891203). Conversely, heat-induced phase separation degrades HPV E7 mRNA, suppressing cervical oncogenicity (PubMed:36288717).
Intrinsic Determinants & Regulations: Phase separation is intrinsically driven by K homology (KH) domains and intrinsically disordered regions (IDRs). The KH3/4 di-domain is essential for phase separation and RNA binding (PubMed:37036576, 32668274), while an IDR upstream of KH1/2 (residues 157-361) and within the N-terminal region (residues 1-320) is critical for condensation (PubMed:32668274, 36214649, 39891203). Mutations in the m6A-binding domain abolish granule formation (PubMed:36288717), and deletion/mutation of the IDR (residues 64-310) impairs phase separation (PubMed:36214649, 39891203). The KH domains and low-complexity region enable strong retention in Stress Granules (PubMed:29463567).
Extrinsic Partners & Regulations: Phase separation is modulated by RNA and protein partners. The lncRNAs RUNX1-IT1 and MNX1-AS1 act as scaffolds, enhancing droplet formation and increasing condensate size/number (PubMed:37036576, 36214649). Client mRNAs (c-Myc and E2F1 3'-UTRs) co-phase separate with IGF2BP1 and enrich within condensates (PubMed:36214649). Poly(A) mRNA associates early with clusters for stress granule maturation (PubMed:32668274). Protein partners include G3BP1, which co-assembles in Stress Granules (PubMed:29463567), and homologous proteins IGF2BP2/IGF2BP3 that co-cluster during granule assembly (PubMed:32668274).

Overall Phase Separation Overview: YTHDF2 undergoes self-driven liquid-liquid phase separation (LLPS) both in vitro and in vivo, forming dynamic liquid-like condensates (PubMed:31388144, 31292544, 31642031, 39823477). It constitutively localizes to P-bodies and relocalizes to stress granules under diverse stressors including arsenite, heat shock, and ER stress (PubMed:37973889, 31388144, 31292544, 39490166, 38926365). Phase separation occurs primarily in the cytoplasm and exhibits rapid fluorescence recovery in FRAP assays, confirming liquid-like material properties with no reported solid-state transitions (PubMed:31388144, 31292544, 39490166).
Functional Summary: YTHDF2 phase separation mediates mRNA regulation during cellular stress by targeting m6A-mRNA to P-bodies for degradation and stress granules for translational repression (PubMed:31388144, 31292544). In stress granules, it recruits EIF2AK1 to phosphorylate eIF2α, inhibiting translation initiation of targets like PTEN mRNA and activating pro-survival AKT signaling (PubMed:39490166). Pathologically, this process promotes malignant transformation during chronic arsenite exposure in keratinocytes and PM2.5-induced lung cancer through accelerated degradation of tumor suppressors like GADD45A mRNA (PubMed:39490166, 39823477). It also stabilizes cellular senescence by repressing cell-cycle mRNAs (PubMed:38926365).
Intrinsic Determinants & Regulations: Phase separation is intrinsically driven by YTHDF2's low-complexity domain (LCD), particularly its glutamine-rich region, which autonomously forms condensates (PubMed:31388144, 31292544, 31642031, 39490166). Mutations in this LCD (Q-to-A substitutions) abolish phase separation (PubMed:31642031, 39490166). The YTH domain is essential for m6A-RNA binding and enhancement of phase separation; W432A and W432A/W486A mutations impair this enhancement without affecting intrinsic LCD-driven condensation (PubMed:31388144, 31642031).
Extrinsic Partners & Regulations: YTHDF2 phase separation is potently enhanced by polymethylated m6A-RNA scaffolds, which lower the saturation concentration for LLPS and increase partition coefficients (PubMed:31388144, 31292544, 31642031). Specific RNA partners include PTEN mRNA and circDNA2, which bind the LCD to promote condensation (PubMed:39490166, 39823477). Protein partners include G3BP1 (co-localizing in stress granules), EIF2AK1 (recruited to condensates), and paralogs YTHDF1/YTHDF3, with all three DF proteins forming heterotypic condensates (PubMed:31388144, 31292544, 39490166). Oxidative stress and arsenite exposure further promote phase separation (PubMed:39490166).

Overall Phase Separation Overview: D3KYQ3 undergoes self-driven phase separation (PubMed:36257947, 36765044, 25562883) primarily within the nucleus where it forms the nuclear pore complex (PubMed:36765044, 25562883). The condensates exhibit hydrogel-like to solid material states, characterized by high intra-phase density and selective permeability properties, with no reported material state transitions (PubMed:36765044, 25562883).
Functional Summary: D3KYQ3 condensates form the selective permeability barrier of the nuclear pore complex, enabling nuclear transport receptor (NTR)-cargo translocation while excluding inert macromolecules (PubMed:36765044, 25562883). Spacer length between FG repeats directly controls barrier selectivity by tuning mesh size, with shorter spacers creating hypercohesive phases that impede NTR entry (PubMed:36765044). Pathological hypercohesion from FSFG mutations disrupts nuclear transport function, while tyrosine substitutions (GLYG) demonstrate evolutionary trade-offs between selectivity and biochemical safety (PubMed:36765044). The phase separation mechanism also explains NTR cooperation effects for large cargo translocation (PubMed:25562883).
Intrinsic Determinants & Regulations: Phase separation is intrinsically driven by FG repeat domains featuring hydrophobic phenylalanine motifs (PubMed:36257947, 36765044, 25562883). Spacer length between motifs critically regulates cohesion: shorter spacers (e.g., 6-8aa) enhance hydrophobic interactions, lowering saturation concentrations and increasing density, while longer spacers reduce cohesion (PubMed:36765044). Mutations altering motif hydrophobicity significantly impact behavior: GLFG→FSFG substitutions cause hypercohesion that impedes nuclear transport receptor (NTR) entry, whereas GLFG→GLYG mutations preserve phase separation but disrupt native NTR binding (PubMed:36765044).
Extrinsic Partners & Regulations: Poly(A) RNA acts as an extrinsic promoter by lowering saturation concentration and enhancing droplet formation (PubMed:36765044). The nuclear transport receptor NTF2 does not alter phase separation thresholds or critical concentrations (PubMed:25562883). No other extrinsic regulators or co-phase separating partners were identified.

Overall Phase Separation Overview: SOD1 exhibits both self-driven and partner-dependent phase separation behaviors (PubMed:36592929, 36416085, 39172789). It autonomously forms liquid-like condensates through self-assembly (PS-self) in its metal-free, disulfide-reduced state (ApoSOD1^{2SH}), driven by conformational disorder in loop IV (aa 49-83) and loop VII (aa 121-142) (PubMed:36416085, 36592929). SOD1 also partitions as a client (PS-other) into CAPRIN1-formed condensates and stress granules (PubMed:39172789, 28377462, 38626504). Primary subcellular localization occurs in the cytoplasm, with consistent association to stress granules (PubMed:39172789, 28377462). Material states range from dynamic liquid droplets to solid aggregates, with frequent liquid-to-solid transitions observed upon oxidation, prolonged incubation, or in mutant forms (PubMed:36592929, 36416085, 39172789). Wild-type SOD1 typically initiates in a liquid state but transitions to fibrillar solids under oxidative stress, while ALS mutants like A4V often form gel/solid aggregates directly (PubMed:36592929, 36416085, 35853451).
Functional Summary: SOD1 phase separation has dual physiological-pathological roles. Physiologically, it localizes to stress granules for mRNA regulation during cellular stress (PubMed:39172789, 28377462). Pathologically, condensates initiate ALS-associated aggregation: liquid-to-solid transitions generate cytotoxic fibrils that cause neuronal death (PubMed:36592929, 36416085). Immature SOD1 undergoes CAPRIN1-driven unfolding in condensates, accelerating aggregation (PubMed:39172789). Mutants (A4V, G85R, G93A) exhibit heightened toxicity, with A4V forming highly cytotoxic aggregates rapidly (PubMed:36592929). Condensates themselves are more toxic than mature aggregates, implicating phase transition dynamics in neurodegeneration (PubMed:36416085). Misfolded SOD1 accumulation in stress granules impairs disassembly, promotes chaperone recruitment, and correlates with TDP-43 depletion—mechanisms linked to ALS progression (PubMed:28377462). Maturation via zinc binding confers resilience against these pathological transitions (PubMed:39172789).
Intrinsic Determinants & Regulations: Phase separation is intrinsically regulated by conformational flexibility in disordered regions: the electrostatic loop (loop VII) and zinc-binding loop (loop IV) enable multivalent interactions essential for self-assembly (PubMed:36592929, 36416085). Key post-translational modifications include oxidation of Cys111 and Trp32, which enhances phase separation and aggregation (PubMed:36592929), and metal-binding status—zinc stabilizes the folded dimer and inhibits phase separation, while metal depletion promotes disorder (PubMed:36416085, 39172789). Disulfide bond formation confers resistance to condensate-driven unfolding (PubMed:39172789). ALS-associated mutations (A4V, G85R, G37R, G93A) disrupt structural stability or metal binding: A4V promotes hydrophobic exposure (PubMed:36592929, 35853451); G85R and I113T compromise zinc coordination (PubMed:36416085); and G93A reduces folding stability (PubMed:36592929). These mutations universally increase aggregation propensity within condensates (PubMed:28377462, 35853451).
Extrinsic Partners & Regulations: Phase separation is modulated by partners and environmental factors. SOD1 partitions into CAPRIN1 condensates as a client, where scaffold interactions remodel its conformational equilibrium toward unfolded states (PubMed:39172789, 38626504). In stress granules, it co-localizes with FUS, G3BP1, and G3BP2, reducing partner mobility and promoting aberrant solidification (PubMed:28377462). Ions critically regulate behavior: Zn²⁺ inhibits/reverses self-driven phase separation (IC₅₀ ~1:2 protein:Zn) (PubMed:36416085), while NaCl enables CAPRIN1 scaffold formation essential for SOD1 recruitment (PubMed:39172789). Cu²⁺ has no effect (PubMed:36416085). Chemical inducers include H₂O₂, which oxidizes Cys111/Trp32 to enhance LLPS and aggregation (PubMed:36592929), and PEI, which accelerates droplet formation (PubMed:36416085). Chaperones (HSP70, HSP27) and ubiquitin are recruited to SOD1-positive condensates for quality control (PubMed:28377462).

Overall Phase Separation Overview: Bovine serum albumin (BSA) undergoes self-driven phase separation in vitro, forming liquid-like condensates (PubMed:37853127, 39642205, 39648588). It primarily associates with artificial coacervate systems rather than natural membrane-less organelles (PubMed:39971992, 37815312, 36511362). BSA exhibits reversible liquid material properties, evidenced by rapid FRAP recovery and spherical droplet morphology (PubMed:39971992, 37815312, 39648588). Under specific conditions, it undergoes material state transitions: photopolymerization drives evolution from homogeneous solutions to multicompartmental structures and vesicles (PubMed:39971992), while high PEG concentrations induce compact coacervates with reduced water content (PubMed:37815312).
Functional Summary: BSA phase separation enables artificial protocell modeling through stable (>300 days) multicompartmental coacervates that enhance enzymatic catalysis (e.g., 8-29.4× lipase activity amplification) via spatial organization (PubMed:39971992). It buffers water potential by liberating hydration water under low-free-water conditions (PubMed:37853127). In crowded environments, BSA regulates model condensate morphology and kinetics, demonstrating how background molecules influence membrane-less organelle formation (PubMed:36511362). These properties have biomedical relevance for protein stabilization in formulations, though no pathological implications were reported (PubMed:39648588).
Intrinsic Determinants & Regulations: BSA phase separation is intrinsically driven by surface-exposed intrinsically disordered regions (IDRs) and unfavorable hydration surfaces that respond to low water potential (PubMed:37853127). Oligomerization into dimers/trimers (association constant K₁ ~10⁴–10⁵ M⁻¹) is essential for phase separation (PubMed:39648588). No domain-specific drivers, PTMs, splicing variants, repeat features, or disease-associated mutations were identified across studies (PubMed:39971992, 37815312, 36511362, 39642205, 39648588).
Extrinsic Partners & Regulations: BSA phase separation is extrinsically regulated by polymers, crowding agents, and small molecules. It forms coacervates with PDADMAC, where sucrose increases droplet size and BSA incorporation, while PEG enhances phase separation density and induces compact complexes via depletion forces (PubMed:37815312). PEG (≥10% w/v) triggers partially segregative phase separation, with PEG partitioning into droplets (PubMed:39648588). Electrostatic interactions drive coacervation with poly-L-lysine (PLL), while Q-dextran enables weak co-phase separation (PubMed:36511362). Proline inhibits phase separation by increasing repulsive interactions and BSA solution stability (PubMed:39642205).

Overall Phase Separation Overview: The prion protein (PrP, P04156) undergoes self-driven liquid-liquid phase separation (LLPS) both in vitro and in vivo, forming dynamic liquid-like condensates that can transition to solid states (PubMed:37805139, PubMed:34737230, PubMed:31821812, PubMed:39333690, PubMed:39826709). These condensates primarily localize to the cytoplasm and plasma membrane, with specific formation at cell-cell interfaces observed under Cu²⁺ exposure (PubMed:37922348, PubMed:39333690). PrP condensates recruit NF-κB signaling components in hepatocellular carcinoma, forming non-canonical membrane-less organelles (PubMed:39333690). Material states range from liquid to hydrogel and solid, with irreversible liquid-to-solid transitions occurring upon aging, oxidative stress, or prolonged metal ion exposure, leading to amyloid formation (PubMed:37922348, PubMed:34737230, PubMed:31821812, PubMed:39826709).
Functional Summary: PrP phase separation governs both physiological and pathological processes. Physiologically, cytoplasmic condensates recruit NF-κB components (TRAF2/6, TAB2/3, TAK1) to activate signaling pathways that drive hepatocellular carcinoma progression via IL-8 upregulation (PubMed:39333690). Short-term Cu²⁺-dependent condensates buffer copper toxicity, mitigating oxidative stress (PubMed:37922348). Pathologically, LLPS nucleates amyloidogenesis: liquid-to-solid transitions in full-length or truncated (Y145Stop) PrP form cytotoxic fibrils linked to prion diseases (CJD, GSS syndrome, familial CAA) (PubMed:37922348, PubMed:34737230, PubMed:39826709). Protective mutations (H177R, N159D, G127V, G127I) inhibit transitions by enhancing fluidity or promoting droplet dissolution, reducing aggregation and cytotoxicity (PubMed:37805139, PubMed:31821812). Chaperones like Ydj1 and Clusterin prevent pathological transitions through dynamic sequestration or co-localization, suggesting quality-control mechanisms (PubMed:39826709, PubMed:39476948).
Intrinsic Determinants & Regulations: Phase separation is intrinsically regulated by PrP's structural domains and mutations. The N-terminal intrinsically disordered region (IDR; residues 23-120/144) drives spontaneous LLPS through electrostatic and hydrophobic interactions, with octapeptide repeats (PHGGGWGQ) and hydrophobic regions (residues 113-135) serving as key drivers (PubMed:34737230, PubMed:39826709). The C-terminal globular domain (residues 121-231) modulates behavior, where α3 helix and disulfide bonding (Cys179-Cys214) are essential for condensate formation and functionality (PubMed:39333690). Disease-associated mutations enhance (A113V/A115V/A117V in Y145Stop) or suppress LLPS: H177R and N159D increase saturation concentrations and droplet fluidity, inhibiting amyloidogenesis (PubMed:37805139), while G127V/G127I mutations promote droplet reversion to solution, preventing liquid-to-solid transitions (PubMed:31821812).
Extrinsic Partners & Regulations: PrP phase separation is extrinsically modulated by ions, biomolecules, and protein partners. Cu²⁺ acts as an essential scaffold for condensation at plasma membranes, with removal by EDTA dissolving condensates, while prolonged exposure generates ROS that trigger pathological transitions (PubMed:37922348). RNA (tRNA, polyU) stoichiometrically tunes LLPS—low ratios lower saturation concentrations but induce gel-like states, whereas high ratios inhibit phase separation entirely (PubMed:34737230, PubMed:39826709). Salt concentration critically regulates behavior: 350 mM NaCl induces homotypic LLPS in Y145Stop, while heterotypic condensates with Ydj1 dissolve at ≥75 mM NaCl (PubMed:39826709). Protein partners include Ydj1, which co-phase separates to form dynamic heterotypic condensates that inhibit amyloidogenesis (PubMed:39826709); Clusterin, which co-localizes to prevent post-cleavage aggregation (PubMed:39476948); and TRAF2/6, TAB2/3, and TAK1, recruited into PrP condensates for NF-κB activation (PubMed:39333690). The prion peptide PrP 106-126 exacerbates cytotoxicity in wild-type but not protective mutants (PubMed:31821812).

Overall Phase Separation Overview: FtsZ (P0A9A6) undergoes both self-driven phase separation (PS-self) and partner-dependent phase separation (PS-other) in the Escherichia coli cytoplasm (PubMed:33581219, 36854378, 36315857, 30523075, 40174834). It forms dynamic, liquid-like regulatory condensates proposed to prevent Z-ring assembly over the nucleoid (PubMed:36854378, 30523075). These condensates exhibit reversible transitions to solid-like FtsZ polymers upon GTP addition, with material states interconverting between liquid droplets and polymeric fibers (PubMed:36854378, 36315857, 30523075, 33581219).
Functional Summary: Phase separation spatially regulates cell division by sequestering FtsZ-GDP near the nucleoid via SlmA-SBS condensates, preventing aberrant Z-ring assembly over chromosomes (PubMed:36854378, 30523075, 36315857). Reversible GTP-driven transitions enable rapid mobilization of FtsZ for divisome formation post-chromosome segregation (PubMed:36854378, 36315857, 30523075). This mechanism facilitates stress adaptation, with condensates proposed to halt division during antibiotic stress or GTP depletion, promoting persister cell formation (PubMed:36854378, 33581219). Coordination with MatP links chromosome segregation to cytokinesis, with condensate dissolution by matS DNA ensuring timely division (PubMed:40174834).
Intrinsic Determinants & Regulations: Phase separation is intrinsically regulated by FtsZ's oligomeric state, with GDP-bound oligomerization enabling multivalent interactions essential for condensation (PubMed:36854378, 33581219). The C-terminal disordered domain (residues 315-383) enhances condensation kinetics, as deletion (FtsZΔCter) reduces condensate size and slows formation while retaining phase separation capability (PubMed:33581219).
Extrinsic Partners & Regulations: Essential extrinsic scaffolds include the SlmA·SBS DNA complex, without which heterotypic condensation cannot occur (PubMed:36854378, 36315857, 30523075). Chemical regulators include: GTP triggering reversible condensate-to-polymer transitions (PubMed:36854378, 36315857, 30523075); potassium glutamate enhancing condensation versus KCl (PubMed:36315857); and high salt (≥300 mM KCl) dissolving condensates (PubMed:36854378, 33581219). Mg²⁺ modulates size and dynamics, reducing exchange rates at higher concentrations (PubMed:36315857). Lipid surfaces promote condensate accumulation and fusion (PubMed:36315857, 40174834), while macromolecular crowders (e.g., dextran) are required for phase separation in vitro (PubMed:30523075, 33581219). Partners include ZapA (client partitioning into condensates; PubMed:36854378) and MatP (forming heterotypic condensates disrupted by matS DNA; PubMed:40174834).

MLO Types: PML nuclear body; Postsynaptic density; Receptor cluster
Overall Phase Separation Overview: Nck requires binding partners for phase separation and does not undergo self-assembly alone (PubMed:30846599, 38161366, 25321392). It forms liquid-like condensates primarily in the cytoplasm (PubMed:30846599, 38161366, 31268421), associating with membrane-associated receptor clusters, signaling complex condensates, and immunological synapse condensates (PubMed:30846599, 38161366, 31268421). The material state remains consistently liquid across studies, with no observed state transitions reported (PubMed:30846599, 38161366, 26553976, 25321392).
Functional Summary: Nck condensates enhance actin nucleation by increasing dwell time of N-WASP/Arp2/3 complexes, enabling stoichiometry-dependent control of actin assembly in processes like podocyte function and immune signaling (PubMed:30846599, 25321392, 26553976). During EPEC infection, condensates facilitate bacterial entry via actin pedestal formation; disruption by p1 inhibitor blocks infection (PubMed:38161366). In T cells, condensates enable radial movement across immunological synapses by coupling to actin networks, with Nck dissipation regulating movement transitions (PubMed:31268421). Dysregulation may contribute to kidney disorders and immune dysfunction, though pathological transitions remain unreported (PubMed:30846599, 38161366).
Intrinsic Determinants & Regulations: Phase separation is driven by multivalent SH2 and SH3 domains that facilitate partner interactions (PubMed:25321392, 30846599, 38161366). The intrinsically disordered linker (L1) between the first two SH3 domains critically enhances phase separation through its basic N-terminal element (KVKRK motif) and overall positive charge, enabling weak electrostatic self-assembly (PubMed:26553976). Mutations reducing positive charge (e.g., L1K/E, L1ΔKVKRK) impair phase separation, while charge-enhancing mutations (e.g., L1basic) promote it (PubMed:26553976). Basic regions in the linker and SH2 domain also mediate actin binding within condensates (PubMed:31268421).
Extrinsic Partners & Regulations: Nck co-phase separates with phosphorylated nephrin (via SH2 domain) and N-WASP (via SH3 domains) to form signaling condensates (PubMed:30846599, 25321392, 26553976). The phosphopeptide 3pY promotes phase separation by mimicking multivalent phosphorylated nephrin, while monovalent phosphopeptides (e.g., Y474) and covalent inhibitor p1 disrupt condensates by competing for SH2 binding (PubMed:38161366). In T cell activation, Nck recruits to LAT condensates via SLP-76 and couples to actin filaments (PubMed:31268421). Stoichiometry of partners modulates condensate dynamics, with trivalent SH3 configurations lowering phase separation thresholds (PubMed:25321392).

Overall Phase Separation Overview: GLH-1 undergoes phase separation as a core structural component of P granules in the C. elegans germline, exhibiting liquid-like material properties in both cytoplasm and nucleus (PubMed:36070689, 32245789, 30833787). These condensates display dynamic behavior including in vivo disassembly during embryogenesis and stress-induced decondensation under imaging conditions (PubMed:32245789, 35801939). Mutations such as DQAD alter material properties, resulting in less dynamic, persistent granules resistant to disassembly (PubMed:32245789).
Functional Summary: GLH-1 phase separation enables mRNA surveillance at nuclear pores, with defective RNA release (DQAD mutant) causing granule mis-sorting to somatic cells and reduced fertility (PubMed:32245789). As a P-compartment scaffold, it maintains germ granule integrity essential for germline development, stem cell maintenance, and meiosis (PubMed:36070689, 34223818). Dysregulation through HERD-1 loss causes aberrant P/Z/M compartment mixing, disorganizing small RNA pathways and prolonging transgenerational epigenetic inheritance (PubMed:39354132). Depletion disrupts P granule coalescence, leading to sterility and embryonic lethality (PubMed:34223818).
Intrinsic Determinants & Regulations: Phase separation is intrinsically driven by FG-repeat regions critical for in vitro condensation, with deletion (GLH-1ΔFG) abolishing phase separation capacity (PubMed:36070689). The DEAD box domain enables ATP-dependent RNA binding and hydrolysis, while residue T663 mediates RNA interactions essential for granule dynamics (PubMed:32245789). FGG repeats facilitate nuclear periphery anchoring without directly driving condensation (PubMed:32245789). Disease-relevant mutations (DAAD, Q368A, T663A, DQAD) impair phase separation through disrupted ATP/RNA binding (PubMed:32245789).
Extrinsic Partners & Regulations: GLH-1 phase separation requires newly transcribed mRNAs for maintenance and dissolves upon RNA depletion (PubMed:32245789). It is anchored within P granules through direct binding to MIP-1 and MIP-2 LOTUS domains, with MIP depletion increasing GLH-1 mobility and mislocalization (PubMed:34223818). HERD-1 regulates GLH-1 interactions, restricting aberrant binding to Z-compartment proteins (ZNFX-1/DEPS-1) to maintain compartment immiscibility (PubMed:39354132). GLH-1 co-phase separates with PRG-1, CSR-1, and PAB-1 in RNA-dependent complexes and requires MEG-3 for proper localization (PubMed:32245789, 30833787).

MLO Types: Centrosome; Destruction complex condensate; Transcriptional condensate
Overall Phase Separation Overview: β-catenin undergoes both self-driven and partner-dependent phase separation, forming dynamic liquid-like condensates (PubMed:39316611, 31563432, 37657935, 36037369, 37873736, 38279052). It localizes to the nucleus and cytoplasm, associating with transcriptional condensates at Wnt-response elements (PubMed:39316611, 37657935), super-enhancer-driven Mediator condensates (PubMed:31563432), destruction complex condensates (PubMed:36037369, 37873736, 38279052), and centrosomal condensates (PubMed:36037369). These condensates exhibit liquid properties including fusion, fission, and rapid FRAP recovery (t½ ~8-60 seconds), with potential hydrogel transitions observed in vitro after prolonged incubation (PubMed:39316611).
Functional Summary: Phase separation regulates β-catenin's dual roles: in destruction complex condensates, it enables phosphorylation and degradation to suppress Wnt signaling and inhibit colorectal cancer growth (PubMed:36037369, 37611590, 37873736, 38279052). Dysregulation (e.g., APC truncations) prevents kinase recruitment, leading to β-catenin accumulation and tumorigenesis (PubMed:38279052). In nuclear transcriptional condensates with LEF1 and MED1, it activates Wnt targets (e.g., c-myc, Sp5), driving stem cell differentiation and tumor proliferation/metastasis (PubMed:39316611, 37657935, 31563432). Centrosomal condensates dissolve upon Wnt activation, facilitating β-catenin stabilization and nuclear translocation (PubMed:36037369).
Intrinsic Determinants & Regulations: Phase separation is intrinsically driven by β-catenin's N-terminal (aa 1–140) and C-terminal intrinsically disordered regions (IDRs), where aromatic residues are essential for homotypic and heterotypic condensation (PubMed:39316611, 31563432). Aromatic-to-alanine mutations in these IDRs abolish phase separation capacity, impairing droplet formation in vitro and transcriptional activation in vivo (PubMed:39316611, 31563432). The IDRs enable autonomous phase separation at concentrations as low as ~5 μM (PubMed:31563432).
Extrinsic Partners & Regulations: β-catenin co-phase separates with multiple partners: LEF1 scaffolds transcriptional condensates at Wnt-response elements (PubMed:39316611, 37657935); MED1 incorporates it into super-enhancer condensates via IDR interactions (PubMed:31563432); Axin1 recruits it into destruction complex condensates stabilized by APC (PubMed:36037369, 37611590, 38279052); and USP10 enhances destruction complex condensation, with AMPK-mediated USP10 phosphorylation strengthening this effect (PubMed:37873736). Kinases (GSK3β, CK1α) partition into destruction condensates for β-catenin phosphorylation (PubMed:36037369, 38279052). Centrosomal condensates dissolve upon Wnt activation, correlating with β-catenin accumulation (PubMed:36037369).

MLO Types: Htt inclusion; Inclusion body; Stress granule
Overall Phase Separation Overview: Huntingtin (HTT) undergoes self-driven phase separation, forming dynamic liquid-like droplets in vitro and in vivo that transition to solid-like or hydrogel states over time (PubMed:34888656, 29754822, 31527136). These condensates localize to the cytoplasm and nucleus, associating with inclusion bodies (PubMed:29358329, 29754822, 31527136) and stress granules under endoplasmic reticulum or oxidative stress (PubMed:40090627, 29754822). Material state transitions—particularly pathological liquid-to-solid conversions—are concentration- and time-dependent, accelerated by polyQ expansions and arginine demethylation (PubMed:34888656, 29754822).
Functional Summary: Physiologically, HTT condensates may serve as dynamic compartments for refolding/degradation via Hsp104-mediated disaggregation in yeast (PubMed:31527136). Pathologically, liquid-to-solid transitions of polyQ-expanded HTT initiate irreversible aggregation in Huntington’s disease, correlating with neuronal toxicity (PubMed:34888656, 29754822, 38654122). Methyl-null mutations exacerbate toxicity, while stress granule recruitment disrupts RNA metabolism and extracellular vesicle secretion (PubMed:40090627, 34888656). Therapeutic strategies targeting phase regulators—e.g., enhancing methylation or profilin binding—reduce aggregation and show neuroprotective effects (PubMed:34888656, 29358329).
Intrinsic Determinants & Regulations: Phase separation is intrinsically driven by HTT's N-terminal exon 1 region, where polyglutamine (polyQ) tract expansion (≥43Q) enables condensation, while the proline-rich domain facilitates reversible liquid-like assembly formation (PubMed:29754822, 29358329). Methylation at arginine residues R200/R205 by PRMT4/6 maintains liquid-like properties and delays solidification; methyl-null mutations (e.g., R200/205K) bypass the liquid phase, directly forming cytotoxic solids (PubMed:34888656). PolyQ length dictates phase behavior: shorter tracts (25Q) require the proline-rich region for assembly, whereas longer tracts (≥97Q) drive rapid solidification even without it (PubMed:29754822).
Extrinsic Partners & Regulations: Phase separation is modulated by molecular crowders (e.g., dextran) that promote droplet formation in vitro (PubMed:34888656, 29754822). Protein partners include profilin-1, which binds monomeric/oligomeric HTT via its polyproline region, suppressing spherical/fibrillar aggregation by shifting phase separation thresholds (PubMed:29358329). In yeast, Hsp104 and Rnq1 scaffold inclusion body formation, with deletion abolishing condensates (PubMed:31527136). Under stress, HTT co-localizes with G3BP1 in stress granules, while mutant CAG-repeat RNA seeds aberrant RNA-protein interactions (PubMed:40090627).

Overall Phase Separation Overview: Grb2 does not undergo self-driven phase separation (class: PS-other) but acts as an essential adaptor that drives phase separation of partner proteins in the cytoplasm, particularly on membrane surfaces (PubMed:35507881, 36322659, 37126554, 31268421). It forms liquid-like condensates associated with signaling hubs at the immunological synapse, plasma membrane, and in oncogenic cytoplasmic granules (PubMed:27056844, 33848463, 34661367). These condensates typically exhibit liquid material properties with fusion and rapid molecular exchange, though they can exhibit solid-like properties in certain oncogenic contexts (PubMed:34661367). No intrinsic material state transitions are reported, but condensate dissolution occurs via phosphatase activity or inhibitor treatment (PubMed:33080222, 35507881).
Functional Summary: Grb2-containing condensates physiologically amplify signal transduction: in TCR pathways, they enable kinetic proofreading by prolonging SOS1 dwell time for precise Ras activation and facilitate actin-coupled radial movement at immunological synapses (PubMed:30846600, 31268421). In EGFR signaling, they enhance SOS-mediated Ras activation efficiency (PubMed:35507881). Pathologically, Grb2 scaffolds oncogenic granules in fusion-driven cancers (EML4-ALK, CCDC6-RET) that constitutively activate Ras/MAPK, PI3K/AKT, and JAK/STAT pathways, driving tumor progression (PubMed:33848463, 34661367, 38805286). Disruption by kinase inhibitors (e.g., alectinib, lorlatinib) or phosphatase activity attenuates signaling, highlighting therapeutic relevance (PubMed:34661367, 35507881).
Intrinsic Determinants & Regulations: The phase separation function of Grb2 is intrinsically regulated by its SH2 and SH3 domains, which enable multivalent interactions. The SH2 domain binds phosphorylated tyrosine residues on scaffold proteins (e.g., LAT, EGFR), while the SH3 domains interact with proline-rich motifs on clients like SOS1 (PubMed:36322659, 30846600, 27056844). Phosphorylation at Y160 disrupts its cross-linking capacity, inhibiting condensation (PubMed:35507881). Neither oligomerization domains nor repeat features drive its behavior, and mutations (e.g., SH2-R86K, SH3-P49L/P206L) abrogate condensate formation by impairing partner binding (PubMed:33848463, 34661367).
Extrinsic Partners & Regulations: Grb2 requires extrinsic partners for phase separation: it crosslinks phosphorylated LAT or EGFR with SOS1 to form core condensates (PubMed:27056844, 30846600, 35507881). In TCR signaling, it recruits SOS1 to LAT clusters, enhancing Ras activation (PubMed:36322659, 31268421). Oncogenic partners include EML4-ALK and CCDC6-RET, where Grb2 scaffolds cytoplasmic granules that constitutively activate Ras/MAPK pathways (PubMed:33848463, 34661367, 38805286). Inhibitors like ceritinib dissolve these granules (PubMed:34661367), while phosphatase treatment reverses membrane-associated condensates (PubMed:33080222, 35507881). Actin binding via basic motifs alters condensate dynamics in cellular contexts (PubMed:31268421).

Overall Phase Separation Overview: HSF1 undergoes self-driven phase separation to form nuclear condensates in response to various stresses including heat shock, oxidative stress, and cadmium exposure (PubMed:40017748, 36971000, 37837696, 32015439, 34067147, 35256776). It primarily localizes to the nucleus where it forms nuclear stress bodies and transcriptional condensates (PubMed:40017748, 36971000, 32015439, 34067147, 35256776). The condensates typically exhibit liquid-like properties initially but undergo transitions to gel-like or solid states under prolonged stress conditions, as evidenced by reduced FRAP recovery and altered morphology (PubMed:40017748, 32015439, 35256776). These state transitions are modulated by oxidative hyper-oligomerization via disulfide bonds and stress duration (PubMed:40017748, 32015439).
Functional Summary: HSF1 phase separation enables rapid transcriptional activation of heat-shock proteins (e.g., HSP70) during stress by forming nuclear condensates that concentrate RNA Pol II and co-activators, thereby maintaining proteostasis and promoting cell survival (PubMed:40017748, 36971000, 37837696, 35256776). Dissolution of dynamic liquid condensates correlates with chaperone induction and viability, while persistent gel-like/solid foci sequester transcriptionally inactive HSF1, reducing HSP expression and priming cells for apoptosis—creating fate heterogeneity (PubMed:32015439, 35256776). Under cadmium stress, phase separation reduces protein aggregation and DNA damage, mitigating toxicity (PubMed:37837696). Pathological liquid-to-solid transitions occur during prolonged stress and are accelerated by mutations (e.g., HSF1Δp), leading to cytotoxicity; this is prevented by HSP70-mediated dissolution (PubMed:32015439, 35256776). In heat stress recovery, condensate formation upregulates HSPs to confer thermal resistance, while inhibition enhances apoptosis (PubMed:34067147).
Intrinsic Determinants & Regulations: Phase separation is intrinsically driven by HSF1's leucine-zipper domains (LZ1-3: residues 121-207; LZ4: residues 380-411) and regulatory domain (RD)/intrinsically disordered region (IDR: aa 221-529) that mediate oligomerization and multivalent interactions (PubMed:40017748, 36971000, 35256776). Disulfide bond formation, particularly at Cys153, promotes hyper-oligomerization and stabilizes α-helical structure under oxidative stress, enabling liquid-to-gel transitions (PubMed:40017748). The DNA-binding domain (DBD: aa 1-110) is essential for cellular condensate formation, while the trans-activating domain (AD: aa 409-529) suppresses phase separation (PubMed:37837696, 36971000). Phosphorylation within the RD, especially at serines, is critical for phase separation capacity, with phosphomimetic mutations (e.g., S326D) abolishing LLPS, while preventing phosphorylation (33Ser-to-Ala mutant) accelerates solidification (PubMed:35256776, 32015439). Mutations like CS5 (C36S/C103S/C153S/C373S/C378S) impair hyper-oligomerization and state transitions, and R71G in DBD abolishes condensate formation (PubMed:40017748, 36971000).
Extrinsic Partners & Regulations: HSF1 phase separation is modulated by extrinsic partners including MED12, which co-condenses with HSF1 IDR in vitro and enhances condensate size and transcriptional activity in cells (PubMed:36971000). DNA scaffolds—particularly HSE arrays and satellite III repetitive sequences—lower the saturation concentration for LLPS and serve as nucleation sites (PubMed:36971000, 35256776, 32015439). HSP70 dissolves condensates via its substrate-binding domain in an ATP-dependent manner, preventing gelation and attenuating transcription (PubMed:35256776). Transcription machinery components (RNA Pol II, BRD4, MED1) co-phase separate with HSF1 to enrich transcriptional apparatuses (PubMed:36971000, 35256776). Chemical regulators include proteotoxic stressors (e.g., MG132, cadmium) that induce condensation, aliphatic alcohols (1,6-hexanediol) that dissolve liquid-like droplets, and topoisomerase inhibitors (mitoxantrone) that suppress/dissolve foci (PubMed:32015439, 34067147). Ionic conditions also modulate behavior, with intermediate salt concentrations promoting assembly (PubMed:36971000).

Overall Phase Separation Overview: Q01130 (SC35/SRSF2) undergoes phase separation primarily in the nucleus, associating with nuclear speckles (PubMed:36150385, 37105967, 37285890, 33731873, 39840526). It exhibits self-driven phase separation (PubMed:37285890) and forms liquid-like condensates in vitro and in vivo (PubMed:31391587, 35752626, 37105967). Its distribution is RNA-dependent, becoming diffuse during mitosis upon RNA degradation (PubMed:37285890) and relocalizing to nucleoli under RNA depletion (PubMed:37105967). The protein also participates in HIV-1-induced membraneless organelles in infected macrophages (PubMed:36314049) and forms aberrant condensates when DYRK3 kinase is inhibited (PubMed:29973724).
Functional Summary: Phase separation organizes nuclear speckles to concentrate splicing machinery, regulating alternative splicing of targets like BECN1 and DNA repair genes (PubMed:38381607, 39840526, 31391587). It facilitates HIV-1 replication by forming viral transcriptional hubs (PubMed:36314049). Dysregulation causes pathological outcomes: WASP deficiency drives aberrant splicing and inflammation via TNF overproduction (PubMed:35752626); DYRK3 inhibition induces mitotic defects through aberrant condensates (PubMed:29973724); and overexpression correlates with tumor pathways in COAD, BRCA, and LUAD cancers (PubMed:37285890). SAMHD1 deficiency also impairs speckle formation (PubMed:36150385).
Intrinsic Determinants & Regulations: Phase separation is intrinsically driven by serine/arginine-rich (SR-rich) domains and intrinsically disordered regions (IDRs), particularly the C-terminal IDR (PubMed:31391587, 37285890). Conserved S/R-rich motifs within disordered regions facilitate condensation (PubMed:37285890). No disease-associated mutations or PTMs directly regulating phase separation were reported.
Extrinsic Partners & Regulations: RNA is essential for condensate formation and maintenance, with loss triggering diffuse distribution during mitosis (PubMed:37285890) and density changes upon depletion (PubMed:37105967). Key protein partners include: WASP, which constrains mobility and modulates speckle organization (PubMed:35752626); DYRK3, acting as a dissolvase to prevent aberrant condensation (PubMed:29973724); SRRM2, which scaffolds Q01130 as a client in condensates (PubMed:38381607); Pol II, incorporated into droplets via hyperphosphorylated CTD (PubMed:31391587, 39266551); and SRSF1/U2AF2/HNRNPA1 for co-phase separation (PubMed:31391587). Additional regulators include USP42 (PubMed:33731873), WAC-RBM12 complexes (PubMed:39840526), and CPSF6 in HIV-1 condensates (PubMed:36314049).

Overall Phase Separation Overview: NPM1 (Q61937) undergoes heterotypic liquid-liquid phase separation primarily within the nucleolar granular component, forming compartmentalized structures through interactions with partners like FBL and rpL5 (PubMed:37202475, 38649740). These condensates exhibit liquid-like properties with rapid FRAP recovery (~90% recovery in 8-53s) but feature network fluid characteristics including spatial inhomogeneities across multiple length scales (PubMed:37202475, 38649740). Under LoNA deficiency, mislocalized NPM1 undergoes pathological acetylation-driven aggregation in the nucleoplasm, transitioning to a solid-like state associated with epigenetic dysregulation (PubMed:37202475).
Functional Summary: NPM1 phase separation establishes nucleolar compartmentalization essential for ribosomal subunit assembly via molecular handoff within granular component network fluids (PubMed:37202475, 38649740). It regulates p53-mediated cell cycle control by sequestering ARF in condensates during homeostasis, with DNA damage-triggered release initiating tumor suppressor activity (PubMed:36220893). Pathological disruption via LoNA deficiency causes nucleolar disassembly, NPM1 acetylation, PRC2 recruitment to embryonic genes, H3K27me3-mediated transcriptional repression, and developmental arrest at the two-cell stage (PubMed:37202475).
Intrinsic Determinants & Regulations: Phase separation is intrinsically driven by NPM1's pentameric oligomerization domain scaffold and acidic regions (A0/A1/A2) that mediate electrostatic interactions with arginine-rich partners (PubMed:38649740). The carboxy-terminal region (aa 211-292) enables LoNA RNA binding, essential for nucleolar compartmentalization (PubMed:37202475). Acetylation of nucleoplasmic NPM1 inhibits phase separation and promotes aggregation, while charge-enhancing mutations (e.g., N130^{+A2}) lower phase separation thresholds and slow condensate dynamics by strengthening electrostatic crosslinking (recovery time 103±8s vs wild-type 53±2s) (PubMed:37202475, 38649740).
Extrinsic Partners & Regulations: NPM1 requires key partners for phase separation: it co-phase separates with FBL to form nucleolar bilayers (GC-like outer phase) scaffolded by LoNA RNA, which reduces saturation concentrations and increases fluidity (PubMed:37202475). It sequesters ARF in condensates during homeostasis but releases it upon Cc competition during DNA damage, evidenced by FRAP mobility shifts (65%→95% recovery) (PubMed:36220893). Ribosomal protein rpL5 acts as essential scaffold, with heterotypic complexation driving phase separation at threshold concentrations (>250-300µM) tunable by electrostatic modifications (PubMed:38649740).

Overall Phase Separation Overview: PSPC1 undergoes self-driven liquid-liquid phase separation (LLPS) in the nucleus, forming dynamic condensates within paraspeckles (PubMed:34490876, 34916619, 36354291). Under osmotic stress, it translocates to the cytoplasm, forming fibrillar aggregates that partially colocalize with stress granules (PubMed:38668381). Its phase separation is concentration-, temperature-, and salt-dependent, exhibiting liquid-like properties with fusion and rapid recovery (PubMed:34490876, 34916619). At high RNA concentrations, it undergoes a pathological liquid-to-solid transition, forming fiber-like aggregates (PubMed:34916619).
Functional Summary: Nuclear phase separation enables PSPC1 to recruit chromatin remodelers (SWI/SNF) and regulate alternative splicing/gene expression (PubMed:36354291). It facilitates Pol II CTD phosphorylation and release, enhancing transcription efficiency (PubMed:34916619), and regulates CHK1 dephosphorylation via PPP5C, critical for oocyte maturation (PubMed:34490876). Under osmotic stress, cytoplasmic aggregation contributes to stress response (PubMed:38668381). Dysregulated phase separation, particularly pathological liquid-to-solid transitions, may underlie cellular dysfunction (PubMed:34916619).
Intrinsic Determinants & Regulations: Phase separation is intrinsically driven by the prion-like domain (PrLD, residues 407-523), with deletion (∆PLD) abolishing condensate formation in vitro and in vivo (PubMed:34490876). Low-complexity sequences (LCS) and the RNA recognition motif (RRM) domain are critical, as mutations (ΔLCS2 and RRMmut: F118A/F120A/K197A/F199A) impair droplet assembly and function (PubMed:34916619). A predicted PrLD also facilitates paraspeckle association (PubMed:36354291).
Extrinsic Partners & Regulations: PSPC1 co-assembles with paraspeckle proteins NONO and SFPQ in cytoplasmic condensates under stress (PubMed:38668381) and requires NEAT1 lncRNA as an essential scaffold for nuclear paraspeckle formation (PubMed:36354291, 37474102). It interacts with ARID1B to recruit the SWI/SNF complex (PubMed:36354291) and co-phase separates with TBP to form transcription condensates incorporating Pol II CTD (PubMed:34916619). RNA bidirectionally regulates PSPC1: low concentrations enhance phase separation and CTD incorporation, while high concentrations dissolve droplets and trigger liquid-to-solid transitions (PubMed:34916619).

Overall Phase Separation Overview: Buc (H0WFA5) undergoes phase separation to form the Balbiani body (Bb) in oocytes and germ plasm (Gp) in embryos (PubMed:30086300, 39793567). As the essential scaffold for Bb assembly, it localizes primarily in the cytoplasm (PubMed:36207377, 27471966, 35065906, 30086300). The condensates display a liquid-like material state during initial formation, characterized by fusion capability and dynamic mobility, which transitions to a solid, hydrogel-like or amyloid state in mature structures (PubMed:35065906, 39793567). This liquid-to-solid transition is developmentally regulated during Bb maturation (PubMed:39793567).
Functional Summary: Buc phase separation is essential for germline development and embryonic patterning. It forms the structural core of the Balbiani body hydrogel, enabling sequestration of maternal mRNAs and organelles for asymmetric distribution during oogenesis (PubMed:35065906, 39793567). This process establishes embryonic polarity and enables germ cell specification via primordial germ cell formation (PubMed:30086300, 39793567). Dysregulation causes pathological consequences: liquid-to-solid transitions in tdrd6a mutants or with RtoK mutations disrupt mRNA stoichiometry, reduce germ cell numbers, and lead to embryonic lethality (PubMed:30086300, 39793567).
Intrinsic Determinants & Regulations: Phase separation is intrinsically driven by Buc's prion-like domain (PLD) and intrinsically disordered regions (IDRs) (PubMed:35065906, 39793567). The N-terminal PLD is essential for aggregation (PubMed:35065906), while a tri-arginine-glycine (tri-RG) motif and symmetric dimethylarginine (sDMA) modifications critically regulate condensate formation (PubMed:30086300). Disease-associated mutations impair functionality: the RtoK mutation disrupts Bb assembly by preventing arginine methylation (PubMed:30086300), and buc-/- knockout abolishes condensate formation entirely (PubMed:39793567).
Extrinsic Partners & Regulations: Buc phase separation is extrinsically modulated by multiple partners. Tdrd6a binds sDMA-modified Buc via Tudor domains, enhancing mobility (55% FRAP recovery vs 35% alone) and promoting functional condensate growth (PubMed:30086300). Microtubules scaffold Buc condensates through dynein-mediated trafficking, prevent disintegration, and control size/shape (PubMed:39793567). Buc co-phase separates with RNA-binding proteins Cirbpa and Cirbpb to integrate maternal mRNAs into the Bb hydrogel (PubMed:35065906). Germ plasm mRNAs serve as client components whose stoichiometric loading depends on proper Buc condensation (PubMed:30086300, 39793567).

Overall Phase Separation Overview: Nephrin (O60500) does not undergo autonomous phase separation but is recruited into heterotypic condensates through partner interactions (PubMed:34330769, 30846599, 25321392). It forms liquid-like condensates in both cytoplasmic membrane-associated clusters and nuclear compartments (PubMed:30846599, 27392146). In the cytoplasm, it localizes to receptor signaling clusters (PubMed:30846599, 25321392), while its intracellular domain (NICD) forms de novo nuclear bodies co-localizing with paraspeckle markers (PubMed:27392146). No material state transitions are reported across studies.
Functional Summary: Phase separation organizes actin regulatory machinery by increasing dwell time of N-WASP/Arp2/3 complexes at membrane clusters, enabling stoichiometry-dependent control of actin nucleation essential for podocyte function and kidney filtration (PubMed:30846599, 25321392). Dysregulation causes proteinuria through disrupted slit diaphragm-cytoskeleton connections (PubMed:34330769). Nuclear condensates of the intracellular domain (NICD) may compete with paraspeckles and serve as a model for complex coacervation of acidic intrinsically disordered regions (PubMed:27392146). Pathological implications include aberrant actin assembly in disease states when phosphorylation or partner stoichiometry is altered (PubMed:25321392, 30846599).
Intrinsic Determinants & Regulations: Phase separation is driven by the disordered cytoplasmic tail containing clustered negative charges (Charge Interaction Elements) and distributed aromatic/hydrophobic residues (Tyr, Leu, Met, Trp) (PubMed:27392146). Phosphorylation at tyrosine residues (Y1176/1193/1217) is essential for multivalent binding (PubMed:25321392, 26553976, 30846599). Charge-patterning mutations significantly regulate behavior: clustered negative charge mutants (CC) enhance phase separation while scattered charge mutants (CS) attenuate it, and point mutations of aromatic residues reduce condensate formation (PubMed:27392146). The PDZ-binding motif (PBM) in the C-terminus is required for recruitment into ternary complexes (PubMed:34330769).
Extrinsic Partners & Regulations: Essential co-phase separation partners include NCK (P16333) and N-WASP (O00401), which form multivalent signaling assemblies on membranes (PubMed:30846599, 25321392, 26553976). Recruitment into slit diaphragm condensates requires MAGI2 (Q86UL8), Dendrin (O94850), and CD2AP (Q9Y5K6) (PubMed:34330769). Nuclear phase separation depends on positively charged scaffolds like supercharged GFP (+25) or oligoarginine peptides that neutralize electrostatic repulsion (PubMed:27392146). The NCK linker domain (particularly its KVKRK motif and net positive charge) enhances condensate formation by promoting weak self-assembly (PubMed:26553976). Phase separation is concentration-dependent and modulated by partner stoichiometry (PubMed:25321392, 30846599).

Overall Phase Separation Overview: Epidermal Growth Factor Receptor (EGFR, P00533) undergoes partner-driven phase separation (class: PS-other) rather than self-assembly. It forms condensates primarily in the cytoplasm on membrane surfaces and is recruited to nuclear paraspeckles (PubMed:35507881, PubMed:34249431, PubMed:33848463). These condensates exhibit liquid-like material properties, characterized by fusion, coarsening, and rapid reversibility, with no observed state transitions under tested conditions (PubMed:35507881, PubMed:36396954, PubMed:34249431). EGFR associates with diverse membrane-less organelles including HOtag-induced cytoplasmic granules and NONO-formed nuclear condensates (PubMed:33848463, PubMed:34249431).
Functional Summary: Condensation enhances SOS-mediated Ras activation and MAPK signaling propagation by concentrating signaling components on membranes (PubMed:35507881). In the nucleus, recruitment into NONO condensates promotes DNA-PK phosphorylation at T2609, accelerating non-homologous end joining DNA repair and conferring tumor radioresistance (PubMed:34249431). Pathological implications include ligand-independent activation through engineered clustering (SIM6-mEGF/SUM5 systems), which induces phosphorylation and endocytosis (PubMed:36396954). Disruption of condensation via Grb2 modifications attenuates signaling, while condensate formation remains compatible with cellular viability and EGF responsiveness (PubMed:35507881, PubMed:35490741).
Intrinsic Determinants & Regulations: Phase separation is intrinsically regulated by EGFR's cytoplasmic tail (residues 991-1186), which contains intrinsically disordered regions with multivalent tyrosine phosphorylation sites (Y1068, Y1086, Y1148, Y1173) essential for partner recruitment (PubMed:35507881). The transmembrane domain exhibits cholesterol sensitivity that influences membrane domain partitioning (PubMed:35490741). Tyrosine phosphorylation by Src-family kinases serves as a primary driver for condensation, enabling Grb2 binding (PubMed:35507881). The extracellular domain facilitates recruitment into engineered condensates via ligand binding (PubMed:36396954).
Extrinsic Partners & Regulations: Phase separation requires extrinsic partners: Grb2 (P62993) acts as an essential crosslinker via SH2 domain binding and dimerization, while SOS^PR (Q07889) enhances condensation extent (PubMed:35507881). Chemical modulators include heptanol, which induces clustering in vivo, and the synthetic HOtag system that forces granule assembly (PubMed:35490741, PubMed:33848463). EGFR is recruited into NONO (Q15233) condensates in the nucleus, facilitated by RNA-enhanced phase separation (PubMed:34249431). Phosphorylated intracellular domains (residues 712-1210) form droplets with SHP2 phosphatase (Q06124) (PubMed:35231400).

Overall Phase Separation Overview: Rubisco (P00877) does not undergo autonomous phase separation but requires the linker protein EPYC1 to form liquid-like condensates (PubMed:36611062, 37195994, 30498228, 31504763). These condensates localize to the cytoplasm within the chloroplast and constitute the core matrix of the pyrenoid, a membrane-less organelle (PubMed:37195994, 28938114). The pyrenoid matrix exhibits liquid-like properties including fusion, internal mixing, and dynamic exchange between condensed and dilute phases (PubMed:28938114, 30498228). Environmentally regulated reversible transitions occur, with dissolution into the stroma under high CO₂ conditions and re-condensation under low CO₂ (PubMed:37195994, 28938114).
Functional Summary: Phase separation with EPYC1 forms the structural basis of the pyrenoid, enabling the CO₂-concentrating mechanism (CCM) that enhances photosynthetic efficiency by up to 60% (PubMed:37195994, 28938114, 30498228). This liquid matrix concentrates Rubisco with carbonic anhydrases and transporters, minimizing photorespiration and contributing to ~30% of global carbon fixation (PubMed:37195994, 31504763). The dynamic liquid properties permit rapid reorganization during cell division and efficient access for regulatory proteins like Rubisco activase (PubMed:28938114).
Intrinsic Determinants & Regulations: Phase separation is intrinsically governed by surface-exposed α-helices (αA and αB) on Rubisco's small subunit (SSU), which mediate binding to EPYC1 (PubMed:31504763, 28938114, 30498228). The L₈S₈ holoenzyme structure provides multivalent interaction sites for EPYC1 binding (PubMed:28938114). Mutations in the SSU, such as M87D/V94D, disrupt EPYC1 binding and abolish phase separation (PubMed:36611062).
Extrinsic Partners & Regulations: EPYC1 is the essential extrinsic partner, forming heterotypic liquid droplets with Rubisco through multivalent interactions (PubMed:36611062, 37195994, 30498228, 31504763). Phase separation is critically modulated by environmental CO₂ levels, with low CO₂ inducing condensation and high CO₂ triggering dissolution (PubMed:37195994, 28938114). The process is salt-sensitive, with droplet formation inhibited at high ionic strength (PubMed:30498228).

MLO Types: Inclusion body; Nuclear speckle; Stress granule
Overall Phase Separation Overview: PABP undergoes both self-driven phase separation (PubMed:36109629, 40102686) and partner-dependent co-phase separation (PubMed:38072230, 11121440) primarily in the cytoplasm. It forms liquid-like condensates (PubMed:38072230, 11121440, 36109629, 40102686) and associates with multiple membrane-less organelles including stress granules (PubMed:11121440, 26777405, 30893049, 36151083), viral mRNP granules within inclusion bodies (PubMed:38072230), P-bodies (PubMed:38565536), mitotic granules (PubMed:29973724), and translation machinery condensates (PubMed:40102686). No material state transitions were reported.
Functional Summary: Physiologically, PABP condensates regulate mRNA triage during stress (PubMed:11121440), activate viral translation (PubMed:38072230), and enhance translation efficiency by concentrating machinery (PubMed:40102686). Pathologically, they drive oncogenesis by stabilizing MYC mRNA in esophageal cancer (PubMed:36109629) and translating leukemogenic transcripts (BCR-ABL1/IDH2) in CML blast crisis (PubMed:40102686). Dysregulation contributes to neurodegenerative pathologies: chronic stress granules evolve into ALS/FTD inclusions (PubMed:30893049), disrupted Golgi condensates cause ribbon fragmentation (PubMed:38992139), and mTOR hyperactivation in STAU1 condensates impairs autophagy (PubMed:38913026).
Intrinsic Determinants & Regulations: Phase separation is intrinsically driven by RNA recognition motifs (RRM1-4) that bind viral/polyadenylated mRNAs (PubMed:38072230, 40102686) and intrinsically disordered regions (IDRs) including a critical IDR3 domain (aa 362-564) essential for self-assembly (PubMed:36109629, 40102686). The MLLE domain is dispensable for phase separation (PubMed:38072230), while deletions in IDR3 abolish condensate formation (PubMed:40102686).
Extrinsic Partners & Regulations: PABP co-phase separates with viral mRNAs in inclusion bodies dependent on RSV proteins N/M2-1 for recruitment (PubMed:38072230), and scaffolds complexes with eIF4G/eIF4E in translation condensates (PubMed:40102686). RNA partners including MTAR1 lncRNA (PubMed:36109629) and poly(A)+ mRNA (PubMed:40102686) enhance condensation, while cellular stressors (arsenite, energy deficiency) induce stress granule recruitment (PubMed:36151083, 11121440). It partitions into condensates formed by G3BP1 (PubMed:30893049), UBAP2L (PubMed:31114027), GM130 (PubMed:38992139), STAU1 (PubMed:38913026), and MEX3A (PubMed:38565536).

Overall Phase Separation Overview: DDX6 undergoes partner-dependent phase separation (class: PS-other) as a core scaffold component of P-bodies in the cytoplasm (PubMed:37370689, 31324804, 38769438, 32302570). It associates with stress granules upon recruitment by UBAP2L (PubMed:32302570). In vitro, DDX6 forms liquid droplets in an ATP/RNA-dependent manner (PubMed:31435012). The material state is consistently described as liquid-like across studies (PubMed:31324804, 32302570, 38769438, 31435012), with no reported state transitions.
Functional Summary: DDX6 phase separation enables translational repression of target mRNAs (including KRAS/NRAS) within P-bodies, with dissolution leading to increased RAS levels and MEK inhibitor resistance (PubMed:37370689). During energy stress, HAX1-scaffolded condensation inhibits global protein synthesis (PubMed:38769438). In YTHDF3 condensates, DDX6 facilitates HSPA13 mRNA decay, suppressing PD-L1 expression and ccRCC malignancy (PubMed:38811341). Interactions with YBX1 suggest roles in exosomal RNA packaging (PubMed:34766549).
Intrinsic Determinants & Regulations: Phase separation is intrinsically regulated by low-complexity domains (LCDs) in the C-terminal region (PubMed:31435012). No specific domains, mutations, or post-translational modifications directly driving DDX6 phase separation were identified in the provided studies.
Extrinsic Partners & Regulations: DDX6 phase separation requires multiple extrinsic partners: LSM14A and EIF4ENIF1 as essential core scaffold components for P-body assembly (PubMed:37370689); UBAP2L for recruitment to stress granules and SG-PB hybrid formation (PubMed:32302570); ubiquitinated HAX1 as a scaffold during energy stress (PubMed:38769438); YTHDF3 for recruitment into mRNA decay condensates (PubMed:38811341); and YBX1 for P-body/exosome interactions (PubMed:34766549). RNA (particularly polyU RNA) and ATP are required for in vitro phase separation (PubMed:31435012).

Overall Phase Separation Overview: Ede1 undergoes self-driven phase separation (class: PS-other) in the cytoplasm, forming condensates at endocytic sites, cortical actin patches, and aberrant endocytic protein deposits (ENDs) (PubMed:35412456, 38235332, 34334089, 39774270). These assemblies typically exhibit liquid-like properties including fusion, fission, and rapid FRAP recovery but can undergo pathological transitions to solid states in chimeric constructs or under high-affinity interactions (PubMed:35412456, 39774270).
Functional Summary: Condensation enables endocytosis initiation by clustering early endocytic proteins, with phase separation loss reducing efficiency by 43% (PubMed:35412456). During stress, Ede1 recruits ADC17 mRNA to cortical actin patches for localized translation of proteasome assembly chaperones, promoting cell survival (PubMed:38235332). As an autophagy receptor, it facilitates clearance of aberrant endocytic assemblies (ENDs) via Atg8/Atg11 pathways—a process requiring liquid-like dynamics, as solidification blocks degradation (PubMed:33207182, 34334089, 39774270).
Intrinsic Determinants & Regulations: Phase separation is intrinsically driven by Ede1's low-complexity region (LCR) and coiled-coil (CC) domains, which mediate multivalent interactions (PubMed:35412456, 33207182, 38235332, 34334089, 39774270). The CC domain enables oligomerization (dimerization/tetramerization), enhancing condensation capacity (PubMed:35412456), while disruption of these domains (e.g., ΔLCR/CC mutation) abolishes phase separation (PubMed:38235332).
Extrinsic Partners & Regulations: Ede1 recruits endocytic machinery proteins (Syp1, Ent1, Sla2, End3, Pan1, Sla1, Las17, Myo5, Abp1, Rvs167) to condensates (PubMed:35412456). It interacts with Atg8 during autophagy and scaffolds Atg11-dependent initiation hubs (PubMed:33207182, 34334089, 39774270).
