Stress-induced recruitment of ADC17/PAC mRNA enables localized translation during rapamycin treatment (PubMed:38235332). High-affinity interactions (e.g., with BFP–3×GBP) trigger liquid-to-solid transitions that impair autophagy (PubMed:39774270).

MLO Types: DNA damage foci; Nucleolus; XY body
Overall Phase Separation Overview: FBL (P35550) undergoes heterotypic phase separation requiring partners to form biomolecular condensates primarily within the nucleolar dense fibrillar component (DFC) (PubMed:34331666, 37202475, 38341436). It exhibits liquid-like material properties under physiological conditions, evidenced by rapid FRAP recovery in vivo (PubMed:34331666, 37202475). Material state transitions occur during cellular differentiation, shifting from spherical liquid-like condensates in undifferentiated cells to irregular gel/solid-like states in myotubes (PubMed:36727534). Environmental perturbations like LIN28A depletion reduce its fluidity and disrupt DFC integrity (PubMed:34331666, 38341436).
Functional Summary: FBL phase separation is physiologically critical for ribosomal biogenesis, facilitating rRNA 2'-O-methylation within DFC condensates (PubMed:34331666, 37202475). Compartmentalization with NPM1 enables proper nucleolar architecture for ribosome assembly (PubMed:37202475). Disruption through LIN28A depletion or rRNA inhibition causes DFC disintegration, reduced rRNA methylation, translational defects, and ribosomal protein mislocalization (PubMed:34331666, 38341436). During myogenesis, nucleolar reorganization involving FBL's material state transition correlates with enhanced translational capacity (PubMed:36727534). Severe phase separation disruption triggers developmental arrest in embryos through NPM1 mislocalization cascades (PubMed:37202475).
Intrinsic Determinants & Regulations: Phase separation of FBL is intrinsically driven by its intrinsically disordered regions (IDRs) that enable multivalent interactions essential for condensate formation within the nucleolar DFC (PubMed:36727534). No specific point mutations, post-translational modifications, or oligomerization domains regulating FBL's phase separation were identified in the provided studies.
Extrinsic Partners & Regulations: FBL's phase separation is extrinsically regulated by RNA scaffolds and protein partners. It co-phase separates with NPM1 to form compartmentalized nucleoli, scaffolded by the long non-coding RNA LoNA which lowers saturation concentration and enhances droplet fluidity (PubMed:37202475). Essential RNA partners include rRNA and snoRNAs that mediate nucleolar localization and condensate maintenance (PubMed:34331666, 38341436). Protein regulators include LIN28A which maintains FBL's dynamic liquid properties in the DFC (PubMed:34331666, 38341436), and NCL which stabilizes condensate integrity (PubMed:34331666). Environmental factors such as temperature shifts and cellular differentiation states modulate its material properties (PubMed:36727534, 38341436).

Overall Phase Separation Overview: Edc3 undergoes self-driven phase separation to form liquid-like condensates (PubMed:36972455) and serves as a core scaffold for P-body assembly in the cytoplasm (PubMed:35876801, 37398029, 39320938, 35269643). It associates with both traditional glucose-deprivation-induced P-bodies and benomyl-induced granules (BIGs), a distinct P-body subtype (PubMed:35876801). These condensates exhibit liquid-like properties—spherical morphology, sensitivity to 1,6-hexanediol, and fusion dynamics—but undergo maturation toward less reversible states over time (PubMed:36972455, 35876801, 35269643).
Functional Summary: Edc3 scaffolds P-body assembly to concentrate mRNA decapping machinery (e.g., Dcp2), enabling stress-responsive mRNA decay/storage during glucose starvation and cytoplasmic fluidization (PubMed:37398029, 36972455). It facilitates chronic P-body accumulation in post-exponential growth phases (PubMed:35269643). Pathologically, Edc3 is degraded via selective autophagy mediated by Med13 and Ksp1, resetting mRNA metabolism post-nitrogen stress to maintain cellular homeostasis (PubMed:39320938).
Intrinsic Determinants & Regulations: Phase separation is intrinsically driven by the Lsm domain (residues 67-282) and YjeF-N domain (residues 283-551), which synergistically lower the saturation concentration (PubMed:36972455). The YjeF-N domain enables self-oligomerization (PubMed:35269643), while an intrinsically disordered region (IDR) mediates partner recruitment (PubMed:39320938). Scaffold function is essential for condensation, though no specific mutations or PTMs are reported (PubMed:37398029).
Extrinsic Partners & Regulations: Edc3 co-phase-separates with protein partners including Dcp2 (co-scaffold with >85% colocalization in P-bodies/BIGs) (PubMed:35876801, 35269643), Pat1 (cooperative scaffolding in heterotypic condensates) (PubMed:36972455), and Dhh1 (PubMed:35269643). It requires untranslated mRNAs for P-body assembly (PubMed:37398029), and RPL41A RNA enhances condensate reversibility (PubMed:36972455). Recruitment to P-bodies during nitrogen starvation depends on Med13, which interacts via Edc3's IDR (PubMed:39320938). Chemical inducers include benomyl (triggering BIGs formation) (PubMed:35876801).

Overall Phase Separation Overview: Ki-67 (P46013) undergoes self-driven liquid-liquid phase separation (LLPS) in physiological contexts, forming dynamic liquid-like condensates (PubMed:37813838, 35513709, 39153474). Its behavior is cell-cycle dependent: during interphase, it localizes to nucleoli via heterotypic interactions, while in mitosis, it forms the perichromosomal layer or enriches at chromatin-cytoplasm interfaces (PubMed:37813838, 35922507, 35513709). During mitotic exit, dephosphorylation triggers cytoplasmic condensate formation (PubMed:39153474). Key locations include the nucleus (chromatin periphery, nucleoli) and cytoplasm, with material properties ranging from highly dynamic liquids to viscoelastic states at high concentrations (PubMed:37813838, 39153474). No material state transitions (e.g., liquid-to-solid) are reported (PubMed:37813838, 39153474).
Functional Summary: Ki-67 LLPS organizes the perichromosomal layer during mitosis, preventing chromosome coalescence by forming a liquid-like surface barrier (PubMed:37813838, 35513709, 40069174). It recruits nucleolar components to chromosomes and regulates heterochromatin organization, with overexpression inducing global heterochromatinization (PubMed:37813838). During mitotic exit, RNA-dependent co-condensation with pre-rRNAs forms a cohesive chromosome coat, driving clustering to facilitate cytoplasmic exclusion and nuclear envelope reassembly (PubMed:39153474, 40069174). Disruption of this process—via phosphomimetic mutations (e.g., 139E), RNA depletion, or CP domain ablation—impairs chromosome segregation and nuclear reformation (PubMed:39153474, 40069174).
Intrinsic Determinants & Regulations: LLPS is intrinsically regulated by Ki-67's repeat domain (RD), where repeat number inversely correlates with saturation concentration (more repeats enhance phase separation) (PubMed:35513709). Multisite phosphorylation exerts context-dependent effects: CDK-mediated phosphorylation promotes LLPS in full-length protein by generating alternating charge blocks in the RD but inhibits it in synthetic repeats when fully phosphorylated (PubMed:37813838, 35513709). Dephosphorylation during mitotic exit is essential for condensate formation, collapsing protein extension to facilitate condensation (PubMed:39153474). Charge-block mimetic mutations (e.g., CBm-3) enhance LLPS, while neutralization mutations (e.g., CBm-1/CBm-2) suppress it (PubMed:35513709). The N-terminal charged patch (CP, aa 496-681) is indispensable for phase separation, whereas the LR domain mediates chromatin binding but is dispensable for LLPS (PubMed:39153474).
Extrinsic Partners & Regulations: Ki-67 co-assembles with nucleolar proteins NCL and NPM1 in condensates, with recruitment modulated by phosphorylation status (PubMed:37813838). During interphase, NPM1 interaction localizes Ki-67 to nucleoli, dissociating in mitosis (PubMed:35513709). Chromatin acts as a scaffold for periphery formation, with Ki-67 enrichment sensitive to chromatin solubility (e.g., disrupted by histone hyperacetylation) (PubMed:35922507). Premature ribosomal RNAs (pre-rRNAs) are essential scaffolds for anaphase condensates, enabling chromosome clustering via co-condensation (PubMed:39153474, 40069174). Chemical regulators include Okadaic acid (enhances LLPS by mimicking phosphorylation) and Purvalanol A (inhibits LLPS via CDK inhibition) (PubMed:37813838).

Overall Phase Separation Overview: Dcp2 undergoes heterotypic phase separation (PS-other) forming liquid-like condensates primarily in the cytoplasm (PubMed:35876801, 35269643, 31285266). It associates with multiple membrane-less organelles including P-bodies under glucose deprivation and stationary phase (PubMed:35876801, 36972455, 35269643, 24862735), Benomyl-induced granules (BIGs) upon microtubule disruption (PubMed:35876801), and Osmotic Shock Foci (OSFs) triggered by hypertonic stress (PubMed:31285266). Condensates exhibit concentration-dependent formation and liquid-like properties evidenced by rapid dissolution with 1,6-hexanediol (PubMed:35876801, 35269643, 24862735), with no reported material state transitions in the provided data.
Functional Summary: Dcp2 condensates function as catalytic hubs for mRNA decapping and decay within P-bodies during stress responses and post-exponential growth phases (PubMed:36972455, 35269643). They enable mRNA storage/decay specialization in BIGs (PubMed:35876801) and facilitate cytoplasmic fluidization during glucose starvation, promoting proteostasis (PubMed:37398029). Chronic accumulation in stationary phase occurs via RNA-independent scaffolding by Nst1 (PubMed:35269643, 35806385). Pathological implications include aberrant phase separation under amyloid-prone conditions observed in related complexes (e.g., Lsm4), though no direct disease linkage is reported for Dcp2 in the provided data (PubMed:26238190).
Intrinsic Determinants & Regulations: Phase separation is driven by structured N-terminal domains and a C-terminal intrinsically disordered region (IDR) that mediate RNA binding and homotypic condensation (PubMed:36972455). Key motifs include helical leucine-rich motifs (HLMs) in the C-terminus (residues 553-741) that facilitate core scaffold assembly (PubMed:24862735). Histidine residue H237 is critical for pH-sensitive behavior, as H237A mutation reduces RNA binding affinity and impairs phase separation under acidic conditions (PubMed:36972455). Distributed histidine residues throughout the sequence confer pH-dependent oligomerization and RNA binding enhancement at lower pH (PubMed:36972455).
Extrinsic Partners & Regulations: Dcp2 co-phase separates with decapping complex partners including Dcp1 (PubMed:35876801, 36972455), Edc3 which scaffolds P-body assembly (PubMed:35876801, 37398029, 35269643), Xrn1 (PubMed:35876801, 36972455), Lsm1/Lsm4 complexes (PubMed:35876801, 26238190), and Nst1 which recruits Dcp2 to condensates independent of RNA influx (PubMed:35806385, 35269643). RNA binding (RPL41A, capped/uncapped RNAs) lowers saturation concentration and enhances condensation, particularly at acidic pH (PubMed:36972455). Environmental triggers include benomyl (inducing BIGs formation via microtubule disruption) (PubMed:35876801), 1M KCl (rapidly forming OSFs within 30 seconds) (PubMed:31285266), and physiological pH shifts where acidic conditions (pH 5.8) promote RNA binding and rescue phase separation at high salt concentrations (PubMed:36972455).

Overall Phase Separation Overview: PSD-95 (P78352) undergoes partner-dependent liquid-liquid phase separation but cannot self-assemble, requiring interaction partners like SynGAP, GKAP, and Shank3 to form condensates (PubMed:36693856, 30078712, 27565345, 38452102). These predominantly liquid-like droplets localize to the cytoplasm and associate with the postsynaptic density (PSD) membrane-less organelle (PubMed:30078712, 38452102, 27565345). The condensates exhibit dynamic liquid properties including fusion and FRAP recovery, but undergo aging transitions toward solid-like states over time as evidenced by increased elastic modulus and hardening (PubMed:30078712).
Functional Summary: PSD-95 phase separation organizes the postsynaptic density by clustering NMDA receptors (via NR2B), concentrating synaptic enzymes like SynGAP, and promoting actin bundling through Shank3 recruitment (PubMed:30078712, 27565345). This dynamically anchors synaptic components, as evidenced by stabilization of GluN2A surface clusters in ternary complexes (PubMed:36693856). The condensates enable activity-dependent plasticity, with SynGAP dispersion during long-term potentiation regulating neuronal excitation (PubMed:27565345). Pathological implications emerge from liquid-to-solid transitions during aging, where hardened condensates with increased elastic modulus (3.5 kPa) may disrupt synaptic function (PubMed:30078712).
Intrinsic Determinants & Regulations: Phase separation is intrinsically regulated by PSD-95's modular domains, with the PDZ1-PDZ2 tandem enabling Stargazin binding (PubMed:31492534) and the PDZ3-SH3-GK (PSG) supramodule facilitating SynGAP interactions (PubMed:27565345). The extended αC helix within PDZ3 is critical for high-affinity binding, as its deletion (p.A399_N410del) disrupts phase separation (PubMed:27565345). Oligomerization capacity is enhanced through partner-induced multimerization, particularly when bound to SynGAP trimers or NR2B tetramers which increase valency (PubMed:30078712, 27565345).
Extrinsic Partners & Regulations: Essential co-phase separation partners include SynGAP, whose trimeric structure nucleates PSD-95 condensation both in vitro and in cells (PubMed:27565345, 38452102). Ternary complexes with FAM81A enhance droplet formation and stability (PubMed:38452102), while GKAP dramatically lowers phase separation thresholds by bridging PSD-95 to Shank3/Homer3 networks (PubMed:30078712). PSD-95 also recruits NMDA receptors via NR2B binding and incorporates into larger condensates with Stargazin (Stg_CT), GluN2A, and Rph3A (PubMed:31492534, 36693856). Within the PSD scaffold, Homer3 tetramerization promotes efficient condensation, while its monomeric isoform Homer1a disperses pre-formed droplets (PubMed:30078712).

Overall Phase Separation Overview: SOS1 (Q07889) undergoes partner-dependent phase separation, requiring Grb2 and phosphorylated LAT for condensate formation, and does not exhibit self-driven phase separation (PubMed:36322659, 37126554, 33080222, 30846600, 27056844, 31268421). It primarily localizes to cytoplasmic membrane-associated signaling hubs, including TCR microclusters at the immunological synapse and oncogenic EML4-ALK foci (PubMed:27056844, 31268421, 34661367). SOS1-containing condensates exhibit liquid-like properties—evidenced by fusion, dynamic exchange, and rapid FRAP recovery—and form exclusively on membrane surfaces (PubMed:27056844, 31268421, 36322659). These condensates remain reversible upon phosphatase treatment or partner disruption, with no material state transitions reported (PubMed:33080222, 36322659).
Functional Summary: SOS1 condensates physiologically amplify Ras/MAPK signaling by concentrating SOS1 at membranes, enabling kinetic proofreading for precise Ras activation in immune responses (PubMed:30846600, 27056844). In T cells, they facilitate actin polymerization, radial movement across the immunological synapse, and signal amplification while excluding phosphatases like CD45 (PubMed:31268421, 27056844). Pathologically, SOS1 recruitment to EML4-ALK V3 liquid-like foci in NSCLC drives oncogenic signaling (RAS/MAPK, PI3K/AKT, JAK/STAT), with disruption impairing cancer cell viability (PubMed:34661367). The condensates also couple protein phase separation to lipid membrane organization, templating raft domain formation (PubMed:37126554, 33080222).
Intrinsic Determinants & Regulations: Phase separation of SOS1 is intrinsically regulated by its proline-rich (PR) domain, which provides multivalent binding sites for Grb2 SH3 domains, enabling cross-linking within the LAT-Grb2-SOS network (PubMed:36322659, 30846600, 27056844). This multivalency lowers the saturation concentration for phase separation and is essential for condensate nucleation (PubMed:27056844, 30846600). No disease-associated mutations or post-translational modifications directly regulating SOS1 phase separation were identified in the provided data.
Extrinsic Partners & Regulations: SOS1 phase separation is extrinsically driven by Grb2, which bridges SOS1 to phosphorylated LAT, forming tripartite condensates (PubMed:36322659, 37126554, 33080222, 30846600, 27056844). These condensates recruit additional partners including SLP-76, Nck, and WASP/N-WASP in T cells, modulating actin coupling and radial movement (PubMed:31268421). SOS1 also partitions into EML4-ALK V1/V3 cytoplasmic foci, where its recruitment is sensitive to ALK inhibitors (e.g., ceritinib, lorlatinib) (PubMed:34661367). Condensate formation requires LAT phosphorylation and is reversible by phosphatases (PubMed:33080222, 36322659).

Overall Phase Separation Overview: SRSF1 (Q07955) undergoes phosphorylation-regulated phase separation primarily within nuclear speckles in the nucleus (PubMed:38638569, 39968932, 39119950, 38381607, 31391587). While capable of self-driven phase separation in its unphosphorylated state (PubMed:39968932), it frequently participates in heterotypic condensates. It forms concentration gradients within nuclear speckles to organize RNA transcripts (PubMed:38638569) and exhibits liquid-like material properties (PubMed:39023093, 31363225, 39968932). Phosphorylation triggers reversible state transitions: unphosphorylated forms promote droplet formation, while hyperphosphorylation inhibits self-assembly but enables co-phase separation with partners (PubMed:39968932, 39023093).
Functional Summary: SRSF1 phase separation spatially organizes pre-mRNA transcripts within nuclear speckles to facilitate spliceosome assembly and splicing regulation (PubMed:38638569, 39968932). Phosphorylation-controlled condensation regulates its nuclear speckle localization, ensuring splicing fidelity (PubMed:39968932). Recruitment into CLK2 condensates under stress induces splicing factor sequestration, intron retention, and cellular senescence, suppressing tumor growth (PubMed:39119950). As a core component of SON+ nuclear speckle subcompartments, it regulates alternative splicing of chromatin-related mRNAs (PubMed:38381607). Dysregulated phase transitions—particularly pathological solidification from liquid states—are implicated in cancer progression (PubMed:39968932).
Intrinsic Determinants & Regulations: Phase separation is intrinsically driven by the Arg/Ser-rich (RS) domain, where repetitive Arg/Ser dipeptides mediate multivalent interactions (PubMed:39968932, 39023093). Phosphorylation status critically regulates behavior: unphosphorylated RS domains drive self-assembly via arginine-mediated interactions, while serine phosphorylation inhibits self-driven phase separation by forming intramolecular salt bridges that reduce intermolecular contacts (PubMed:39968932). Hyperphosphorylation of the RS domain enhances electrostatic-driven co-phase separation with partners like U1-70K BAD1 (PubMed:39023093). RNA-binding domains (RRMs) contribute to partner recruitment and RNA-dependent modulation (PubMed:38638569, 31363225).
Extrinsic Partners & Regulations: SRSF1 co-phase separates with multiple partners: U1-70K via RS-BAD1 domain interactions enhanced by hyperphosphorylation (PubMed:39023093); CLK2 which recruits SRSF1 into stress-induced condensates (PubMed:39119950); and hnRNPA1 with antagonistic positioning effects in nuclear speckles (PubMed:38638569). It scaffolds hyperphosphorylated RNA Pol II CTD (PubMed:31391587) and co-assembles with splicing factors (TRA2B, RBMX) in RNA-dependent condensates (PubMed:31363225). RNA concentration bidirectionally modulates phase behavior—low levels promote assembly while high concentrations dissolve condensates (PubMed:31363225). Buffer ions (e.g., phosphate vs. arginine) competitively regulate phosphorylation-dependent phase separation (PubMed:39968932).

Overall Phase Separation Overview: CIRBP undergoes self-driven phase separation (PubMed:22579281, 32234784, 24267890), forming RNA-dependent liquid-like condensates in the Cytoplasm and Nucleus (PubMed:34738012, 32234784). It associates with Stress Granules under various stressors including cold shock, oxidative stress, and proteotoxic stress (PubMed:34738012, 32234784, 33991007). While typically exhibiting liquid-like properties with fusion capabilities in RNA-containing environments (PubMed:34738012, 32234784, 33991007), its low-complexity domain can also form hydrogel states in vitro (PubMed:22579281, 24267890).
Functional Summary: Phase separation enables CIRBP recruitment to stress granules for mRNA stabilization during cellular stress (e.g., cold, oxidative, UV stress), promoting cell survival (PubMed:34738012, 32234784, 33991007). Dysregulation via phosphorylation or arginine methylation impairs stress granule association, potentially contributing to neurodegeneration and cancer (PubMed:34738012, 32234784). ATP depletion during stress correlates with condensate formation, indicating metabolite-regulated dynamics (PubMed:33991007), while pathological hydrogel transitions may occur through heterotypic interactions with amyloidogenic proteins (PubMed:22579281).
Intrinsic Determinants & Regulations: Phase separation is intrinsically driven by the Arginine-Glycine/Glycine-rich (RG/RGG) domain (aa 68-137/90-137) (PubMed:34738012, 32234784, 33991007, 24267890), with the RNA Recognition Motif (RRM) domain (aa 1-90) contributing to nucleotide binding (PubMed:33991007). Phosphorylation at S97/S115/S130 and arginine methylation at R94/R101/R105/R112/R116 within the RG/RGG region inhibit LLPS and stress granule recruitment (PubMed:34738012). Phosphomimetic mutations (S97D/S115D/S130D) similarly impair condensate formation (PubMed:34738012), while arginine methylation weakens binding to inhibitory transport factors (PubMed:32234784).
Extrinsic Partners & Regulations: RNA scaffolds like (UG)₁₂ RNA are essential for LLPS induction at low concentrations but suppress phase separation at high concentrations (PubMed:34738012, 32234784, 33991007). Transport factors TNPO1 and TNPO3 inhibit LLPS and stress granule recruitment by binding the RG/RGG region and displacing RNA (PubMed:32234784). ATP competitively inhibits RNA binding to the RG/RGG domain, dissolving condensates (PubMed:33991007). CIRBP co-phase separates with proteins including FUS and hnRNPA2, exhibiting heterotypic trapping in hydrogels and copolymerization (PubMed:22579281).

Overall Phase Separation Overview: Interferon regulatory factor 3 (IRF3) undergoes self-driven liquid-liquid phase separation (LLPS) forming dynamic liquid-like nuclear condensates upon viral infection, dependent on deacetylation of its DNA-binding domain (DBD) (PubMed:35879450, 35879453). It also participates in co-phase separation within mitochondrial MAVS signaling platforms (PubMed:37188808), cytoplasmic AXIN1 condensates (PubMed:39384753), and pathological NF2m condensates (PubMed:34453890). Primary subcellular locations include the nucleus and cytoplasm (PubMed:35879450, 39384753), with condensates exhibiting liquid material properties characterized by rapid fluorescence recovery, fusion, and sensitivity to 1,6-hexanediol (PubMed:35879450, 34453890, 35879453). No material state transitions are reported for IRF3 alone, though it undergoes maturation within NF2m condensates (PubMed:34453890).
Functional Summary: IRF3 phase separation is physiologically critical for antiviral immunity. Nuclear condensates bound to ISRE DNA compartmentalize IRF7 and MED1, forming hubs for efficient transcription of type I interferons (IFN-I) and interferon-stimulated genes (PubMed:35879450). Cytoplasmic recruitment into MAVS and AXIN1 condensates facilitates TBK1-mediated phosphorylation and interferon production (PubMed:37188808, 39384753). Dysregulation leads to pathology: acetylation or SIRT1 deficiency impairs LLPS, increasing viral susceptibility in aging (PubMed:35879450, 35879453); pathological NF2m condensates sequester IRF3 to suppress cGAS-STING signaling and promote tumorigenesis (PubMed:34453890); and viral NS80 viroplasms sequester IRF3 to evade immune responses (PubMed:39194247).
Intrinsic Determinants & Regulations: IRF3 phase separation is intrinsically regulated by its DNA-binding domain (DBD), intrinsically disordered region (IDR), and IRF-associated domain (IAD), which are essential for LLPS, while its inhibitory domain (ID) suppresses it (PubMed:35879450). Deacetylation of lysine residues K39 and K77 in the DBD by SIRT1 drives phase separation, with acetylation at these sites inhibiting condensate formation (PubMed:35879450, 35879453). A SUMO-interacting motif (SIM; residues 391-VDLHI-395) enables recruitment into MAVS condensates, while phosphorylation at Ser386/Ser396 disrupts SIM-mediated interactions (PubMed:37188808). Deletion mutations (d-DBD, d-IDR, d-IAD) impair LLPS, whereas d-ID enhances it, and acetyl-mimicking mutations (K39Q/K77Q) abrogate phase separation (PubMed:35879450).
Extrinsic Partners & Regulations: IRF3 phase separation is extrinsically modulated by nucleic acids, proteins, and chemicals. ISRE DNA acts as an essential scaffold, lowering saturation concentration and promoting droplet formation (PubMed:35879450, 35879453). It co-phase separates with IRF7 and MED1 in transcriptional condensates (PubMed:35879450), and is recruited into MAVS platforms via SIM-SUMO interactions (PubMed:37188808), AXIN1 signaling hubs (PubMed:39384753), and pathological NF2m aggregates (PubMed:34453890). During viral infection, IRF3 is sequestered within NS80 viroplasms to evade immunity (PubMed:39194247). SIRT1 agonists enhance LLPS by promoting deacetylation, while inhibitors (e.g., EX527) suppress it (PubMed:35879450).

Overall Phase Separation Overview: EB1 (Q15691) undergoes self-driven liquid-liquid phase separation (LLPS) to form dynamic, liquid-like condensates both in vitro and in vivo (PubMed:38323478, 36536176, 39749826). These condensates localize primarily to the cytoplasm and associate with the spindle apparatus, centrosome, and microtubule plus-ends, forming evolutionarily conserved structures termed 'EB1 bodies' that exhibit rapid fusion, fission, and fluorescence recovery (PubMed:38323478, 36536176, 39749826). While wild-type EB1 condensates maintain liquid properties, pathological mutations (e.g., EB1-hnRNPA1D262V) can trigger liquid-to-gel/solid transitions (PubMed:36536176). Acetylation at Lys220 enhances self-assembly but disrupts co-condensation with partners (PubMed:38323478).
Functional Summary: EB1 condensates serve as biochemical hubs that compartmentalize microtubule regulators (TIP150, MCAK) and tubulin, enabling precise regulation of microtubule dynamics (growth rate, catastrophe frequency), plus-end tracking, and kinetochore-microtubule attachments during mitosis (PubMed:38323478, 36536176). Disruption via mutations (e.g., K174Q, KR6Q) or acetylation causes spindle misorientation, chromosome misalignment, anaphase delay, and reduced kinetochore tension (PubMed:38323478, 36536176, 39749826). EB1 exhibits neuroprotective functions by suppressing tau LLPS/aggregation, delaying pathological transitions linked to tauopathies (PubMed:38445984). Recruitment to CLIP-170 condensates suggests roles in +TIP network superstructures (PubMed:34890409).
Intrinsic Determinants & Regulations: EB1 phase separation is intrinsically driven by multivalent interactions among its N-terminal calponin homology (CH) domain, C-terminal coiled-coil EB homology (EBH) domain, and intrinsically disordered linker region (IDR; residues 126-183), with the EBH domain enabling essential dimerization (PubMed:36536176). Electrostatic interactions mediated by conserved lysine/arginine residues in the IDR constitute critical molecular grammar: Lys174 acylation (mimicked by K174Q) attenuates LLPS by disrupting self-association, while charge-cluster mutations enhance it (PubMed:36536176, 39749826). Acetylation at Lys220 promotes self-phase separation but inhibits partner recruitment, and mutations (e.g., KR6Q: K174Q/R176Q/K178Q/K180Q/K182Q/R183Q) or IDR deletion abolish LLPS (PubMed:38323478, 36536176).
Extrinsic Partners & Regulations: EB1 co-phase separates with scaffolding partners TIP150 and MCAK, which synergistically lower its phase separation threshold, enhance condensate dynamics, and stabilize droplet structure (PubMed:38323478, 36536176). Tubulin is enriched within EB1 condensates as a reservoir for microtubule growth (PubMed:36536176). Ionic conditions modulate LLPS, with optimal droplet formation at 150 mM KCl (PubMed:36536176). EB1 inhibits tau phase separation and aggregation by binding tau (Kd = 2.5 µM), increasing droplet mobility, and delaying liquid-to-solid transitions (PubMed:38445984). Conversely, EB1 is recruited to CLIP-170-induced cytoplasmic condensates (PubMed:34890409).

MLO Types: Inclusion body; p62 cluster; Stress granule
Overall Phase Separation Overview: p62 undergoes partner-dependent phase separation primarily in the cytoplasm, forming liquid-like condensates associated with inclusion bodies and p62 clusters (PubMed:34862482, 31434890, 30126895, 33822768). These condensates exhibit hydrogel properties when interacting with DAXX in vitro (PubMed:31434890) and require NBR1 for liquid droplet formation in vivo (PubMed:31916398). Phase separation is inhibited by caspase-6-mediated cleavage at D256 during inflammatory stress (TNFα/LPS) and induced by mitochondrial fragmentation through redox-dependent mechanisms (PubMed:34862482, 33822768).
Functional Summary: Phase separation regulates autophagy and NRF2-mediated stress responses, with inhibition impairing autophagic function (PubMed:34862482). Condensates facilitate KEAP1 sequestration and NRF2 activation during oxidative stress (PubMed:31434890, 31916398). Pathological dysregulation occurs through persistent condensates resistant to autophagy clearance (PubMed:30126895) and redox-dependent formation of large condensates during mitochondrial dysfunction, contributing to retinal pigment epithelium impairment in macular degeneration (PubMed:33822768).
Intrinsic Determinants & Regulations: Phase separation is intrinsically regulated by PB1 and UBA domains (inferred from human homology) (PubMed:34862482). Key modifications include inhibitory cleavage at D256 by caspase-6 (PubMed:34862482), oxidation of cysteines at positions 105/113 during mitochondrial stress (PubMed:33822768), and phosphorylation at Ser351 associated with condensate formation (PubMed:30126895). DAXX-induced oligomerization promotes phase separation, while the P392L mutation reduces DAXX interaction and impairs puncta formation (PubMed:31434890).
Extrinsic Partners & Regulations: Essential co-phase separation partners include polyubiquitinated proteins (PubMed:34862482), DAXX which promotes oligomerization and droplet formation (PubMed:31434890), and NBR1 which enables liquid droplet formation (PubMed:31916398). Condensates incorporate KEAP1, NRF2, and polyubiquitin (PubMed:30126895). Phase separation is inhibited by inflammatory stressors (TNFα/CHX/LPS) that trigger cleavage (PubMed:34862482) but promoted by mitochondrial fragmentation through redox changes (PubMed:33822768).

Overall Phase Separation Overview: YTHDF3 undergoes self-driven liquid-liquid phase separation (LLPS) in vitro and forms dynamic, liquid-like condensates primarily in the cytoplasm (PubMed:38811341, 31388144, 31292544). It associates with stress granules under diverse stress conditions including oxidative stress, heat shock, arsenite exposure, and cellular senescence (PubMed:32451507, 31292544, 38926365). The protein also forms punctate condensates not classified under predefined membrane-less organelles (PubMed:38811341). No material state transitions were reported under tested conditions (PubMed:38811341, 31388144, 31292544).
Functional Summary: Phase separation enables YTHDF3 to suppress clear cell renal cell carcinoma (ccRCC) malignancy and immune evasion by degrading HSPA13 mRNA via DDX6 recruitment, downregulating PD-L1 and enhancing CD8⁺ T-cell activity (PubMed:38811341). It is essential for stress granule formation and m6A-mRNA recruitment during oxidative stress (PubMed:32451507, 31292544). Disruption of phase separation via IDR mutations abolishes tumor suppression (PubMed:38811341). YTHDF3's presence in stress granules is exploited by SARS-CoV-2 for potential viral replication through interaction with the nucleocapsid protein (PubMed:34780058).
Intrinsic Determinants & Regulations: Phase separation is intrinsically driven by YTHDF3's low-complexity domain (LCD) and N-terminal intrinsically disordered region (IDR, residues 288-360) (PubMed:31388144, 38811341, 31292544). The YTH domain is essential for stress granule functionality (PubMed:32451507). Glutamine-to-alanine substitutions in the IDR disrupt phase separation, abolish condensate formation, and impair tumor-suppressive functions (PubMed:38811341).
Extrinsic Partners & Regulations: YTHDF3 phase separation is enhanced by multivalent RNA scaffolds, particularly mRNAs with multiple m6A residues which significantly increase partition coefficients (PubMed:31388144, 31292544). It co-phase separates with paralogs YTHDF1 and YTHDF2 to form heterotypic condensates (PubMed:31292544). Within condensates, YTHDF3 recruits DDX6 to facilitate HSPA13 mRNA degradation and co-localizes with G3BP1 to promote stress granule assembly (PubMed:38811341, 32451507). YTHDF3 interacts with SARS-CoV-2 nucleocapsid protein in stress granules, potentially facilitating viral hijacking (PubMed:34780058).

Overall Phase Separation Overview: FIP200 (RB1CC1) undergoes both self-driven and partner-dependent phase separation, forming liquid-like condensates primarily in the cytoplasm (PubMed:36198318, 36394358, 30853400). It associates with autophagosome initiation sites on the endoplasmic reticulum (ER) through FIP200/ATG13/ULK1 complex condensates and forms distinct RB1CC1 bodies (PubMed:36198318, 36394358). The protein exhibits rapid fusion/fission dynamics and FRAP recovery consistent with liquid material states, though no phase transitions are reported under studied conditions (PubMed:36198318, 36394358).
Functional Summary: FIP200 phase separation is essential for autophagy, assembling dynamic initiation complexes on the ER that recruit downstream components (e.g., LC3) and develop into autophagosomes (PubMed:36198318, 36394358). Dysregulation via persistent Ca²⁺ oscillations or IDR disruption causes accumulation of unclosed autophagic structures, impairing autophagy flux (PubMed:36198318, 36394358). Acetylation-dependent stabilization at K276 is crucial for canonical autophagy function in breast cancer cells (PubMed:36394358). The protein's modulation of p62 phase separation further regulates selective autophagy pathways (PubMed:30853400).
Intrinsic Determinants & Regulations: Phase separation is intrinsically driven by multiple domains: The N-terminal intrinsically disordered region (IDR, residues 212-295) autonomously enables liquid-liquid phase separation (LLPS) (PubMed:36394358), while coiled-coil domains (CC1, CC2) and termini (NTD, CTD) regulate puncta dynamics and stability during Ca²⁺-triggered assembly (PubMed:36198318). The C-terminal region (CTR) forms a dimeric 'Claw' domain that modulates partner condensates (PubMed:30853400). Key mutations include ΔIDR (impairs formation), ΔCC1 (slows dynamics), ΔNTD/ΔCTD (abolish formation), and CTR point mutations (F1574A, R1573D, R1584A) that disrupt interactions (PubMed:36198318, 30853400). Acetylation at K276 by CREBBP enhances protein stability, indirectly promoting puncta formation (PubMed:36394358).
Extrinsic Partners & Regulations: Phase separation is primarily triggered by Ca²⁺ ions, with puncta forming near ER-associated transients (PubMed:36198318). Essential partners include ATG13, which scaffolds LLPS and co-partitions into condensates (PubMed:36198318). ULK1 and ATG101 are recruited as clients but are non-essential for initial phase separation (PubMed:36198318). The acetyltransferase CREBBP stabilizes FIP200 to enhance puncta formation (PubMed:36394358). Spatial organization is modulated by ATG9 vesicles, whose absence causes aberrant puncta (PubMed:36198318). FIP200 CTR recruitment slows phase separation of ubiquitinated proteins in p62 condensates (PubMed:30853400).

Protein Name: Mediator of RNA polymerase II transcription subunit 1
Gene Names: Med1 Crsp210 Drip205 Pbp Pparbp Trap220 Trip2
Overall Phase Separation Overview: MED1 undergoes both self-driven phase separation via its intrinsically disordered region (IDR) and partner-dependent phase separation, primarily occurring in the nucleus (PubMed:31398323, 34605568, 29930091). It associates with transcriptional condensates including super-enhancers, Mediator condensates, and YAP-induced transcriptional hubs (PubMed:29930091, 34605568, 33606996). The material state is typically liquid-like, exhibiting rapid fluorescence recovery and fusion dynamics, with no explicit state transitions reported (PubMed:34605568, 29930091). DNA scaffolding significantly reduces the concentration threshold for partner-dependent condensation (PubMed:31398323).
Functional Summary: MED1 phase separation enables transcriptional regulation by concentrating RNA polymerase II and coactivators at super-enhancers, facilitating non-linear recruitment of machinery (PubMed:31398323, 29930091). It is essential for Mediator complex assembly, where disruption via IDR-exon skipping impairs transcription and causes cell death (PubMed:34605568). MED1's IDR rescues phase separation capacity in defective transcription factors, restoring reprogramming efficiency (PubMed:34038708). In pathological contexts, MED1 partitions into YAP condensates to maximize CD155 expression, promoting tumor immune evasion and anti-PD-1 therapy resistance (PubMed:33606996).
Intrinsic Determinants & Regulations: Phase separation is intrinsically driven by MED1's intrinsically disordered region (IDR), with the C-terminal IDR encoded by the last exon being particularly critical (PubMed:31398323, 34038708, 34605568, 29930091). Disruption of this IDR via SRSF3-dependent alternative splicing abolishes nuclear condensate formation (PubMed:34605568). The IDR mediates weak multivalent interactions essential for transcriptional condensate assembly and stability (PubMed:31398323, 29930091).
Extrinsic Partners & Regulations: MED1 co-phase separates with transcription factors including OCT4 in a DNA-dependent manner, where DNA scaffolding reduces the critical saturation concentration by 68-fold (PubMed:31398323, 34038708). It interacts interdependently with Mediator components (MED4, MED15) for condensate assembly (PubMed:34605568, 34789250). MED1 partitions into YAP transcriptional condensates alongside TEAD4 and EP300 (PubMed:33606996) and forms condensates that incorporate BRD4 and RNA polymerase II (PubMed:29930091). IFN-γ induces MED1 recruitment into transcriptional hubs (PubMed:33606996).

Overall Phase Separation Overview: RIM1α (Q9JIR4) undergoes self-driven liquid-liquid phase separation (LLPS) to form dynamic liquid-like condensates, primarily in the cytoplasm (PubMed:30661983, 34031393, 33202250). It associates with presynaptic active zone condensates through multivalent interactions and exhibits constitutive phase separation behavior in cellular systems (PubMed:34031393, 33761347). The protein forms spherical droplets that undergo fusion and display partial-to-high mobility in FRAP assays, with full-length RIM1α showing reduced mobility compared to truncated forms (PubMed:30661983, 33202250). No material state transitions were reported across studies (PubMed:30661983, 34031393, 33202250).
Functional Summary: RIM1α condensates organize presynaptic active zones by clustering voltage-gated calcium channels into nano-domains, positioning them near synaptic vesicles for precise, efficient neurotransmitter release (PubMed:30661983, 33202250). They mediate synaptic vesicle tethering through lipid-dependent coating mechanisms, reconstituting functional reserve and tethered vesicle pools (PubMed:33202250, 38552623). Recruitment into Liprin-α3 condensates enhances vesicle docking and readily releasable pool size during PKC activation (PubMed:34031393). While no pathological transitions were reported, reduced synaptic levels impair vesicle priming and release kinetics (PubMed:34031393).
Intrinsic Determinants & Regulations: Phase separation is intrinsically driven by RIM1α's N-terminal region (aa 1-480), PDZ domain, C2A domain, and proline-rich motifs (PRMs) (PubMed:30661983). The N-terminal region significantly enhances LLPS capacity, while PRM motifs (particularly PRM1 and PRM2) are essential for multivalent interactions, as their deletion weakens or abolishes condensate formation (PubMed:30661983, 33202250). C2 domains facilitate lipid binding and vesicle coating on condensate surfaces (PubMed:33202250). No PTMs, splicing variants, or oligomerization features were explicitly identified as regulators in the provided data.
Extrinsic Partners & Regulations: RIM1α requires co-scaffold partners for physiological phase separation: RIM-BP2 drives LLPS via SH3 domain-PRM interactions (PubMed:30661983, 33202250, 33761347), while ELKS1/2 enhances condensate formation through PDZ-binding motifs (PubMed:33202250, 33761347). Liprin-α3 recruits RIM1α into PKC-activated condensates that modulate vesicle priming (PubMed:34031393). Voltage-gated calcium channels (e.g., CACNA1B) act as enriched clients that promote LLPS and cluster within condensates via C-terminal interactions (PubMed:30661983, 33202250). Negatively charged lipids (DOPS, PI(4,5)P2) enable synaptic vesicle coating on condensate surfaces (PubMed:33202250). Munc13-1 co-localizes in Liprin-α3/RIM1α condensates to regulate neurotransmitter release (PubMed:34031393).

Overall Phase Separation Overview: SRRM2 undergoes self-driven liquid-liquid phase separation (LLPS) both in vitro and in vivo, forming dynamic, liquid-like condensates primarily within nuclear speckles in the nucleus (PubMed:38381607, 35929045, 39798570, 39755675). It also forms mitotic granules during cell division (PubMed:29973724). The material state is typically liquid, exhibiting rapid FRAP recovery and droplet fusion (PubMed:38381607, 39755675, 39798570), but undergoes tunable state transitions: phosphorylation by DYRK3 increases liquidity while dephosphorylation by PP1 enhances cohesion toward a gel-like state (PubMed:39755675). Additionally, serine mutations in RS domains reduce condensate liquidity (PubMed:38381607).
Functional Summary: SRRM2 scaffolds nuclear speckles to regulate pre-mRNA splicing, particularly for exons with weak splice sites and short flanking introns (e.g., in FES and MUC1 genes), maintaining protein domain integrity and influencing innate immunity (via FES isoforms) and oncogenesis (via MUC1 isoforms) (PubMed:35929045, 39798570, 38381607). During mitosis, its granules control splicing factor availability (PubMed:29973724). Phosphorylation-modulated material states govern mRNA retention: dephosphorylation increases nuclear/speckle mRNA retention, while phosphorylation promotes release for export and translation (PubMed:39755675). Pathologically, mislocalization to tau aggregates causes aberrant splicing and contributes to neurodegeneration in tauopathies (PubMed:33848474).
Intrinsic Determinants & Regulations: Phase separation is intrinsically driven by SRRM2's RS domains (RS1/RS2) that mediate essential homotypic oligomerization for nucleation, alongside NCK and IDR regions that facilitate condensate coalescence (PubMed:38381607). The UPR (undeca-amino acid) and DPR (dodeca-amino acid) repeats, particularly within UPR3, are critical for LLPS propensity (PubMed:35929045, 39798570). Mutations such as ΔRS1/ΔRS2 abolish phase separation, while ΔNCK/ΔIDR yield smaller, non-coalesced condensates (PubMed:38381607). Serine residues in RS domains fine-tune liquidity independently of phosphorylation; substitutions (e.g., RS<sub>S-A</sub>) reduce dynamics (PubMed:38381607).
Extrinsic Partners & Regulations: RNA, including mRNA and poly(A) RNA, acts as a scaffold that lowers the saturation concentration for LLPS and promotes condensate formation (PubMed:38381607, 35929045). SRRM2 co-phase separates with splicing factors U2AF1, SRSF2, and RBM25, which partition selectively into its condensates (PubMed:38381607). Chemical inhibition of DYRK3 by GSK-626616 induces mitotic granule formation (PubMed:29973724). Enzymatic regulators include DYRK3 kinase, which phosphorylates SRRM2 to increase mobility/liquidity, and PP1 phosphatase, which dephosphorylates it to enhance cohesion (PubMed:39755675). SRRM2 also interacts with SMNDC1 within nuclear speckles (PubMed:37587144).

Overall Phase Separation Overview: CAR-1 undergoes partner-dependent phase separation (classified as PS-other) primarily in the cytoplasm, with additional nuclear localization observed under stress conditions (PubMed:35801939, 24176641). It associates with membrane-less organelles including P-bodies, germ granules (P granules, Z granules), and germ plasm bodies (grPBs) (PubMed:37505984, 37703874, 24176641). CAR-1 forms viscoelastic semiliquid condensates in arrested oocytes, exhibiting slow fusion kinetics and elastic responses to stress (PubMed:24176641). Material state transitions occur: diffuse-to-condensed transitions are triggered by developmental arrest or imaging stress (PubMed:35801939, 24176641), while pathological liquid-to-solid transitions occur upon loss of regulatory partners like CGH-1, forming immobile aggregates (PubMed:24176641).
Functional Summary: CAR-1 condensates regulate maternal mRNA during oogenesis by stoichiometrically buffering repressed mRNAs and repressors in arrested oocytes, maintaining cytosolic repressor availability while sequestering targets like spn-4 mRNA (PubMed:37703874, 24176641). They organize germ granules into functional sub-compartments (P/Z granules), enabling transgenerational gene silencing through small RNA factor enrichment (PubMed:37505984). Upon fertilization, rapid condensate dissolution mobilizes RNPs for translation (PubMed:24176641). Pathologically, loss of CGH-1 triggers solid-state transitions forming cytotoxic aggregates, modeling neurodegenerative disease mechanisms (PubMed:24176641). Disruption of condensation (e.g., via PUF-5 depletion) causes embryonic lethality due to aberrant mRNA translation (PubMed:37703874).
Intrinsic Determinants & Regulations: No intrinsic domains, motifs, post-translational modifications, or mutations driving CAR-1 phase separation are reported in the provided data (PubMed:39167497, 37505984, 37703874, 35801939, 24176641).
Extrinsic Partners & Regulations: CAR-1 phase separation is scaffolded by partner proteins: CGH-1 is essential for condensate formation and germ granule interactions, with car-1 depletion dispersing CGH-1 foci (PubMed:37505984). PUF-5 acts as a critical structural component for P-body integrity; its depletion dissolves CAR-1 condensates and disrupts mRNA buffering (PubMed:37703874, 24176641). CAR-1 co-assembles with repressed mRNAs in condensates (PubMed:37703874, 24176641) and segregates into subdomains with PGL-1/PATR-1 in germ plasm bodies (PubMed:24176641). Stress-induced condensation occurs rapidly under imaging conditions (PubMed:35801939). CAR-1 also partially colocalizes with MEX-3 and LIN-41 in ectopic condensates upon CCT chaperonin depletion (PubMed:39167497).

Overall Phase Separation Overview: MECP2 exhibits conflicting phase separation behavior in the nucleus, primarily associating with heterochromatin condensates or chromocenters. While some studies report liquid-like condensate formation through self-assembly in murine cells (PubMed:32698189, 35156529, 35809564), others find no evidence of liquid-liquid phase separation, attributing localization solely to DNA methylation-dependent binding (PubMed:38719804, 32101700). Disease-associated truncation mutations (e.g., R168X, R186*) consistently disrupt nuclear partitioning regardless of the proposed mechanism (PubMed:35809564, 32698189, 38719804). No material state transitions were reported across studies.
Functional Summary: In phase separation models, MeCP2 condensates organize heterochromatin architecture, facilitate chromatin compaction, recruit effectors like HP1α, and regulate transcriptional silencing (PubMed:32698189, 35156529). Disruption by Rett syndrome mutations causes aberrant chromatin organization, reduced HP1α recruitment, and transcriptional dysregulation, contributing to disease pathogenesis (PubMed:32698189, 35156529, 35809564). Alternative models attribute MeCP2's function strictly to DNA methylation-dependent gene regulation without phase separation involvement, with Rett mutations impairing DNA binding rather than condensate dynamics (PubMed:38719804, 32101700).
Intrinsic Determinants & Regulations: The methyl-CpG binding domain (MBD) is universally essential for heterochromatin localization, whether through direct DNA binding or phase separation mechanisms (PubMed:32698189, 38719804, 35156529). Studies proposing phase separation identify the C-terminal IDR-2 with basic patches and N-terminal IDR as key drivers via multivalent interactions, while residues 168-254 mediate self-oligomerization required for condensate formation (PubMed:32698189, 35156529). Rett syndrome mutations (R111G, R133C, T158M, R168X, R186*, R255X, R306C) disrupt these processes by impairing DNA binding, self-interaction, or domain functionality (PubMed:32698189, 35809564, 35156529, 38719804).
Extrinsic Partners & Regulations: DNA serves as a critical scaffold, with methylated DNA significantly enhancing condensate formation by lowering the saturation concentration in phase separation models (PubMed:32698189). MeCP2 co-localizes with HP1α in heterochromatin condensates and recruits client proteins like TBLR1-CTD via its NID domain (PubMed:32698189). DNA methylation also modulates compartment size by restricting droplet growth and increasing protein immobilization (PubMed:35156529). No extrinsic partners or regulators were identified in studies disputing phase separation (PubMed:35809564, 38719804, 32101700).

Overall Phase Separation Overview: ZNFX-1 undergoes phase separation to form Z granules, initially colocalizing with P granules in early germline blastomeres before forming independent liquid-like condensates in later developmental stages (PubMed:36750365, 29769721). These dynamic structures exhibit rapid fluorescence recovery (t½ = 8s) and spherical morphology, characteristic of liquid states (PubMed:29769721, 33438773). In adult germ cells, Z granules assemble into ordered tri-condensate PZM assemblages with P granules and Mutator foci (PubMed:29769721). The protein primarily localizes to cytoplasmic subdomains but exhibits nuclear presence during early development (PubMed:29769721, 36750365). ZNFX-1 condensates undergo pathological liquid-to-solid transitions when deprived of the regulator ZSP-1, resulting in hardened granules with abolished mobility (PubMed:33438773).
Functional Summary: ZNFX-1 condensates organize RNA-silencing machinery for transgenerational epigenetic inheritance, concentrating silencing factors to mark mRNAs complementary to inherited siRNAs (PubMed:29769721, 33438773). They enable pUG RNA–siRNA cycling, where dysregulation prolongs epigenetic inheritance and disrupts germline small RNA pathways (PubMed:39354132). Pathological transitions to solid states cause germline immortality defects and RNAi inheritance failure, as demonstrated by temperature-sensitive mortal germline phenotypes in zsp-1 mutants (PubMed:33438773, 29769721). The PZM tri-condensate architecture spatially coordinates RNA processing pathways, with compartment mixing in herd-1 mutants leading to global disorganization of germline regulatory networks (PubMed:39354132, 29769721). Z granule integrity is essential for segregating silencing machinery to germline blastomeres during development (PubMed:33438773, 29769721).
Intrinsic Determinants & Regulations: No specific intrinsic domains, mutations, or molecular features driving ZNFX-1 phase separation were identified in the provided studies (PubMed:36750365, 39354132, 29769721, 33438773). All examined papers reported 'Not Specified' for domains, PTMs, oligomerization states, or mutations in key_drivers sections, indicating no experimentally confirmed intrinsic regulators within the analyzed dataset.
Extrinsic Partners & Regulations: ZNFX-1 phase separation is modulated by multiple extrinsic partners: It co-assembles with WAGO-4 to form core Z granule scaffolds, with physical interaction confirmed by co-immunoprecipitation (PubMed:29769721, 33438773). RNA binding is essential, as pUG RNAs recruit ZNFX-1 to condensates and enable transgenerational epigenetic inheritance functions (PubMed:39354132). The protein ZSP-1 maintains condensate liquidity by localizing to granule surfaces; its absence triggers liquid-to-solid transitions evidenced by abolished FRAP recovery (PubMed:33438773). Early localization depends on PGL-1 scaffolding within P granules, with segregation failures observed in P granule-defective mutants (PubMed:29769721). Additionally, ZNFX-1 occupies distinct subdomains with PRG-1 within shared granules, positioned near cytoplasmic edges (PubMed:36750365).

Gene Names: ARID1A BAF250 BAF250A C1orf4 OSA1 SMARCF1
Overall Phase Separation Overview: ARID1A undergoes self-driven phase separation (PubMed:39095374, 38326345) to form dynamic, liquid-like condensates primarily in the nucleus (PubMed:39095374, 37788668, 38326345), with potential cytoplasmic localization (PubMed:38326345). It associates with transcriptional condensates and chromatin remodeling hubs (PubMed:39095374) and partitions into ectopic condensates (PubMed:34018649). The condensates exhibit rapid fluorescence recovery after photobleaching (FRAP), fusion events, and concentration-dependent formation thresholds (1.13-2.5 μM) (PubMed:39095374, 37788668, 38326345). No explicit material state transitions are reported under standard conditions, though pathological mutations may promote solid-like states (PubMed:37788668).
Functional Summary: ARID1A condensates regulate chromatin remodeling and oncogene activation (e.g., TFAP2B/CDK14/SOX6) via enhancer targeting in Ewing’s sarcoma, essential for tumor proliferation and invasion (PubMed:39095374). They concentrate cBAF interaction networks for chromatin accessibility and transcriptional activation (PubMed:37788668). Dysregulation—through IDR mutations or ectopic recruitment into FUS-DDIT3 condensates—disrupts genomic localization, causing gene expression defects linked to cancer and neurodevelopmental disorders (PubMed:37788668, 34018649). Pathological mutations may promote cytotoxic solid-like states (PubMed:37788668).
Intrinsic Determinants & Regulations: Phase separation is intrinsically driven by prion-like domains (PrLDs) and intrinsically disordered regions (IDRs), particularly IDR1 and tyrosine-rich segments (PubMed:39095374, 37788668, 38326345). Tyrosine residues are critical drivers, as tyrosine-to-serine mutations (e.g., PrLD(Y/S), 42YS, 29Y-to-S) abolish condensation (PubMed:39095374, 37788668, 38326345). Deletion of disordered domains (ΔDD, ΔIDR1) or core-binding regions (CBR) prevents phase separation (PubMed:39095374, 37788668). The ARID DNA-binding domain modulates DNA-enhanced condensation, with mutations (e.g., DBDmut) reducing condensate count and slowing dynamics (PubMed:37788668). Glutamine residues moderately regulate saturation concentration, as Q-to-G mutations increase Csat (PubMed:38326345). Cancer-associated mutations (R774C/R1223C) retain liquid-like properties (PubMed:39095374).
Extrinsic Partners & Regulations: ARID1A phase separation is modulated by nucleic acids and partner proteins. DNA and nucleosomes enhance condensation and reduce saturation concentration, while RNA has no effect (PubMed:37788668). It co-condenses with the oncofusion protein EWS/FLI1, essential for oncogenic hub function (PubMed:39095374), and mutually recruits transcription factors (NFIA, TEAD1, cJUN) in an IDR1-dependent manner (PubMed:37788668). ARID1A exhibits strong co-partitioning with FUS, SS18, and ARID1B (partition coefficients: 51-162) (PubMed:38326345) and enriches in FUS-DDIT3 ectopic condensates (partition coefficient: 15±4) (PubMed:34018649).

MLO Types: Centrosome; Nuclear speckle; Spindle apparatus; Stress granule
Overall Phase Separation Overview: DYRK3 undergoes self-driven phase separation to form liquid-like condensates in the cytoplasm and nucleus (PubMed:29973724, PubMed:23415227, PubMed:33738926, PubMed:39755675). It associates with stress granules, nuclear speckles, centrosomes (pericentriolar matrix), spindle apparatus, and P-granule-like structures (PubMed:29973724, PubMed:33738926, PubMed:23415227, PubMed:39755675). These condensates exhibit dynamic properties including fusion and rapid FRAP recovery but undergo liquid-to-solid transitions upon kinase inactivation (e.g., via K218M mutation or inhibitors like GSK-626616) (PubMed:23415227).
Functional Summary: DYRK3 condensates regulate stress adaptation, mitosis, and mRNA processing. During stress, partitioning into granules protects DYRK3 from aggregation; active DYRK3 dissolves stress granules to restore mTORC1 signaling and translation (PubMed:33738926, PubMed:23415227). In mitosis, dissolution of nuclear/cytoplasmic condensates prevents aberrant co-condensation, ensuring proper spindle assembly and cell division; loss of activity causes multipolar spindles and delays (PubMed:29973724). DYRK3 phosphorylates nuclear speckle scaffolds (e.g., SRRM2, SON), reducing cohesion and mRNA retention, with inhibition promoting nuclear mRNA accumulation (PubMed:39755675). Dysregulation (e.g., via Hsp90 inhibition or ALS-linked FUS mutations) impairs granule disassembly, contributing to cytotoxicity and neurodegeneration (PubMed:33738926).
Intrinsic Determinants & Regulations: Phase separation is intrinsically driven by DYRK3's intrinsically disordered N-terminal domain (NTD), essential for partitioning into stress granules and nuclear speckles (PubMed:29973724, PubMed:33738926, PubMed:23415227). Phosphorylation regulates solubility: tyrosine autophosphorylation in the activation loop (YXY) maintains kinase activity, while serine/threonine phosphorylation in unstructured domains modulates condensation propensity (PubMed:29973724, PubMed:33738926). Disease-relevant mutations (e.g., K218M, NTD deletion) impair kinase activity, disrupt partitioning, and promote aberrant solidification (PubMed:29973724, PubMed:23415227).
Extrinsic Partners & Regulations: DYRK3's phase separation is extrinsically regulated by partner proteins and chemicals. It co-condenses with SRRM1, PCM1, ZNF207, PABP1, SON, and SRRM2 in hybrid structures, with dissolution requiring kinase activity (PubMed:29973724, PubMed:39755675). Hsp90 stabilizes cytosolic DYRK3; inhibition by geldanamycin or 17AAG promotes partitioning into condensates and delays stress granule disassembly (PubMed:33738926). Chemical inhibitors (GSK-626616, harmine) trap DYRK3 in stabilized condensates by blocking kinase activity, while PARylation enhances co-partitioning with partners like PARP1 (PubMed:29973724, PubMed:23415227).

Overall Phase Separation Overview: ERα (P03372) is predominantly nuclear-localized and associates with transcriptional condensates, nuclear speckles, and TiPARP nuclear bodies (PubMed:32482854, 33850322, 30449618, 30833784). It exhibits context-dependent phase separation behavior: primarily recruited to heterotypic condensates formed by partners like TiPARP, SRC-1, or MED1 (PubMed:32482854, 33850322, 30449618), though one study demonstrates autonomous, ligand-induced self-assembly into liquid-like condensates (PubMed:30833784). Material states range from dynamic liquids to hydrogels, with pathological liquid-to-gel transitions observed under chronic estrogen stimulation (PubMed:30833784).
Functional Summary: ERα condensates regulate estrogen-dependent transcription: 1) Recruitment to TiPARP bodies enables ubiquitination and degradation, suppressing tumor growth (PubMed:32482854), 2) Co-condensation with SRC-1 or MED1 activates estrogen-responsive genes (PubMed:33850322, 30449618), and 3) Acute self-assembly facilitates MegaTrans complex formation for enhancer activation and chromosomal looping (PubMed:30833784). Pathological liquid-to-gel transitions under chronic estrogen stimulation reduce transcriptional competence, potentially contributing to disease (PubMed:30833784).
Intrinsic Determinants & Regulations: Phase separation is intrinsically regulated by ERα's intrinsically disordered region (IDR), enabling autonomous condensate formation (PubMed:30833784). The ligand-binding domain conformationally changes upon estrogen binding, promoting heterotypic interactions with partners like MED1 (PubMed:30449618). No disease-associated mutations directly modulating phase separation were reported.
Extrinsic Partners & Regulations: ERα phase separation is extrinsically modulated by multiple partners: 1) TiPARP scaffolds recruitment to nuclear bodies (PubMed:32482854), 2) SRC-1 enables pathway-specific co-phase separation upon estrogen activation (PubMed:33850322), 3) MED1 forms heterotypic droplets enhanced by β-estradiol (PubMed:30449618), and 4) GATA3 co-assembles into shared condensates while TFF1e eRNA accelerates droplet fluidity (PubMed:30833784). Estrogen universally promotes these interactions.

Organism: Human respiratory syncytial virus A (strain A2)
Overall Phase Separation Overview: The N protein (P03418) undergoes partner-dependent phase separation (class: PS-other) requiring the P protein and RNA to form dynamic, liquid-like cytoplasmic inclusion bodies (IBs) or viral factories (PubMed:38072230, 37210029, 32963000, 37762166). It transitions from an aggregated state to liquid condensates when complexed with P and RNA, exhibiting reversible behavior sensitive to stoichiometric balances and environmental conditions (PubMed:37210029).
Functional Summary: N-P phase separation scaffolds viral factories (IBs) that compartmentalize viral RNA synthesis and replication (PubMed:37210029, 32963000, 37762166). These condensates recruit cellular proteins like PABP to activate viral mRNA (PubMed:38072230). Dysregulation—such as cyclopamine-induced hardening when M2-1 is present—disrupts liquid dynamics and inhibits replication, highlighting the critical role of condensate fluidity in viral pathogenesis (PubMed:37762166).
Intrinsic Determinants & Regulations: Phase separation is intrinsically regulated by N's oligomerization domains (N-/C-arms), which enable RNA binding essential for forming functional decameric rings (NRNA complexes). Mutations disrupting RNA binding (e.g., K170A/R185A) abolish phase separation competence, while RNA-bound oligomeric states are critical for scaffold formation (PubMed:32963000, 37210029).
Extrinsic Partners & Regulations: N requires extrinsic partners for phase separation: the P protein acts as a co-scaffold for heterotypic LLPS and rescues NRNA aggregates into condensates (PubMed:37210029, 32963000, 37762166); host RNA (~70nt) prevents irreversible aggregation and enables NRNA complex formation (PubMed:37210029, 32963000). Crowding agents (e.g., Ficoll ≥5%) facilitate in vitro condensation (PubMed:32963000), while cyclopamine reduces protein mobility within condensates (PubMed:37762166).

Overall Phase Separation Overview: NPM1 undergoes phase separation primarily through heterotypic interactions (PS-other class) and localizes to the granular component of the nucleolus in the nucleus (PubMed:35607824, 37943867, 31399547, 27212236). It forms liquid-like condensates that exhibit rapid fusion dynamics and complete FRAP recovery under physiological conditions (PubMed:27212236). These condensates can undergo material state transitions: actinomycin D treatment reduces granular component area (PubMed:35607824), while light-induced oligomerization via Cry2olig fusion triggers a liquid-to-gel transition that hinders molecular mobility and prevents coalescence (PubMed:31399547). NPM1-rich phases are immiscible with FIB1-rich dense fibrillar components, forming core-shell structures (PubMed:27212236).
Functional Summary: NPM1 phase separation facilitates ribosome assembly by concentrating ribosomal proteins and pre-ribosomal particles in the granular component, with low-viscosity liquid properties enabling dynamic exchange during rRNA processing (PubMed:27212236, 35607824). Disruption through actinomycin D halts ribosome biogenesis, correlating with reduced condensate area (PubMed:35607824). Pathological gelation transitions disrupt rRNA processing flux, causing toxic accumulation of early precursors and depletion of mature intermediates (PubMed:31399547). Engineered binding to dense fibrillar component proteins can override normal compartmentalization rules, demonstrating functional plasticity (PubMed:37943867).
Intrinsic Determinants & Regulations: Phase separation is intrinsically driven by the N-terminal oligomerization domain (OD) enabling pentamerization and the C-terminal RNA recognition motif (RRM) for rRNA binding, with both domains required for condensate formation (PubMed:27212236). Oligomerization through the OD creates radial interaction networks critical for phase separation, as deletion of either OD or RRM domains abolishes nucleolar localization and condensate formation (PubMed:27212236, 31399547). Light-induced oligomerization via Cry2olig fusion further demonstrates that enforced oligomerization drives pathological gelation (PubMed:31399547).
Extrinsic Partners & Regulations: NPM1 phase separation is extrinsically regulated by rRNA, which acts as an essential scaffold enabling condensation at physiological concentrations (PubMed:27212236). It forms immiscible phases with the dense fibrillar component protein FIB1, resulting in core-shell organization through differential surface tension (PubMed:27212236). Environmental conditions significantly modulate behavior: actinomycin D reduces condensate area by halting rRNA synthesis (PubMed:35607824), while blue light activation of opto-NPM1 triggers gelation (PubMed:31399547). NPM1 also interacts with ribosomal assembly partners including Pes1, Gtpbp4, Ncl, and Npm3 within the granular component (PubMed:35607824).

Overall Phase Separation Overview: Vasa (P09052) undergoes self-driven phase separation in vitro, forming liquid-like condensates through its N-terminal intrinsically disordered region (PubMed:37980572). In vivo, it is recruited into phase-separated condensates within germ granules (cytoplasmic and nuclear) and nuage granules, primarily localized in the cytoplasm and nucleus (PubMed:37384531, 25842866, 30260314). These condensates exhibit liquid-like properties, characterized by rapid molecular exchange (FRAP recovery half-time ~5 seconds in spermatocyte piNG-bodies) and hydrogel-like stability in nuclear granules (PubMed:25842866, 30260314). While Vasa can nucleate cytoplasmic condensates independently in somatic cells (PubMed:30260314), its enrichment in germ granules depends on Oskar-mediated recruitment (PubMed:37384531, 30260314). No material state transitions (e.g., liquid-to-solid) were explicitly reported under studied conditions (PubMed:37384531, 25842866, 30260314).
Functional Summary: Vasa phase separation is physiologically essential for germline development. As a core component of germ granules, it enables primordial germ cell formation, embryonic patterning, and germ cell fate determination (PubMed:37384531, 30260314). In nuage granules, Vasa condensates maintain structural integrity for piRNA-dependent silencing of transposable elements (e.g., retrotransposons) and repetitive genomic elements (e.g., Stellate repeats), ensuring genomic stability (PubMed:25842866). Pathologically, impaired Vasa expression disrupts nuage granule integrity, causing transposon mobilization and repeat overexpression, which compromises germline function (PubMed:25842866).
Intrinsic Determinants & Regulations: Phase separation of Vasa is intrinsically driven by its N-terminal intrinsically disordered region (IDR), which is sufficient to form Ca²⁺-responsive condensates in vitro (PubMed:37980572). When expressed alone in somatic cells, full-length Vasa self-assembles into cytoplasmic condensates, confirming intrinsic phase separation capability (PubMed:30260314). No specific domains, mutations, or post-translational modifications regulating phase separation were detailed in the provided studies (PubMed:37384531, 25842866, 30260314, 37980572).
Extrinsic Partners & Regulations: Vasa phase separation is extrinsically regulated by Oskar, which recruits Vasa into cytoplasmic and nuclear germ granules (PubMed:37384531, 30260314). In nuage granules, Vasa serves as a scaffold for partner proteins including Aubergine, AGO3, Spindle-E, Armitage, Tudor, Krimper, and Tejas, though their recruitment dependence on Vasa was inferred from prior knowledge (PubMed:25842866). The ion Ca²⁺ promotes phase separation of the Vasa N-terminal IDR in vitro (PubMed:37980572). While germ granule mRNAs are not required for Vasa enrichment in granules (PubMed:37384531), RNAs are hypothesized targets within nuage granules (PubMed:25842866).

Overall Phase Separation Overview: Nucleolin (NCL) undergoes phase separation primarily within the nucleolus, localizing to both the dense fibrillar component (DFC) and granular component (GC) (PubMed:34331666, 36727534, 38341436, 32101700, 34515347). Its phase separation is RNA-dependent and requires partners like LIN28A for proper condensate formation (PubMed:34331666, 38341436). NCL exhibits liquid-like properties in undifferentiated cells, evidenced by FRAP recovery and preferential internal mixing (PubMed:32101700, 34331666, 36727534). However, during cellular differentiation or under stress, it undergoes material state transitions to solid-like or hydrogel states, correlating with altered nucleolar morphology (PubMed:36727534, 38341436).
Functional Summary: NCL phase separation maintains nucleolar integrity for ribosomal subunit assembly and ribosome biogenesis, with condensate reorganization during myogenesis correlating with increased rRNA production and translational capacity (PubMed:34331666, 36727534, 38341436). Disruption via rRNA inhibition, LIN28A dysfunction, or GAR domain deletion causes nucleolar disassembly ('caps', scattering, or fragmentation), leading to ribosomal protein mislocalization and reduced translation (PubMed:34331666, 38341436, 34515347). mTOR-dependent condensate reorganization is essential for cellular differentiation efficiency (PubMed:36727534).
Intrinsic Determinants & Regulations: NCL phase separation is intrinsically regulated by its RNA recognition motifs (RRMs), which dominate LLPS-dependent nucleolar stability, and its glycine-arginine-rich (GAR) domain (amino acids 646-697), which facilitates nucleolar partitioning (PubMed:34515347). Deletion of the GAR domain (ΔGAR) reduces nucleolar accumulation by ~50% but does not abolish phase separation capacity, indicating the RRMs' primary role in condensate maintenance (PubMed:34515347).
Extrinsic Partners & Regulations: NCL phase separation requires rRNA as an essential scaffold, with rRNA availability directly modulating condensate formation and stability (PubMed:34331666, 36727534, 38341436). It co-phase separates with LIN28A, which promotes NCL's incorporation into DFC ring-like condensates; LIN28A mutations or truncations disrupt NCL's nucleolar organization (PubMed:34331666, 38341436). Hypoosmotic stress rapidly dissolves NCL condensates (>50% reduction within 2 minutes), demonstrating environmental sensitivity (PubMed:34515347).

Overall Phase Separation Overview: PARP1 undergoes DNA-dependent phase separation, forming biomolecular condensates primarily in the nucleus (PubMed:36092926, 38320550, 37851801, 34083132). Its phase separation requires partner molecules like damaged DNA and is classified as PS-other, indicating non-self-driven assembly (PubMed:39496836, 38320550). PARP1 associates with DNA damage foci, chromocenters, and transcriptional condensates (PubMed:36092926, 38320550, 37851801). The material state transitions from solid-like (viscous, limited FRAP recovery) to liquid-like (complete FRAP recovery, fusion) upon autoPARylation (PubMed:39496836). Re-entrant phase behavior occurs at high DNA concentrations (PubMed:39496836).
Functional Summary: Physiologically, PARP1 condensates organize DNA repair by bridging broken ends, concentrating repair factors (XRCC1/LIG3), and enhancing ligation efficiency (PubMed:39496836, 38320550). They facilitate transcriptional elongation in biomolecular condensates and regulate stress responses via FUS recruitment (PubMed:37851801, 26317470). Pathologically, PARP1 trapping in condensates by inhibitors (e.g., olaparib) causes synthetic lethality in cancer, while KAT6A-mediated sequestration promotes PARP inhibitor resistance in ovarian cancer (PubMed:38320550, 38973255). Dysregulated liquid-to-solid transitions of PARP1-recruited partners (e.g., FUS) are linked to neurodegenerative diseases like ALS (PubMed:26317470). PARylation also globally halts transcription during DNA damage by dissolving CycT1 condensates (PubMed:35393539).
Intrinsic Determinants & Regulations: Phase separation is intrinsically driven by PARP1's zinc finger (ZnF) domains (residues 1-378), which are essential for DNA binding and condensation (PubMed:39496836, 38320550). AutoPARylation enhances condensation proportionally to PAR chain length and increases condensate fluidity (PubMed:39496836). Key mutations impair phase behavior: E988Q (PARylation-deficient) prevents NAD⁺-induced decondensation, caspase-3 cleavage abolishes condensation, and ZnF truncations (e.g., ΔZnF1, ΔZnF3) disrupt co-condensation with DNA (PubMed:39496836, 38320550). DNA-driven multimerization through stereospecific binding to free ends is critical for assembly (PubMed:38320550).
Extrinsic Partners & Regulations: Damaged DNA is an essential scaffold for condensation, with length/structure-dependent promotion and re-entrant behavior at high concentrations (PubMed:39496836, 38320550). PAR chains enhance condensation dynamics and recruit partners like FUS, which stabilizes condensates against dissolution (PubMed:39496836, 38320550, 26317470). Key protein partners include FUS (recruited via PAR binding), XRCC1/LIG3 (form multiphase repair condensates), CycT1 (PARylation disrupts its phase separation), KAT6A (co-phase separates to sequester PARP1), and transcriptional machinery (e.g., POLR2A, NONO) (PubMed:39496836, 35393539, 38973255, 37851801). Chemical regulators include NAD⁺ (dissolves condensates via PARylation) and PARP inhibitors (e.g., olaparib) that trap PARP1 in condensates (PubMed:38320550, 39496836).

Overall Phase Separation Overview: Tau (P10637) undergoes phase separation to form liquid-like condensates primarily in the cytoplasm, as observed in induced neural stem cells (iNSCs) and neurons (PubMed:37060562, 37949856). These condensates manifest as dynamic, transient nanoclusters in presynapses and larger clusters in axons, with properties sensitive to 1,6-hexanediol and activity-dependent regulation (PubMed:37949856). Tau also forms developmentally regulated, Triton X-100-resistant puncta along microtubules in neurons (PubMed:31481790). While typically liquid, Tau aggregates recruit nuclear speckle components like SRRM2 in pathological conditions (PubMed:33848474).
Functional Summary: Physiologically, Tau condensates regulate synaptic vesicle mobility and presynaptic organization in an activity-dependent manner (PubMed:37949856) and facilitate transdifferentiation by reactivating the IkB-NF-κB-CCND1 axis (PubMed:37060562). Pathologically, Tau aggregates recruit nuclear speckle components (PubMed:33848474), while dysregulated condensates contribute to synaptic defects in tauopathies (PubMed:37949856). Tau ubiquitination within TRIAD3A condensates promotes autophagic degradation (PubMed:39009640).
Intrinsic Determinants & Regulations: Tau phase separation is intrinsically regulated by its intrinsically disordered region (IDR) and microtubule-binding region (MTBR) (PubMed:37060562, 37949856). The MTBR is essential, as mutations (I277P/I308P) reduce LLPS propensity, and truncation (ΔTau74) abolishes condensate formation (PubMed:37949856). Activity-dependent phosphorylation modulates Tau mobility and presynaptic redistribution, while dephosphorylation enhances condensate stability (PubMed:37949856).
Extrinsic Partners & Regulations: Tau co-localizes with SRRM2 in cytosolic aggregates in tauopathy models (PubMed:33848474). Additionally, Tau partitions into TRIAD3A condensates where it undergoes ubiquitination, indicating regulation by TRIAD3A-mediated phase separation (PubMed:39009640).

Overall Phase Separation Overview: Ape1 undergoes self-driven liquid-liquid phase separation (LLPS) to form biomolecular condensates in the cytoplasm (PubMed:36217212, 31995729, 39774270). These condensates exhibit liquid-like properties including reversibility, fusion capability, and sensitivity to 1,6-hexanediol (PubMed:31995729, 36217212). They associate primarily with pre-autophagosomal structures (PAS), serving as scaffolds for PAS formation during selective autophagy (PubMed:36217212). Temperature critically regulates LLPS: droplets form at ≤33°C but reversibly disassemble at 40°C (PubMed:36217212). Over time or due to mutations (e.g., P22L), liquid condensates undergo pathological transitions to solid states with impaired dynamics (PubMed:31995729).
Functional Summary: Ape1 condensates are essential for the Cvt pathway, scaffolding PAS assembly to deliver cargo to vacuoles via selective autophagy (PubMed:36217212, 31995729). Liquidity enables efficient membrane sequestration, while solidification (via aging or P22L mutation) impairs degradation and disrupts cellular homeostasis (PubMed:31995729). Temperature-sensitive disassembly halts vacuolar transport, linking LLPS regulation to proteostasis (PubMed:36217212). Aberrant phase transitions contribute to cytotoxicity, with implications for proteinopathy diseases (PubMed:31995729). Ape1 also participates in osmotic shock foci formation during hyperosmotic stress response (PubMed:31285266).
Intrinsic Determinants & Regulations: Phase separation is intrinsically driven by the N-terminal propeptide, which mediates trimerization of Ape1 dodecamers to enable higher-order assembly (PubMed:31995729). Full-length Ape1 is sufficient for LLPS, but C-terminal GFP tagging reduces thermostability (PubMed:36217212). The P22L mutation induces irreversible liquid-to-solid transitions by enhancing propeptide interactions, while L11S prevents assembly entirely (PubMed:31995729). Oligomerization through dodecamer formation is essential for phase separation (PubMed:39774270). K12R mutation does not alter LLPS behavior (PubMed:36217212).
