Intrinsic Determinants & Regulations: Phase separation of Shank3 is intrinsically driven by its Proline-Rich Motif (PRM), which mediates binding to IRSp53 via SH3 domain interactions (PubMed:35819332). Deletion of the PRM region (ΔPRM) abolishes phase separation capacity, demonstrating its essential role. Additionally, its Homer-Binding Sequence (HBS) enables critical interactions with Homer1 during PSD condensate assembly (PubMed:37318128).
Extrinsic Partners & Regulations: Shank3 co-phase separates with IRSp53 via SH3-PRM interactions, forming essential scaffold complexes (PubMed:35819332). It also integrates into core PSD condensates with GKAP and Homer1, where this tripartite assembly directly enables actin bundling (PubMed:37318128). The splice isoform Homer1a acts as a dominant-negative regulator, dispersing pre-formed Shank3-containing condensates and destabilizing associated actin bundles (PubMed:37318128).

Overall Phase Separation Overview: DEPS-1 undergoes phase separation as a scaffold protein essential for germ granule organization in Caenorhabditis elegans cytoplasm. It forms dynamic, perinuclear condensates within P granules (PubMed:36750365, 32843637) and Z compartments (PubMed:39354132), requiring partner interactions rather than self-assembly (class: PS-other). Its material state exhibits liquid-like behavior with dynamic ~250 nm clusters that intertwine with partners under molecular crowding conditions, though no material state transitions are reported (PubMed:32843637).
Functional Summary: DEPS-1 phase separation organizes germ granules for small RNA regulation, enabling piRNA-dependent silencing and secondary endo-siRNA production against targets. It bridges P granules and mutator foci, with disruption causing malformed granules, PRG-1 mislocalization, and desilencing of piRNA sensors (PubMed:36750365, 32843637). Dysregulation through HERD-1 loss extends transgenerational epigenetic inheritance by disorganizing RNA pathways and promoting pathological compartment mixing (PubMed:39354132).
Intrinsic Determinants & Regulations: Phase separation is intrinsically regulated by DEPS-1's PIWI Binding Site (PBS) motif, which mediates direct interaction with PRG-1. Deletion of this motif disrupts condensate formation, leading to cytoplasmic diffusion and loss of elongated granule morphology (PubMed:32843637).
Extrinsic Partners & Regulations: DEPS-1's phase separation is extrinsically modulated by multiple partners: it forms intertwining clusters with PRG-1 via PBS-mediated binding (PubMed:32843637), associates with EDG-1 which regulates condensate size (enlargement upon EDG-1 knockdown) (PubMed:32843637), and interacts with HERD-1 which limits DEPS-1's valence for cross-compartment binding. Loss of HERD-1 enhances DEPS-1 interaction with GLH-1, causing aberrant mixing of germ granule compartments (PubMed:39354132).

Overall Phase Separation Overview: DDX21 undergoes self-driven phase separation (PubMed:37029300, 34326237) primarily in the nucleus, where it associates with nucleoli, nuclear speckles (PubMed:37979585), and virus-modified paraspeckles during viral infection (PubMed:39592606). It forms condensates exhibiting liquid-like properties in vitro and in colorectal cancer cells (PubMed:37029300, 37979585) and gel-like states when coating nucleolar subcompartments (PubMed:34326237). DDX21 undergoes material state transitions, including a SLERT RNA-induced gel-to-liquid transition that modulates condensate dynamics (PubMed:34326237).
Functional Summary: DDX21 phase separation regulates ribosome biogenesis by controlling fibrillar center/dense fibrillar component (FC/DFC) liquidity and size in nucleoli, influencing Pol I transcription (PubMed:34326237, 37979585). Its condensates promote colorectal cancer metastasis via EMT pathway activation through MCM5 upregulation (PubMed:37029300). During viral infection, DDX21 recruitment to virus-modified paraspeckles supports viral RNA processing (PubMed:39592606). Dysregulation—including dense cluster formation suppressing transcription, SAMHD1-deficiency impairing nucleolar enrichment (PubMed:36150385), or pathological mutations—contributes to nucleolar dysfunction and disease (PubMed:37979585, 34326237).
Intrinsic Determinants & Regulations: Phase separation is intrinsically driven by the N-terminal intrinsically disordered region (IDR; aa 1-182) (PubMed:37029300) and involves both N-terminal (aa 1-300) and C-terminal domains (aa 600-783), while the helicase core domain (aa 301-599) inhibits separation (PubMed:37979585). Oligomerization via the N-terminus is critical (PubMed:37979585), with multivalent N/C-terminal IDR interactions enabling clustering (PubMed:34326237). Key regulatory features include: phosphorylation by CK2 modulating separation propensity (PubMed:37979585); RGG motif mutations (e.g., R681A/R685A) reducing phase separation (PubMed:37979585); acidic IDR mutations (E/D→A) disrupting condensation (PubMed:37029300); and disease-associated conformational mutants (e.g., DDX21_DAT) promoting dense clustering through augmented intermolecular interactions (PubMed:34326237).
Extrinsic Partners & Regulations: RNA partners including rRNA, snoRNA (PubMed:37979585) and SLERT lncRNA regulate DDX21 condensation, with SLERT binding RecA domains to induce hypomultimerization and phase transitions (PubMed:34326237). DDX21 interacts with fibrillarin (FBL) in core-shell nucleolar structures (PubMed:34326237) and participates in virus-modified paraspeckles through association with SFPQ, NONO, NEAT1 RNA, viral ORF11, and RNA processing factors like hnRNP U and DDX17 (PubMed:39592606).

MLO Types: Nuclear speckle; p62 cluster; PML nuclear body
Overall Phase Separation Overview: DAXX (Q9UER7) undergoes self-driven phase separation via its C-terminal intrinsically disordered region (IDR), forming liquid-like condensates in vitro (PubMed:30244836, 31845799), but frequently requires partners for phase separation in cellular contexts (PubMed:35809564, 35194189, 36822200, 31434890). It localizes to the nucleus and cytoplasm (PubMed:36822200, 31434890) and associates with PML nuclear bodies, SPOP/DAXX bodies, and p62 bodies (PubMed:35809564, 35194189, 30244836, 31434890, 36822200). Condensates exhibit liquid-like properties (PubMed:36822200, 30244836), though complexes with SPOP transition from gel-like to liquid-like states depending on DAXX concentration (PubMed:31845799). The R318* truncation mutation impairs phase separation (PubMed:35809564).
Functional Summary: DAXX phase separation enables ubiquitination and degradation via SPOP co-condensation, with disruption leading to DAXX accumulation and cancer pathogenesis (PubMed:30244836, 31845799). In cytoplasm, p62 co-condensation regulates redox homeostasis by sequestering Keap1 and activating Nrf2-mediated stress responses (PubMed:31434890). Pathologically, HRE DNA-enhanced phase separation drives epigenetic silencing of the C9orf72 promoter via chromatin remodeling, contributing to motor neuron degeneration in ALS/FTD (PubMed:36822200). Dysregulation in transcriptional condensates is implicated in cancer (PubMed:35809564).
Intrinsic Determinants & Regulations: Phase separation is intrinsically driven by DAXX's C-terminal IDR, where oppositely charged blocks enable homotypic assembly (PubMed:30244836, 31845799). This region contains five SPOP-binding motifs (SB motifs) critical for heterotypic phase separation (PubMed:30244836, 31845799) and a distinct segment (182-230aa) that mediates p62 interactions (PubMed:31434890). The R318* truncation mutation reduces condensate partitioning by removing interaction domains (PubMed:35809564), while the C9orf72 HRE DNA-binding capacity enhances phase separation valency (PubMed:36822200).
Extrinsic Partners & Regulations: DAXX phase separation is extrinsically modulated by partners: SPOP triggers gel-like or liquid-like co-assemblies depending on DAXX stoichiometry (PubMed:30244836, 31845799); p62 acts as a scaffold for co-phase separation, with DAXX driving p62 condensation (PubMed:31434890); and C9orf72 hexanucleotide repeat expansion (HRE) DNA promotes phase separation in a repeat-length-dependent manner (PubMed:36822200). DAXX is recruited to PML bodies via SUMO-SIM interactions (PubMed:35194189) and recruits epigenetic regulators (ATRX, SUV39H1, HDAC1) into condensates (PubMed:36822200).

Overall Phase Separation Overview: AGO2 undergoes partner-dependent phase separation primarily in the cytoplasm, forming liquid-like condensates associated with multiple membrane-less organelles including endoplasmic reticulum (ER)-associated condensates, RNA-processing bodies (P-bodies), and stress granules (PubMed:35325613, 29576456, 40056914). Under hyperosmotic stress, it co-assembles into non-canonical condensates distinct from P-bodies or stress granules (PubMed:32857953). These condensates exhibit liquid-like properties with fusion/fission events but reduced molecular mobility in cellular contexts (PubMed:35325613, 29576456), and material state transitions are not explicitly reported across studies.
Functional Summary: AGO2 phase separation enables mRNA regulation through compartmentalized activities: In ER condensates, it recruits Ltn1 to ubiquitinate nascent peptides of membrane/secretory proteins, linking miRNA silencing to ribosome quality control (PubMed:35325613). In P-bodies, condensation with TNRC6B sequesters target mRNAs and concentrates deadenylation machinery (CCR4-NOT), accelerating decay >100-fold (PubMed:29576456). Pathologically, amyloid beta oligomers enhance phase separation, contributing to miRNA dysfunction in Alzheimer's disease, while HuR-mediated inhibition restores regulatory activity (PubMed:40056914).
Intrinsic Determinants & Regulations: Phase separation is intrinsically driven by three conserved domains: 1) The N-terminal LBM1 motif essential for lipid-mediated condensation on the ER, where ΔLBM1 mutation abolishes phase separation (PubMed:35325613); 2) The PIWI domain containing tryptophan-binding pockets (P590/R688) that enable multivalent interactions with TNRC6B in P-bodies, with pocket mutations impairing droplet formation (PubMed:29576456); and 3) The miRNA-binding domain critical for ATP-dependent P-body targeting, where Y529E mutation reduces condensation (PubMed:40056914).
Extrinsic Partners & Regulations: Phase separation is extrinsically regulated by diverse partners and conditions: 1) Lipid scaffolds (PI(4,5)P2) drive ER membrane condensation (PubMed:35325613); 2) Protein partners include TNRC6B (reciprocal driver in P-bodies via GW-PIWI interactions), Ltn1 (co-assembles in ER condensates), and DCP1A (co-condenses during hyperosmotic stress) (PubMed:29576456, 35325613, 32857953); 3) RNA (miRNA targets) is sequestered within condensates (PubMed:29576456); 4) Physicochemical factors modulate behavior—ATP dependence, osmolarity, viscosity, and salt concentration affect P-body targeting, while amyloid beta oligomers enhance condensation (PubMed:40056914); and 5) The RNA-binder HuR inhibits phase separation by sequestering miRNAs (PubMed:40056914).

Overall Phase Separation Overview: IGF2BP2 undergoes RNA-nucleated phase separation in the cytoplasm, forming condensates scaffolded by circHIPK3 (PubMed:39041323) or facilitated by TRIM15-mediated ubiquitination (PubMed:38657551). These condensates exhibit liquid-like properties including fusion and rapid fluorescence recovery (PubMed:38657551). IGF2BP2 associates with stress granules, where it co-clusters with homologous IGF2BP proteins during osmotic stress responses (PubMed:32668274).
Functional Summary: Phase separation enables circHIPK3-mediated sequestration of IGF2BP2, facilitating competing endogenous RNA (ceRNA) function to regulate mRNA stability of targets like STAT3 despite stoichiometric imbalance (PubMed:39041323). In pancreatic cancer, condensate formation concentrates IGF2BP2 to enhance m6A reader activity, stabilizing TLR4 mRNA and promoting tumor progression (PubMed:38657551). IGF2BP2 also contributes to stress granule initiation during osmotic stress by forming early mRNA-associated clusters that recruit core components like G3BP1 and TIA1 (PubMed:32668274).
Intrinsic Determinants & Regulations: Phase separation is intrinsically regulated by predicted disordered low-complexity domains and K63-linked ubiquitination at lysine residues K462 and K487 (PubMed:38657551). Mutations at these sites (K462R, K487R) significantly impair phase separation and disrupt functional outcomes (PubMed:38657551).
Extrinsic Partners & Regulations: Essential extrinsic regulators include the RNA circHIPK3, which nucleates condensate formation as a stoichiometric scaffold (PubMed:39041323), and TRIM15, which mediates K63 ubiquitination to promote phase separation (PubMed:38657551). K63 polyubiquitin chains directly induce phase separation in vitro (PubMed:38657551). During stress granule assembly, IGF2BP2 co-clusters with IGF2BP1/IGF2BP3 and associates with poly(A) mRNA (PubMed:32668274).

Overall Phase Separation Overview: RNase E (A0A290MSE1) undergoes self-driven phase separation to form liquid-like biomolecular condensates (BR-bodies) in the cytoplasm (PubMed:37558691, 38865176). It serves as a scaffold and driver component of BR-bodies, with phase separation being RNA-dependent and sensitive to phosphate and magnesium ion concentrations (PubMed:37558691, 37815915). No material state transitions were reported across studies (PubMed:37558691, 37815915, 38865176).
Functional Summary: Phase separation organizes the mRNA decay machinery within BR-bodies, enhancing PNPase ribonuclease activity 3.4-fold and altering substrate specificity toward poly(A) RNA (PubMed:37558691, 37815915). Crucially, condensation accelerates cleavage of RNase E's own 5' UTR RNA, enabling precise autoregulation of protein levels that optimizes global mRNA decay and cellular fitness; dysregulation causes severe growth defects (PubMed:38865176). This process couples nutrient availability (phosphate) to decay efficiency, providing a regulatory mechanism for stress adaptation (PubMed:37558691, 38865176).
Intrinsic Determinants & Regulations: Phase separation is intrinsically driven by the C-terminal domain (CTD, residues 451-898), particularly its intrinsically disordered region (IDR) with charged blocks that mediate multivalent interactions (PubMed:37558691, 37815915, 38865176). The CTD alone is sufficient for condensation (PubMed:37558691). Deletion of the entire IDR (ΔIDR) abolishes phase separation (PubMed:38865176), while a C-terminal truncation (∆PNP-BS) preserves homotypic condensation but disrupts client recruitment (PubMed:37558691).
Extrinsic Partners & Regulations: Phase separation requires RNA scaffolds, including long unstructured RNAs, total cellular RNA, and the 5' UTR RNA, which lower the saturation concentration and accelerate condensation kinetics (PubMed:37558691, 37815915, 38865176). Key modulators include: 1) PNPase recruitment via specific protein-protein interactions that enhance enzymatic activity (PubMed:37558691); 2) Ribosomal protein S1 and MetK, which dissolve condensates through RNA competition and direct binding respectively (PubMed:37815915); and 3) Ions, where phosphate (≥6 mM) disrupts condensation by competing with multivalent interactions, while magnesium (≤12 mM) is required for stability (PubMed:37558691).

Overall Phase Separation Overview: EML4-ALK undergoes self-driven phase separation to form cytoplasmic condensates, with material properties varying by variant: variant 1 (V1) forms static, solid-like foci resistant to 1,6-hexanediol, while variant 3 (V3) forms dynamic, liquid-like droplets capable of fusion and exhibiting partial fluorescence recovery in FRAP assays (PubMed:38284990, 33976114, 34661367). These condensates occur exclusively in the cytoplasm across human cancer cell lines, murine tumors, and tumor-derived organoids, with no association to canonical membrane-less organelles (PubMed:38284990, 33976114, 34661367). No material state transitions were reported.
Functional Summary: Phase separation hyperactivates JAK-STAT, RAS/MAPK, and PI3K/AKT pathways, driving malignant transformation, tumorigenesis, and adeno-to-squamous transition (AST) in lung adenocarcinoma (PubMed:38284990, 33976114). AST confers resistance to ALK inhibitors (lorlatinib), reversible via JAK1/2 inhibition (ruxolitinib) (PubMed:38284990). V1 solid foci act as persistent signaling hubs associated with disease resilience, while V3 liquid foci correlate with aggressive NSCLC progression (PubMed:34661367). Disruption via 21S mutation or conformational inhibitors impairs signaling, proliferation, and tumor growth (PubMed:33976114, 34661367).
Intrinsic Determinants & Regulations: Phase separation is intrinsically driven by aromatic residues (tyrosine/phenylalanine) within the EML4 N-terminal domain (exon 1-13), with the 21S mutation (aromatic→serine) abolishing condensate formation (PubMed:38284990, 33976114). For V1, the partial TAPE domain (blades 12N/5) stabilizes solid-like foci, while EML4 trimerization domains enable oligomerization (PubMed:34661367). For V3, ALK kinase domain dimerization drives cross-linking, with conformation-sensitive mutations (K1150M, F1174L, R1275Q) modulating foci assembly (PubMed:34661367). The L1196M mutation enhances cytoplasmic phase separation but does not alter material state (PubMed:38284990, 33976114).
Extrinsic Partners & Regulations: Condensates recruit signaling partners including GRB2, SOS1, pPLCγ2(Y759), PI3K p85β, pC-KIT(Y721), and phosphorylated STAT3, which co-localize within foci to amplify oncogenic signaling (PubMed:33976114, 34661367). ALK inhibitors differentially modulate behavior: alectinib enhances foci formation in both variants, while ceritinib and lorlatinib dissolve V3 droplets and redirect protein to microtubules (PubMed:34661367). Phase separation is independent of ALK catalytic activity but requires active kinase conformation for V3 assembly (PubMed:33976114, 34661367).

Overall Phase Separation Overview: Polo-like kinase 4 (Plk4) undergoes self-driven phase separation via autophosphorylation of its cryptic polo-box (CPB) domain, forming nanoscale spherical condensates primarily in the cytoplasm at centrosomes (PubMed:31672968, 33323015). These condensates function as procentriole assembly matrices and exhibit liquid-like dynamics in cells, including fusion competence and fluorescence recovery after photobleaching (FRAP), but transition to gel/solid states in vitro or upon prolonged incubation (PubMed:31672968). Plk4 initially forms hollow spherical assemblies that undergo a transition to inside-filled condensates upon binding STIL, with size modulation occurring during the cell cycle (enlargement in G1, shrinkage in mitosis) (PubMed:33323015).
Functional Summary: Plk4 phase separation enables centriole biogenesis by forming symmetry-breaking condensates that recruit STIL and Sas6 to initiate procentriole assembly, while evading βTrCP-mediated degradation through clustering (PubMed:31672968, 33323015). Dysregulation causes pathological outcomes: condensation-proficient mutations (e.g., S698E/S700E/T704E/T707D) induce aberrant centriole amplification, elongated condensates, and genomic instability linked to cell viability defects (PubMed:31672968, 33323015).
Intrinsic Determinants & Regulations: Phase separation is intrinsically regulated by the cryptic polo-box (CPB) domain (residues 581-808), where autophosphorylation of the PC3 motif (S698, S700, T704, T707) exposes hydrophobic surfaces that drive condensation (PubMed:31672968, 33323015). Phospho-mimicking mutations (S698E/S700E/T704E/T707D) enhance phase separation and enable Cep152-independent assembly (PubMed:31672968, 33323015). Hydrophobic residues in the disordered PB2-tip loop (Y750, L752, V758, L761) are essential, as alanine substitutions abolish condensation (PubMed:31672968). Catalytically inactive mutations (K41M) disrupt spherical assembly formation (PubMed:33323015).
Extrinsic Partners & Regulations: Plk4 phase separation is extrinsically modulated by partner proteins. STIL binds Plk4 and converts hollow condensates into inside-filled assemblies competent for Sas6 recruitment, with full-length STIL required for maturation (PubMed:31672968, 33323015). Plk4 also partitions into Deup1-generated condensates, which spatially compartmentalize Plk4 in the cytoplasm (PubMed:33658185). Sas6 colocalizes with Plk4 in condensates but does not autonomously drive phase separation (PubMed:31672968, 33323015).

Overall Phase Separation Overview: FCA (O04425) undergoes self-driven phase separation via its prion-like domain to form liquid-like nuclear condensates (FCA bodies) in Arabidopsis thaliana (PubMed:31043738). These dynamic bodies exhibit liquid properties including fusion and rapid fluorescence recovery in vivo (PubMed:31043738). Formation occurs exclusively in the nucleus and depends on RNA scaffolds and regulatory partners (PubMed:35621186, 31043738). In heterologous yeast systems, the prion domain forms non-heritable aggregates but does not exhibit classical phase separation behavior (PubMed:27114519).
Functional Summary: FCA nuclear bodies compartmentalize 3'-end RNA processing factors to regulate proximal polyadenylation of target transcripts like COOLAIR, controlling flowering time in Arabidopsis (PubMed:35621186, 31043738). This process is functionally dependent on FLL2-mediated phase separation, as demonstrated by impaired polyadenylation and reduced nuclear bodies in the sof78 FLL2 mutant (PubMed:31043738). No pathological transitions were reported across studies.
Intrinsic Determinants & Regulations: Phase separation is intrinsically driven by FCA's prion-like domain (PrLD, residues 504-714), which is necessary and sufficient for autonomous liquid droplet formation in vitro (PubMed:31043738). A shorter prion domain fragment (residues 632-711) demonstrates inherent aggregation propensity, forming SDS-resistant oligomers and foci in yeast (PubMed:27114519). The RRM domain lacks phase separation capability (PubMed:31043738).
Extrinsic Partners & Regulations: FCA phase separation requires RNA scaffolds and protein partners. m6A-modified RNAs are essential scaffolds for nuclear body formation in vivo, with condensate formation impaired in m6A writer (fip37-4) and reader (ect2/3/4) mutants (PubMed:35621186). Arabidopsis total RNA enhances full-length FCA puncta formation in vitro (PubMed:31043738). The coiled-coil protein FLL2 acts as a critical co-phase separation partner, promoting nuclear body formation through direct partitioning interactions with FCA-PrLD in vitro and genetic dependency in vivo (PubMed:31043738).

Overall Phase Separation Overview: Dcp2 (O13828) does not undergo self-driven phase separation alone but requires partners like Pat1 or Edc3 to form liquid-like condensates in the cytoplasm (PubMed:32513655, 24862735, 33767388). It is a core component of P-bodies, where it associates through multivalent interactions (PubMed:24862735, 33767388). The condensates exhibit liquid properties, including droplet fusion and homogeneous distribution, though material properties can be altered by mutations like Y220G, which increases viscosity and induces substructures (PubMed:33767388). No explicit state transitions (e.g., liquid-to-solid) were reported.
Functional Summary: Phase separation clusters Dcp2 into P-bodies to regulate mRNA decay. Without Edc3, condensates repress decapping by stabilizing Dcp2's inactive conformation; Edc3 activates decapping 90-fold within condensates via conformational rewiring (PubMed:33767388). This compartmentalization enhances substrate binding and stress response (PubMed:24862735, 33767388). Dysregulation—such as the Y220G mutation—causes aberrant decapping activity and altered material properties, disrupting mRNA decay homeostasis (PubMed:33767388).
Intrinsic Determinants & Regulations: Phase separation is intrinsically regulated by Dcp2's C-terminal region, which contains helical leucine-rich motifs (HLMs) that mediate multivalent binding to partners (PubMed:32513655, 24862735). Valency is critical: constructs with five HLMs phase-separate at lower concentrations than those with four, while single-HLM mutants abolish phase separation (PubMed:24862735). Low-complexity regions (residues 274–504) are sufficient to drive condensation (PubMed:33767388). The Y220G mutation disrupts material properties, causing viscous condensates with impaired fusion and substructures (PubMed:33767388). Inhibitory motifs (IMs) also regulate phase behavior by stabilizing inactive conformations (PubMed:33767388).
Extrinsic Partners & Regulations: Dcp2's phase separation requires extrinsic scaffolds: Pat1 enables condensation via oligomerization-driven multivalent HLM interactions (PubMed:32513655), while Edc3 reduces the critical concentration 20-fold through dimerization-dependent binding to HLMs (PubMed:24862735, 33767388). Dcp1 is incorporated into condensates but disrupts phase separation when in excess by competing for intermolecular interactions (PubMed:33767388). Edc3 concentration modulates dynamics, slowing FRAP recovery at higher levels (PubMed:33767388). RNA is recruited into condensates but does not initiate phase separation (PubMed:33767388).

Overall Phase Separation Overview: DAXX undergoes partner-dependent phase separation rather than self-driven assembly, forming condensates in both the nucleus and cytoplasm (PubMed:35809564, 37926283, 36175410, 31434890). It associates with multiple membrane-less organelles including SPOP-DAXX nuclear bodies, PML nuclear bodies, and cytoplasmic p62 clusters (PubMed:37926283, 36175410, 31434890). These assemblies typically exhibit liquid-like material states, with no observed state transitions reported (PubMed:37926283, 31434890).
Functional Summary: DAXX-containing condensates serve as active compartments for SPOP-mediated ubiquitination, with dysregulation linked to endometrial/skin cancers (PubMed:37926283, 35809564). Within PML bodies, DAXX contributes to repression of transposable elements and stem cell state regulation (PubMed:36175410). Cytoplasmic DAXX-p62 condensates activate Nrf2-mediated stress responses, promoting cellular survival (PubMed:31434890).
Intrinsic Determinants & Regulations: DAXX phase separation is intrinsically regulated by its multivalent C-terminal region containing five SPOP-binding motifs that enable crosslinking (PubMed:37926283). The N-terminal domain is essential for promoting p62 oligomerization and phase separation (PubMed:31434890). A truncation mutation (R318*) disrupts condensate incorporation by removing critical interaction domains (PubMed:35809564).
Extrinsic Partners & Regulations: DAXX phase separation is extrinsically modulated by SPOP, forming co-condensates enhanced by SPOP interfacial mutations (R221C/R354H) despite weakened discrete binding (PubMed:37926283). It partitions into PML nuclear bodies induced by arsenic-mediated oxidative stress (PubMed:36175410). In the cytoplasm, DAXX drives p62 liquid phase condensation by inducing oligomerization (PubMed:31434890).

Protein Name: BUB3-interacting and GLEBS motif-containing protein ZNF207
Overall Phase Separation Overview: BuGZ (ZNF207) undergoes self-driven phase separation forming temperature-dependent liquid droplets in vitro (PubMed:26388440), but does not autonomously form condensates in centrosomal contexts, instead co-phase separating with Aurora-A (PubMed:38746663). It localizes to cytoplasm and nucleus, associating with centrosomes, spindle matrix, nuclear speckles, and splicing speckles (PubMed:38746663, 29973724, 26388440). Material states are liquid-like, demonstrated by droplet dynamics in vitro and in spindle matrices (PubMed:26388440, 29973724), with no observed state transitions reported.
Functional Summary: BuGZ enables centrosome maturation, separation, and microtubule nucleation by enhancing Aurora-A phase separation (PubMed:38746663). It is essential for spindle matrix assembly via phase separation, ensuring proper spindle microtubule organization and chromosome alignment (PubMed:26388440, 29973724). Pathological sequestration in mitotic granules upon DYRK3 inhibition disrupts spindle matrix assembly, causing mitotic defects (PubMed:29973724).
Intrinsic Determinants & Regulations: Phase separation is intrinsically driven by hydrophobic residues (Phe/Tyr) within its disordered low-complexity region, where mutation of 15 Phe/Tyr residues to serine (mBuGZ15S) disrupts phase transition and function (PubMed:26388440). Low-complexity regions are also critical for its phase behavior (PubMed:29973724).
Extrinsic Partners & Regulations: BuGZ co-phase separates with Aurora-A, enhancing Aurora-A's centrosomal phase separation via direct N-terminal binding (PubMed:38746663). Its mitotic behavior is regulated by DYRK3 kinase activity, which prevents sequestration in aberrant granules; inhibition of DYRK3 by GSK-626616 induces granule formation and co-localization with PABP (PubMed:29973724).

Protein Name: Cleavage and polyadenylation specificity factor subunit 5
Overall Phase Separation Overview: CPSF5 (O43809) does not autonomously undergo liquid-liquid phase separation (LLPS) but is recruited as a client protein into nuclear speckle condensates driven by CPSF6, forming CPSF5₂-CPSF6₂ tetramers (PubMed:37414787, 37777964). It localizes exclusively to the nucleus and associates with nuclear speckles (PubMed:37414787, 37777964). In vitro, CPSF5 co-phase separates with CPSF6 under macromolecular crowding conditions (10% PEG-4000/Ficoll-400), forming liquid-like condensates (PubMed:38762180). No material state transitions were reported.
Functional Summary: CPSF5-containing condensates are critical for productive wild-type HIV-1 infection; disruption reduces infectivity 33-fold (PubMed:37414787). As part of the CFIm complex within CPSF6 condensates, CPSF5 regulates alternative polyadenylation: condensate integrity promotes distal poly(A) site usage (longer 3' UTRs), particularly for cell-cycle genes like CCND2. Disrupted condensate formation in cancer cells shortens 3' UTRs, upregulates oncogenes, and accelerates proliferation (PubMed:37777964).
Intrinsic Determinants & Regulations: No intrinsic drivers for autonomous phase separation were identified, as CPSF5 lacks self-assembly capability (PubMed:37777964). Its recruitment into condensates is mediated entirely through heterotypic interactions with CPSF6, forming stable CPSF5₂-CPSF6₂ tetramers (PubMed:37414787, 37777964).
Extrinsic Partners & Regulations: CPSF6 is the essential scaffold for CPSF5 recruitment, with co-phase separation occurring in nuclear speckles (PubMed:37414787, 37777964). HIV-1 infection induces condensate formation (PubMed:37414787), while macromolecular crowding agents (10% PEG-4000/Ficoll-400) promote in vitro co-condensation (PubMed:38762180). CPSF5 recruitment is modulated by CLK2 kinase activity: hyperphosphorylation of CPSF6 disrupts condensates, whereas CLK2 inhibition (SM04690) enhances CPSF5 incorporation (PubMed:37777964).

Overall Phase Separation Overview: AKAP95 (O43823) undergoes self-driven phase separation to form dynamic, liquid-like condensates in vitro and in nuclear foci in vivo (PubMed:33235917, PubMed:32719551). These condensates associate with nuclear speckles and transcriptional condensates marked by Pol II Ser2 phosphorylation (PubMed:32719551). The wild-type protein exhibits liquid material properties characterized by rapid diffusion and fusion capabilities, but undergoes pathological liquid-to-solid transitions when tyrosine residues are mutated to phenylalanine (YF), resulting in reduced dynamics and slower diffusion (PubMed:33235917, PubMed:32719551).
Functional Summary: AKAP95 phase separation regulates splicing of cancer-related genes (e.g., CCNA2, SMAD6) and transcription of the hnRNPUL1-S isoform, promoting tumorigenesis in breast and ovarian cancers (PubMed:33235917, PubMed:38711442, PubMed:32719551). Liquid-like condensates support mRNA processing and suppress nonsense-mediated decay, enabling cell proliferation and oncogenic transformation (PubMed:32719551). Pathological solidification (YF mutation) or disruption (101-210 deletion) impairs splicing/transcriptional regulation, reduces tumor growth, and in ovarian cancer, diminishes PARP1 expression—thereby increasing sensitivity to PARP inhibitors like niraparib (PubMed:38711442, PubMed:32719551).
Intrinsic Determinants & Regulations: Phase separation is intrinsically driven by the intrinsically disordered region (IDR) spanning residues 101-210, which enables multivalent interactions (PubMed:33235917, PubMed:38711442, PubMed:32719551). Tyrosine residues within this region are critical regulators: mutation to alanine (YA) or serine (YS) abolishes condensation, while phenylalanine substitution (YF) enhances condensation propensity but promotes pathological liquid-to-solid transitions (PubMed:33235917, PubMed:32719551). Chimeric studies confirm that condensation capability—rather than domain specificity—is functionally essential (PubMed:33235917).
Extrinsic Partners & Regulations: Cellular RNA binds AKAP95's zinc finger domain and modulates condensate dynamics by restricting droplet mobility and fusion (PubMed:32719551). No other extrinsic regulators or co-phase separating partners were reported in the provided data.

Overall Phase Separation Overview: LSD1 (O60341) undergoes both self-driven and partner-dependent phase separation primarily in the nucleus (PubMed:36877164, 39523439, 38461301). It associates with distinct membrane-less organelles including super-enhancer condensates, chromatin sub-compartments (CSCs), and ALT telomeres (PubMed:36877164, 39523439, 38461301). Condensates typically exhibit liquid-like properties (droplet fusion, rapid FRAP recovery ~90%, dissolution by 1,6-hexanediol), but can undergo pathological transitions to solid states when induced by chemicals like N-methyl mesoporphyrin IX (NMM) (PubMed:36877164, 39523439, 38461301).
Functional Summary: LSD1 phase separation serves critical roles in transcriptional regulation and genome maintenance: 1) In super-enhancer condensates, it concentrates oncogenic transcription machinery (LSD1/FOXA1/BRD4) to drive castration-resistant prostate cancer, with disruption impairing tumor growth (PubMed:36877164); 2) In chromatin sub-compartments with NEK6, it enhances local histone demethylation rates ~10-fold for efficient gene silencing, where IDR deletion abolishes silencing activity (PubMed:39523439); 3) At ALT telomeres, TERRA-driven condensates enrich Rad51AP1 to promote R-loop formation and homology-directed repair essential for cancer cell viability, with nucleic acid-binding mutants disrupting telomere maintenance (PubMed:38461301). Pathologically, chemical disruption or liquid-to-solid transitions impair these functions across contexts (PubMed:36877164, 38461301).
Intrinsic Determinants & Regulations: The N-terminal intrinsically disordered region (IDR; aa 1-165) is the primary intrinsic driver of LSD1 phase separation, essential for condensate formation across all contexts (PubMed:36877164, 39523439, 38461301). Phosphorylation at S126 by NEK6 significantly modulates phase separation properties: the phosphomimetic S126E mutation enhances formation kinetics, increases droplet mobility (FRAP t½ ~5s), and reduces aging, while the non-phosphorylatable S126A shows opposite effects (PubMed:39523439). Deletion of the IDR (ΔN-LSD1 or Δ191) abolishes condensate formation, and nucleic acid-binding mutations (3KE) disrupt TERRA-driven phase separation (PubMed:36877164, 38461301, 39523439).
Extrinsic Partners & Regulations: LSD1 phase separation is extrinsically regulated by multiple partners: 1) TERRA RNA acts as essential scaffold, driving length/structure-dependent condensation and lowering saturation concentration (PubMed:38461301); 2) NEK6 co-phase separates with LSD1, serving as a scaffold for chromatin sub-compartment formation and phosphorylating S126 to modulate material properties (PubMed:39523439); 3) BRD4 stabilization in enhancer condensates is disrupted by LSD1 inhibitors (PubMed:36877164); 4) Rad51AP1 co-partitions to synergize R-loop formation in telomeric condensates (PubMed:38461301); 5) Histone peptides and DNA incorporate into IDR droplets (PubMed:39523439). Small molecules regulate behavior: N-methyl mesoporphyrin IX (NMM) induces liquid-to-solid transitions, while 1,6-hexanediol dissolves condensates (PubMed:36877164, 38461301).

Overall Phase Separation Overview: MUT-16 undergoes self-driven liquid-liquid phase separation to form Mutator foci in the cytoplasm of C. elegans germ cells (PubMed:30036386). These perinuclear condensates associate with P granules and exhibit liquid-like properties including spherical morphology, rapid FRAP recovery (t½ = 7.2 sec), dissolution by 1,6-hexanediol, and temperature-sensitive reversibility (PubMed:30036386). Mutator foci represent a distinct subcompartment of germ granules (M compartment) that positions adjacent to P granules (PubMed:36750365, 39354132, 30036386). At high overexpression concentrations in somatic cells, MUT-16 forms non-spherical structures suggesting possible liquid-to-solid state transitions (PubMed:30036386).
Functional Summary: Mutator foci concentrate RNA-silencing machinery—including RRF-1 RdRP and pUG RNA–siRNA cycling factors—to enable efficient 22G-RNA amplification for germline RNA interference and transposon silencing (PubMed:30036386, 39354132). This compartmentalization is essential for endo-siRNA production, with loss of foci causing defective RNAi and transposable element inactivation (PubMed:36750365, 39354132). The condensates spatially coordinate mRNA sorting via association with nuclear pores and P granules (PubMed:30036386). Under impaired E granule assembly, MUT-16 foci serve as backup sites for EGO-1-mediated 5′-derived 22G-RNA synthesis, preserving fertility and RNAi capacity (PubMed:38987544).
Intrinsic Determinants & Regulations: Phase separation of MUT-16 is intrinsically driven by its C-terminal region (aa 773-1050), specifically the J, K, and L segments (PubMed:30036386). This region is necessary and sufficient for foci formation, with larger C-terminal fragments enhancing condensate robustness (PubMed:30036386). Mutations within these domains—including p.Y774_Q885del (ΔJ), p.F886_Y946del (ΔK), p.N948_V1034del (ΔL), and p.Y387_Y946del (ΔE-K)—severely disrupt foci assembly despite normal protein expression levels (PubMed:30036386).
Extrinsic Partners & Regulations: MUT-16 functions as a scaffold that recruits core Mutator complex proteins including MUT-2, MUT-15, RDE-2, MUT-14, RRF-1, RDE-8, and NYN-1 into condensates (PubMed:30036386). It enriches ≥86 proteins in the M compartment via proximity-dependent interactions (PubMed:39354132). Spatial organization involves juxtaposition with PRG-1-containing P granules at germ granule peripheries (PubMed:36750365). Under E granule-disrupting conditions, MUT-16 foci host residual EGO-1 complexes (PubMed:38987544). Artificial tethering forces mixing between MUT-16 condensates and P granule components like PGL-1 (Pearson’s R = 0.85) (PubMed:39354132).

Overall Phase Separation Overview: WAGO-4 (O62275) undergoes phase separation primarily through co-assembly into Z granules, requiring partner proteins rather than self-driven assembly (PubMed:37505984, 29769721, 33438773). It localizes exclusively to the cytoplasm and transitions from P granules in early germline blastomeres to distinct liquid-like Z granules during later developmental stages (PubMed:29769721). These Z granules exhibit liquid properties including spherical morphology, rapid fluorescence recovery, and fusion competence (PubMed:29769721), but undergo pathological liquid-to-solid transitions when regulatory components like ZSP-1 are absent, resulting in hardened condensates with reduced mobility (PubMed:33438773).
Functional Summary: WAGO-4 phase separation enables transgenerational epigenetic inheritance by concentrating 22G-RNAs and silencing factors within Z granules for mRNA targeting (PubMed:37505984, 29769721). Disruption through CGH-1 depletion or WAGO-4 mutation abolishes RNAi inheritance and causes germline mortality (PubMed:37505984, 29769721). Pathological solidification via ZSP-1 loss dysregulates endogenous siRNA networks, impairs piRNA silencing, and compromises germline immortality (PubMed:33438773). These findings establish liquid Z granules as essential hubs for RNA-directed heritable gene silencing in C. elegans.
Intrinsic Determinants & Regulations: No intrinsic domains, mutations, or structural features directly regulating WAGO-4 phase separation were identified across the provided studies (PubMed:37505984, 29769721, 33438773). All experiments examined full-length protein behavior without domain-specific manipulations, indicating the current evidence points to extrinsic rather than intrinsic drivers for its condensate formation.
Extrinsic Partners & Regulations: WAGO-4 phase separation is critically regulated by protein partners: Its Z granule integration requires physical interaction with ZNFX-1, confirmed through co-immunoprecipitation and colocalization (PubMed:29769721, 33438773). Early localization depends on PGL-1 scaffolding in P granules (PubMed:29769721), while stability and RNA loading require CGH-1 helicase activity, with depletion causing condensate dissolution (PubMed:37505984). The peripheral regulator ZSP-1 maintains Z granule liquidity; loss of ZSP-1 triggers liquid-to-solid transitions, causing granule enlargement and abolished fluorescence recovery (PubMed:33438773).

Overall Phase Separation Overview: SURF6 (O75683) does not undergo self-driven phase separation (class_ 'PS-other') and exclusively forms heterotypic condensates through partner-dependent interactions, primarily with NPM1 (PubMed:29483575, 30498217, 30981631). It localizes to the nucleus and associates with the nucleolar granular component (PubMed:29483575). SURF6 forms liquid-like droplets in vitro when complexed with NPM1, exhibiting rapid fusion and FRAP recovery, with no reported material state transitions (e.g., liquid-to-solid) in the provided data (PubMed:29483575, 30498217, 30981631).
Functional Summary: SURF6-NPM1 phase separation scaffolds the liquid-like matrix of the nucleolar granular component, enabling spatial organization of ribosome biogenesis (PubMed:29483575, 30498217). Disruption by poly(PR) displaces SURF6 from condensates, sequestering rRNA into static puncta and impairing ribosome assembly—a mechanism linked to nucleolar stress and cytotoxicity in C9-ALS (PubMed:30981631). Genetic deletion of SURF6 disrupts ribosome biogenesis and reduces cell viability, underscoring its essential role in cellular homeostasis (PubMed:29483575).
Intrinsic Determinants & Regulations: The phase separation of SURF6 is intrinsically regulated by its arginine-rich motifs (R-motifs), which mediate multivalent electrostatic interactions with acidic tracts of partner proteins like NPM1 (PubMed:29483575, 30498217, 30981631). Key regions include residues 1-182 and 299-326, where R-motifs enable scaffold binding without homotypic assembly capability (PubMed:29483575, 30498217, 30981631). No PTMs, splicing variants, or disease-associated mutations modulating its phase behavior were reported.
Extrinsic Partners & Regulations: SURF6 requires the scaffold protein NPM1 for heterotypic phase separation, driven by electrostatic complementarity between SURF6's R-motifs and NPM1's acidic tracts (PubMed:29483575, 30498217, 30981631). Molecular crowding agents (e.g., PEG-8000) enhance this LLPS by reducing saturation concentrations (PubMed:30498217). Poly(PR) dipeptide repeats disrupt native interactions by competitively displacing SURF6 from NPM1 condensates (PubMed:30981631). SURF6 integrates into NPM1 droplets with adaptive stoichiometry, forming core-shell architectures where SURF6 enriches the core (PubMed:30498217).

Overall Phase Separation Overview: ELF3 (O82804) undergoes self-driven phase separation to form thermoresponsive condensates in the nucleus and cytoplasm (PubMed:35621186, 32848244). These condensates, referred to as ELF3 bodies or speckles, exhibit liquid-like properties in vivo and in vitro, with reversible formation at elevated temperatures (PubMed:32848244, 39113361, 35621186). In vitro studies reveal that these liquid droplets can undergo a time-dependent transition to a gel-like state after approximately 30 minutes (PubMed:39113361).
Functional Summary: Phase separation enables thermosensory regulation of the Evening Complex (ELF3-ELF4-LUX), repressing target genes like PIF4 and GI to control hypocotyl elongation and flowering in Arabidopsis thaliana (PubMed:35621186, 32848244). Loss of phase separation in ELF3-BdPrD mutants abolishes thermal responsiveness, disrupting temperature-dependent gene regulation and developmental processes (PubMed:32848244).
Intrinsic Determinants & Regulations: Phase separation is intrinsically driven by ELF3's prion-like domain (PrD), which is essential for thermoresponsive behavior (PubMed:35621186, 39113361, 32848244). Within this domain, the polyglutamine (polyQ) repeat length modulates phase separation propensity, with longer repeats increasing speckle formation frequency (PubMed:32848244). Substitution of the PrD with the Brachypodium distachyon ortholog (BdPrD) completely abolishes phase separation (PubMed:32848244).
Extrinsic Partners & Regulations: Phase separation is regulated by temperature and pH, with condensation induced at higher temperatures (PubMed:39113361, 32848244, 35621186). The protein partner ELF4 stabilizes the soluble state and inhibits phase separation, as demonstrated by reduced speckling upon ELF4 overexpression (PubMed:32848244). Additionally, m6A-modified RNAs are essential for condensate formation in vivo, with impaired ELF3 body assembly observed in m6A writer/reader mutants (PubMed:35621186).

Overall Phase Separation Overview: Synapsin 1 (O88935) undergoes both self-driven and partner-dependent phase separation to form liquid-like condensates primarily in the cytoplasm, specifically associated with synaptic vesicle (SV) clusters (PubMed:37250768, 34496937, 33202250). It exhibits self-assembly capability in vitro and in synaptic contexts, forming dynamic condensates that cluster SVs (PubMed:33202250). However, in heterologous cellular systems, it requires partners like Endophilin A1 or Synaptophysin for droplet formation (PubMed:37250768, 34496937). The condensates consistently display liquid material properties, with no reported state transitions under standard conditions (PubMed:37250768, 34496937, 33202250).
Functional Summary: Synapsin 1 phase separation is critical for organizing synaptic vesicle clusters in presynaptic terminals, enabling activity-dependent dispersion and reassembly during neuronal stimulation (PubMed:37250768). It facilitates SV pool maintenance by recruiting endocytic machinery (e.g., Endophilin A1) and spatially segregating vesicle pools through encapsulation of RIM/RIM-BP condensates (PubMed:33202250, 37250768). This mechanism underpins synaptic function during neurotransmission, with dysregulation potentially impacting vesicle reservoir dynamics (PubMed:34496937, 33202250).
Intrinsic Determinants & Regulations: Phase separation is intrinsically regulated by Synapsin 1's C-terminal intrinsically disordered region (IDR), which is polybasic and contains 31 positively charged residues (21 arginines) (PubMed:34496937). Additionally, a fragment encompassing the dimerization domain (domain C) and disordered domain (domain D) is sufficient for autonomous phase separation and synaptic vesicle clustering (PubMed:33202250). The full-length protein enables immiscibility with and encapsulation of RIM/RIM-BP condensates, a function lost in truncated constructs (PubMed:33202250).
Extrinsic Partners & Regulations: Synapsin 1 phase separation is extrinsically modulated by key partners: it coacervates with Synaptophysin via π-cation interactions, essential for condensate formation in cellular systems (PubMed:34496937, 37250768). Endophilin A1 facilitates Synapsin 1 droplet assembly through mutual co-localization in condensates (PubMed:37250768). Synapsin 1 also co-phase separates with Intersectin (ITSN) and coacervates with small unilamellar vesicles (SUVs) or synaptic vesicles (SVs) to form condensates (PubMed:33202250).

Overall Phase Separation Overview: MED1 undergoes self-driven phase separation (PubMed:36535377, 37156794) to form liquid-like transcriptional condensates primarily in the nucleus (PubMed:36535377, 37156794). It serves as a core scaffold for transcriptional condensates at super-enhancers and co-localizes with transcription factors like CEBPA, AR, and BRD4 (PubMed:37516962, 36535377, 37156794). MED1 also forms heterotypic condensates with partner proteins such as CEBPA in vitro (PubMed:37516962). These condensates exhibit liquid-like properties with rapid internal dynamics (mobile fraction ~96%, FRAP t½ ~3s) (PubMed:36535377).
Functional Summary: MED1 phase separation drives formation of transcriptional hubs at super-enhancers that concentrate RNA polymerase II and co-activators to activate cell-identity genes (PubMed:36535377, 37156794). These condensates are essential for androgen receptor-mediated oncogenic transcription in prostate cancer (PubMed:36535377). Depletion or phosphorylation-inhibition of MED1 disrupts AR condensate formation and reduces target gene expression (PubMed:36535377). Dysregulation is linked to cancer progression through aberrant activation of oncogenes (PubMed:37156794). MED1 condensates also compartmentalize transcriptional machinery during heat shock response via co-phase separation with HSF1 (PubMed:35256776) and regulate autophagy genes through co-localization with TFEB condensates (PubMed:33290690).
Intrinsic Determinants & Regulations: Phase separation of MED1 is intrinsically driven by its intrinsically disordered region (IDR, residues 948-1574) (PubMed:36535377). Deletion of the IDR disrupts phase separation capacity (PubMed:37156794), while phosphorylation within the IDR (particularly at T1457) regulates recruitment to condensates and functional activity (PubMed:36535377). The charge-patterning and block architecture of the IDR enable selective partitioning of client proteins like CTR9 and SPT6 (PubMed:36603581).
Extrinsic Partners & Regulations: MED1 co-phase separates with multiple transcription factors: It enhances androgen receptor (AR) droplet formation in vitro, lowering AR's concentration threshold for phase separation (PubMed:36535377); forms heterotypic condensates with CEBPA (PubMed:37516962); and mutually scaffolds condensates with BRD4 (PubMed:37156794). MED1 phosphorylation at T1457 promotes co-condensation with AR, while inhibition by THZ1 (CDK7 inhibitor) reduces phosphorylation and condensate recruitment (PubMed:36535377). Estrogen enhances MED1's co-phase separation with estrogen receptor (ER) (PubMed:30449618), and MED1 incorporates MYC into condensates (PubMed:30449618). Charge-patterned IDRs of client proteins (CTR9, SPT6) partition selectively into MED1 condensates (PubMed:36603581).

Overall Phase Separation Overview: MYC undergoes self-driven phase separation via multivalent electrostatic interactions, forming reversible salt-sensitive liquid droplets in vitro (PubMed:39343006). It is also recruited to partner-driven condensates including TiPARP nuclear bodies (PubMed:32482854) and MED1 transcriptional condensates (PubMed:30449618). Located primarily in the nucleus, MYC associates with transcriptional condensates where wild-type forms liquid-like droplets, while mutations can induce irreversible solid-like aggregates (PubMed:39343006).
Functional Summary: MYC phase separation modulates transcriptional output: Recruitment to TiPARP condensates promotes ubiquitination and degradation, suppressing transcriptional activity and inhibiting tumor growth (PubMed:32482854). Mutations enhancing phase separation (e.g., ΔE242-E261) increase transcriptional activity of oncogenes (CD47, GLUT1, CDCA7, PDL1, TERT) and promote cancer cell proliferation (PubMed:39343006).
Intrinsic Determinants & Regulations: MYC phase separation is intrinsically driven by its C-terminal basic region helix-loop-helix leucine zipper (bHLHLZ) domain through multivalent electrostatic interactions (PubMed:39343006). The negatively charged E242-E261 segment inhibits phase separation; its deletion or specific mutations (E253A/E254A/E255A, E257A/D258A/E259A, E260A/E261A) enhance phase separation and promote irreversible aggregation (PubMed:39343006).
Extrinsic Partners & Regulations: MYC is recruited to TiPARP nuclear condensates where it undergoes ubiquitination and degradation (PubMed:32482854). It co-phase separates with the transcriptional coactivator MED1 in vitro, incorporating into MED1 droplets (PubMed:30449618). No extrinsic non-protein regulators are reported.

Overall Phase Separation Overview: FTH1 undergoes partner-dependent phase separation to form liquid-like cytoplasmic condensates, requiring NCOA4 as an essential scaffold (PubMed:36066504, 39988734). These cytosolic condensates do not associate with predefined membrane-less organelles (PubMed:36066504, 39988734). One study tested FTH1 in engineered nuclear condensates for CRISPRa applications but observed minimal regulatory capacity (PubMed:40087540). No material state transitions were reported.
Functional Summary: FTH1 condensates facilitate ferritin degradation via macroautophagy and endosomal microautophagy (ferritinophagy), enabling iron release during deficiency (PubMed:36066504). This process is mechanosensitive: condensates promote ferroptosis under high tension by releasing iron, while impaired phase separation under low tension confers ferroptosis resistance (PubMed:39988734). Recruitment to iron-induced NCOA4 condensates modulates ferritin fate—sequestering NCOA4 initially to prevent degradation, then delivering ferritin to lysosomes during prolonged iron exposure (PubMed:35318808). Engineered nuclear condensates showed minimal gene regulatory capacity in CRISPRa systems (PubMed:40087540).
Intrinsic Determinants & Regulations: No intrinsic domains, mutations, or specific protein regions driving FTH1 phase separation were identified across studies (PubMed:36066504, 39988734, 40087540). Phase separation is primarily regulated extrinsically through partners and environmental cues.
Extrinsic Partners & Regulations: NCOA4 is the critical extrinsic scaffold for FTH1 condensate formation, with colocalization and rescue experiments confirming its essential role (PubMed:36066504, 39988734). Mechanical tension regulates this process: high tension (stiff substrates/sparse cells) promotes liquid condensate formation while low tension (soft substrates/dense cells) suppresses it (PubMed:39988734). FTH1 interacts with ferritin light chain (FTL) within condensates as part of the ferritin complex, though FTL is dispensable for initial assembly (PubMed:36066504). FTH1 also partitions into solid-like NCOA4 condensates induced by iron (Fe(III)) (PubMed:35318808).

Organism: Human respiratory syncytial virus A (strain A2)
Overall Phase Separation Overview: P03421 undergoes both self-driven and partner-dependent phase separation. It forms homotypic liquid condensates in vitro via its C-terminal α-helical molten globule domain, exhibiting reversible temperature-dependent dissolution (PubMed:37210029). In vivo, it co-phase separates with nucleoprotein N in the cytoplasm to form dynamic, liquid-like viral inclusion bodies (factories) (PubMed:37210029, 32963000, 37762166). These condensates display rapid FRAP recovery (t₁/₂ ~80s in vitro; 100% recovery in 2s in cells), fusion capability, and spherical morphology (PubMed:37210029). Material state transitions include stoichiometry-dependent shifts between aggregates and droplets with N-RNA complexes, and M2-1/cyclopamine-induced hardening to less dynamic states (PubMed:37210029, 37762166).
Functional Summary: P-N condensates form viral factories compartmentalizing RNA synthesis/replication, acting as scaffolds that recruit cellular proteins (e.g., HSP70) and rescue aggregated nucleoproteins (PubMed:37210029, 32963000). Dysregulated phase transitions have pathological consequences: Irreversible hardening by cyclopamine-M2-1 complexes inhibits viral replication, while Y102L mutation confers antiviral resistance (PubMed:37762166). Stoichiometric imbalances cause N-RNA aggregation, disrupting viral gene expression (PubMed:37210029). Sequential assembly from P-N nuclei to factories organizes viral transcription machinery, with disrupted dynamics impacting pathogenesis (PubMed:37210029, 32963000).
Intrinsic Determinants & Regulations: Phase separation is intrinsically governed by multivalent domains: The C-terminal α-helical molten globule (aMG, residues 172-206) serves as the primary homotypic driver, stabilized by helical structure (PubMed:37210029). Both N-terminal intrinsically disordered (IDD) and aMG domains are essential for optimal behavior (PubMed:37210029, 32963000). The oligomerization domain and C-terminal residues (including F241) act as critical scaffolds, with ΔF241 abolishing phase separation (PubMed:32963000). Key mutations include a3mut (G172S/R174A/E175G) in αC1 helix that destabilizes aMG and reduces homotypic LLPS, and Y102L in the M2-1 binding region (residues 95-110) conferring cyclopamine resistance (PubMed:37210029, 37762166).
Extrinsic Partners & Regulations: Essential heterotypic partners include nucleoprotein N (P03418), enabling stoichiometrically tuned condensates that rescue N-RNA aggregates (PubMed:37210029, 32963000). M2-1 protein enhances P mobility within condensates but enables cyclopamine-induced hardening (PubMed:37762166). Chemical regulators: 2,2,2-Trifluoroethanol stabilizes aMG helicity, promoting homotypic LLPS (4-fold critical concentration reduction at 5% TFE) (PubMed:37210029). NaCl modulates homotypic LLPS (required at low concentrations, deforms droplets >200 mM) (PubMed:37210029). Crowding agents (Ficoll ≥5%) enable in vitro phase separation (PubMed:32963000). Cyclopamine reduces P mobility in condensates when M2-1 is present (FRAP recovery drops from 70% to 15-40%) (PubMed:37762166).

Organism: Influenza A virus (strain A/Puerto Rico/8/1934 H1N1)
Overall Phase Separation Overview: The nucleoprotein (NP) of Influenza A virus (P03466) undergoes partner-dependent phase separation to form viral inclusions primarily in the cytoplasm, with nuclear localization also observed (PubMed:37013374, 30967547). These inclusions exhibit liquid-like properties including fusion, fission, dynamic exchange, and sensitivity to osmotic shock under physiological conditions (PubMed:37013374, 30967547). However, they undergo concentration-dependent liquid-to-solid transitions when treated with nucleozin, resulting in hardened, immobile condensates (PubMed:37013374, 37894933). A fraction of inclusions may naturally transition toward gel-like states over time, as evidenced by partial 1,6-hexanediol resistance and immobile FRAP components (PubMed:30967547).
Functional Summary: Liquid viral inclusions facilitate selective influenza genome assembly by concentrating vRNPs to enable stochastic interactions essential for replication and genetic reassortment (PubMed:37013374, 30967547). Pathological solidification via nucleozin-induced NP polymerization disrupts these dynamic functions, halting viral replication and confirming material state as a viable antiviral target (PubMed:37013374, 37894933). Notably, inclusion formation is independent of immune evasion mechanisms, as condensate disruption does not alter interferon responses (PubMed:30967547).
Intrinsic Determinants & Regulations: Phase separation of NP requires the full-length protein within viral ribonucleoprotein (vRNP) complexes, where multivalency drives condensate formation (PubMed:37013374, 30967547, 37894933). The Y289H mutation confers resistance to nucleozin-induced hardening by preventing small molecule binding and subsequent NP polymerization (PubMed:37013374). Nucleozin binding at specific NP sites induces oligomerization, which directly triggers the liquid-to-solid transition by stabilizing vRNP interactions (PubMed:37894933).
Extrinsic Partners & Regulations: NP phase separation is critically regulated by extrinsic partners: The host protein Rab11 acts as an essential scaffold, with its GTP-bound form required for inclusion formation and vesicular trafficking dependence (PubMed:37013374, 30967547). Influenza vRNA serves as an integral structural component of vRNP complexes that drives initial condensate assembly (PubMed:30967547). The small molecule nucleozin potently modulates material state by binding NP to induce polymerization, overriding Rab11 dependence and promoting liquid-to-solid transitions (PubMed:37013374, 37894933).

Protein Name: DNA-directed RNA polymerase II subunit RPB1
Overall Phase Separation Overview: RPB1 (P04050) exhibits distinct phase separation behaviors in vitro versus in vivo. In vitro, its unphosphorylated carboxy-terminal domain (CTD) undergoes self-driven liquid-liquid phase separation (LLPS), forming dynamic liquid-like droplets (PubMed:39266551, 30127355). However, in living Saccharomyces cerevisiae cells, RPB1 does not form phase-separated condensates; instead, its CTD mediates spatial confinement within subnuclear regions enriched for active genes without phase transition (PubMed:38548891). The protein is exclusively nuclear (PubMed:38548891, 30127355, 30605674) and associates with heat shock-induced gene coalescence foci (PubMed:30605674). Yeast CTD forms less stable droplets than human CTD due to shorter repeat length, showing rapid fluorescence recovery (PubMed:30127355). Phosphorylation dissolves liquid droplets, while dephosphorylation restores LLPS (PubMed:39266551).
Functional Summary: CTD-mediated spatial confinement optimizes transcriptional efficiency by enhancing RNAPII's diffusive search for chromatin targets, accelerating pre-initiation complex formation, and regulating burst kinetics (e.g., at HSP82 locus) (PubMed:38548891). Disruption via CTD truncation impairs these functions. RPB1 is required for Hsf1-driven coalescence of heat shock genes into nuclear foci, enabling rapid transcriptional activation during stress; loss of RPB1 abolishes this gene reorganization and compromises stress response (PubMed:30605674). While in vitro CTD phase separation may reflect concentration-dependent regulatory mechanisms, in vivo functions occur without phase separation.
Intrinsic Determinants & Regulations: Phase separation and spatial confinement are intrinsically regulated by RPB1's CTD and its modifications. The CTD's heptad repeats (YSPTSPS) drive both behaviors: longer repeats enhance confinement and chromatin binding in vivo (PubMed:38548891), while repeat length determines droplet stability in vitro (PubMed:30127355). Phosphorylation at Ser5/Ser2 inhibits LLPS, and phosphomimetic mutations (e.g., T4E, S7E) abolish droplet formation (PubMed:39266551). Dephosphorylation promotes phase separation, with phosphorylation state acting as a reversible switch (PubMed:39266551, 30127355). CTD truncations disrupt nuclear confinement and reduce chromatin binding (PubMed:38548891).
Extrinsic Partners & Regulations: Specific partners enable phase separation of phosphorylated CTD states. PIN1 induces LLPS of Ser5-phosphorylated CTD via its WW domain (PubMed:39266551). SCAF4 promotes LLPS of CTD phosphorylated at both Ser5 and Ser2, while RPRD1b specifically induces phase separation of Ser2-phosphorylated CTD (PubMed:39266551). RPB1 also functions as an essential partner for Hsf1, enabling coalescence of heat shock protein genes into subnuclear foci during stress response (PubMed:30605674).

Overall Phase Separation Overview: Glycinin (P04776) undergoes self-driven liquid-liquid phase separation (LLPS) in vitro, forming viscous liquid condensates that exhibit viscoelastic properties (PubMed:37217523, 37770422). These condensates display salinity-dependent behavior with material properties modulated by sodium chloride concentrations (PubMed:37217523, 37770422). They undergo liquid-to-hollow transitions via internal phase separation upon salinity shifts (PubMed:37217523) and exhibit reentrant dissolution at high salt (PubMed:37770422). While primarily studied in vitro with model membranes, the protein is proposed to function in plant vacuolar contexts, though no direct subcellular locations or membrane-less organelle associations are evidenced in the provided data.
Functional Summary: Glycinin condensates facilitate membrane remodeling through wetting transitions that alter lipid packing and fluidity (PubMed:37217523, 37770422). They stabilize damaged membranes by nucleating at pore sites to prevent vesicle collapse (PubMed:37968398). These properties suggest roles in plant vacuolar compartmentalization during seed development and potential applications in synthetic biology for tunable protocell design (PubMed:37217523, 37770422, 37968398).
Intrinsic Determinants & Regulations: Phase separation is intrinsically driven by the full-length hexameric structure of Glycinin, with no specific domains, mutations, or post-translational modifications identified as regulators in the provided data (PubMed:37217523, 37770422, 37968398). The oligomeric state (360 kDa hexamer) contributes to high condensate viscosity and surface tension (PubMed:37217523).
Extrinsic Partners & Regulations: Sodium chloride (NaCl) is the primary extrinsic regulator, serving as an essential scaffold for LLPS that modulates phase boundaries, material properties (viscosity, surface tension), wetting behavior, and droplet morphology (PubMed:37217523, 37770422). Condensate formation is triggered by pH decreases or salt increases and exhibits reentrant dissolution at high salinity (PubMed:37968398, 37770422). No protein partners were identified.

Overall Phase Separation Overview: HSPB1 (HSP27) does not undergo autonomous phase separation but partitions into and modulates biomolecular condensates formed by partner proteins (PubMed:36075972, 32231288, 36701233). It localizes primarily to the cytoplasm and associates with stress granules (PubMed:28377462, 32231288), TDP-43 cytoplasmic condensates (PubMed:36075972), SQSTM1/p62 condensates on damaged lysosomes (PubMed:37194327, 36701233), and FUS aggregates (PubMed:32231288). HSPB1 maintains liquid-like properties of these condensates (PubMed:36075972, 32231288, 36701233) and prevents pathological liquid-to-solid transitions (PubMed:36075972, 32231288).
Functional Summary: HSPB1 maintains proteostasis by preventing pathological condensate transitions: it preserves TDP-43 liquidity to enable stress recovery and prevent ALS-associated aggregation (PubMed:36075972); sustains SQSTM1/p62 condensate dynamics for autophagosome biogenesis during lysophagy, with defects linked to neurodegeneration (PubMed:37194327, 36701233); and inhibits FUS amyloid formation, protecting against ALS (PubMed:32231288). Dysregulation of HSPB1-mediated control correlates with irreversible liquid-to-solid transitions in TDP-43/FUS condensates, driving cytotoxicity in ALS and FTD (PubMed:36075972, 32231288).
Intrinsic Determinants & Regulations: HSPB1's regulatory function is governed by its N-terminal domain (NTD) and oligomerization state (PubMed:32231288). Phosphorylation at S15/S78/S82 disrupts multimerization, switching its activity: under basal conditions, multimeric HSPB1 inhibits client phase separation; under stress, phosphorylated HSPB1 partitions into condensates to preserve liquidity (PubMed:32231288). Phosphorylation is essential for recruitment to SQSTM1/p62 condensates (PubMed:36701233). The alpha-crystallin domain (ACD) directly binds client proteins like FUS to inhibit amyloid formation when exposed by demultimerization (PubMed:32231288).
Extrinsic Partners & Regulations: HSPB1 partitions into TDP-43 condensates, delaying liquid-to-gel transitions and inhibiting fibrillization (PubMed:36075972). It co-localizes with SQSTM1/p62 on damaged lysosomes, maintaining condensate liquidity for lysophagy (PubMed:37194327, 36701233). For FUS, HSPB1 inhibits phase separation under non-stress conditions but co-phase separates upon phosphorylation to prevent amyloid transitions (PubMed:32231288). HSPB1 is recruited to SOD1-positive stress granules during proteotoxic stress (PubMed:28377462) and requires partner proteins (TDP-43, SQSTM1, FUS) for condensate incorporation (PubMed:36075972, 36701233, 32231288).

Overall Phase Separation Overview: The measles virus nucleoprotein (N, UniProt P04851) undergoes partner-dependent phase separation, requiring interaction with the viral phosphoprotein (P) to form liquid-like condensates. In vitro, N and P co-assemble into dynamic droplets dependent on salt concentration (PubMed:32270045). In vivo, this interaction drives formation of cytoplasmic viral inclusion bodies (IBs) that serve as replication factories (PubMed:39194235, 31375591). While N alone forms nuclear aggregates (PubMed:39194235), co-expression with P yields spherical cytoplasmic condensates exhibiting liquid-like properties including fusion and rapid component exchange in small puncta (PubMed:31375591). These condensates undergo a time- and size-dependent material state transition from liquid to gel-like/solid states in larger structures (PubMed:31375591).
Functional Summary: N-P phase separation creates functional viral replication compartments that concentrate RNA and replication machinery. In vitro condensates accelerate nucleocapsid assembly kinetics by 3-4 fold compared to dilute phases (PubMed:32270045). In vivo inclusion bodies serve as replication factories that evade host immune responses (PubMed:39194235). The liquid-to-gel material state transition in mature IBs may provide protective advantages by shielding viral components while maintaining replication efficiency (PubMed:31375591).
Intrinsic Determinants & Regulations: Phase separation is intrinsically regulated by N's C-terminal domains. The TAIL domain (including residues 460-525) mediates essential interactions with P's XD domain, with the S491L mutation abolishing phase separation in vitro (PubMed:32270045). In vivo, the C-terminal molecular recognition element (MoRE)-containing unstructured region (aa 392-525) is critical for inclusion body formation, as its deletion prevents normal condensate assembly (PubMed:31375591). RNA-binding capability is dispensable for phase separation, demonstrated by unaffected IB formation in RNA-binding mutants (K180A/R194A/R354A) (PubMed:31375591).
Extrinsic Partners & Regulations: N's phase separation is extrinsically scaffolded by the viral phosphoprotein (P), which is essential for condensate formation both in vitro (PubMed:32270045) and in vivo (PubMed:39194235, 31375591). RNA localizes to N-P condensates and triggers nucleocapsid assembly in vitro (PubMed:32270045). Cellular machinery modulates condensate dynamics: dynein-mediated transport facilitates IB growth and perinuclear localization (PubMed:31375591), while Casein Kinase 2 phosphorylation of P enhances condensate size (PubMed:31375591).

Overall Phase Separation Overview: HP1a undergoes self-driven phase separation (class PS-self) to form dynamic liquid-like condensates primarily in the nucleus, specifically within heterochromatin domains (PubMed:28636597, 31866201). These condensates exhibit liquid properties during initial formation (spherical droplets, fusion, rapid dynamics) but mature into structures containing both liquid and stable compartments, as evidenced by increased immobile fractions and reduced circularity (PubMed:28636597). Phase separation can occur autonomously in vitro but is strongly enhanced by partners like H3K9me3-modified nucleosome arrays (PubMed:30425322) and Prospero (PubMed:31866201).
Functional Summary: HP1a phase separation drives heterochromatin domain formation, enabling genome stability, DNA repair, and transcriptional silencing by regulating molecular access through phase boundaries (PubMed:28636597). Crucially, during neural development, Prospero recruits HP1a into condensates that expand H3K9me3+ heterochromatin domains, irreversibly silencing self-renewal genes to ensure terminal neuronal differentiation; disruption of this co-condensation mechanism leads to tumorigenesis (PubMed:31866201).
Intrinsic Determinants & Regulations: Phase separation is intrinsically driven by HP1a's N-terminal tail and hinge domains containing intrinsically disordered regions (IDRs) and low-complexity sequences (PubMed:28636597). Chromo shadow domain-mediated dimerization critically stabilizes condensates, as disruption by the I191E mutation increases mobility and reduces hexanediol resistance (PubMed:28636597). While exhibiting weak autonomous phase separation capability, HP1a's intrinsic properties facilitate co-assembly with partners (PubMed:31866201).
Extrinsic Partners & Regulations: Key extrinsic modulators include: 1) HP4 and HP5, which co-assemble with HP1a into heterochromatin domains and require HP1a for localization (PubMed:28636597); 2) H3K9me3-modified nucleosome arrays, essential for phase separation in chromatin contexts (PubMed:30425322); and 3) Prospero, which dramatically enhances HP1a's phase separation and droplet fusion ability through co-condensation, forming continuous heterochromatin crescents (PubMed:31866201). Partner binding via the W200 residue stabilizes the immobile fraction of condensates (PubMed:28636597).

Overall Phase Separation Overview: U1-70K (SNRNP70) undergoes self-driven liquid-liquid phase separation (LLPS) in the nucleus, forming dynamic liquid-like condensates that can transition to solid aggregates (PubMed:36073763, 31723601). It associates with nuclear condensates, nuclear bodies, and nuclear speckles, where it co-localizes with CPSF6, PABPN1, and U2 snRNA (PubMed:36073763, 31723601, 38381607). The protein also co-phase separates with partners like SRSF1 in vitro (PubMed:39023093). Liquid-to-solid transitions occur in cellular environments and are modulated by concentration, time, and environmental factors (PubMed:31723601, 36073763).
Functional Summary: Physiologically, U1-70K LLPS regulates RNA processing by recruiting CPSF6 to alternative polyadenylation sites and modulating PABPN1-mediated repression, while co-phase separation with SRSF1 ensures spliceosome assembly fidelity (PubMed:36073763, 39023093). Pathologically, liquid-to-solid transitions—accelerated by prolonged expression or environmental stressors—promote cytotoxic aggregate formation linked to Alzheimer’s disease, where U1-70K co-aggregates with tau (PubMed:31723601, 36073763). These transitions are driven by LC domain motifs and represent a key mechanism in neurodegeneration (PubMed:31723601).
Intrinsic Determinants & Regulations: Phase separation is intrinsically driven by low-complexity domains LC1 (residues 231-306, also termed BAD1) and LC2 (residues 317-407), which contain repetitive basic-acidic motifs enabling multivalent electrostatic interactions (PubMed:36073763, 31723601, 39023093). The LC1 domain undergoes a conformational switch from α-helix to β-strand/random coil upon partner binding (PubMed:39023093). Arginine-to-alanine mutations in LC1 disrupt phase separation and partner interactions (PubMed:36073763). Basic residues are essential for droplet formation, while acidic residues stabilize morphology (PubMed:31723601).
Extrinsic Partners & Regulations: U1-70K co-phase separates with protein partners including PABPN1 (driving its liquid-to-aggregate transition), CPSF6 (recruited to nuclear condensates), and SRSF1 (via BAD1-phosphorylated RS domain interactions) (PubMed:36073763, 39023093). This co-assembly is regulated by phosphorylation of both U1-70K BAD1 and SRSF1 (PubMed:39023093). Small molecules modulate material states: aspartic acid induces solid aggregates, while arginine maintains liquid states but disrupts droplet morphology (PubMed:31723601). Phase separation is sensitive to pH and salt concentrations, with larger droplets forming at acidic pH (PubMed:31723601).

Overall Phase Separation Overview: SlmA does not undergo self-driven phase separation but acts as an essential scaffold for heterotypic condensate formation when bound to SBS DNA and in complex with FtsZ (PubMed:36854378, 36315857, 30523075). These condensates are liquid-like and form in the nucleoid-associated region in vivo (PubMed:36854378, 30523075). They exhibit reversible transitions, such as disassembly upon GTP addition and reassembly upon GTP depletion, as part of the FtsZ-SlmA-SBS complex (PubMed:36854378, 30523075).
Functional Summary: SlmA-mediated condensates enable nucleoid occlusion, spatially regulating bacterial cell division by sequestering FtsZ near chromosomes to prevent aberrant Z-ring assembly and DNA damage (PubMed:36854378, 36315857, 30523075). This dynamic sequestration allows timed release of FtsZ for divisome formation at midcell post-segregation (PubMed:30523075) and may confer stress survival benefits by halting division under adverse conditions (PubMed:36854378).
Intrinsic Determinants & Regulations: The phase separation behavior of SlmA is intrinsically regulated by its DNA-binding domain, which is essential for recognizing SBS sequences and forming a tetrameric complex that enables multivalent interactions with FtsZ (PubMed:36854378).
Extrinsic Partners & Regulations: SlmA requires extrinsic partners for phase separation: it forms condensates only in complex with FtsZ and SBS DNA (PubMed:36854378, 36315857, 30523075). The formation and properties of these condensates are modulated by ions (e.g., KCl reduces condensate size) (PubMed:36854378), potassium glutamate enhances formation (PubMed:36315857), macromolecular crowders (e.g., dextran) promote phase separation via volume exclusion (PubMed:30523075), and lipid surfaces (e.g., E. coli lipid bilayers) facilitate condensate accumulation and fusion (PubMed:36315857).

Overall Phase Separation Overview: HSP70 (P0DMV8) does not undergo autonomous phase separation but is recruited into various membraneless organelles through heterotypic interactions (PubMed:33335017, 39804774). It localizes to both nucleus and cytoplasm, associating with stress-induced condensates including BAG2 degradation condensates (80.7% colocalization), TDP-43 anisosomes (6-16× enrichment in liquid cores), p62 nuclear condensates, TDP-43 nuclear condensates (NCs), and Negri bodies (PubMed:35654899, 33335017, 34385323, 28680096, 39804774). Within these compartments, HSP70 maintains liquid-like states with rapid fluorescence recovery (t½=3s in anisosome cores), but its delocalization can trigger liquid-to-gel transitions in client condensates (PubMed:33335017, 39804774).
Functional Summary: HSP70 serves as a chaperone guardian in biomolecular condensates, preventing pathological transitions: in BAG2 condensates, it enables ubiquitin-independent proteasomal degradation of clients like Tau (PubMed:35654899); in TDP-43 assemblies, it sustains liquidity to avert neurotoxic aggregation linked to ALS/FTD (PubMed:33335017, 36930291); in p62 hubs, it facilitates stress-responsive protein quality control (PubMed:34385323); and in Negri bodies, it supports viral replication machinery concentration (PubMed:28680096).
