Dysregulation—through delocalization (e.g., during prolonged poly-PR stress), ATP depletion, or inhibition—triggers gelation of TDP-43 condensates, causing phospho-TDP-43 oligomerization, cytotoxicity (7.7% LDH increase), and TDP-43 proteinopathy (PubMed:39804774, 33335017).
Intrinsic Determinants & Regulations: No intrinsic domains or features driving autonomous HSP70 phase separation are identified, as it lacks self-assembly capability (PubMed:33335017, 39804774). Its regulatory function in condensates is mediated by ATP-dependent chaperone activity, where ATP hydrolysis maintains liquidity of host condensates like TDP-43 anisosomes and nuclear condensates (PubMed:33335017, 39804774). Inhibition of HSP70 ATPase activity reduces fluidity and promotes pathological transitions in client condensates (PubMed:33335017, 39804774).
Extrinsic Partners & Regulations: HSP70 recruitment requires partner-driven condensation: it co-phase separates with BAG2 in degradation condensates during hyperosmotic/proteasome stress (PubMed:35654899), enriches in TDP-43 anisosomes dependent on RNA-binding deficient TDP-43 variants (PubMed:33335017), partitions into p62 nuclear condensates under heat/oxidative stress (PubMed:34385323), incorporates into Negri bodies via viral P protein interactions (PubMed:28680096), and maintains TDP-43 NC fluidity through NEAT1 RNA scaffolding (PubMed:39804774). Key modulators include ATP levels (depletion causes irreversible liquid-to-solid transitions), proteasome inhibition (enhances TDP-43 demixing), and poly-PR dipeptide (induces NC maturation) (PubMed:33335017, 39804774).

Overall Phase Separation Overview: Histone H1.4 (P10412) undergoes phase separation exclusively through partner-dependent mechanisms (class: PS-other) primarily in the nucleus (PubMed:32111972). It forms liquid-like condensates with short dsDNA (300-bp) in vitro (PubMed:37432033) and associates with heterochromatin (chromocenters) and nucleoli (PubMed:32111972). With chromatin scaffolds, its C-terminal domain promotes a transition toward solid-like material states characterized by increased density and reduced dynamics (PubMed:31543265). No material state transitions were explicitly reported across studies.
Functional Summary: H1.4 phase separation regulates chromatin architecture by promoting longer nucleosome linkers in higher eukaryotes (PubMed:31543265) and organizing heterochromatin domains (PubMed:32111972). Pathologically, its failure to be displaced by MeCP2 in Rett syndrome results in aberrant H1.4-dominated chromatin architecture, contributing to neurodevelopmental defects (PubMed:32111972). The evolutionary conservation of H1 expression correlates with its role in tuning chromatin phase separation properties (PubMed:31543265).
Intrinsic Determinants & Regulations: Phase separation is intrinsically driven by the disordered C-terminal domain (CTD), which is necessary and sufficient for altering chromatin condensate density and dynamics (PubMed:31543265). Post-translational modifications, particularly acetylation of histone tails, modulate the material properties of chromatin droplets (PubMed:31543265). While the lysine-rich CTD is implicated in DNA-driven phase separation, this remains inferred rather than experimentally validated (PubMed:37432033).
Extrinsic Partners & Regulations: H1.4 requires nucleic acid scaffolds: short dsDNA (300-bp) is essential for droplet formation but inhibited by longer DNA (PubMed:37432033), while nucleosomal arrays/chromatin enhance phase separation (PubMed:31543265, 32111972). It competes with MeCP2 for chromatin binding, forming mutually exclusive condensates where functional MeCP2 displaces H1.4 from heterochromatin to nucleoli. Rett syndrome mutations in MeCP2 abolish this competition, trapping H1.4 in heterochromatin (PubMed:32111972).

Protein Name: Calcium/calmodulin-dependent protein kinase type II subunit alpha
Overall Phase Separation Overview: CaMKIIα does not undergo autonomous phase separation (class: PS-other) but is recruited into biomolecular condensates via partner interactions, primarily within the cytoplasm and postsynaptic density (PSD) of dendritic spines (PubMed:33235361, PubMed:38440150). It forms liquid-like condensates (PubMed:33235361, PubMed:38440150) and undergoes dissolution rather than state transitions, dispersing upon calcium-dependent activation (PubMed:36599935, PubMed:33235361, PubMed:38440150).
Functional Summary: Phase separation with GluN2B and PSD scaffolds is critical for basal synaptic transmission and long-term potentiation maintenance, organizing PSD nano-domains for synaptic plasticity (PubMed:36827181, PubMed:33235361). Activity-dependent shuttling between Shank3 and GluN2B condensates decodes calcium oscillations, driving structural LTP through SAPAP phosphorylation and PSD enlargement (PubMed:33235361). In dendritic spines, dissolution of layered condensates upon activation regulates scaffolding dynamics essential for spine enlargement; dysregulation may cause synaptic dysfunction (PubMed:36599935, PubMed:38440150, PubMed:33235361).
Intrinsic Determinants & Regulations: Phase separation capacity is intrinsically regulated by CaMKIIα's short unstructured linker (30 amino acids), where lengthening abolishes co-phase separation with GluN2B (PubMed:36827181). Phosphorylation at T286 and kinase activity are essential, as the D135N kinase-dead mutant fails to influence condensate formation (PubMed:33235361). Activation via calcium/calmodulin binding triggers dispersal from condensates (PubMed:33235361, PubMed:38440150).
Extrinsic Partners & Regulations: CaMKIIα co-phase separates with GluN2B as an essential scaffold partner (PubMed:36827181, PubMed:33235361) and with PSD proteins (PSD-95, SAPAP, Shank3, Homer3) in reconstituted assemblies (PubMed:36827181, PubMed:33235361). It also forms layered condensates with SORBS2, SHANK3, and GKAP in dendritic spines (PubMed:38440150, PubMed:36599935). Calcium ions trigger translocation to GluN2B/PSD-95 condensates upon activation, while phosphatase PP2A mediates dispersal via dephosphorylation (PubMed:33235361).

Protein Name: Eukaryotic peptide chain release factor subunit 1
Overall Phase Separation Overview: Sup45 (P12385) undergoes phase separation primarily in the cytoplasm, forming aggregates during heat shock that exhibit liquid-like fusion during dissolution (PubMed:38025775). It associates with stress granules under stress conditions, including heat stress and energy depletion (PubMed:38942013, 37759770). The condensates display both solid and liquid material states, with reversible disassembly observed upon glucose addition (PubMed:37759770) and fusion indicating liquid-like behavior during dissolution (PubMed:38025775).
Functional Summary: Sup45 phase separation facilitates stress response through incorporation into stress granules during heat stress and energy depletion (PubMed:38942013, 37759770). These condensates disassemble upon glucose-induced recovery, indicating a regulated role in stress adaptation (PubMed:37759770).
Intrinsic Determinants & Regulations: No intrinsic domains, mutations, or features driving phase separation of Sup45 were identified in the provided studies (PubMed:38025775, 38942013, 37759770).
Extrinsic Partners & Regulations: Sup45 requires the ubiquitin-like modifier Urm1 for efficient condensation and stress granule incorporation, evidenced by defective assembly in urm1Δ cells (PubMed:38942013). It co-assembles with the translation termination factor Sup35 in cytoplasmic condensates (72% colocalization) and associates with the stress granule marker Pub1 (76% colocalization) (PubMed:37759770). mRNA is essential for condensate formation, as cycloheximide treatment prevents puncta assembly (PubMed:37759770).

Overall Phase Separation Overview: PHYB undergoes self-driven phase separation to form photobodies in the nucleus, exhibiting concentration- and environment-dependent material states. Under dim light or lower temperatures, it forms liquid-like condensates that transition to gel-like states under high PHYB concentrations or strong light (PubMed:38664420, 35728588). Photobodies associate with specific subnuclear sites including chromocenters and nucleolar regions (PubMed:38684657). These phase-separated compartments demonstrate reversible temperature sensitivity, dissolving at ≥25°C and reforming at 15-20°C (PubMed:35728588).
Functional Summary: Photobody formation spatially segregates antagonistic PHYB functions: facilitating PIF degradation in the nucleoplasm while stabilizing PIFs within condensates to balance hypocotyl elongation during photomorphogenesis (PubMed:38664420, 38684657). Temperature-dependent phase transitions enable direct thermosensing, regulating thermomorphogenesis through selective recruitment of signaling components like PIF3/PIF4 into biomolecular hubs (PubMed:35728588). Photobody association with chromocenters suggests roles in chromatin organization, with dissolution of thermo-sensitive photobodies at elevated temperatures disrupting growth regulation (PubMed:38684657). Phase separation is indispensable for environmental signal integration in plant adaptive responses (PubMed:35728588).
Intrinsic Determinants & Regulations: Phase separation is intrinsically driven by the C-terminal module through homodimerization, which provides essential multivalency (PubMed:38664420, 35728588, 38684657). The intrinsically disordered N-terminal extension (NTE) modulates phase behavior, containing RGG/VGG/SGG motifs that confer thermosensitivity and light responsiveness (PubMed:35728588). Critical mutations include D1040V (disrupting dimerization and abolishing phase separation), Y276H (constitutively active), and N-terminal truncations that impair condensate formation (PubMed:38664420, 35728588, 38684657).
Extrinsic Partners & Regulations: PHYB co-phase separates with client transcription factors including PIF3, PIF4, and PIF5, recruiting them into photobodies for functional sequestration (PubMed:38664420, 35728588). Phase separation is extrinsically regulated by red light (660 nm), which triggers photobody assembly through phytochrome activation (PubMed:38664420). Temperature acts as a direct modulator, with dissolution occurring at ≥25°C and reassembly at 15-20°C via NTE-mediated sensitivity (PubMed:35728588). Environmental factors including light intensity and R:FR ratio dynamically regulate photobody size and distribution (PubMed:38684657).

Overall Phase Separation Overview: NP (P18272) undergoes phase separation to form cytoplasmic viral inclusion bodies (IBs) or viral factories (VFs), which serve as membraneless organelles for viral replication (PubMed:37306660, 37598728, 37443171). While capable of self-assembly into IB-like structures when bound to cellular RNA in cells, its in vitro phase separation requires the essential partner VP35 (PubMed:37598728, 37306660). These condensates typically exhibit liquid-like properties including fusion and dynamic molecular exchange, but undergo material state transitions to more solid-like states modulated by IB size (smaller IBs more liquid), RNA binding (solidifies), and VP35 co-expression (enhances liquidity) (PubMed:37306660).
Functional Summary: NP phase separation forms functional viral factories that spatially coordinate Ebola virus RNA synthesis (replication/transcription) and nucleocapsid assembly by concentrating viral components (VP35, VP30, L) and host factors like HSP90 (PubMed:37306660, 37598728, 37443171). These condensates serve as essential platforms for viral replication, with disruption of NP-VP35 complex formation (via VP35-derived peptides) inhibiting inclusion body formation and potently blocking viral infection (PubMed:37598728). Material state transitions toward solid-like states, driven by RNA binding or absence of VP35, may impact replication efficiency through altered condensate dynamics (PubMed:37306660).
Intrinsic Determinants & Regulations: Phase separation is intrinsically driven by NP oligomerization mediated by N-terminal residues Y21 and H22, which are essential for condensate formation (PubMed:37306660). The N-terminal domain (NTD, residues 25-384) is critical for complex phase separation with VP35 (PubMed:37598728). RNA binding through residues K160, R171, and R174 promotes condensate solidification, with RNA-binding-deficient mutants exhibiting increased liquidity (PubMed:37306660). While intrinsically disordered regions (IDRs) are dispensable for phase behavior regulation (residues 500-739 deletion shows unchanged dynamics), residues 481-500 are crucial for VP35 interaction (PubMed:37306660, 37443171).
Extrinsic Partners & Regulations: VP35 (Q05127) is an essential extrinsic regulator that scaffolds NP-VP35 complex formation in vitro and enhances NP condensate liquidity in cellular contexts (PubMed:37598728, 37306660, 37443171). RNA binding solidifies condensates, with cellular RNA enabling NP-alone IB formation in cells (PubMed:37306660, 37598728). Ions modulate phase separation reversibly, with low NaCl (150mM) promoting and high NaCl (500mM) inhibiting droplet formation (PubMed:37598728). Viral polymerase L (Q05318) reduces NP-VP35 condensate liquidity in ternary complexes, while VP24 (Q05322) alters morphology to network-like structures (PubMed:37443171).

Overall Phase Separation Overview: SON forms immiscible, viscoelastic condensates within nuclear speckles in the nucleus, exhibiting minimal molecular dynamics (PubMed:38381607). Its material properties are regulated by phosphorylation: dephosphorylation increases cohesion (rendering it more viscoelastic), while phosphorylation decreases cohesion (making it more liquid-like) (PubMed:39755675). As a core scaffold, SON maintains nuclear speckle integrity, with depletion disrupting speckle organization (PubMed:39798570).
Functional Summary: SON phase separation regulates alternative splicing of chromatin-related mRNAs and organizes nuclear speckle subcompartments that selectively enrich clients like SRSF1 and U2 snRNA (PubMed:38381607). Phosphorylation-dependent cohesion dynamics directly control mRNA retention within speckles, with dephosphorylation increasing nuclear mRNA retention (PubMed:39755675). SON depletion disrupts pre-mRNA 3' end processing genome-wide and enlarges RBBP6 foci, confirming its essential role in maintaining nuclear speckle structure for efficient gene expression (PubMed:39798570).
Intrinsic Determinants & Regulations: The phase separation of SON is intrinsically regulated by phosphorylation states. Dephosphorylation enhances condensate cohesion and viscoelasticity, whereas phosphorylation reduces cohesion, promoting liquid-like dynamics (PubMed:39755675).
Extrinsic Partners & Regulations: SON's phase separation is extrinsically modulated by phosphatase PP1 (complexed with NIPP1), which dephosphorylates SON to increase cohesion and mRNA retention in nuclear speckles (PubMed:39755675). Conversely, the kinase DYRK3 phosphorylates SON, reducing cohesion and promoting mRNA release (PubMed:39755675). SON also functionally interacts with SRRM2 as a co-scaffold; their co-depletion disrupts nuclear speckle integrity (PubMed:39798570).

Overall Phase Separation Overview: TFEB undergoes self-driven phase separation (PubMed:35293953, 33290690, 33290695), forming liquid-like condensates primarily in the nucleus, where it associates with transcriptional condensates (PubMed:33290690, 33290695). Under specific conditions (e.g., high salt), it also forms cytoplasmic condensates (PubMed:35293953). These condensates exhibit liquid properties including rapid fluorescence recovery and spherical morphology, but demonstrate rigid interfacial boundaries and low fusion propensity (PubMed:35293953). Material state transitions occur from liquid to solid-like states in aged droplets, accelerated by small molecules or in disease models (PubMed:35293953).
Functional Summary: TFEB phase separation facilitates the assembly of dynamic transcriptional condensates that activate autophagy and lysosomal gene expression (PubMed:33290690, 33290695). Modulation of condensate material properties by Ro-3306 or vanillic acid enhances TFEB transcriptional activity, increasing lysosomal biogenesis and clearance of toxic aggregates (e.g., mutant huntingtin) independently of nuclear translocation (PubMed:35293953). Inhibition of phase separation by IPMK suppresses this transcriptional program and lysosomal function (PubMed:33290690, 33290695). Pathological liquid-to-solid transitions, accelerated by small molecules or disease conditions, impair condensate dynamics and may contribute to cytotoxicity (PubMed:35293953).
Intrinsic Determinants & Regulations: The phase separation of TFEB is intrinsically driven by its basic helix-loop-helix (bHLH) domain (PubMed:35293953, 33290690, 33290695). Charged residues (arginine/lysine) within this domain regulate fusion propensity, interfacial tension, and viscosity (PubMed:35293953). Mutation of eight basic residues to alanine (bHLH-B8A) reduces the LLPS concentration threshold, increases fusion frequency, and decreases surface rigidity (PubMed:35293953). Deletion of the bHLH domain abolishes phase separation capacity (PubMed:33290690, 33290695).
Extrinsic Partners & Regulations: TFEB phase separation is modulated by several extrinsic regulators. The protein IPMK binds directly to TFEB's bHLH domain, inhibiting phase separation and dissolving preformed condensates (PubMed:33290690, 33290695). Within nuclear condensates, TFEB co-localizes with the transcriptional co-activator MED1 and associates with target mRNAs like LAMP1 (PubMed:33290690, 33290695). Sodium ions (Na⁺) are essential for condensation, with droplet formation showing salt-concentration dependence and high salt inducing cytoplasmic puncta (PubMed:35293953). Small molecules Ro-3306 and vanillic acid initially increase droplet size and fusion but promote pathological liquid-to-solid transitions over time (PubMed:35293953).

Protein Name: Mediator of RNA polymerase II transcription subunit 15
Gene Names: GAL11 ABE1 MED15 RAR3 SDS4 SPT13
Overall Phase Separation Overview: Med15 undergoes partner-driven phase separation to form liquid-like condensates in the nucleus (PubMed:39717019, 36327976). It associates with transcriptional condensates during heat shock and co-phase separates with transcription factors Gcn4 and Msn2 in vitro, forming spherical droplets that exhibit fusion and sensitivity to 1,6-hexanediol (PubMed:39717019, 30449618, 36327976). These condensates recruit transcriptional machinery including Pol II and drive inter-chromosomal gene coalescence during stress responses (PubMed:36327976).
Functional Summary: Med15 condensates facilitate transcriptional activation of amino acid biosynthesis genes via Gcn4 and stress response genes via Msn2 (PubMed:39717019, 30449618). During heat shock, they enable 3D genome reorganization through intergenic coalescence of HSR genes, concentrating Mediator/Pol II for rapid stress response and cellular thermotolerance (PubMed:36327976). Dysregulation via leucine-rich inserts (e.g., 12L-Q1R) causes non-functional aggregation, impairing gene expression and stress adaptation (PubMed:39717019).
Intrinsic Determinants & Regulations: Phase separation is intrinsically regulated by Med15's Q1R region (amino acids 117-239), which is sufficient for co-condensation with transcription factors (PubMed:39717019). The polyglutamine (Q1) tract composition modulates activity and interaction strength but is not essential for droplet formation (PubMed:39717019). Leucine-rich sequences (e.g., 12L mutation) disrupt liquid properties, leading to non-functional aggregates (PubMed:39717019).
Extrinsic Partners & Regulations: Med15 co-phase separates with transcription factors Gcn4 and Msn2 in vitro, forming dynamic heterotypic droplets dependent on Gcn4's aromatic residues (PubMed:39717019, 30449618). During heat shock (39°C), it is recruited into Hsf1-driven transcriptional condensates with >70% co-localization, a process dissolved by 1,6-hexanediol (PubMed:36327976). Hsp70 represses condensate formation by binding Hsf1's CE2 domain, while Hsf1's N-terminal activation domain promotes Med15 recruitment (PubMed:36327976).

Gene Names: XRN1 DST2 KEM1 RAR5 SEP1 SKI1
Overall Phase Separation Overview: Xrn1 undergoes self-driven phase separation in vitro to form condensates enhanced by acidic pH (PubMed:36972455). In vivo, it primarily acts as a client protein recruited into liquid-like P-bodies and benomyl-induced granules (BIGs) in the cytoplasm (PubMed:35876801, 35806385, 27374333). These condensates exhibit liquid-like properties, including rapid dissolution upon 1,6-hexanediol treatment and fusion dynamics (PubMed:35876801, 35806385).
Functional Summary: Xrn1 phase separation facilitates mRNA decay by concentrating 5’→3’ exonuclease activity within P-bodies and BIGs, enabling efficient substrate degradation (PubMed:36972455, 27374333). This compartmentalization is scaffolded by proteins like Nst1, which assembles decapping complexes independent of RNA influx (PubMed:35806385). Differential composition of specialized condensates like BIGs suggests context-specific roles in mRNA regulation (PubMed:35876801).
Intrinsic Determinants & Regulations: The intrinsic phase separation of Xrn1 is pH-sensitive, with condensate formation significantly enhanced at pH 5.8 compared to neutral pH (PubMed:36972455). No specific domains, mutations, or post-translational modifications driving this behavior were identified in the provided data.
Extrinsic Partners & Regulations: Xrn1 recruitment to condensates is modulated by extrinsic partners: it co-scaffolds P-bodies and BIGs with core decapping proteins Dcp2, Edc3, Lsm1, and Dcp1, showing >85% colocalization (PubMed:35876801). It partitions into heterotypic condensates with Dcp1 and Dcp2 in vitro (PubMed:36972455) and is recruited to RNA-independent P-body scaffolds formed by Nst1 (PubMed:35806385). mRNA enhances Xrn1 partitioning into condensates, with ~2-fold increased recruitment in mRNA-accumulating mutants (PubMed:27374333), while RPL41A RNA tightens binding affinity at acidic pH (PubMed:36972455). Benomyl chemically induces BIG formation, a distinct P-body subtype (PubMed:35876801).

Overall Phase Separation Overview: Dbp1 undergoes phase separation primarily driven by its low-complexity domain (LCD) and RG/RGG motifs (PubMed:38637545, 39222785, 31435012). It forms liquid-like condensates in vitro, as observed through droplet formation and fusion (PubMed:38637545, 31435012), and exhibits temperature-dependent aggregation behavior modulated by RGG motif spacing (PubMed:39222785). While subcellular locations and membrane-less organelle associations are not specified in the provided data, phase separation occurs in purified protein systems and is sensitive to ionic conditions (PubMed:38637545).
Functional Summary: Dbp1 regulates RNA-containing organelles through ATP-dependent phase separation, where ATP hydrolysis induces compartment turnover and RNA release, suggesting control over RNA flux in biochemical reaction centers (PubMed:31435012). In engineered condensates (Dbp1-NOX fusion), phase separation creates a cationic microenvironment that enhances enzymatic activity (increased kcat) by concentrating substrates/cofactors, with greater enhancement observed in nanoclusters versus micron-sized condensates, demonstrating potential as designed biocatalytic microreactors (PubMed:38637545).
Intrinsic Determinants & Regulations: Phase separation is intrinsically regulated by the N-terminal LCD (residues 1-155) featuring a +11 net charge that enables multivalent electrostatic interactions through arginine/aromatic residues (PubMed:38637545). Critical spacing (≤6 amino acids) between RG/RGG motifs is required, with increased RGG repeats enhancing phase separation when properly spaced (PubMed:39222785). The dimeric state of fused partner proteins may further promote multivalent interactions (PubMed:38637545). Mutations altering RGG motif spacing (e.g., N78R with 6aa spacing) enable aggregation, while larger spacings (>63aa) prevent phase separation (PubMed:39222785).
Extrinsic Partners & Regulations: Dbp1 phase separation requires ATP and RNA as essential co-factors for liquid droplet formation in vitro (PubMed:31435012). When fused to NOX (Dbp1-NOX), condensates selectively recruit NADH (Kp=12.5±3.3) and FAD (Kp=4.7±1.1) via electrostatic attraction, enhancing enzymatic activity within the dense phase (PubMed:38637545). Phase separation is inhibited by NaCl concentrations >300 mM, which dissolve both micron-sized condensates and nanoclusters (PubMed:38637545).

Overall Phase Separation Overview: APC undergoes self-driven phase separation (class: PS-self) to form biomolecular condensates (PubMed:37047451, 38279052, 33060621). It primarily localizes to the cytoplasm and nucleus, associating with destruction complex condensates and centrosome-associated structures (PubMed:35867833, 36037369, 38279052). These condensates exhibit liquid-like properties, evidenced by droplet fusion and rapid FRAP recovery, but undergo pathological liquid-to-solid transitions when aged or under specific conditions (PubMed:33060621, 38279052).
Functional Summary: APC phase separation organizes the β-catenin destruction complex, concentrating kinases (GSK3β/CK1α) to enable efficient β-catenin phosphorylation and degradation, thereby suppressing Wnt signaling (PubMed:36037369, 38279052, 33060621). In colorectal cancer, truncating mutations (e.g., R1450*/R876*) maintain condensate formation but disrupt kinase recruitment, leading to β-catenin accumulation, nuclear translocation, and Wnt-driven tumorigenesis (PubMed:38279052, 33060621). Centrosomal association with Dvl2 condensates fine-tunes Wnt signal transduction during cell cycle progression, dissolving during mitosis while remaining dispensable for pathway activation (PubMed:35867833). Pathological liquid-to-solid transitions generate cytotoxic aggregates linked to disease progression (PubMed:33060621).
Intrinsic Determinants & Regulations: Phase separation is intrinsically driven by multiple disordered regions: the ASAD domain (residues 396-426) utilizes hydrophobic patches (Leu3/Ile7/Tyr10/Trp17) and charged residues (PubMed:37047451), while 20R repeats (e.g., 20R3 SLSAL motif, 20R5 SLSSL motif) and SAMP motifs provide essential multivalency (PubMed:33060621, 37047451). A critical IDR (aa2157-2653) autonomously drives liquid droplet formation (PubMed:38279052). Phosphorylation at specific sites (S1501/S1505/S1504/S1507 in 20R3; S1857/S1861/S1863 in 20R5) inhibits phase separation, narrowing or abolishing droplet formation (PubMed:37047451). Disease-associated truncations (R1450*, R876*) retain phase separation capacity but disrupt functional organization (PubMed:38279052).
Extrinsic Partners & Regulations: APC co-phase separates with Axin through multivalent interactions, significantly enhancing condensate stability and reducing Axin's critical concentration for assembly (PubMed:33060621, 38279052). It recruits β-catenin, GSK3β, and CK1α into destruction complexes for phosphorylation cascades, though kinase recruitment fails in APC-truncated mutants (PubMed:36037369, 38279052). APC also colocalizes within Dvl2 centrosomal condensates alongside Wnt components like Axin1 and LRP6 (PubMed:35867833). Phase separation is salt-sensitive, following the Hofmeister series, with droplet formation optimized at intermediate ionic strengths (186-336 mM) (PubMed:37047451).

Overall Phase Separation Overview: Oskar (P25158) undergoes self-driven phase separation to form biomolecular condensates independently in both cytoplasm and nucleus, primarily associated with Germ Granules (PubMed:37384531, 30260314). These condensates exhibit hybrid material properties: liquid-like dynamics (fusion, FRAP recovery <40-46.8%) coexist with hydrogel-like stability (resistance to dissolution, persistent anchoring) (PubMed:37384531, 30260314). Granules mature through state transitions from small solid structures to hollow cores in primordial germ cells (PubMed:30260314). Oskar nucleates granule assembly in vivo and heterologous systems (HEK293T/S2R+ cells), with RNA-independent nucleation but RNA-modulated size control (PubMed:37384531, 39112465). Additional associations include Endoplasmic Reticulum and Nuclear Pore Complexes (PubMed:37384531).
Functional Summary: Oskar-mediated phase separation nucleates germ granules essential for primordial germ cell specification, embryonic patterning, and mRNA regulation (e.g., nanos sequestration) (PubMed:37384531, 30260314). Nuclear granules promote germ cell divisions, with ablation reducing germ cell numbers by 39.3% (PubMed:30260314). Aberrant phase transitions may underlie pathologies through aggregation or dysregulated mRNA handling (PubMed:37384531). Spatiotemporal control of granule number, size, and distribution is critical for developmental fidelity (PubMed:37384531).
Intrinsic Determinants & Regulations: Phase separation is intrinsically driven by synergistic action of multiple domains: linker regions L1/L2, LOTUS, and SGNH, with no single domain being essential (PubMed:30260314). The short isoform (lacking N-terminal 138aa) is necessary and sufficient for condensation, while the long isoform fails to form granules (PubMed:30260314). The RNA-binding SGNH domain is dispensable for nucleation, though its deletion (ΔSGNH) yields larger granules (PubMed:37384531, 30260314). Nuclear localization signal 1 (NLS1) is critical for nuclear granule assembly, with CRISPR-mediated ablation (OskΔNLS) eliminating nuclear granules and impairing germ cell proliferation (PubMed:30260314). Oligomerization, low-complexity sequences, and RNA-binding capacity are dispensable for condensation (PubMed:30260314).
Extrinsic Partners & Regulations: Oskar recruits protein partners including Vasa (core component with similar dynamics), Aubergine (RNA-dependent recruitment), and Piwi (nuclear granule client) (PubMed:37384531, 30260314). Germ granule mRNAs (e.g., nanos, pgc) limit condensate size and enable compositional specificity but are dispensable for nucleation and persistence (PubMed:37384531). MBP recruitment dissolves nuclear condensates via light-induced dissolution (PubMed:39112465). RNA removal increases granule size without dissolution, confirming RNA's role as a size modulator rather than scaffold (PubMed:37384531).

Overall Phase Separation Overview: Ydj1 undergoes self-driven phase separation in vitro, forming hydrogel-like condensates (PubMed:33229560), and participates in cytoplasmic foci formation during osmotic shock in vivo (PubMed:31285266). It does not undergo homotypic phase separation under certain conditions but co-phase separates with partners like the prion variant Y145X to form dynamic liquid-like condensates (PubMed:39826709). Ydj1 associates with stress granules through recruitment into Pab1 condensates (PubMed:35490076) and forms osmotic shock foci (PubMed:31285266).
Functional Summary: Ydj1 contributes to stress response by forming cytoplasmic foci during osmotic shock (PubMed:31285266) and regulating Pab1 condensate disassembly during heat stress (PubMed:35490076). Through heterotypic phase separation with Y145X, it prevents pathological amyloid formation by sequestering the prion variant in dynamic condensates, serving a protein quality control function (PubMed:39826709).
Intrinsic Determinants & Regulations: Phase separation of Ydj1 is intrinsically driven by its flexible G/F-rich region, enabling self-assembly into hydrogel-like condensates (PubMed:33229560).
Extrinsic Partners & Regulations: Ydj1 co-phase separates with the prion protein variant Y145X via electrostatic and hydrophobic interactions, forming dynamic liquid condensates inhibited by high salt concentrations (≥75 mM NaCl) (PubMed:39826709). It interacts with RNA to form multiphasic condensates (PubMed:39826709) and is recruited into Pab1 condensates where it inhibits their dispersal (PubMed:35490076).

MLO Types: Htt inclusion; Hyperosmotic shock foci; Stress granule
Overall Phase Separation Overview: Hsp104 (P31539) is a cytoplasmic disaggregase that regulates phase transitions of various biomolecular condensates in Saccharomyces cerevisiae. It associates with stress granules (PubMed:35490076, 26359986, 26238190), osmotic shock foci (PubMed:31285266), and mutant Huntingtin inclusion bodies (PubMed:31527136). Hsp104 facilitates material state transitions, enabling solid-to-liquid phase transitions of heat-induced aggregates (e.g., FlucSM) for dissolution (PubMed:38025775) and promoting amyloid formation during Nup100FG condensate maturation (PubMed:39725032). It co-localizes with heat-induced aggregates of proteins like Osh3 (PubMed:32169085).
Functional Summary: Hsp104-mediated phase regulation is crucial for cellular proteostasis. It enables clearance of heat-induced aggregates (e.g., FlucSM) through chaperone-assisted dissolution, preventing proteostasis collapse (PubMed:38025775). In stress granules, Hsp104 facilitates Pab1 condensate disassembly for stress recovery (PubMed:35490076). It scaffolds cytoprotective mutant Huntingtin inclusion bodies that enable dynamic mHtt exchange and degradation (PubMed:31527136). Dysregulation contributes to pathological outcomes, as Hsp104 promotes amyloid-like maturation of Nup100FG condensates (PubMed:39725032), while its absence impairs aggregate dissolution and cellular fitness (PubMed:38025775, 35490076).
Intrinsic Determinants & Regulations: No intrinsic molecular features (e.g., domains, mutations, PTMs) driving Hsp104 phase separation are described in the provided literature (PubMed:38025775, 35490076, 31285266, 26359986, 26238190, 32169085, 31527136, 39725032).
Extrinsic Partners & Regulations: Hsp104 function is modulated through interactions with client proteins and environmental stressors. It is essential for the dissolution of FlucSM aggregates via solid-to-liquid phase transitions (PubMed:38025775) and disassembles Pab1 condensates in concert with Hsp70 and Sis1 (PubMed:35490076). Hsp104 co-localizes with misfolded proteins in Nrp1-containing stress granules (PubMed:26238190) and Osh3 aggregates during heat stress (PubMed:32169085). It scaffolds mutant Huntingtin inclusion body formation (PubMed:31527136) and promotes amyloid maturation of Nup100FG condensates (PubMed:39725032). Heat stress (42°C) induces its recruitment to aggregates (PubMed:32169085).

Protein Name: Peroxisomal long-chain fatty acid import protein 1
Overall Phase Separation Overview: Pat1 (P34230) exhibits context-dependent phase separation behavior. It undergoes self-driven phase separation in vitro to form dynamic liquid-like condensates that mature into aspherical networks with reduced reversibility over time (PubMed:36972455). However, in vivo and in heterotypic contexts, it primarily acts as an essential scaffold for P-body assembly without forming homotypic condensates (PubMed:35876801, 30648970). It localizes to the cytoplasm and associates exclusively with P-bodies, showing specific recruitment under glucose deprivation conditions (PubMed:35876801, 36972455, 30648970). Material state transitions from liquid-like to less reversible structures are observed in vitro, accelerated by time but delayed by RNA (PubMed:36972455).
Functional Summary: Pat1-mediated phase separation is essential for stress-responsive mRNA regulation. As a core scaffold, it enables P-body assembly for mRNA decay and storage during glucose deprivation and other stresses (PubMed:35876801, 36972455, 30648970). By concentrating decay factors like Dhh1 and antagonizing Not1-mediated disassembly, it maintains functional mRNA processing compartments critical for cell viability under stress (PubMed:30648970). Differential inclusion in P-body subtypes suggests functional partitioning of mRNA substrates (PubMed:35876801). While no direct pathological implications were reported, phosphorylation provides regulatory control that could prevent aberrant condensation (PubMed:30648970, 35876801).
Intrinsic Determinants & Regulations: Phase separation is intrinsically regulated by distinct domains: the central structured domain (aa 241-422) serves as the primary driver for homotypic LLPS in vitro (PubMed:36972455), while the N-terminal domain (Dhh1-binding via DETF motif) and C-terminal RNA-binding domain are essential for heterotypic P-body assembly (PubMed:30648970). Phosphorylation at S456/S457 by PKA inhibits RNA binding and suppresses P-body formation (PubMed:30648970, 35876801). Mutations disrupting Dhh1-binding (Pat1⁴ᴬ⁻ᴰʰʰ¹) or mimicking phosphorylation (Pat1ᴱᴱ) impair scaffolding function (PubMed:30648970). Acidic pH enhances phase separation propensity (PubMed:36972455).
Extrinsic Partners & Regulations: Pat1's phase separation is extrinsically regulated by cooperative partners and RNA. It co-assembles with Dhh1, Edc3, and Lsm1-7 proteins in heterotypic condensates, forming epistatic interaction networks essential for P-body integrity (PubMed:36972455, 30648970). RNA molecules (RPL41A, MFA2 mRNA, polyU) play dual roles: they lower the concentration threshold for condensation and delay maturation by maintaining reversibility (PubMed:36972455, 30648970). Not1 dissolves condensates via ATPase activation (PubMed:30648970). Environmental factors modulate behavior: acidic pH promotes assembly while physiological salt concentrations regulate droplet formation (PubMed:36972455).

Overall Phase Separation Overview: BMI1 (P35226) does not undergo self-driven phase separation under basal conditions and primarily acts as a client protein recruited into partner-driven condensates within the nucleus (PubMed:37756159, 34620850, 33169020). It associates with nuclear bodies and Polycomb bodies, exhibiting enrichment in CBX2-driven condensates (PubMed:37756159, 33169020). Upon light-induced oligomerization, BMI1 forms dynamic liquid-like condensates characterized by rapid fluorescence recovery and fusion behavior (PubMed:34620850). These condensates maintain a liquid state without reported material state transitions under tested conditions (PubMed:34620850, 33169020).
Functional Summary: BMI1 phase separation facilitates epigenetic silencing through PRC1-mediated formation of repressive chromatin compartments. These condensates enable reading of H3K27me3 marks and writing of H2AK119Ub repressive histone modifications, driving chromatin compaction (PubMed:34620850). Pathological hyper-clustering of BMI1 condensates—observed in MLL4-deficient states—increases nuclear stiffness, impairs mesenchymal stem cell differentiation, and contributes to Kabuki syndrome pathogenesis (PubMed:33169020). Dysregulation disrupts nuclear architecture without reported cytotoxicity (PubMed:33169020).
Intrinsic Determinants & Regulations: Phase separation of BMI1 is intrinsically regulated by its RAWUL oligomerization domain, which is essential for de novo condensate formation. Removal of this domain (ΔOD mutation) abolishes phase separation capacity (PubMed:34620850). In contrast, the intrinsically disordered region (IDR) is dispensable for droplet formation but partially mediates self-interaction within condensates (PubMed:34620850). No disease-associated mutations or post-translational modifications directly regulating phase separation were reported (PubMed:37756159, 34620850, 33169020).
Extrinsic Partners & Regulations: BMI1 phase separation is extrinsically modulated through heterotypic interactions with multiple partners. It is recruited into condensates formed by CBX2 scaffolds and co-assembles with RING1B in Polycomb bodies (PubMed:37756159, 33169020). BMI1 reciprocally recruits PRC1 components PHC1 and RNF2 into its own condensates, demonstrating bidirectional partnership within the complex (PubMed:34620850). Condensate formation is enriched at H3K27me3-marked chromatin regions and exhibits hyper-clustering upon MLL4 loss-of-function (PubMed:33169020).

Overall Phase Separation Overview: NF2 (P35240) exhibits context-dependent phase separation behaviors. Wild-type NF2 undergoes self-driven phase separation (PS-self) forming solid-like condensates in the cytoplasm that age into detergent-resistant fibers in vitro and in mammalian cells (PubMed:39116228). However, specific mutants demonstrate distinct behaviors: the c.770-784del mutant forms liquid-like cytoplasmic puncta requiring LATS for co-phase separation (PS-other), while patient-derived FERM domain mutants (L46R/L64P/L141P) form liquid-like condensates induced by activated IRF3 (PubMed:36300003, 34453890). Material states range from liquid to solid, with wild-type NF2 undergoing liquid-to-solid transitions in vitro (PubMed:39116228).
Functional Summary: Phase separation has significant pathophysiological consequences. Cytoplasmic NF2mut-LATS condensates sequester LATS from the plasma membrane, inhibiting Hippo signaling and promoting meningioma tumorigenesis (PubMed:36300003). For FERM mutants, IRF3-induced condensates sequester TBK1/IRF3 and recruit RACK1-PP2A to dephosphorylate TBK1, suppressing cGAS-STING signaling and compromising antiviral defense, DNA damage responses, and antitumor immunity (PubMed:34453890). Pathological condensates in human schwannomas correlate with tumorigenesis, and liquid-to-solid transitions in wild-type NF2 may contribute to cytotoxicity (PubMed:34453890, 39116228).
Intrinsic Determinants & Regulations: Phase separation is intrinsically regulated by NF2's structural domains and mutations. The FERM domain's hydrophobic core stability controls phase behavior, where mutations (L46R/L64P/L141P) cause conformational changes promoting oligomerization (PubMed:34453890). The LATS-binding domain (residues 69-100) is essential for co-phase separation with LATS, while the IDR (308-590) is dispensable (PubMed:36300003). Phosphorylation at S518 by TBK1 stabilizes an open conformation facilitating oligomerization (PubMed:34453890). The c.770-784del mutation in the F3 module disrupts membrane binding, enabling cytoplasmic condensation (PubMed:36300003).
Extrinsic Partners & Regulations: Phase separation is extrinsically regulated by partner proteins and signaling contexts. LATS acts as essential co-scaffold for c.770-784del mutant condensates, forming heterogeneous cytoplasmic droplets (PubMed:36300003). For FERM mutants, activated IRF3 directly induces phase separation via FERM domain binding, while TBK1 recruitment enables phosphorylation-dependent regulation (PubMed:34453890). The RACK1-PP2A complex is functionally recruited into mutant condensates to deactivate TBK1 (PubMed:34453890). Phase separation requires innate immune activation (MAVS/STING pathways) and is disrupted by 1,6-hexanediol (PubMed:34453890).

Overall Phase Separation Overview: Nup62 (P37198) exhibits context-dependent phase separation behavior primarily associated with the nuclear pore complex (PubMed:36690069, 36482422, 34059832). While it does not undergo self-driven phase separation alone in certain conditions (PubMed:36690069), it forms non-spherical assemblies under molecular crowding (PubMed:34059832). Nup62 readily co-phase separates with partners like FUS into amorphous, solid-like assemblies with reduced dynamics (PubMed:36690069, 34059832), and co-aggregates with TDP-43 into amyloid-like fibrils in pathological contexts (PubMed:36482422). RNA promotes its incorporation into liquid-like FUS droplets, demonstrating material state versatility (PubMed:34059832).
Functional Summary: Nup62's aberrant phase transitions disrupt nucleocytoplasmic transport and contribute to neurodegeneration. Cytoplasmic co-phase separation with FUS or co-aggregation with TDP-43 mislocalizes nuclear pore components, impairing transport in amyotrophic lateral sclerosis (ALS) and frontotemporal dementia (FTD) (PubMed:36690069, 36482422, 34059832). These pathological solid assemblies recruit phospho-TDP-43 and form amyloid-like fibrils (PubMed:36482422). Therapeutic dissolution of aggregates by KPNB1 restores transport and reduces toxicity, highlighting potential treatment strategies (PubMed:36482422).
Intrinsic Determinants & Regulations: Phase separation is intrinsically regulated by Nup62's domain architecture. Its C-terminal domain (CTD, aa 301–522) with coiled-coil structure is essential for FUS binding and co-phase separation (PubMed:36690069). The N-terminal domain (NTD, aa 1–300) contains phenylalanine-glycine (FG) repeats that mediate multivalent interactions for TDP-43 co-aggregation (PubMed:36482422, 34059832). Mutation of NTD phenylalanines (F->A) abolishes modulatory effects on FUS droplets, confirming their functional role (PubMed:36690069).
Extrinsic Partners & Regulations: Nup62's phase behavior is extrinsically modulated by protein partners and molecular conditions. It co-phase separates with FUS to form solid-like assemblies, accelerated by FUS interaction (PubMed:36690069, 34059832). Co-aggregation with TDP-43 occurs via FG-repeat/PrLD interactions, forming pathological hydrogels (PubMed:36482422). RNA promotes Nup62 incorporation into liquid FUS droplets, inhibiting aberrant assembly (PubMed:34059832). The karyopherin KPNB1 dissolves aggregates by disrupting FG interactions (PubMed:36482422). Ionic strength modulates phase separation, with higher salt concentrations reducing assembly formation (PubMed:36690069).

Overall Phase Separation Overview: Ph (P39769) undergoes phase separation primarily driven by its SAM domain, forming liquid-like condensates in the nucleus and cytoplasm (PubMed:36412795, 38257239, 33154383). It associates with Polycomb bodies – membrane-less organelles involved in gene regulation – where its condensates exhibit fusion dynamics and chromatin interactions (PubMed:36412795, 38257239). While typically liquid-like, these condensates can transition to an arrested non-fusing state when exposed to specific partners like PRC1ΔPh (PubMed:38257239).
Functional Summary: Ph condensates form functional Polycomb bodies that compact chromatin and create biochemical compartments for epigenetic regulation (PubMed:36412795, 38257239, 33154383). They recruit PRC1 components and enhance H2A ubiquitylation ~2-fold, crucial for gene silencing (PubMed:33154383, 38257239). Sequential action with PSC-CTR establishes stable repressed chromatin domains (PubMed:38257239). Disruption via domain deletions (e.g., ΔIDR2 causing chromatin exclusion) or polymerization mutations impairs normal epigenetic function (PubMed:36412795, 33154383).
Intrinsic Determinants & Regulations: Phase separation is intrinsically regulated by multiple domains: The SAM domain is essential for polymerization and condensate formation (PubMed:36412795, 38257239, 33154383), while HD1/FCS domains are required for DNA binding (PubMed:33154383). Three N-terminal IDRs (IDR1-aa1-400, IDR2-aa400-800, IDR3-aa800-1200) modulate behavior: IDR2 promotes chromatin binding and small condensates, IDR1 and IDR2 synergize to enhance nucleation, while IDR3 inhibits other IDRs (PubMed:36412795). Acetylation prevents DNA binding and phase separation (PubMed:33154383). Polymerization-interface mutations (L1547R, L1565R) impair but don't abolish phase separation, yielding smaller condensates (PubMed:33154383, 38257239).
Extrinsic Partners & Regulations: Chromatin/DNA serves as an essential scaffold for phase separation (PubMed:38257239, 33154383). RNA incorporates into condensates (PubMed:33154383), while high salt (>125 mM NaCl) inhibits formation (PubMed:33154383). ATP (8 mM) dissolves condensates (PubMed:33154383). Exposure to PRC1 lacking Ph (PRC1ΔPh) or PSC-CTR triggers liquid-to-arrested state transitions (PubMed:38257239).

Overall Phase Separation Overview: MATR3 undergoes self-driven phase separation forming liquid-like condensates primarily in the nucleus, with additional cytoplasmic localization observed under mutation conditions (PubMed:35252808, 33097688, 31019288). It forms dynamic, shell-like spherical structures (anisosome-like) in the nucleus, exhibiting rapid FRAP recovery indicative of liquid properties (PubMed:35252808). Disease-associated mutations (S85C, P154S, T622A) induce material state transitions from liquid to gel/solid states characterized by irregular morphology and loss of dynamics (PubMed:35252808). The F115C mutation enables cytoplasmic aggregation and phase separation (PubMed:33097688).
Functional Summary: Aberrant MATR3 phase separation is mechanistically linked to neurodegenerative pathologies. Disease mutations (S85C, P154S, T622A) cause pathological liquid-to-solid transitions that drive proteotoxicity in amyotrophic lateral sclerosis (ALS) and frontotemporal dementia (FTD) (PubMed:35252808). The F115C mutant contributes to TDP-43 pathology in ALS and frontotemporal lobar degeneration by forming cytoplasmic aggregates that recruit TDP-43 (PubMed:33097688). These pathological transitions lead to cytotoxic fibril formation and are rescued by engineered Hsp104 variants that reverse misfolding (PubMed:35252808).
Intrinsic Determinants & Regulations: Phase separation is intrinsically driven by MATR3's N-terminal intrinsically disordered region (IDR; aa 1-397) and modulated by RNA recognition motifs (RRMs) (PubMed:35252808, 31019288). The IDR enables multiple foci formation while RRMs prevent coalescence into single large structures (PubMed:35252808). RRM2 deletion promotes phase separation, indicating RNA binding normally suppresses condensation (PubMed:31019288). Disease mutations significantly alter behavior: S85C inhibits droplet formation and stability, P154S/T622A cause liquid-to-solid transitions with impaired mobility, and F115C enables cytoplasmic aggregation (PubMed:35252808, 33097688, 31019288).
Extrinsic Partners & Regulations: MATR3 phase separation is regulated by RNA availability and protein partners. RNA binding suppresses condensation, with impaired RNA binding (via RRM2 deletion) enhancing phase separation (PubMed:31019288). MATR3 recruits TDP-43 into condensates when TDP-43's RNA-binding capability is compromised (RRM1-disabled constructs) or as isolated prion-like domains (PubMed:31019288). The F115C mutant forms cytoplasmic aggregates that co-phase separate with and recruit TDP-43 (PubMed:33097688).

Overall Phase Separation Overview: SOX2 (P48431) exhibits distinct phase separation behaviors across cellular contexts. It undergoes self-driven reentrant phase separation in vitro, forming liquid-like droplets at both low (50 mM) and high (2.15 M) KCl concentrations, with high circularity (>95%) indicating liquid properties (PubMed:33597515). In the nucleus, SOX2 forms heterogeneous distributions characterized by diffuse 'islands' and sparse diffraction-limited foci, displaying phase separation behavior classified as PS-other (PubMed:36309135). It co-condenses with p300 to form transcriptional condensates (PubMed:33651988) but does not associate with predefined membrane-less organelles. SOX2 disrupts condensates of steroid receptors like glucocorticoid receptor (GR) without direct binding (PubMed:36309135).
Functional Summary: SOX2 phase separation functionally modulates transcriptional programs. By disrupting steroid receptor condensates (e.g., GR) and redistributing coactivators like NCoA-2, it alters transcriptional outcomes (PubMed:36309135). Its co-condensation with p300 enables formation of transcriptional clusters, potentially regulating gene activation (PubMed:33651988). Aberrant SOX2 expression in cancer may dysregulate steroid hormone responses through these condensate-modifying activities (PubMed:36309135).
Intrinsic Determinants & Regulations: The phase separation of SOX2 is intrinsically regulated by its Transactivation Domain (TAD, amino acids 121-317), which drives co-condensation with p300 (PubMed:33651988). No other intrinsic domains, mutations, post-translational modifications, or oligomerization features regulating its phase behavior are reported in the provided data.
Extrinsic Partners & Regulations: SOX2 phase separation is modulated by key extrinsic partners and conditions. It co-condenses with p300 scaffold protein through interactions mediated by its TAD domain (PubMed:33651988). SOX2 redistributes coactivator NCoA-2 to its nuclear islands without direct binding and disrupts GR condensates (PubMed:36309135). Ion concentration critically regulates its behavior, with KCl inducing reentrant phase separation (droplet formation at 50 mM and 2.15 M KCl, absence at 500 mM) through hydrophobic and non-ionic interactions (PubMed:33597515).

Overall Phase Separation Overview: C/EBPα (P49715) undergoes self-driven phase separation to form liquid-like condensates in vitro and forms dynamic nuclear foci in vivo, primarily localized in the nucleus (PubMed:37516962, 37903757). It associates with transcriptional condensates and forms nuclear foci that partially colocalize with MED1 during cellular processes like B cell-to-macrophage transdifferentiation and hematopoiesis (PubMed:37516962). The condensates exhibit liquid-like properties including rapid fluorescence recovery after photobleaching (FRAP), droplet fusion, and spherical morphology. Material state transitions to solid aggregates are not observed, though aromatic residue mutations (e.g., AroLITE) or heterodimerization with C/EBPα-p30 can inhibit phase separation (PubMed:37516962, 37903757, 38969762).
Functional Summary: Phase separation drives chromatin compartment switching and long-range hub formation during cellular differentiation, activating myeloid genes (e.g., CSF1R, PU1) while repressing B cell genes (e.g., EBF1) (PubMed:37516962). Enhanced condensation capacity correlates with genomic binding strength and reprogramming efficiency (PubMed:38969762). In acute myeloid leukemia (AML), liquid-liquid phase separation is essential for differentiation induced by chemotherapeutic agents; pathological inhibition by C/EBPα-p30 contributes to AML progression by disrupting condensate formation and myeloid gene activation (PubMed:37903757). Mutations impairing phase separation (e.g., AroLITE, S16A) disrupt chromatin reorganization and transcriptional rewiring during transdifferentiation (PubMed:37516962, 37903757).
Intrinsic Determinants & Regulations: Phase separation is intrinsically driven by the N-terminal intrinsically disordered region (IDR, residues 1–255), where hydrophobic interactions involving aromatic residues (including specific tyrosines and phenylalanines) are essential (PubMed:37516962). Optimized dispersion of aromatic residues (AroPERFECT) enhances liquid-like dynamics and functional activity, while substitutions (AroLITE) abolish homotypic condensation (PubMed:38969762, 37516962). Homodimerization via the leucine zipper domain (residues 287–322) and phosphorylation at serine 16 (S16) critically promote phase separation, with phosphomimetic mutations (S16E) enhancing condensate formation (PubMed:37903757).
Extrinsic Partners & Regulations: C/EBPα co-condenses with transcriptional regulators including MED1 (which enhances droplet size), PU1, PPARG2, and IKAROS in heterotypic nuclear foci, demonstrating cooperative assembly in transcriptional hubs (PubMed:37516962). Hyperosmotic stress induced by mannitol triggers phase separation in cells, while heterodimerization with the isoform C/EBPα-p30 inhibits condensation by disrupting homodimerization at high stoichiometric ratios (PubMed:37903757). No extrinsic chemical partners beyond mannitol were identified across studies (PubMed:38969762, 37516962, 37903757).

Overall Phase Separation Overview: VASP undergoes self-driven phase separation (class: PS-self) to form dynamic liquid-like condensates in vitro, exhibiting fusion, wetting, and rapid fluorescence recovery after photobleaching (FRAP) (PubMed:37425724, 38405682, 39914390). These condensates are primarily cytoplasmic and associate with focal adhesions where they partition into LIMD1 biomolecular condensates (PubMed:33891898). Actin polymerization within droplets drives morphological transitions from spheres to rings, ellipsoids, and linear bundles; this liquid state can shift toward solid-like behavior under high crowding conditions (10% PEG) that impair deformation (PubMed:38405682).
Functional Summary: VASP phase separation orchestrates actin cytoskeletal remodeling by mediating competition between filament branching (Arp2/3-dependent) and bundling, enabling formation of aster structures that model filopodia emergence from lamellipodia during cell migration (PubMed:37425724, 38405682). This process facilitates force-sensitive recruitment to focal adhesions via LIMD1 condensates, regulating adhesion maturation, cellular traction forces, and stiffness-guided migration (durotaxis) (PubMed:33891898). Liquid-like droplet properties are essential for actin filament reorganization into bundles; impairment of F-actin binding or excessive crowding disrupts bundling capability, highlighting the mechanistic link between condensate fluidity and cytoskeletal function (PubMed:38405682, 39914390).
Intrinsic Determinants & Regulations: VASP phase separation is intrinsically regulated by its tetramerization domain, which enables multivalent interactions essential for condensate formation (PubMed:37425724, 38405682, 39914390). Mutations in functional domains critically modulate behavior: RK236,237EE substitutions in the G-actin binding (GAB) domain reduce actin partitioning but permit partial droplet deformation, while KR275,276EE/K278E/K280E mutations in the F-actin binding (FAB) domain prevent internal filament organization and abolish deformation (PubMed:38405682). The EVH1 domain facilitates co-condensation with partners through multivalent proline-rich interactions (PubMed:39914390).
Extrinsic Partners & Regulations: VASP condensates recruit actin monomers and filaments, whose polymerization drives droplet deformation and bundle formation (PubMed:37425724, 38405682, 39914390). The Arp2/3 complex modulates actin organization: it inhibits bundling at low actin:VASP ratios but promotes aster formation with core-spoke architecture at high ratios, requiring N-WASP for activation (PubMed:37425724). VASP co-condenses with Lamellipodin via EVH1-mediated interactions, enhancing actin bundling without crowding agents (PubMed:39914390). Additionally, VASP partitions into LIMD1 condensates at focal adhesions under mechanosensitive regulation (PubMed:33891898).

Overall Phase Separation Overview: VCP (p97) does not autonomously undergo phase separation but is recruited to various membrane-less organelles including arsenite-induced stress granules in the cytoplasm, FUS cytoplasmic granules, and nuclear proteasome foci (PubMed:29804830, 35445401, 32025036). It regulates the material properties of these condensates, facilitating stress granule clearance through proteasomal recruitment and modulating FUS granule stability via ATP-dependent mechanisms without undergoing autonomous state transitions (PubMed:29804830, 35445401).
Functional Summary: VCP serves as a critical regulator of proteostasis within condensates: it enables stress granule clearance by recruiting the 26S proteasome to degrade ubiquitylated substrates, prevents aberrant granule persistence linked to ALS/IBMPFD, and acts as a biphasic timer for FUS granule dissolution to inhibit pathological fibrillization (PubMed:29804830, 35445401). In nuclear proteasome foci, it enhances degradation efficiency under hyperosmotic stress (PubMed:32025036). Dysfunction via mutations (R155H) or impaired recruitment accelerates liquid-to-solid transitions in stress granules and FUS condensates, directly contributing to neurodegenerative pathogenesis (PubMed:29804830, 35445401).
Intrinsic Determinants & Regulations: The hexameric AAA ATPase domains of VCP, containing 12 ATPase domains, intrinsically enable its regulatory function by hydrolyzing ATP to modulate condensate stability (PubMed:35445401). Pathogenic mutations including R155H impair stress granule clearance capacity, while the A232E mutation in the ATPase domain alters FUS granule dynamics and promotes cytoplasmic mislocalization (PubMed:29804830, 35445401).
Extrinsic Partners & Regulations: VCP recruitment is mediated by scaffold proteins: ZFAND1 recruits it to arsenite-induced stress granules, FUS enables its colocalization to cytoplasmic granules, and RAD23B/UBE3A facilitate nuclear proteasome focus association (PubMed:29804830, 35445401, 32025036). Its function is modulated by ATP concentrations (optimal at ~1mM) where ATP depletion rigidifies FUS granules, while arsenite stress specifically induces its interactions with degradation machinery (PubMed:35445401, 29804830). Pathological FUS P525L mutation reduces VCP affinity, extending granule persistence (PubMed:35445401).

Protein Name: Eukaryotic translation initiation factor 3 subunit B
Overall Phase Separation Overview: eIF3η is recruited into stress granules in the cytoplasm through partner-dependent mechanisms rather than self-driven phase separation (PubMed:39306064, 30893049, 29262335). It forms puncta co-localizing with the scaffold proteins G3BP1 and G3BP2 under Cr(VI), arsenic, or rG4C2 RNA stress, exhibiting liquid-like material properties within these condensates (PubMed:39306064, 29262335, 30893049). No material state transitions are reported for eIF3η itself.
Functional Summary: eIF3η enrichment in stress granules facilitates stress-induced translational arrest during cellular stress responses (PubMed:29262335). Pathologically, aberrant condensation driven by expanded rG4C2 RNA disrupts RNA granule homeostasis, contributing to C9-ALS/FTD pathogenesis (PubMed:29262335). Its consistent presence in stress granules under diverse stressors (Cr(VI), arsenic, optical induction) confirms its role as a core stress response component (PubMed:39306064, 30893049).
Intrinsic Determinants & Regulations: No intrinsic domains, mutations, or molecular features driving eIF3η phase separation are specified in the provided data (PubMed:39306064, 30893049, 29262335).
Extrinsic Partners & Regulations: eIF3η recruitment requires extrinsic scaffolds: It co-localizes with G3BP1 and G3BP2, which are essential for stress granule integrity (PubMed:39306064). Condensation is RNA-dependent, as rG4C2 repeats promote its partitioning into stress granules in a length- and structure-sensitive manner, with optimal assembly at intermediate salt concentrations (PubMed:29262335). eIF3η also co-partitions with multiple stress granule components including PABP, TDP-43, TIA1, eIF4G, FUS, and polyadenylated mRNAs in optically induced G3BP1 scaffolds (PubMed:30893049).

Overall Phase Separation Overview: Histone H1 undergoes partner-dependent phase separation, requiring nucleic acids or proteins rather than self-assembly (PubMed:35484234, PubMed:31952807, PubMed:37468629). It forms condensates primarily in the nucleus, associating with replication fork puncta, nucleolus, and heterochromatin (PubMed:35484234, PubMed:31952807). The material state is substrate-dependent: gel-like with ssDNA/RNA, liquid-like with dsDNA/nucleosomes, and viscous liquid-like when co-phase separating with ProTα (PubMed:35484234, PubMed:37468629). ATP induces transitions from dynamically arrested to liquid-like states in polynucleosome condensates (PubMed:31952807).
Functional Summary: H1 phase separation stabilizes replication forks by shielding ssDNA from mechanical stress and organizes genome maintenance machinery into nuclear puncta during replication stress (PubMed:35484234). In heterochromatin, it scaffolds transcriptionally repressive domains whose ATP-dependent dynamics facilitate chromatin remodeling (PubMed:31952807). Co-phase separation with ProTα forms nuclear condensates enabling rapid partner exchange for chromatin organization and transcriptional regulation (PubMed:37468629). Dysregulation, particularly through CTD impairment, is linked to DNA damage response pathologies (PubMed:35484234).
Intrinsic Determinants & Regulations: Phase separation is intrinsically driven by the disordered C-terminal domain (CTD), which is lysine-rich and essential for nucleic acid-mediated condensation (PubMed:35484234, PubMed:31952807). The N-terminal domain (NTD) contributes secondarily, as its truncation reduces phase separation propensity and increases droplet fluidity (PubMed:35484234). The globular domain alone shows minimal phase separation capacity (PubMed:35484234). The high positive charge (+53) of full-length H1 enables electrostatic interactions with negatively charged partners (PubMed:37468629).
Extrinsic Partners & Regulations: Essential scaffolds include ssDNA (inducing gel-like droplets, enhanced by longer lengths/lower GC content), RNA (stronger driver than ssDNA), dsDNA, and nucleosomes (forming liquid-like droplets) (PubMed:35484234). H1 co-phase separates with prothymosin α (ProTα) through charge complementarity, forming viscous coacervates where each H1 molecule interacts with ~8 ProTα molecules (PubMed:37468629). ATP promotes liquid-like behavior in polynucleosome condensates and is required for in vivo droplet formation (PubMed:31952807). Phase separation is salt-sensitive, with higher KCl concentrations suppressing coacervation by screening electrostatic interactions (PubMed:37468629, PubMed:31952807).

Overall Phase Separation Overview: Rabies virus phosphoprotein (P69479) undergoes self-driven phase separation (PS-self) to form liquid condensates both in vitro and in vivo, primarily within the cytoplasm and nucleus (PubMed:36480574, 36989298, 39645030). It serves as a core scaffold for Negri bodies (viral factories) and associates with nucleoli, exhibiting liquid-like properties including fusion and rapid fluorescence recovery (PubMed:36480574, 36989298, 28680096). These condensates undergo pathological liquid-to-gel transitions upon aging (>3h) in vitro and display thermoresponsive behavior with lower critical solution temperature (LCST) characteristics, showing reversibility below 30°C (PubMed:36480574, 39645030).
Functional Summary: Phase separation enables formation of viral factories (Negri bodies) for RNA transcription/replication, concentrating viral components and facilitating membrane envelopment (PubMed:36480574, 39645030, 28680096). It supports immune evasion through nucleolar association and microtubule bundling, while pathological liquid-to-gel transitions stabilize compartments but may contribute to cytotoxicity (PubMed:36989298, 36480574). Mutations impairing phase separation (e.g., Ni-CE/L56P/L58P/L66P/F81P/N226H) cause viral attenuation, confirming its essential role in infectivity (PubMed:36989298).
Intrinsic Determinants & Regulations: Phase separation is intrinsically driven by the C-terminal domain (CTD, aa 195-297), dimerization domain (P_MD, aa 90-133), and globular P_CTD, which form cooperative networks with intrinsically disordered regions IDR1/IDR2 (PubMed:36480574, 36989298, 39645030). Key mutations disrupting phase separation include L56P/L58P/L66P/F81P in IDR1 and N226H in P_CTD, which impair conformational switching, while truncation of the dimerization domain (PΔ90-133) abolishes phase separation entirely (PubMed:36989298, 39645030).
Extrinsic Partners & Regulations: P69479 requires co-phase separation with viral nucleoprotein N (P16285) for stable condensate formation in cellular systems and Negri body assembly (PubMed:36480574, 28680096). RNA (poly(A) and viral) concentrates within droplets, enhancing stability and modulating dissolution dynamics, while intermediate salt concentrations (90–150 mM NaCl) enable reentrant phase separation governed by dipole-dipole interactions (PubMed:36480574, 39645030).

Overall Phase Separation Overview: GluN2B (Q01097) requires partner proteins for phase separation and does not undergo self-assembly (PubMed:31492534, 33927400, 38452102). It is primarily located in the cytoplasm and associates with the postsynaptic density (PSD) as a key membrane-less organelle (PubMed:33927400, 38452102). The protein forms dynamic liquid-like condensates in vitro and in cellular contexts, with its material state consistently characterized as liquid across studies (PubMed:33927400, 38452102). No material state transitions were reported under standard conditions, though it partitions into distinct subphases within multicomponent assemblies (PubMed:33927400).
Functional Summary: GluN2B phase separation organizes postsynaptic nanodomains by anchoring CaMKII condensates at synapses and segregating NMDARs from AMPARs during plasticity (PubMed:33927400). This compartmentalization aligns postsynaptic receptor nanodomains with presynaptic release sites, facilitating trans-synaptic signaling and synaptic reorganization during plasticity (PubMed:33927400). In PSD assemblies, GluN2B co-phase separation with PSD-95, SynGAP, and FAM81A contributes to synaptic structure maintenance, where FAM81A knockdown reduces PSD-95 puncta size and neuronal firing frequency (PubMed:38452102). The persistent liquid-phase organization mediated by CaMKII T286 phosphorylation provides a mechanism for activity-dependent synaptic trapping of client proteins like Tiam1 (PubMed:33927400).
Intrinsic Determinants & Regulations: Phase separation of GluN2B is intrinsically regulated by its carboxyl-terminal domain (CTD), particularly through a T-site binding motif that mediates essential interactions (PubMed:33927400). Specific point mutations in this region—L1298A/R1300Q (LR/AQ) and R1300Q/S1303D (RS/QD)—completely abolish phase separation capacity by disrupting CaMKII binding (PubMed:33927400). The CTD enables multivalent interactions that drive condensation behavior, though no additional domains, PTMs, or oligomerization features were identified as regulators in the available data (PubMed:33927400, 38452102).
Extrinsic Partners & Regulations: GluN2B phase separation is extrinsically modulated by multiple partners: CaMKII serves as the essential scaffold for co-condensation in a strictly Ca²⁺-dependent manner (PubMed:33927400); PSD-95 and SynGAP act as core co-scaffolds that enable ternary complex formation (PubMed:38452102); FAM81A facilitates and stabilizes incorporation into PSD condensates (PubMed:38452102); and Stargazin (STGc) contributes to phase segregation within multicomponent assemblies (PubMed:33927400). The Tiam1 peptide becomes trapped within GluN2B-containing condensates in an activity-dependent manner (PubMed:33927400). Calcium ions are required for initial condensation nucleation, while phosphorylation at CaMKII T286 enables persistent phase segregation after Ca²⁺ removal (PubMed:33927400).

Overall Phase Separation Overview: Nup49 (Q02199) undergoes self-driven phase separation (PS-self) forming liquid condensates in vitro that exhibit dynamic properties including droplet fusion and rapid fluorescence recovery (PubMed:31723007). These condensates associate with nuclear and cytoplasmic compartments, specifically localizing to the nuclear pore complex (NPC) and daughter-specific cytosolic condensates (PubMed:39356635, 17082456). The protein transitions from liquid droplets to hydrogel/solid states over time, as evidenced by microfluidic device clogging and FRAP immobility when incorporated into heterotypic assemblies (PubMed:31723007, 17082456).
Functional Summary: Nup49 condensates form a selective permeability barrier that replicates NPC functionality, excluding inert molecules while permitting nuclear transport receptor-mediated cargo import (PubMed:31723007). Within daughter-specific cytosolic condensates, it contributes to proper NPC assembly during yeast cell division; disruption of these condensates correlates with aging phenotypes and proteostasis decline (PubMed:39356635). Through heterotypic hydrogel formation with other FG-nucleoporins like Nsp1, Nup49 establishes essential barrier properties for nucleocytoplasmic transport, with hydrogel disruption proving lethal in yeast (PubMed:17082456).
Intrinsic Determinants & Regulations: Phase separation is intrinsically driven by Nup49's GLFG-repeat domain within its N-terminal disordered region (residues 1-249) (PubMed:31723007, 17082456). This domain confers inherent liquid-like properties to condensates, demonstrated by low insolubility in sedimentation assays and high circularity in vivo (PubMed:39356635). The GLFG motifs facilitate heterotypic interactions with other FG-nucleoporins, enabling integration into hydrogel networks (PubMed:17082456).
Extrinsic Partners & Regulations: Nup49 phase separation is modulated by partner proteins and chemical conditions. It co-assembles with Nsp1 in both daughter-specific cytosolic condensates and heterotypic hydrogels, where Nsp1 promotes liquid-like properties and reduces aggregation (PubMed:39356635, 17082456). The chemical TMAO assists phase separation by tuning solvent conditions to prevent amorphous aggregation (PubMed:31723007). Nuclear transport receptors (Importin α/β) enable cargo import into droplets without co-phase separating, facilitating selective permeability (PubMed:31723007).

Overall Phase Separation Overview: Nup100 undergoes self-driven phase separation (PubMed:39356635, 25562883, 39725032), forming condensates in the cytoplasm and nucleus (PubMed:39356635, 39725032). In the absence of modulators, it exhibits aggregation-prone behavior, forming solid-like hydrogel particles that replicate nuclear pore complex permeability by excluding inert molecules while allowing nuclear transport receptor influx (PubMed:25562883, 39356635). With modulators like Nsp1 and Kap95, it adopts a liquid-like state (PubMed:39356635). Over time, condensates undergo maturation from liquid-like to gel-like and ultimately solid/amyloid-like states (PubMed:39725032).
Functional Summary: Phase separation recapitulates nuclear pore complex permeability, enabling selective nuclear transport receptor influx while excluding inert molecules (PubMed:25562883). Proper modulation by Nsp1 and Kap95 prevents pathological aggregation and maintains proteostasis (PubMed:39356635). However, aberrant liquid-to-solid transitions form cytotoxic aggregates, mitigated by chaperones like DNAJB6b to preserve nuclear pore functionality (PubMed:39725032).
Intrinsic Determinants & Regulations: Phase separation is intrinsically driven by the FG domain (residues 1-580), where hydrophobic FG motifs mediate multivalent interactions (PubMed:39356635, 25562883, 39725032). This domain facilitates ultra-rapid phase separation at low critical concentrations (~200 nM) without kinetic barriers (PubMed:25562883).
Extrinsic Partners & Regulations: Nsp1 and Kap95 suppress aggregation and promote liquid-like states by reducing insoluble fractions and increasing condensate circularity (PubMed:39356635). NaCl enhances phase separation by screening electrostatics and strengthening hydrophobic interactions, following Hofmeister series effects (PubMed:39725032). The chaperone DNAJB6b delays liquid-to-solid transitions and maintains dynamic states (PubMed:39725032), while Hsp104 fragments fibrils during amyloid formation (PubMed:39725032). Crowding agents like PEG3350 promote homogeneous, circular condensates (PubMed:39725032).

Overall Phase Separation Overview: CcmM (Q03513) undergoes context-dependent phase separation in the cytoplasm of Synechococcus elongatus, primarily associated with β-carboxysome formation. Its M35 isoform requires Rubisco for phase separation, forming dynamic liquid condensates via SSUL-Rubisco interactions (PubMed:30675061, 34759380). The M58 isoform undergoes self-driven phase separation through γCAL domain-mediated homodimerization and electrostatic interactions, forming immobile solid-like condensates that serve as scaffolds for the pre-carboxysome matrix (PubMed:34759380). Material properties are redox-regulated: oxidation enhances M58 homodemixing while reducing M35 mobility, with transitions between reducing (cytosolic) and oxidizing (carboxysome interior) environments modulating condensate dynamics (PubMed:30675061, 34759380).
Functional Summary: Phase separation concentrates Rubisco and carbonic anhydrase (CcaA) into immobile pre-carboxysome condensates under reducing cytosolic conditions, enabling efficient encapsulation into β-carboxysomes for spatial co-localization in CO₂ fixation (PubMed:30675061, 34759380). This facilitates a specialized microenvironment that enhances carbon fixation while avoiding photorespiration, with Rubisco remaining enzymatically active within condensates (PubMed:34759380). Redox-regulated dynamics are essential for functional restructuring: oxidation in the carboxysome interior promotes M58 homodemixing and reduces M35 mobility, facilitating metabolic repair and carbon-concentrating mechanism efficiency (PubMed:34759380). Dysregulation via mutations (e.g., cysteine→serine) disrupts condensate dynamics, causing abnormal carboxysome morphology, reduced cellular fitness, and 10-20× increased CO₂ requirements (PubMed:30675061, 34759380).
Intrinsic Determinants & Regulations: Phase separation is intrinsically regulated by: 1) SSUL domains mediating Rubisco binding in both isoforms (PubMed:30675061, 34759380); 2) γCAL domains enabling M58 homodimerization via head-to-head trimer stacking and electrostatic γCAL-SSUL interactions (PubMed:34759380); 3) Redox-sensitive disulfide bonds in SSUL domains - oxidation enhances M58 homodemixing and stabilizes M58-Rubisco interactions while reducing M35 mobility (PubMed:30675061, 34759380); 4) Oligomerization state - trimeric M58 provides high local SSUL concentration for enhanced Rubisco avidity, whereas monomeric M35 exhibits lower affinity (PubMed:34759380). Key mutations disrupting phase separation include γCAL dimerization mutants (R164D/D172K), SSUL charge-reversal mutations (R251D/R252D/R298D), and cysteine→serine mutations (C279S/C395S) that impair disulfide formation (PubMed:30675061, 34759380).
Extrinsic Partners & Regulations: Essential partners include: Rubisco, which co-phase separates with M35 to form dynamic liquid droplets and is recruited into M58 scaffolds with high avidity (PubMed:30675061, 34759380); CcaA, which binds M58's γCAL domain via its C-terminal C2 peptide to form immobile condensates (PubMed:34759380). Environmental modulators include: 1) Redox state - oxidation enhances M58 homodemixing and stabilizes M58-Rubisco interactions while reducing M35 dynamics (PubMed:30675061, 34759380); 2) Salt concentration - high KCl (>100mM) impairs M35-Rubisco and M58-CcaA interactions but minimally affects M58-Rubisco binding (PubMed:34759380); 3) Raf1 chaperone, which prevents non-productive M58-RbcL₈ interactions (PubMed:34759380). Within multiprotein condensates, M58 acts as an immobile scaffold while M35 introduces partial mobility (PubMed:34759380).

Overall Phase Separation Overview: eIF4G (Q04637) does not undergo self-driven phase separation but is recruited as a client protein to biomolecular condensates in the cytoplasm (PubMed:38421168, 38072230, 30893049). It associates with viral inclusion body-associated granules (IBAGs) during respiratory syncytial virus infection, where it concentrates translation machinery (PubMed:38421168, 38072230), and partitions into stress granules under cellular stress conditions (PubMed:30893049, 36151083). Its material state within condensates is not explicitly characterized in the provided data.
Functional Summary: eIF4G condensate recruitment enables compartmentalized translation initiation. In viral contexts, it enhances RSV replication efficiency by concentrating translation machinery within IBAGs for selective viral mRNA translation (PubMed:38421168, 38072230).
