Intrinsic Determinants & Regulations: Intrinsic drivers are not explicitly identified, though full-length Aβ(1-40) and Aβ42 peptides inherently undergo phase separation (PubMed:37718544, 39854227). No specific domains, mutations, or PTMs were reported as regulators in the provided studies.
Extrinsic Partners & Regulations: Phase separation is critically modulated by environmental factors and partners: Low pH (pH 3) and polyP induce Aβ(1-40) LLPS and fibril acceleration (PubMed:37718544); phospholipids are essential scaffolds for Aβ42 membrane condensates (PubMed:39854227); APP-C99 incorporates into GSAP-16K condensates via direct interaction (PubMed:35298330); and high NaCl concentrations (≥300 mM) inhibit GSAP-16K droplet formation, indirectly affecting APP-C99 sequestration (PubMed:35298330).

Overall Phase Separation Overview: Fyn (P06241) exhibits partner-dependent phase separation behavior primarily in the cytoplasm without autonomous droplet formation (PubMed:36258016, 30397184). It forms nanoclusters when in an open conformation, enhanced by recruitment into Tau-P301L biomolecular condensates (PubMed:36258016), and co-phase separates with hnRNPA2 to form liquid-like droplets via its SH3 domain (PubMed:30397184). Fyn associates with stress granules and Tau-P301L condensates (PubMed:36258016, 30397184), with material states ranging from liquid-like droplets in hnRNPA2 complexes to non-specified nanoclusters in neuronal contexts (PubMed:30397184, 36258016). No material state transitions were reported.
Functional Summary: Fyn phase separation has significant pathological implications in neurodegeneration. Tau-P301L condensate-mediated nanoclustering amplifies Fyn/ERK/S6 signaling, contributing to Alzheimer's disease and frontotemporal lobar degeneration with tauopathy (PubMed:36258016). Co-phase separation with hnRNPA2 in transport granules is proposed to position Fyn for phosphorylation-dependent granule disassembly and mRNA release, though this mechanism requires experimental validation (PubMed:30397184). Pathological immobilization in Tau condensates represents a key mechanism in Fyn-mediated neurodegeneration (PubMed:36258016).
Intrinsic Determinants & Regulations: Phase separation is intrinsically regulated by conformational changes and domain-specific interactions. Transition to an open conformation via disruption of SH3-PPII linker or SH2-pY531 interactions drives nanoclustering (PubMed:36258016). Dephosphorylation at Y531 promotes this open state and clustering (PubMed:36258016). The SH3 domain is essential for inducing and co-phase separating with hnRNPA2 (PubMed:30397184). Mutations modulate behavior: Y531F enhances clustering while K299M (kinase-dead) partially rescues clustering when combined with Y531F (PubMed:36258016).
Extrinsic Partners & Regulations: Fyn phase separation is extrinsically regulated by specific protein partners. Tau (MAPT) scaffolds Fyn recruitment into Tau-P301L condensates, immobilizing Fyn nanoclusters and amplifying downstream signaling, as demonstrated by co-localization and reduced mobility in sptPALM (PubMed:36258016). Fyn's SH3 domain induces hnRNPA2 liquid-liquid phase separation, incorporating Fyn into droplets and delaying disease-mutant (P298L) aggregation under low-salt conditions (PubMed:30397184).

Overall Phase Separation Overview: Progesterone Receptor (PR, P06401) undergoes ligand-dependent phase separation in the nucleus to form transcriptional condensates (PubMed:35881789, 18931262). It forms liquid-like droplets in vivo, evidenced by Brownian motion coalescence dynamics, dissolution with 1,6-hexanediol, and fluorescence recovery after photobleaching (FRAP) (PubMed:35881789, 18931262). Condensates exhibit viscoelastic properties due to chromatin interactions and reach a steady-state nanoscale size (~70 nm radius) via regulated molecular escaping (PubMed:35881789). Dimerization-deficient mutants form solid cytoplasmic aggregates instead of nuclear condensates (PubMed:18931262).
Functional Summary: PR phase separation into transcriptional condensates regulates hormone-responsive gene expression by amplifying transcriptional output and prolonging DNA binding (PubMed:35881789, 18931262). Aberrant condensates in endometrial/breast cancers correlate with poor prognosis (PubMed:18931262). Disruption via mutations (e.g., dimerization-deficient, NMTS, or DBD mutants) abolishes transcriptional activity (PubMed:18931262). Arrested nanoscale condensate growth prevents transcriptional collapse or excessive chromatin condensation, maintaining regulatory fidelity (PubMed:35881789).
Intrinsic Determinants & Regulations: Phase separation is intrinsically driven by the N-terminal intrinsically disordered region (IDR) and hinge region IDR (PubMed:35881789). Dimerization via the hinge region (aa 1432-1567) is essential for condensate formation, while the DNA-Binding Domain (DBD, Cys587) ensures proper nuclear localization and mobility (PubMed:18931262). The Nuclear Matrix Targeting Sequence (NMTS, Leu690/Leu691) mediates chromatin anchoring, and mutations in these domains (e.g., C587A in DBD, NMTS mutants) disrupt phase separation, leading to aberrant aggregation or diffuse distribution (PubMed:18931262).
Extrinsic Partners & Regulations: The hormone R5020 is essential for phase separation initiation, acting as a tunable regulator with a critical concentration threshold (10^-10 M) (PubMed:35881789). Chromatin provides a viscoelastic environment within condensates, with ~90% of PR molecules DNA-bound (PubMed:35881789). PR forms heterodimers with isoform PRB (P06400) in shared nuclear foci, confirmed by FRET (PubMed:18931262). ATP-dependent mechanisms are required for nuclear retention of condensates (PubMed:18931262).

Overall Phase Separation Overview: eIF4E (P06730) is recruited to biomolecular condensates as a client protein (PS-other class) in the cytoplasm, associating with viral mRNP condensates within respiratory syncytial virus (RSV) inclusion bodies (PubMed:38072230), stress granules (PubMed:40090627), and PABPC1-driven liquid-like condensates enriched in translation machinery (PubMed:40102686). Its material state within these condensates is not specified in the provided studies, and no material state transitions were reported.
Functional Summary: eIF4E's condensate recruitment facilitates viral mRNA translation within RSV inclusion bodies (PubMed:38072230) and serves as a stress granule marker during cellular stress responses (PubMed:40090627). In CML blast crisis, its incorporation into PABPC1 condensates selectively enhances translation of leukemogenic mRNAs (e.g., BCR-ABL1, IDH2), driving disease progression and therapy resistance; pharmacological disruption of these condensates overcomes treatment resistance (PubMed:40102686).
Intrinsic Determinants & Regulations: No intrinsic molecular features (e.g., specific domains, mutations, or post-translational modifications) driving eIF4E phase separation were reported in the provided studies (PubMed:38072230, PubMed:40090627, PubMed:40102686).
Extrinsic Partners & Regulations: eIF4E recruitment to condensates requires extrinsic partners: eIF4G1 is essential for its incorporation into viral mRNP condensates within RSV inclusion bodies (PubMed:38072230). In chronic myeloid leukemia (CML) cells, eIF4E is recruited as a co-scaffold into PABPC1-driven condensates, stabilized by interactions with eIF4G and dependent on poly(A)+ RNA scaffolding for condensate formation (PubMed:40102686).

Protein Name: DNA repair and recombination protein RAD52
Overall Phase Separation Overview: Rad52 (P06778) undergoes self-driven liquid-liquid phase separation (LLPS) in the nucleus of Saccharomyces cerevisiae, forming dynamic condensates at DNA damage sites referred to as DNA repair centers or foci (PubMed:32019927, 33543712). These liquid-like droplets exhibit characteristic behaviors including fusion, dripping, wetting, and rapid molecular exchange in vivo, and form in vitro under low-salt conditions (PubMed:32019927). The condensates display confined diffusion and scale dynamically with DNA break number, maintaining liquid properties (viscosity: 1-2.4 Pa.s) under physiological conditions (PubMed:33543712). A material state transition to a gel-like hydrogel occurs upon SUMOylation, characterized by reduced mobility and increased density (PubMed:33543712).
Functional Summary: Rad52 phase separation enables genome stability by clustering DNA damage sites into repair centers that concentrate repair machinery like Rad51 and facilitate homology search (PubMed:32019927, 33543712). These condensates coordinate microtubule-mediated transport: they concentrate tubulin, project aster-like microtubules (aster-DIMs), and mobilize damaged DNA to the nuclear periphery for repair (PubMed:32019927). Dysregulation via SUMOylation-induced gelation, 1,6-hexanediol treatment, or Δ307 mutation causes defective damage clustering, hyperactivated DNA damage checkpoints (e.g., Rad53 phosphorylation), and genome instability (PubMed:32019927, 33543712).
Intrinsic Determinants & Regulations: Phase separation is intrinsically driven by Rad52's intrinsically disordered region (IDR) and multivalent interactions mediated by its prion-like (PLD) and arginine-glycine-glycine (RGG) domains (PubMed:32019927, 33543712). Oligomerization into multimers is essential for LLPS, with ≈62% of molecules existing as multimers in vivo (PubMed:33543712). The C-terminal truncation mutant Δ307 (lacking residues 307-471) abolishes phase separation due to disruption of the disordered domain (PubMed:32019927). SUMOylation post-translational modification induces a liquid-to-gel transition, reducing diffusion coefficients and confinement radii within foci (PubMed:33543712).
Extrinsic Partners & Regulations: Rad52 phase separation requires nucleation at double-strand breaks via RPA-coated single-stranded DNA (ssDNA), where the Rfa1 subunit (P22336) acts as a scaffold for condensate assembly (PubMed:33543712). Nuclear microtubule filaments (pti-DIMs) promote droplet fusion and clustering, with computational models confirming microtubule-generated flows drive optimal fusion at 90° angles (PubMed:32019927). Condensate formation is salt-dependent in vitro, being optimal under low ionic conditions (PubMed:32019927). The aliphatic alcohol 1,6-hexanediol dissolves condensates in vivo and disrupts repair function (PubMed:32019927, 33543712).

Protein Name: T-cell surface glycoprotein CD3 epsilon chain
Overall Phase Separation Overview: CD3E undergoes partner-driven phase separation (class: PS-other) primarily in the cytoplasm, forming TCR signalosomes at immunological synapses (PubMed:37399423). It assembles dynamic liquid-like condensates with Lck kinase via multivalent ionic interactions, exhibiting fusion/fission events and FRAP recovery. These condensates undergo dissolution upon phosphorylation-induced Csk recruitment, with no aging to solid states reported (PubMed:37399423). An engineered CD3ε motif (EB6I) enables self-phase separation through cation-π interactions in synthetic systems (PubMed:39609126).
Functional Summary: CD3E condensates form signaling hubs ('TCR signalosomes') that amplify Lck activity and CD3 phosphorylation, enhancing T-cell activation through enzyme-substrate proximity (PubMed:37399423). Dissolution by Csk provides self-terminating feedback for dynamic immune responses (PubMed:37399423). Engineered CD3ε motifs (EB6I) in CARs induce phase separation, improving immunological synapse maturation, signaling efficiency, cytotoxicity against low-antigen tumors, and antitumor efficacy in murine models of blood and solid cancers (PubMed:39609126).
Intrinsic Determinants & Regulations: Phase separation is intrinsically regulated by CD3E's cytoplasmic tail motifs: the basic residue-rich sequence (BRS), proline-rich sequence (PRS), and RK motifs drive multivalent ionic interactions (PubMed:37399423). Phosphorylation at ITAM tyrosines (Y1/Y2) serves as a molecular switch, altering binding preferences from Lck to Csk (PubMed:37399423). Mutations (mBRS, mPRS, RK mutant) impair condensation, while CD3ε-YYFF mutations prevent dissolution (PubMed:37399423). An engineered EB6I motif derived from CD3ε enables cation-π interaction-driven self-phase separation (PubMed:39609126).
Extrinsic Partners & Regulations: CD3E phase separation requires Lck as an essential scaffold, with co-condensation mediated by ionic interactions between CD3E motifs and Lck domains (UD-SH3-SH2) (PubMed:37399423). Phosphorylated CD3E recruits Csk, whose SH2 domain competitively dissolves condensates to terminate signaling (PubMed:37399423). In engineered contexts, CD3ε-derived motifs partner with CD3ζ and CD28 in chimeric antigen receptors (CARs) to enable self-phase separation (PubMed:39609126).

Overall Phase Separation Overview: RET alone does not undergo liquid-liquid phase separation (LLPS) and instead forms aggregates (PubMed:38805286). However, when fused to partner proteins like CRY2 or CCDC6, it forms cytoplasmic condensates. The CRY2-RET fusion exhibits light-induced LLPS with liquid-like properties (PubMed:38805286), while the CCDC6-RET fusion forms de novo membraneless cytoplasmic protein granules (PubMed:33848463). No material state transitions are reported.
Functional Summary: RET fusion phase separation drives pathological signaling cascades. CRY2-RET condensates enhance RET kinase activity and Ras/MAPK signaling (PubMed:38805286). CCDC6-RET granules facilitate oncogenic Ras/MAPK hyperactivation through GRB2 recruitment and RAS-GTP enrichment, establishing signal niches that promote cancer progression (PubMed:33848463). This dysregulated signaling underlies RET fusion-related malignancies.
Intrinsic Determinants & Regulations: Phase separation in RET fusion proteins is intrinsically driven by oligomerization domains of fusion partners. For CRY2-RET, light-induced oligomerization of the CRY2 domain enables LLPS (PubMed:38805286). In CCDC6-RET, the coiled-coil domain (CC) of CCDC6 is essential for granule formation, as its deletion (ΔCC) abolishes condensation while retaining kinase activity (PubMed:33848463). RET kinase activity itself is dispensable for granule formation, evidenced by the kinase-deficient K147M mutant forming granules (PubMed:33848463).
Extrinsic Partners & Regulations: Phase separation is modulated by extrinsic factors: light triggers CRY2-RET condensation (PubMed:38805286), while CCDC6-RET granules recruit GRB2 in a kinase-dependent manner (disrupted by K147M mutation) and enrich RAS-GTP (PubMed:33848463). Both fusion proteins amplify Ras/MAPK signaling through granule-localized activation mechanisms (PubMed:38805286, 33848463).

Overall Phase Separation Overview: Synaptophysin (P08247) does not undergo self-driven phase separation but requires the partner protein Synapsin (P17600) for co-condensation (PubMed:39223639, 39947282). It localizes to the cytoplasm and associates with synaptic vesicle condensates (termed synapsin-SV condensates), exhibiting liquid-like material properties in these membrane-less organelles (PubMed:39223639, 39947282). No material state transitions were reported.
Functional Summary: Synaptophysin-Synapsin co-condensation enables synaptic vesicle clustering at nerve terminals, which is essential for neurotransmission (PubMed:39223639, 39947282). This process maintains distinct vesicle pools through segregation mechanisms, and disruption of vesicle organization (e.g., on Rab5 mutant-induced endosomes) impairs sorting (PubMed:39223639). The condensates generate interphase pH gradients proposed to regulate vesicular ATPase activity and neurotransmitter loading, contributing to neuronal function (PubMed:39947282).
Intrinsic Determinants & Regulations: The phase separation of Synaptophysin is intrinsically regulated by its cytoplasmic intrinsically disordered region (IDR; residues 233–313), which is enriched in aromatic residues and enables heterotypic interactions with Synapsin (PubMed:39947282). No specific mutations, post-translational modifications, or oligomerization features were identified as key drivers.
Extrinsic Partners & Regulations: Synaptophysin's phase separation is extrinsically dependent on Synapsin (P17600), which scaffolds its co-condensation into synaptic vesicle clusters (PubMed:39223639, 39947282). Without Synapsin, Synaptophysin fails to form condensates and remains scattered in the cytoplasm (PubMed:39223639). The heterotypic interactions between Synaptophysin's IDR and Synapsin's C-terminal IDR are essential for condensate formation (PubMed:39947282).

Overall Phase Separation Overview: Fluc (P08659) does not autonomously undergo phase separation but is recruited into synthetic biomolecular condensates formed by cationic peptides and ATP in vitro (PubMed:36342014). In vivo, within the cytoplasm of HEK293 cells, Fluc undergoes temperature-dependent phase separation, forming aggresome-like amorphous inclusions at 37°C and needle-shaped crystal-like solid inclusion bodies at hypothermic temperatures (25–31°C) (PubMed:38876374).
Functional Summary: The recruitment of Fluc into synthetic coacervates enhances its enzymatic reaction rate and bioluminescence quantum yield, which may improve the reliability of bioluminescence imaging (PubMed:36342014). In cellular environments, the temperature-dependent crystallization of Fluc under conditions of substrate insufficiency modulates the soluble enzyme availability and protein turnover rate, suggesting a role in enzyme storage (PubMed:38876374).
Intrinsic Determinants & Regulations: No intrinsic regulators of phase separation were identified in the provided studies for Fluc (PubMed:36342014, 38876374).
Extrinsic Partners & Regulations: Fluc is recruited into biomolecular condensates formed by the cationic peptides poly-L-arginine (PLR) and poly-L-lysine (PLL) in the presence of ATP, which enhances its enzymatic activity and bioluminescence quantum yield (PubMed:36342014). Additionally, the small molecules D-luciferin, CycLuc1, HPBT, and PBT inhibit the temperature-dependent crystallization of Fluc in the cytoplasm, thereby preventing the formation of solid inclusion bodies (PubMed:38876374).

Overall Phase Separation Overview: Vimentin (P08670) undergoes heterotypic phase separation (PS-other) in the cytoplasm, forming liquid-like condensates under specific conditions (PubMed:38331785, 39079387). These condensates associate with membrane complexes but not classical membrane-less organelles. Under oxidative stress (e.g., diamide/H₂O₂), vimentin filaments reversibly remodel into motile, spherical droplets exhibiting liquid properties including FRAP recovery, fusion capability, and 1,6-hexanediol sensitivity (PubMed:39079387). This transition is reversible upon stress removal, though prolonged stress causes irreversible damage (PubMed:39079387).
Functional Summary: Physiologically, reversible phase separation protects vimentin from oxidative damage, enabling filament reassembly post-stress and serving as a cellular adaptation mechanism (PubMed:39079387). Pathologically, in bacterial infections (e.g., Streptococcus suis), vimentin participates in ENO-RPSA-VIM co-condensates on host cell surfaces. These condensates elevate intracellular Ca²⁺, disrupt mitochondrial function, and induce apoptosis in brain endothelial cells, contributing to meningitis pathogenesis (PubMed:38331785).
Intrinsic Determinants & Regulations: Phase separation is intrinsically regulated by cysteine residue C328, as its oxidation triggers filament-to-droplet remodeling (PubMed:39079387). The C328A mutation confers resistance to both oxidant-induced condensation and 1,6-hexanediol dissolution, confirming this residue's essential role (PubMed:39079387).
Extrinsic Partners & Regulations: Vimentin co-phase separates with ribosomal protein SA (RPSA) and bacterial enolase (ENO), forming heterotypic membrane condensates where ENO scaffolds RPSA-VIM interactions (PubMed:38331785). Oxidative stressors (diamide, H₂O₂) rapidly induce liquid condensate formation, while elevated Ca²⁺ enhances condensation dynamics (PubMed:38331785, 39079387).

Protein Name: DNA-directed RNA polymerase II subunit RPB1
Overall Phase Separation Overview: RNA Polymerase II (Pol II, UniProt P08775) forms phase-separated transcriptional condensates in the nucleus through co-assembly with partners like Mediator complex and PSPC1 (PubMed:29930094, 38194964, 34916619). It localizes to transcriptional condensates at super-enhancers and dynamically partitions into splicing-factor condensates during elongation (PubMed:31391587, 38194964). These condensates exhibit liquid-like properties—demonstrating rapid fluorescence recovery (t½ ~10-60s), coalescence, and sensitivity to hexanediol dissolution—with diameters typically ranging from 300-560 nm (PubMed:29930094, 31391587, 34916619). Phosphorylation-dependent transitions regulate its compartmentalization between transcriptional and splicing condensates (PubMed:31391587).
Functional Summary: Pol II condensates functionally regulate transcription through spatial coordination: proximity (<1 µm) to gene loci (e.g., Sox2, Esrrb) enhances transcriptional bursting by increasing mRNA output 2-fold and burst size by ~57% (PubMed:38194964, 29930094). This facilitates 'dynamic kissing' interactions between enhancers and promoters, compartmentalizing transcription machinery (PubMed:29930094). Phosphorylation-mediated partitioning into splicing condensates enables co-transcriptional RNA processing (PubMed:31391587). Dissolution of condensates (via JQ1 or PSPC1 degradation) disrupts global transcription and stem cell identity maintenance (PubMed:29930094, 34916619).
Intrinsic Determinants & Regulations: Phase separation of Pol II is intrinsically regulated by post-translational modifications, particularly phosphorylation at Serine 2 (Ser2) of its C-terminal domain (CTD), which drives its transition from transcriptional condensates to splicing-factor condensates during elongation (PubMed:31391587). No specific domains (e.g., IDRs), mutations, or oligomerization features were identified as primary drivers in the studied contexts (PubMed:38194964, 31391587).
Extrinsic Partners & Regulations: Pol II phase separation is modulated by multiple extrinsic partners: it co-scaffolds transcriptional condensates with Mediator complex, exhibiting colocalization in >90% of nuclear clusters (PubMed:29930094, 38194964), and associates with PSPC1 in RNA-dependent condensates essential for chromatin binding (PubMed:34916619). DNA elements—including the Sox2 super-enhancer (SCR) and CTCF sites—are critical for condensate integrity and transcriptional enhancement (PubMed:38194964). Chemical inhibitors dissolve condensates (JQ1 within 15 min; hexanediol gradually) (PubMed:29930094, 34916619), while splicing factors (e.g., SRSF2) serve as co-scaffolds in elongation-phase condensates (PubMed:31391587).

Overall Phase Separation Overview: Synapsin (P09951) undergoes both self-driven liquid-liquid phase separation (LLPS) in vitro, forming liquid-like droplets that exhibit fusion and rapid fluorescence recovery (PubMed:37597184), and partner-dependent phase separation with ITSN to form condensates that cluster synaptic vesicles (PubMed:38552623). The material state of self-assembled droplets is liquid, with no observed state transitions (PubMed:37597184).
Functional Summary: The ITSN-coassembled condensates organize synaptic vesicles into a reserve pool for activity-dependent mobilization during neurotransmission (PubMed:38552623). No pathological implications or disease associations are reported.
Intrinsic Determinants & Regulations: Phase separation is intrinsically regulated by the length of its C-terminal intrinsically disordered region (IDR), where longer IDR isoforms (e.g., 1a) form larger droplets with higher molecular mobility than shorter IDR isoforms (e.g., 1b) (PubMed:37597184). No mutations, post-translational modifications, or oligomerization features are reported as regulators.
Extrinsic Partners & Regulations: Synapsin requires the co-scaffold protein ITSN for heterotypic condensate formation (PubMed:38552623). These condensates incorporate vesicle phospholipids as clients, enabling synaptic vesicle clustering (PubMed:38552623). No chemical/ionic regulators are described.

Overall Phase Separation Overview: TmaR (P0A8M6) undergoes self-driven phase separation to form polar biomolecular condensates in the cytoplasm of Escherichia coli, primarily during stationary phase (PubMed:36577380, 40100851). These condensates, identified as distinct membraneless organelles ('TmaR condensates'), exhibit liquid-like properties with dynamic client recruitment and RNA-dependent formation (PubMed:40100851). TmaR serves as a heterotypic scaffold, enabling co-condensation with partners like Hfq and enzyme I (EI) (PubMed:36577380, 40100851).
Functional Summary: TmaR condensates spatially regulate cellular processes by scaffolding Hfq-mediated RNA chaperone activity for stress-responsive sRNA/mRNA localization and stability (PubMed:36577380). They control metabolism through sequestration of EI (modulating sugar uptake) and protect flagellar RNAs to maintain motility (PubMed:40100851). Disruption of phase separation via helical mutations or patch defects impairs carbon metabolism, motility, and stress adaptation (PubMed:36577380, 40100851).
Intrinsic Determinants & Regulations: Phase separation is intrinsically driven by a coiled-coil domain (two α-helices) and an N-terminal disordered region (IDR) functioning as a sticker domain (PubMed:36577380, 40100851). Helical mutations (L11A/E14A/L15A in Helix1; L48A/E51A/L52A in Helix2) impair self-clustering (PubMed:36577380). Key residues in Patch I (F8, V11, R16) and Patch II (A84, E85, D87) regulate partner recruitment, with mutations (e.g., F8L, V11I, R16P, D87H) disrupting co-phase separation (PubMed:40100851).
Extrinsic Partners & Regulations: TmaR forms heterotypic condensates with protein partners including Hfq (co-scaffold for polar assembly) and enzyme I (EI), validated through co-IP, co-localization, and in vitro reconstitution (PubMed:36577380, 40100851). Phase separation is RNA-dependent, recruiting flagellar RNAs for functional regulation (PubMed:40100851). Mutations in Patch I/II specifically impair EI recruitment without abolishing self-clustering (PubMed:40100851).

Overall Phase Separation Overview: Dps undergoes self-driven phase separation under crowded conditions (e.g., with PEG) and co-phase separates with DNA to form liquid-like condensates in vitro, exhibiting rapid fluorescence recovery (PubMed:36963493). It associates with the bacterial nucleoid and forms multiphasic heterotypic condensates with HU proteins (HU-A and HU-B) and DNA, characterized by demixed subdomains where Dps-rich regions localize within larger HU-rich condensates (PubMed:36963493). Under non-crowded conditions, Dps requires DNA for phase separation, forming stable condensates that nucleate preferentially at DNA bridging sites in supercoiled DNA (PubMed:38572752). While typically liquid-like, these condensates can exhibit stable immobile properties under certain conditions and are known to form crystalline structures during prolonged stress in vivo, though explicit liquid-to-solid transitions were not observed in these in vitro studies (PubMed:36963493, 38572752).
Functional Summary: Dps-DNA phase separation compacts and protects the bacterial nucleoid during stress conditions (e.g., starvation, oxidative stress), enabling rapid genome reorganization through cooperative DNA bridging (PubMed:36963493, 38572752). This process facilitates extreme nucleoid condensation in stationary-phase E. coli, with multiphasic heterotypic condensates involving HU proteins potentially serving as organizational precursors to crystalline Dps-DNA structures formed under prolonged stress (PubMed:36963493). The stable condensates can capture additional DNA strands without free Dps, suggesting a role in nucleoid accretion and protection (PubMed:38572752).
Intrinsic Determinants & Regulations: Phase separation of Dps is intrinsically driven by its dodecameric oligomerization state, which enables DNA bridging contacts essential for condensation (PubMed:36963493, 38572752). Key structural features include intrinsically disordered regions (IDRs) throughout its sequence, charge clusters, and a basic N-terminal tail (amino acids 1-13) that facilitate multivalent DNA binding (PubMed:36963493). The disordered N-terminal domain specifically mediates cooperative DNA interactions that enhance nucleation kinetics (PubMed:38572752).
Extrinsic Partners & Regulations: DNA acts as an essential extrinsic partner for Dps phase separation under non-crowded conditions, with supercoiled DNA providing optimal bridging sites for rapid nucleation (PubMed:36963493, 38572752). Dps forms heterotypic multiphasic condensates with HU proteins (HU-A/HU-B) and DNA, where Dps-rich subdomains localize within HU-rich scaffolds (PubMed:36963493). Macromolecular crowding agents like PEG 6000 enable self-assembly without DNA (PubMed:36963493). DNA topology critically regulates condensation kinetics, with supercoiled DNA compacting faster than relaxed or linear DNA due to preferential nucleation at plectonemes (PubMed:38572752).

Overall Phase Separation Overview: HU-A (P0ACF0) undergoes heterotypic phase separation requiring partner molecules, classified as PS-other, forming liquid-like condensates. It phase separates with LPS to form spherical condensates (PubMed:39445815) and undergoes complex coacervation with DNA (e.g., 4WJ, salmon testis DNA) to form dynamic, spherical droplets exhibiting rapid fluorescence recovery, indicative of liquid material state (PubMed:36963493). No material state transitions were reported under studied conditions.
Functional Summary: HU-A phase separation with DNA facilitates bacterial nucleoid formation and chromosome compaction in Escherichia coli, contributing to dynamic genome organization during growth phases (PubMed:36963493). Its phase separation with HU-B may regulate nucleoid architecture in logarithmic growth phase, while interactions with LPS suggest potential relevance to biofilm formation (PubMed:39445815, 36963493).
Intrinsic Determinants & Regulations: Phase separation propensity is intrinsically regulated by oligomerization states and disordered regions. HU-A exists primarily in dimeric form, with lower multimericity correlating with poorer phase separation ability compared to HU-B (PubMed:36963493). Intrinsically disordered regions (IDRs) contribute to phase separation tendency. The E34K-V42L double mutation enhances multimericity (promoting dimer/octamer formation) and significantly improves phase separation efficiency by reducing critical saturation concentration (PubMed:36963493).
Extrinsic Partners & Regulations: Phase separation requires extrinsic partners: HU-A co-phase separates with LPS (PubMed:39445815) and depends on nucleic acids (4WJ DNA, salmon testis DNA) for condensate formation under standard conditions (PubMed:36963493). HU-B dramatically enhances HU-A's phase separation, enabling condensate formation at lower concentrations through heterotypic co-assembly (PubMed:36963493). HU-A also forms multiphasic heterotypic condensates with Dps and DNA, where Dps-rich subdomains localize within larger HU-A-rich condensates (PubMed:36963493).

Overall Phase Separation Overview: HU-B undergoes heterotypic phase separation primarily through interactions with nucleic acids and other biomolecules, classified as PS-other (PubMed:39445815, 36963493). It forms dynamic, liquid-like condensates with DNA that exhibit rapid FRAP recovery and droplet fusion, while forming gel-like condensates with LPS (PubMed:39445815). With various DNA forms (4WJ, dsDNA, ssDNA) and RNA (poly(U)), it establishes spherical liquid droplets in vitro, both with and without crowding agents (PubMed:36963493). Condition-dependent material transitions occur, such as reduced liquidity when LPS is added to HU-DNA condensates (PubMed:39445815).
Functional Summary: HU-B phase separation is functionally crucial for bacterial chromosome organization, facilitating nucleoid compaction and accretion through DNA coacervation, with its superior phase separation ability compared to HU-A potentially explaining differential compaction during growth phases (PubMed:36963493). In biofilm formation, HU-B acts as a 'molecular glue' in extracellular matrices by bridging LPS-coated bacterial cells and DNA, where LPS-modulated matrix liquidity supports structural integrity and cellular embedment (PubMed:39445815). Multiphasic condensates with Dps may represent organizational intermediates in nucleoid architecture, while heterotypic assemblies with HU-A enable emergent condensate properties during stress responses (PubMed:36963493).
Intrinsic Determinants & Regulations: Phase separation is intrinsically regulated by HU-B's oligomerization state, with dimeric, tetrameric, and octameric forms exhibiting enhanced phase separation capability at lower saturation concentrations compared to HU-A (PubMed:36963493). DNA-binding surfaces, including both canonical and non-canonical sites, are essential for electrostatic interactions with nucleic acids and LPS phosphates (PubMed:39445815). Intrinsically disordered regions (IDRs) contribute to phase separation propensity, while the F47W mutation serves as an experimental tool without functional impact (PubMed:39445815, 36963493).
Extrinsic Partners & Regulations: HU-B phase separation is extrinsically modulated by multiple partners: DNA (4WJ, dsDNA, ssDNA) acts as an essential scaffold for liquid condensate formation, significantly lowering critical saturation concentrations (PubMed:39445815, 36963493). LPS promotes gel-like condensates and reduces liquidity in HU-DNA complexes through competitive binding (PubMed:39445815). Protein partners include HU-A, whose phase separation is enhanced through co-assembly into heterotypic condensates, and Dps, forming multiphasic condensates with demixed subdomains (PubMed:36963493). Ionic strength (KCl) inhibits phase separation at high concentrations (500 mM), while poly(U) RNA also drives coacervation (PubMed:39445815, 36963493).

Overall Phase Separation Overview: P0C717 undergoes phase separation in the cytoplasm, forming liquid-like condensates both in vitro and in vivo (PubMed:36250941, 34015248). Its phase separation is intrinsically driven by a conserved basic cluster and requires DNA induction, with no reported material state transitions or specific membrane-less organelle associations (PubMed:36250941, 34015248).
Functional Summary: P0C717 phase separation mediates immune evasion by restricting cGAS-DNA condensate formation, thereby inhibiting the cGAS-STING pathway (PubMed:34015248).
Intrinsic Determinants & Regulations: Phase separation is intrinsically regulated by a conserved basic cluster within an intrinsically disordered region, as evidenced by the complete abolition of condensate formation in the 4A mutant (K120A/K121A/R122A/R123A) (PubMed:36250941).
Extrinsic Partners & Regulations: Double-stranded DNA (dsDNA) acts as an essential extrinsic inducer of phase separation, required for both in vitro droplet formation and cellular puncta assembly (PubMed:34015248).

Overall Phase Separation Overview: HSF1 (P10961) undergoes self-driven phase separation to form inducible, dynamic transcriptional condensates in the nucleus upon heat shock or proteotoxic stress (PubMed:36327976, 30605674). These liquid-like condensates, sensitive to dissolution by 1,6-hexanediol, exhibit rapid spatiotemporal dynamics with distinct demixing (formation), intermixing (rearrangement), and remixing (dissolution) phases. They specifically associate with heat shock response (HSR) genes and drive inter-chromosomal gene coalescence, forming compartments distinct from nucleoli or nuclear pores (PubMed:36327976).
Functional Summary: HSF1 condensates enable 3D genome reorganization by driving inter-chromosomal coalescence of HSR genes, concentrating Mediator/Pol II for rapid transcriptional activation during stress, and promoting cellular thermotolerance (PubMed:36327976, 30605674). Dysregulation impairs function: loss of intergenic coalescence (ΔNTAce2AAA mutant) reduces fitness, while disrupted condensate dynamics (e.g., via impaired Pol II recruitment) abolishes stress response (PubMed:36327976, 30605674).
Intrinsic Determinants & Regulations: Phase separation is intrinsically regulated by HSF1's N-terminal activation domain (NTA), which promotes condensate formation and intergenic interactions among HSR genes, and the C-terminal activation domain (CTA), essential for Mediator recruitment and intergenic interactions (PubMed:36327976). Key mutations alter phase behavior: the CE2 mutation prevents Hsp70 binding and causes constitutive clustering without intergenic coalescence; ΔNTA abolishes clustering; and ΔNTAce2AAA forms constitutive clusters lacking gene coalescence (PubMed:36327976).
Extrinsic Partners & Regulations: HSF1 phase separation is extrinsically modulated by partners including the chaperone Hsp70, which represses clustering by binding the CE2 domain (evidenced by constitutive clustering in ce2AAA mutants) (PubMed:36327976). HSF1 co-phase separates with transcriptional machinery: Med15 and Rpb3 show >70% co-localization in condensates, while RNA polymerase II subunit Rpb1 is essential for HSR gene coalescence (PubMed:36327976, 30605674). HSR genes act as genomic anchors for condensate localization (PubMed:36327976).

Overall Phase Separation Overview: HSPA5 (BiP) does not undergo autonomous phase separation but is recruited into biomolecular condensates through partner-driven mechanisms (PubMed:37253728, 33335017, 39946235). It localizes to multiple subcellular compartments including the cytoplasm, nucleus, and ER membrane, associating with distinct membrane-less organelles: stress-induced CERFs (Coalescence of ER Fragments) in adipocytes (PubMed:37253728), nuclear anisosomes (PubMed:33335017), and ER-associated SCOTIN condensates (PubMed:39946235). Its material state varies contextually—exhibiting solid-like properties in CERFs and SCOTIN condensates (low FRAP recovery, TEM morphology) but liquid-like behavior in anisosome cores (rapid FRAP) (PubMed:37253728, 33335017, 39946235). Pathological liquid-to-solid transitions occur in CERFs through age-dependent hardening and in anisosomes upon ATP depletion (PubMed:37253728, 33335017).
Functional Summary: HSPA5 condensates have dual physiological-pathological roles: In CERFs, HSPA5 coating mitigates LPL aggregation toxicity during proteostasis failure, enabling adipocyte survival but contributing to age-related metabolic dysfunction upon solidification (PubMed:37253728). In anisosomes, HSPA5 maintains TDP-43 liquidity via ATP-dependent chaperone activity; its failure drives pathological aggregation in ALS, FTD, and Alzheimer's disease (PubMed:33335017). Conversely, HSPA5 sequestration by SCOTIN condensates depletes free chaperone pools, dissociating HSPA5 from ER stress sensors (IRE1/PERK/ATF6) to trigger UPR activation and apoptosis—implicated in interferon responses and cancer (PubMed:39946235).
Intrinsic Determinants & Regulations: No intrinsic domains or sequence features of HSPA5 driving its phase separation were reported in the provided studies. Its incorporation into condensates is exclusively partner-dependent, requiring scaffold proteins for recruitment (PubMed:37253728, 33335017, 39946235).
Extrinsic Partners & Regulations: HSPA5 phase separation is extrinsically regulated by three key partners: LPL scaffolds core-shell condensates where HSPA5 forms the outer layer in CERFs, reducing turbidity and slightly increasing mobility (PubMed:37253728); RNA-binding deficient TDP-43 recruits HSPA5 into liquid cores of nuclear anisosomes, with enrichment confirmed by proteomics (6-16×) (PubMed:33335017); and SCOTIN sequesters HSPA5 in ER-associated condensates dependent on SCOTIN's proline-rich domain (PRD)-mediated condensation (PubMed:39946235). ATP levels critically regulate liquidity—depletion drives irreversible solidification in anisosomes (PubMed:33335017).

Overall Phase Separation Overview: Bik1 (P11709) undergoes self-driven liquid-liquid phase separation (LLPS) both autonomously and within the Kar9-Bim1-Bik1 ternary complex, forming liquid-like condensates (PubMed:36536177, 39885130). It localizes to the cytoplasm and associates with the '+TIP body' condensate at microtubule plus-ends, exhibiting persistent liquid properties without observed state transitions (PubMed:36536177).
Functional Summary: Bik1 LLPS drives +TIP body formation, enabling persistent microtubule plus-end tracking and mechanical coupling to actin cables for spindle positioning during yeast mitosis/mating (PubMed:36536177, 39885130). Its fractal condensate organization provides high viscosity at low protein concentrations, facilitating force transmission (PubMed:39885130). Disruption (e.g., bik1Δ combined with Kar9 mutants) causes severe spindle misalignment and mitotic defects (PubMed:36536177).
Intrinsic Determinants & Regulations: Phase separation is intrinsically driven by the N-terminal CAP-Gly domain and C-terminal QQFF motif (EEY/F-like), both essential for autonomous condensation (PubMed:36536177, 39885130). The coiled-coil domain mediates conformational rearrangements enabling higher-order oligomerization, while truncations (e.g., ΔQQFF) abolish phase separation (PubMed:39885130). Self-association interfaces facilitate multivalency, though specific mutation effects remain uncharacterized (PubMed:36536177).
Extrinsic Partners & Regulations: Bik1 co-phase separates with Kar9 and Bim1 in a cooperative ternary network, where Kar9 significantly lowers the critical concentration for droplet formation (PubMed:36536177). Bim1 binds Bik1 via CAP-Gly-EEY/F interactions, resolubilizing Bik1 in Kar9's absence but enriching 27-fold within ternary condensates (PubMed:36536177).

Overall Phase Separation Overview: EBNA2 undergoes self-driven phase separation (PubMed:31941785) to form liquid-like condensates primarily in the nucleus and occasionally in the cytoplasm (PubMed:34400762). These condensates are enriched at superenhancer sites (e.g., MYC, Runx3) (PubMed:31941785) and induce accessible chromatin domains (ACDs) (PubMed:34400762). The condensates exhibit liquid-like properties including rapid fluorescence recovery after photobleaching (FRAP), fusion dynamics, and sensitivity to 1,6-hexanediol (PubMed:31941785, 34400762). No pathological material state transitions were observed under normal conditions (PubMed:31941785, 34400762).
Functional Summary: EBNA2 condensates enable Epstein-Barr virus-mediated oncogenesis by recruiting transcriptional machinery to superenhancer sites, activating key target genes (e.g., MYC, Runx3) for B-cell transformation (PubMed:31941785). They reorganize host chromatin into accessible domains (ACDs), recruiting p300 to acetylate H3K27 and hijack epigenetic regulation of host genes (e.g., SYK, autoimmune loci) (PubMed:34400762).
Intrinsic Determinants & Regulations: Phase separation is intrinsically driven by EBNA2's intrinsically disordered region (IDR, aa 145-441) (PubMed:31941785) and requires its N-terminal dimerization domains (Dim1/Dim2) for self-association (PubMed:34400762). Proline residues are essential, as mutation to alanine (P-to-A) abolishes condensate formation (PubMed:31941785). Disruption occurs when negative charges are introduced via poly-glutamic acid tracts (Nter-8E mutation), which interfere with phase separation (PubMed:34400762).
Extrinsic Partners & Regulations: EBNA2 recruits the histone acetyltransferase p300 to its condensates through its C-terminal transactivation domain (C-TAD) (PubMed:34400762). Phase separation is sensitive to environmental conditions: it is disrupted by 1,6-hexanediol (PubMed:31941785, 34400762) and suppressed by increasing NaCl concentrations (>50mM) (PubMed:31941785).

Overall Phase Separation Overview: Nsp1 (P14907) undergoes both self-driven phase separation to form hydrogels via phenylalanine-mediated cross-linking in vitro (PubMed:17082456) and co-phase separation with partners to form liquid-like cytosolic condensates in daughter cells during division (PubMed:39356635). It localizes to the nucleus and cytoplasm, associating primarily with the nuclear pore complex and daughter-specific cytosolic condensates (PubMed:39356635, 17082456). While Nsp1 itself forms reversible hydrogels in vitro (PubMed:17082456), it modulates material state transitions in other FG-nucleoporins, promoting liquid-like properties and preventing pathological aggregation (PubMed:39356635).
Functional Summary: Nsp1 hydrogel formation constitutes the nuclear pore complex permeability barrier, enabling size-selective transport essential for yeast viability (PubMed:17082456). Its cytosolic condensates maintain FG-nucleoporins in liquid-like, assembly-competent states for daughter-cell NPC biogenesis, with reduced levels causing aging-mimetic defects in proteostasis and NPC function (PubMed:39356635). Dysregulation leads to pathological aggregation of client proteins, while Nsp1 overexpression attenuates toxicity of ALS-linked polyPR peptides, highlighting its role in cellular surveillance against condensation defects (PubMed:39356635, 17082456).
Intrinsic Determinants & Regulations: Phase separation is intrinsically driven by Nsp1's FG domain, where phenylalanine residues within FG/FSFG motifs are essential for hydrogel formation via inter-repeat cross-linking (PubMed:17082456). Charged spacers in the extended domain (residues 187-601) enable surfactant-like activity critical for modulating client condensates (PubMed:39356635). Mutations disrupting hydrophobic interactions (e.g., F→S substitutions) abolish hydrogel formation (PubMed:17082456), while spacer-randomized mutations impair phase-modulating capabilities and reduce condensate circularity (PubMed:39356635).
Extrinsic Partners & Regulations: Nsp1 co-phase separates with nuclear transport receptor Kap95 (79% co-localization) as co-scaffolds in daughter-specific condensates and cooperatively modulates FG-nucleoporin liquidity (PubMed:39356635). It incorporates GLFG-repeat domains from nucleoporins Nup116, Nup49, Nup57, and Nup145 into heterotypic hydrogels (PubMed:17082456) and shows 97% co-localization with RNA helicase Dbp5 in cytoplasmic foci (PubMed:39356635). Nsp1's phase behavior enables cooperative regulation with Kap95 to suppress aggregation of FG-Nups like Nup100 and Nup116 by promoting liquid-like states (PubMed:39356635).

Overall Phase Separation Overview: p33 (P15962) undergoes self-driven phase separation (class: PS-self) to form gel-like condensates (vir-condensates) within viral replication organelles (VROs) in the cytoplasm (PubMed:38515267). These condensates sequester host proteins and exhibit hydrogel properties with no FRAP recovery in vitro, while in planta dynamics are constrained by ER/actin meshworks (PubMed:38515267). p33 additionally scaffolds liquid-like puncta of autophagy proteins within VROs, characterized by partial FRAP recovery (PubMed:38484009). No material state transitions are reported.
Functional Summary: Phase separation enables viral replication by concentrating glycolytic enzymes for local ATP production within VROs; IDR1 mutations impair this process and reduce replication (PubMed:38515267). Simultaneously, p33 sequesters ATG8f and NBR1 in condensates to inhibit autophagic flux, evading antiviral degradation while enriching phosphatidylethanolamine and PI3P lipids for membrane biosynthesis (PubMed:38484009). This dual mechanism supports viral immune evasion and replication efficiency.
Intrinsic Determinants & Regulations: Phase separation is intrinsically driven by the IDR1 region, which is essential for droplet formation (PubMed:38515267). The p33:p33/p92 domain stabilizes the gel-like state, while charged residues within IDR1 are critical for phase separation (PubMed:38515267). Mutations significantly alter behavior: IDR1m1 (charged segment mutant) reduces droplet formation, DIDR1 abolishes VRO formation, and DIDR2 increases droplet size while maintaining the gel state (PubMed:38515267). The N-terminal region (aa 1-82) facilitates ATG8f binding but does not directly drive phase separation (PubMed:38484009).
Extrinsic Partners & Regulations: p33 recruits glycolytic/fermentation enzymes (ADH1, FBA2, GAPDH, PGK1, PK, PDC1) and RPN11 into condensates via co-partitioning, enabling localized ATP production (PubMed:38515267). It also scaffolds autophagy proteins ATG8f and NBR1 into liquid-like puncta, with direct interactions mediated through its N-terminal domain (PubMed:38484009). Condensate integrity depends on hydrophobic/electrostatic interactions, evidenced by partial dissolution with 1,6-hexanediol treatment (PubMed:38515267, 38484009).

Overall Phase Separation Overview: H1.5 (P16401) undergoes partner-dependent phase separation classified as PS-other. In vivo, phase separation is inferred through binding with RNA SNHG8 (PubMed:35140358). In vitro, the CH1 domain (residues 115-225) forms phase-separated droplets with DNA (PubMed:30301810). Material state remains unspecified across studies, with no reported state transitions.
Functional Summary: Phase separation regulates chromatin organization: SNHG8 binding modulates chromatin condensation in vivo (PubMed:35140358). The CH1-DNA model demonstrates phosphorylation-dependent control of higher-order chromatin structuring, where phosphorylation disrupts condensate formation (PubMed:30301810).
Intrinsic Determinants & Regulations: The CH1 domain (residues 115-225) is critical for phase separation (PubMed:30301810). Phosphorylation at S157, S175, and S193 disrupts droplet formation, maintaining complexes in the bulk phase instead of phase-separating (PubMed:30301810).
Extrinsic Partners & Regulations: Phase separation requires extrinsic partners: RNA SNHG8 in vivo, evidenced by RNA pull-down and ChIRP assays (PubMed:35140358), and 36-bp DNA in vitro, where titration causes turbidity indicative of coacervation (PubMed:30301810).

Overall Phase Separation Overview: H1.2 undergoes partner-dependent phase separation in the nucleus, requiring DNA or RNA scaffolds for condensation (PubMed:35140358, 34108453). In vitro, it forms liquid-like droplets with DNA or nucleosome arrays, exhibiting spherical morphology, fusion competence, and rapid fluorescence recovery (PubMed:34108453). No material state transitions were observed under tested conditions (PubMed:34108453).
Functional Summary: Phase separation mediates chromatin organization: condensate formation regulates DNA accessibility, with ubiquitylation (e.g., K64) promoting transcriptionally active states by preventing heterochromatin compaction (PubMed:34108453). SNHG8-dependent modulation of H1.2 condensation further influences chromatin binding dynamics, linking RNA interactions to chromatin architecture (PubMed:35140358).
Intrinsic Determinants & Regulations: Phase separation is modulated by site-specific ubiquitylation within functional domains: modifications at K17 (N-terminal domain) and K64 (globular domain) significantly increase condensate number while reducing droplet size without altering liquid-like dynamics or partition coefficients (PubMed:34108453). Ubiquitylation at K206 also influences phase behavior but with distinct effects on chromatosome stability (PubMed:34108453).
Extrinsic Partners & Regulations: DNA acts as an essential electrostatic scaffold for LLPS, with droplet formation occurring only in its presence and dissolving at high ionic strength (PubMed:34108453). The RNA SNHG8 binds H1.2 and regulates condensation, where SNHG8 loss promotes increased chromatin binding and phase separation (PubMed:35140358).

Overall Phase Separation Overview: PTBP1 undergoes partner-dependent phase separation, primarily driven by multivalent interactions with RNA and protein partners (PubMed:32908311). It forms liquid-like condensates in the nucleus, specifically associating with the inactive X chromosome (Xi) territory and nuclear speckles (PubMed:32908311). These condensates exhibit dynamic liquid properties including droplet fusion in vitro and viscoelastic behavior in vivo (PubMed:32908311). PTBP1 also participates in supramolecular complexes (SMACs) with dynamic exchange kinetics, as observed through FRAP analysis (PubMed:34813726).
Functional Summary: PTBP1 condensates are essential for X-chromosome inactivation, anchoring Xist RNA to the Xi territory to establish heritable gene silencing and epigenetic memory (PubMed:32908311). Within supramolecular complexes (SMACs), PTBP1 contributes to dynamic protein gradients that regulate proximal chromatin regions, with partitioning mediated by intrinsically disordered regions being critical for transcriptional repression (PubMed:34813726).
Intrinsic Determinants & Regulations: Phase separation is intrinsically regulated by PTBP1's RNA recognition motif (RRM) domains that enable multivalent RNA binding, with the C-terminal region being critical for valency (PubMed:32908311). Disruption of these features through C-terminal truncation (ΔC) impairs condensate formation, while the Y247Q mutation specifically ablates heterotypic protein interactions (PubMed:32908311).
Extrinsic Partners & Regulations: Phase separation is extrinsically regulated by the Xist E-repeat RNA, which serves as a scaffold for multivalent binding and droplet nucleation (PubMed:32908311). Heterotypic protein interactions with MATR3 stabilize condensates through RNase-resistant binding, while CELF1 synergistically enhances phase separation by lowering the concentration threshold for droplet formation (PubMed:32908311).

Overall Phase Separation Overview: NELFE (P18615) undergoes partner-dependent phase separation as an essential component of the NELF complex in the nucleus (PubMed:33548202, 36603581). Under cellular stress (e.g., heat shock, arsenic exposure), the entire heterotetrameric NELF complex forms liquid-like transcriptional condensates that exhibit dynamic properties including fusion and rapid fluorescence recovery (PubMed:33548202). These condensates serve as nuclear counterparts to cytosolic stress granules and require the intrinsically disordered tentacle domain (aa 139-380) of NELFE for formation (PubMed:33548202). While wild-type NELFE tentacle doesn't partition into MED1IDR condensates, an engineered 'blocky' variant with charge patterning gains partitioning capability (PubMed:36603581).
Functional Summary: Phase separation of the NELF complex containing NELFE drives stress-induced transcriptional downregulation by stabilizing promoter-proximally paused RNA Polymerase II at housekeeping genes, which is essential for cell survival under stress (PubMed:33548202). These condensates represent nuclear counterparts to cytosolic stress granules that coordinate global stress responses (PubMed:33548202). Artificially engineered partitioning of the 'blocky' NELFE variant into MED1IDR condensates mislocalizes the NELF complex, repressing transcription and demonstrating functional consequences of aberrant compartmentalization (PubMed:36603581).
Intrinsic Determinants & Regulations: Phase separation of NELFE is intrinsically regulated by its intrinsically disordered tentacle domain (residues 139-380), which is necessary and sufficient for NELF complex condensation through heterotypic interactions with NELFA's IDR (PubMed:33548202). Deletion of this domain (Δ139-380) abolishes phase separation (PubMed:33548202). Charge patterning within the tentacle domain is a critical determinant: engineered 'blocky' variants with alternating charge blocks gain partitioning capability into MED1IDR condensates, unlike the wild-type sequence (PubMed:36603581).
Extrinsic Partners & Regulations: NELFE co-phase separates exclusively as part of the heterotetrameric NELF complex with partners NELFA, NELFB, and NELFC (PubMed:33548202). Complex condensation is regulated antagonistically by post-translational modifications: SUMOylation mediated by ZNF451/UBC9 promotes condensation, while phosphorylation by P-TEFb (CDK9) inhibits it by weakening intermolecular interactions and increasing mobility (PubMed:33548202). NELF condensates enrich S5-phosphorylated RNA Polymerase II CTD with distal non-consensus repeats and are dissolved by 1,6-hexanediol treatment (PubMed:33548202). The engineered 'blocky' NELFE variant partitions into MED1IDR condensates as a client (PubMed:36603581).

Overall Phase Separation Overview: XRCC1 (P18887) does not undergo self-driven phase separation (class: PS-other) but partitions into condensates through partner-dependent mechanisms. It forms inhomogeneous multiphase assemblies primarily driven by poly(ADP-ribose) (PAR), localizing into PARP1 condensates where it exhibits enhanced enrichment upon PARylation (PubMed:39496836, 36361989). XRCC1 co-phase separates with FUS in PAR-containing systems and forms distinct multiphase structures with DNA ligase III (LIG3) (PubMed:39496836, 36361989).
Functional Summary: XRCC1 condensates organize DNA repair machinery, enhancing DNA ligation efficiency through multiphase assemblies with LIG3 (PubMed:39496836). PAR-dependent coassemblies with FUS propose a role in damage-site organization, potentially facilitating DNA repair complex formation (PubMed:36361989).
Intrinsic Determinants & Regulations: No intrinsic domains, mutations, or structural features driving XRCC1 phase separation are reported in the provided studies (PubMed:39496836, 36361989).
Extrinsic Partners & Regulations: XRCC1 phase separation is extrinsically regulated by nucleic acids and protein partners. PAR chains are essential for inducing its microphase separation and co-assembly with FUS (PubMed:36361989). PARP1 acts as a scaffold for XRCC1 partitioning, with PARylation enhancing enrichment ~2-fold (PubMed:39496836). XRCC1 forms functional multiphase condensates with LIG3 and co-localizes with FUS in shared droplets under PAR-rich conditions (PubMed:39496836, 36361989).

Overall Phase Separation Overview: Nucleolin (NCL) undergoes phase separation primarily within the nucleolus, where it functions as a structural component (PubMed:36150385, 34515347, 39108718). Its phase separation behavior is classified as PS-other, requiring partners rather than self-assembly (PubMed:34515347, 36150385). Nucleolin partitions into nuclear condensates through domain-specific mechanisms, with its glycine-arginine rich (GAR) domain contributing to localization while RNA recognition motifs (RRMs) dominate phase separation stability (PubMed:34515347). It forms liquid-like condensates, evidenced by rapid FRAP recovery when its intrinsically disordered region (IDR) functionally rescues defects in other nucleolar proteins (PubMed:39108718). These condensates undergo dissolution upon ssRNA accumulation (PubMed:36150385).
Functional Summary: Nucleolin phase separation is essential for nucleolar integrity and function. Dissolution of its condensates by ssRNA accumulation impairs nucleolar organization (PubMed:36150385). Through heterotypic interactions, it contributes to mitotic organization via recruitment to Ki-67 condensates in the perichromosomal layer (PubMed:37813838). Critically, its phase separation capability maintains ribosome biogenesis and prevents proteotoxic stress, as demonstrated by rescue of protein synthesis deficits, reduced p53 activation, and improved cell survival when its IDR compensates for FBL defects in neural progenitor cells (PubMed:39108718). Impairment of these phase separation functions links to ribosomopathy-like defects including protein synthesis deficiency and developmental delays (PubMed:39108718).
Intrinsic Determinants & Regulations: Phase separation of nucleolin is intrinsically regulated by its glycine-arginine rich (GAR) domain, an intrinsically disordered region (IDR) essential for nucleolar partitioning (PubMed:34515347). Deletion of this domain (ΔGAR) significantly reduces nucleolar localization while maintaining nuclear presence (PubMed:34515347). The RNA recognition motifs (RRMs) play a dominant role in maintaining phase separation stability under stress conditions (PubMed:34515347). The functional importance of the GAR domain as a phase separation driver is confirmed by its ability to replace the IDR of FBL and rescue nucleolar phase separation defects in mutant cells (PubMed:39108718).
Extrinsic Partners & Regulations: Nucleolin phase separation is modulated by RNA and protein partners. Single-stranded RNA (ssRNA) dissolves nucleolar condensates, as demonstrated by microinjection reducing nucleolin intensity by ~50% (PubMed:36150385). Nucleolin co-assembles with Ki-67 in phosphorylation-dependent condensates, forming liquid-like foci observable in optoDroplet systems (PubMed:37813838). This co-assembly occurs alongside nucleophosmin (NPM1) within heterotypic condensates (PubMed:37813838). Nucleolin's IDR serves as a functional phase separation motif that rescues defects in FBL when swapped, indicating cooperative interactions with nucleolar components (PubMed:39108718).

Overall Phase Separation Overview: TRIM21 (P19474) exhibits dual phase separation-related behaviors. It undergoes self-driven liquid-liquid phase separation (LLPS) in vitro and forms dynamic liquid-like cytoplasmic puncta in human cells, primarily driven by its coiled-coil domain (PubMed:37879251). Alternatively, under oxidative stress, it associates with membrane-less organelles (MLOs) like stress granules (SGs) in the cytoplasm without undergoing phase separation itself, instead regulating G3BP1 condensation through ubiquitination (PubMed:36692217).
Functional Summary: TRIM21 phase separation promotes autophagosome nucleation and autophagy activation, leading to reduced p62 levels, increased LC3-II conversion, and inhibition of cell proliferation (PubMed:37879251). Alternatively, through G3BP1 ubiquitination, TRIM21 regulates stress granule homeostasis, preventing pathological SG accumulation linked to neurodegenerative diseases like ALS-FTD and supporting cell survival (PubMed:36692217).
Intrinsic Determinants & Regulations: The coiled-coil (CC) domain (residues 80-220) is the primary intrinsic driver of TRIM21 phase separation, containing predicted low-complexity disordered regions essential for condensate formation. Deletion of this domain (ΔCC) completely abolishes phase separation capability (PubMed:37879251).
Extrinsic Partners & Regulations: TRIM21 interacts with G3BP1 under oxidative stress, inhibiting its phase separation via K63-linked ubiquitination (PubMed:36692217). During autophagy-related phase separation, TRIM21 co-localizes with LC3B in cytoplasmic puncta, though LC3B's direct role in modulating phase separation remains unspecified (PubMed:37879251).

Overall Phase Separation Overview: TFE3 undergoes self-driven phase separation to form liquid-like condensates in the nucleus (PubMed:35293953, 33290695). These condensates exhibit low fusion propensity and are associated with transcriptional condensates (PubMed:35293953). Under cellular stress, TFE3 forms nuclear puncta (PubMed:33290695). No material state transitions were reported in these studies.
Functional Summary: TFE3 phase separation is associated with transcriptional condensates, suggesting a role in transcriptional regulation (PubMed:35293953). However, specific functional consequences were not detailed in the provided studies (PubMed:35293953, 33290695).
Intrinsic Determinants & Regulations: Phase separation of TFE3 is driven by its full-length protein structure, as both studies utilized full-length constructs and observed self-assembly without identifying specific domains, mutations, or post-translational modifications as regulators (PubMed:35293953, 33290695).
Extrinsic Partners & Regulations: TFE3 phase separation is unaffected by the protein partner IPMK, as co-addition in vitro did not inhibit droplet formation and cellular depletion did not alter puncta formation (PubMed:33290695). The compounds Ro-3306 and vanillic acid, which modulate related proteins, show no effect on TFE3 condensate properties (PubMed:35293953).

Overall Phase Separation Overview: TBP (P20226) undergoes self-driven phase separation (class: PS-self), forming liquid-like condensates primarily in the nucleus, where it associates with transcriptional condensates (PubMed:32386547). In vitro, phase separation requires molecular crowding agents like dextran to form liquid droplets, otherwise forming fiber-like aggregates (PubMed:34916619). Pathological glutamine repeat expansion (53Q) inhibits its phase separation capacity (PubMed:32386547).
Functional Summary: TBP phase separation compartmentalizes Pol II CTD within transcriptional condensates, facilitating efficient transcription (PubMed:34916619). Dysregulation, particularly inhibition of phase separation by pathological glutamine repeat expansion (53Q), disrupts transcriptional condensate formation and is linked to spinocerebellar ataxia type 17 (SCA17) (PubMed:32386547).
Intrinsic Determinants & Regulations: Phase separation is intrinsically driven by TBP's intrinsically disordered region (IDR) (PubMed:32386547). Pathological mutations, specifically the glutamine repeat expansion (53Q) within the IDR, disrupt phase separation (PubMed:32386547). The protein's high intrinsic disorder content (51% IDR) further supports phase separation propensity (PubMed:34916619).
Extrinsic Partners & Regulations: TBP co-phase separates with the scaffold protein PSPC1, forming larger condensates that enhance incorporation of Pol II C-terminal domain (CTD) (PubMed:34916619). Phase separation is critically dependent on extrinsic crowding agents (e.g., 10% dextran) to achieve liquid-like states in vitro (PubMed:34916619).

Overall Phase Separation Overview: OCT4 undergoes both self-driven and partner-dependent phase separation (PubMed:34038708, 31398323). It forms liquid-like condensates primarily in the nucleus, associating with genomic loci to reorganize topologically associating domains (TADs) (PubMed:34038708). These condensates exhibit dynamic liquid properties including rapid FRAP recovery and fusion capability (PubMed:34038708). DNA scaffolding stabilizes condensate formation at low protein concentrations (PubMed:31398323).
Functional Summary: OCT4 condensates concentrate chromatin loops to drive TAD reorganization during somatic cell reprogramming, redistributing super-enhancers to activate pluripotency genes like Dppa5a (PubMed:34038708). This enables efficient induced pluripotent stem cell (iPSC) generation, as phase separation disruption reduces reprogramming efficiency while IDR fusion restores it (PubMed:34038708). OCT4-mediated condensates also recruit transcriptional machinery (RNA Pol II, BRD4) to enhancers, enabling exponential transcriptional activation at high motif-density loci (PubMed:31398323).
Intrinsic Determinants & Regulations: Phase separation is intrinsically driven by OCT4's intrinsically disordered regions (IDRs), particularly through acidic residues (E/D) and a critical 3-amino acid motif (aa 324-326) in the C-terminal IDR (PubMed:34038708). The acidic activation domain mediates essential interactions with partners like MED1 (PubMed:31398323). Mutations disrupting these features - including acidic-to-alanine substitutions and deletion of residues 324-326 - abolish phase separation capacity both in vitro and in vivo (PubMed:34038708, 31398323).
Extrinsic Partners & Regulations: OCT4 phase separation requires cooperative partnerships with MED1 and DNA scaffolds containing multivalent binding sites (e.g., ODNA_20) (PubMed:31398323). DNA binding lowers the critical saturation concentration (C_sat) by 68-fold compared to DNA-free conditions (PubMed:31398323). Heterologous IDRs like FUS IDR can rescue phase separation in OCT4 mutants (PubMed:34038708). Condensate stability depends on DNA scaffolding at low protein concentrations, becoming resistant to DNase I degradation only at high concentrations (PubMed:31398323).

Overall Phase Separation Overview: Nucleolin (Ncl) undergoes phase separation within the nucleus, specifically associating with the nucleolus's granular component (GC) and dense fibrillar component (DFC) (PubMed:35607824, 37943867). It exhibits variable compartmentalization: while predominantly localizing to GC, it also occupies DFC with inter-experiment variability, and its isolated N-terminal intrinsically disordered region (IDR) distributes non-specifically throughout nucleolar compartments (PubMed:37943867). Material state and transitions were not explicitly characterized in the provided studies.
Functional Summary: Ncl's phase separation facilitates ribosome assembly and pre-rRNA transcription by enabling dynamic movement between nucleolar compartments during ribosome biogenesis stages (PubMed:35607824, 37943867). Its dual GC/DFC localization supports functional integration across these subcompartments, particularly in coordinating ribosomal subunit maturation and nuclear export processes (PubMed:37943867).
Intrinsic Determinants & Regulations: Phase separation is primarily driven by Ncl's N-terminal IDR (residues 1-270), which features a high negative charge (net -40 at pH 7) and intrinsically disordered properties (PubMed:37943867). This domain alone localizes broadly throughout the nucleolus but cannot confer specific compartment targeting when fused to other proteins (PubMed:37943867). A predicted C-terminal FG-rich IDR, nuclear localization signal (NLS), and nucleolar localization signal (NoLS) were noted but not experimentally validated (PubMed:35607824, 37943867).
Extrinsic Partners & Regulations: No extrinsic regulators, partner proteins, or environmental modulators (e.g., ions, chemicals) were reported for Ncl's phase separation in the provided studies (PubMed:35607824, 37943867).

Overall Phase Separation Overview: Fbl (P22232) undergoes phase separation and localizes to the dense fibrillar component (DFC) of the nucleolus in the nucleus, acting as a canonical marker for this compartment (PubMed:35607824, 37943867). It forms punctate structures that exhibit stress-responsive material state transitions: heat shock causes fragmentation and dispersion into the granular component, while actinomycin D induces condensation; recovery occurs after stress removal (PubMed:35607824). Phase separation is sensitive to 1,6-hexanediol, indicating involvement of hydrophobic interactions (PubMed:37943867).
Functional Summary: Fbl phase separation is essential for ribosome biogenesis, enabling pre-rRNA methylation within the DFC compartment (PubMed:35607824, 37943867). Stress-induced disruption (e.g., heat shock) correlates with compromised rRNA processing, directly linking condensate integrity to cellular function (PubMed:35607824).
Intrinsic Determinants & Regulations: The N-terminal intrinsically disordered region (IDR; residues 1-89) of Fbl is RG-repeat rich with a net positive charge (+17) but is not essential for phase separation or DFC localization, as its removal does not prevent compartmentalization (PubMed:37943867). An IDR was predicted but not experimentally verified as a key driver (PubMed:35607824).
Extrinsic Partners & Regulations: Fbl co-phase separates with protein partners including Nop56, Gar1, Nhp2, and Snu13, forming essential rRNA modification complexes in the DFC, as evidenced by co-localization (PubMed:35607824). rRNA serves as a scaffold for DFC assembly (PubMed:35607824). Phase separation is disrupted by 1,6-hexanediol, indicating regulation by hydrophobic interactions (PubMed:37943867).

Overall Phase Separation Overview: Spa2 (P23201) undergoes self-driven liquid-liquid phase separation (LLPS) via intrinsically disordered regions (IDRs), forming dynamic liquid condensates in the cytoplasm and at the bud tip within the polarisome complex (PubMed:38802374, 31699995). This behavior is concentration-dependent and modulated by ionic strength, with condensates exhibiting liquid-like properties including fusion and rapid fluorescence recovery after photobleaching (FRAP) (PubMed:38802374, 31699995).
Functional Summary: Phase separation enables rapid actin remodeling during glucose starvation by nucleating ADP-actin monomers and bundling filaments, stabilizing actin cables against cofilin-mediated severing (PubMed:38802374). At the bud tip, Spa2 concentrates Aip5 for polarized actin assembly and ensures reversible stress storage of Aip5, preventing irreversible aggregation and facilitating rapid actin reassembly upon recovery (PubMed:31699995). In spa2Δ mutants, Aip5 forms pathological solid-like aggregates that disrupt actin dynamics and impair cell growth (PubMed:31699995).
Intrinsic Determinants & Regulations: Phase separation is intrinsically driven by two distinct IDRs: an N-terminal IDR (aa 1-281) enabling homotypic LLPS and ADP-actin wetting/bundling, and a C-terminal IDR (aa 1151-1305) independently facilitating LLPS (PubMed:38802374, 31699995). A dimeric core (aa 281-535) enables actin binding, with engineered trimerization enhancing nucleation/bundling by mimicking IDR multivalency (PubMed:38802374).
Extrinsic Partners & Regulations: Spa2 co-phase separates with ADP-actin filaments, wetting and bundling them via IDR-mediated multivalency (PubMed:38802374). It scaffolds Aip5 into liquid condensates, converting amorphous Aip5 assemblies into dynamic states (PubMed:31699995). LLPS is suppressed at high KCl concentrations (>250 mM) and is sensitive to ionic strength (PubMed:38802374).

Overall Phase Separation Overview: Sis1 (P25294) undergoes self-driven phase separation (PubMed:33229560), forming liquid droplets in vitro (PubMed:33229560) and hydrogel-like condensates in vivo within the cytoplasm during hyperosmotic stress (PubMed:31285266). It associates with Osmotic Shock Foci (PubMed:31285266) and regulates the disassembly of stress-triggered Pab1 condensates (PubMed:35490076).
Functional Summary: Sis1-containing Osmotic Shock Foci facilitate rapid cellular adaptation to osmotic stress (PubMed:31285266). As a chaperone, Sis1 is essential for disassembling Pab1 hydrogel condensates during heat stress recovery, promoting cellular fitness by enabling chaperone-mediated dispersal (PubMed:35490076).
Intrinsic Determinants & Regulations: The phase separation of Sis1 is intrinsically driven by its full-length protein structure (residues 1-352) (PubMed:33229560).
Extrinsic Partners & Regulations: Sis1's condensate formation is triggered by hyperosmotic stress in vivo (PubMed:31285266). Functionally, it requires interaction with Hsp104 and Hsp70 for efficient disassembly of Pab1 condensates during heat stress (PubMed:35490076).

Overall Phase Separation Overview: Rnq1 (P25367) undergoes phase separation in the cytoplasm of Saccharomyces cerevisiae, exhibiting distinct assembly states regulated by prion backgrounds (PubMed:26238190). In [pin−] cells, it forms dynamic, liquid-like non-amyloid assemblies sensitive to hexanediol, while in [PIN+] backgrounds, it transitions to solid-like, Thioflavin T-positive amyloid aggregates (PubMed:26238190). Rnq1 associates with insoluble protein deposits (IPOD) and colocalizes with prion-like aggregates (PubMed:27114519), and is essential for the formation of mutant Huntingtin (mHtt) inclusion bodies – gel-like, non-membrane-bound compartments (PubMed:31527136).
Functional Summary: Rnq1 serves as a critical scaffold for protein aggregation pathways, determining the structural properties of mutant Huntingtin inclusion bodies – dynamic, gel-like compartments proposed to sequester toxic polyglutamine-expanded proteins (PubMed:31527136). Its prion-like switching between liquid and amyloid states under [PIN+] regulation demonstrates a functional role in conformational memory and strain formation (PubMed:26238190). This behavior positions Rnq1 as a key modulator of protein homeostasis, where dysregulated phase transitions contribute to aggregation pathologies (PubMed:26238190, 31527136).
Intrinsic Determinants & Regulations: Phase separation of Rnq1 is intrinsically driven by its prion-like domain (PLD), which facilitates conformational switching and higher-order assembly (PubMed:26238190, 31527136). This domain enables the formation of distinct oligomeric states and governs its role as a scaffold for amyloid conversion in yeast (PubMed:26238190, 27114519).
Extrinsic Partners & Regulations: Rnq1's phase behavior is extrinsically regulated by the [PIN+] prion, which promotes amyloid conversion and SDS-resistant polymerization (PubMed:26238190). It functionally interacts with mutant Huntingtin (mHtt), where genetic deletion (rnq1Δ) abolishes mHtt inclusion body formation (PubMed:31527136). Rnq1 also colocalizes with the Arabidopsis thaliana protein LD at insoluble protein deposits, suggesting cross-species prion interactions (PubMed:27114519). Hexanediol dissolves its non-amyloid assemblies, confirming sensitivity to chemical disruptors (PubMed:26238190).

Overall Phase Separation Overview: U2AF2 (P26369) does not undergo autonomous phase separation but is recruited to membrane-less organelles in both cytoplasmic and nuclear compartments. In the cytoplasm, it localizes to eCAGr RNA foci (PubMed:37592155), while in the nucleus, it associates with splicing condensates at active genes (PubMed:31391587). The material state of these condensates and any phase transitions remain unspecified in both studies.
Functional Summary: Cytoplasmic recruitment to eCAGr RNA foci may contribute to RNA toxicity through protein sequestration, though direct functional evidence is lacking (PubMed:37592155). The functional role in nuclear splicing condensates remains unspecified, with no pathological implications or disease associations reported across the studies (PubMed:31391587, 37592155).
Intrinsic Determinants & Regulations: No intrinsic domains, mutations, or sequence features driving phase separation were identified in the provided studies. Both papers reported no specified domains, PTMs, or mutations influencing recruitment behavior (PubMed:37592155, 31391587).
Extrinsic Partners & Regulations: U2AF2 recruitment is modulated by eCAGr RNA, which forms cytoplasmic condensates that sequester the protein (PubMed:37592155). No additional extrinsic regulators, molecular partners, or environmental modulators were reported in the provided studies.

Overall Phase Separation Overview: PTBP1 (P26599) undergoes RNA-dependent liquid-liquid phase separation (LLPS) in vitro, classified as partner-driven phase separation (PS-other) (PubMed:34916619, 29425497). It forms droplets that incorporate RNA polymerase II C-terminal domain (Pol II CTD) and requires RNA scaffolds for assembly. Phase separation is enhanced by macromolecular crowding agents (BSA, PEG) and fusion with intrinsically disordered regions (IDRs) (PubMed:29425497). Subcellular locations and membrane-less organelle associations are not specified in the provided data.
Functional Summary: PTBP1 phase separation enhances RNA polymerase II engagement with DNA templates, promoting transcriptional regulation in vitro (PubMed:34916619). This behavior provides a model system for studying ribonucleoprotein (RNP) granule assembly mechanisms driven by specific protein-RNA interactions (PubMed:29425497). The crowding-enhanced phase separation demonstrates how cellular environments modulate biomolecular condensate formation (PubMed:29425497).
Intrinsic Determinants & Regulations: Phase separation is driven by PTBP1's RNA-binding domains that facilitate specific RNA interactions (PubMed:29425497).
