Overall Phase Separation Overview: Kib (A0A0B4LH59) undergoes phase separation classified as PS-other upon overexpression in Drosophila melanogaster, forming spherical cytoplasmic condensates that recruit Hpo (PubMed:36807601). These condensates exhibit concentration-dependent formation and sensitivity to macromolecular crowding but lack explicit characterization of material state or transitions (PubMed:36807601).
Functional Summary: Kib's phase separation activates Hpo signaling by nucleating condensates that recruit Hpo, thereby promoting kinase activation and growth regulation in Drosophila follicle epithelium (PubMed:36807601).
Intrinsic Determinants & Regulations: The phase separation of Kib is intrinsically driven by intrinsically disordered regions (IDRs) and PPXY motifs, which enable condensate formation (PubMed:36807601).
Extrinsic Partners & Regulations: Kib condensates recruit Hpo as a client protein, demonstrated by co-localization in condensates induced by Kib overexpression (PubMed:36807601).

Overall Phase Separation Overview: HIV-1 Integrase (IN) undergoes self-driven phase separation to form liquid-like, fusion-competent condensates in the nucleus (PubMed:38762180). These nuclear condensates are distinct from CPSF5/6 complexes and potentially associate with viral pre-integration complexes (PubMed:38762180). Aggregation occurs in E. coli-expressed complexes, though no explicit liquid-to-solid transition is reported (PubMed:38762180).
Functional Summary: LLPS regulates sequential enzymatic steps: it inhibits 3′ processing (pre-nuclear entry) but enhances strand transfer within nuclear condensates to optimize viral integration efficiency (PubMed:38762180). Dysregulation may contribute to HIV-1 integration efficiency and latency by locking IN in an integration-competent conformation (PubMed:38762180).
Intrinsic Determinants & Regulations: Phase separation is intrinsically driven by intrinsically disordered regions (IDRs) at the N-terminus, C-terminus, and interdomain (NTD-CCD linker), alongside multivalent interactions (PubMed:38762180). Post-translational modifications—including phosphorylation (S24, S255), acetylation (K173), and methylation—enhance LLPS efficiency in mammalian complexes (PubMed:38762180).
Extrinsic Partners & Regulations: LEDGF is essential for stable LLPS, enhancing condensate abundance, with mammalian IN-LEDGF/p75 complexes forming 3-fold more condensates than E. coli complexes (PubMed:38762180). Viral DNA (U5 sequence) and target DNA co-phase separate to form functional 'intasomes' within condensates, exhibiting high colocalization (Pearson r = 0.96) (PubMed:38762180).

Overall Phase Separation Overview: ATXN2 undergoes phase separation in the cytoplasm, forming multiple small granules in its wildtype form. Deletion of the PAM2 motif (ΔPAM2 mutant) results in the formation of a single large granule under normal conditions (PubMed:37295429).
Functional Summary: The functional implications of ATXN2 phase separation were not specified in the provided data (PubMed:37295429).
Intrinsic Determinants & Regulations: The phase separation of ATXN2 is intrinsically regulated by its PAM2 motif, as deletion of this domain alters condensate morphology by transforming multiple small granules into a single large granule (PubMed:37295429).
Extrinsic Partners & Regulations: No extrinsic regulators or partners modulating ATXN2 phase separation were reported in the provided data (PubMed:37295429).

Overall Phase Separation Overview: NF-κB p65 (UniProt:A0A0D9R6K4) is recruited to bovine respiratory syncytial virus (bRSV) Inclusion Bodies (IBs) in the cytoplasm of Vero cells, exhibiting phase separation behavior classified as PS-other. These viral IBs sequester p65 in gel-like states, blocking its nuclear translocation. The condensates form in vivo and maintain structural integrity under stress (e.g., resisting hypotonic shock), with larger IBs (>10 µm²) demonstrating irreversible retention capabilities (PubMed:32878896).
Functional Summary: Sequestration in viral IBs disrupts NF-κB signaling by preventing nuclear translocation of p65, representing a viral immune evasion strategy. This irreversible confinement in gel-like condensates compromises cellular defense mechanisms during infection, as evidenced by sustained p65 retention in IBs post-hypotonic shock (PubMed:32878896).
Intrinsic Determinants & Regulations: No intrinsic drivers (domains, PTMs, mutations, or structural features) regulating phase separation were identified in the study. Experiments focused exclusively on full-length endogenous protein without characterizing specific regulatory regions or modifications (PubMed:32878896).
Extrinsic Partners & Regulations: Phase separation is extrinsically regulated by viral infection, with bRSV-induced Inclusion Bodies serving as the primary scaffold for recruitment. No protein partners, ions, or chemical modulators were reported; sequestration relies exclusively on the viral IB environment in infected Vero cells (PubMed:32878896).

Overall Phase Separation Overview: MetK (A0A0H3C5U2) undergoes RNA-dependent phase separation, forming small condensates in vitro, and dissolves condensates formed by RNase E. This behavior classifies as PS-other, indicating phase separation driven by external factors rather than self-assembly. Subcellular location and MLO associations were not specified (PubMed:37815915).
Functional Summary: As S-adenosylmethionine synthase, MetK acts as a metabolic sensor regulating BR-body assembly. Its phase separation capacity is weak but functionally significant, dissolving RNase E condensates to modulate BR-body dynamics during cellular metabolism (PubMed:37815915).
Intrinsic Determinants & Regulations: No intrinsic domains, mutations, or structural features driving phase separation were identified. The full-length protein lacking intrinsically disordered regions (IDRs) was studied, but no specific drivers were reported (PubMed:37815915).
Extrinsic Partners & Regulations: Total RNA promotes weak condensation of MetK through RNA binding with weak affinity. Conversely, MetK dissolves RNase E-containing condensates via direct protein-protein interactions, as demonstrated in bacterial two-hybrid assays and in vitro/vivo dissolution experiments (PubMed:37815915).

Overall Phase Separation Overview: Rbm14b (A0A0R4IJ04) undergoes self-driven phase separation, forming liquid-like droplets both in vitro and in vivo through its intrinsically disordered region (IDR) (PubMed:31636951). It localizes to nuclear and cytoplasmic compartments, associating with stress granules under oxidative stress, nuclear RNP compartments, and nucleolar caps following actinomycin D treatment (PubMed:31636951). The material state remains liquid-like, with no observed phase transitions reported (PubMed:31636951).
Functional Summary: Phase separation is essential for dorsoventral patterning via BMP signaling regulation and formation of RNP compartments that modulate RNA metabolism (splicing, transcript stability) (PubMed:31636951). Loss of phase separation disrupts punctate localization and stress granule recruitment, leading to dorsalization and transcriptome dysregulation (PubMed:31636951).
Intrinsic Determinants & Regulations: Phase separation is intrinsically driven by the C-terminal IDR (amino acids 256-556), which is necessary and sufficient for droplet formation (PubMed:31636951). Tyrosine residues within this domain are critical, as evidenced by the zRbm14bIDR18S mutation (18 tyrosine-to-serine substitutions) abolishing phase separation capacity (PubMed:31636951).
Extrinsic Partners & Regulations: Rbm14b co-phase separates with BuGZ (Q7ZXV8) in vitro, forming intermingled droplets (PubMed:31636951). Its behavior is modulated by extrinsic stressors: arsenite induces recruitment to stress granules, while actinomycin D triggers localization to nucleolar caps (PubMed:31636951).

Overall Phase Separation Overview: ATG8a (UniProt: A0A0X9SCL6) is recruited to Viral Replication Organelles (VROs) formed by Tomato bushy stunt virus (TBSV) and Carnation Italian ringspot virus (CIRV) in the cytoplasm and nucleus of Nicotiana benthamiana, forming punctate structures through phase separation driven by viral partners rather than self-assembly (class: PS-other). This recruitment is less prominent than its paralog ATG8f, though the specific material state (e.g., liquid/solid) and transitions remain uncharacterized (PubMed:38484009).
Functional Summary: Phase separation-mediated recruitment of ATG8a to VROs serves a pro-viral function, as knockdown experiments show reduced TBSV replication. This implicates ATG8a condensates in facilitating viral replication processes within host cells (PubMed:38484009).
Intrinsic Determinants & Regulations: No intrinsic domains, mutations, or molecular features driving ATG8a phase separation were identified in the study; experiments exclusively examined the full-length protein (e.g., GFP-ATG8a) without specifying regulatory domains or modifications (PubMed:38484009).
Extrinsic Partners & Regulations: ATG8a phase separation is extrinsically regulated by the viral replication proteins p33 and p36, which recruit ATG8a into VROs. This recruitment was confirmed via Bimolecular Fluorescence Complementation (BiFC) assays demonstrating direct interactions in infected Nicotiana benthamiana leaves (PubMed:38484009).

Overall Phase Separation Overview: XopR undergoes self-driven liquid-liquid phase separation (LLPS) via electrostatic interactions, forming reversible, dynamic liquid droplets in vitro (PubMed:34210966). It localizes to cortical condensates at the plasma membrane-actin cytoskeleton (PM-AC) continuum rather than predefined membrane-less organelles (PubMed:34210966). These liquid condensates exhibit fusion events and rapid dynamics with low interfacial energy (~1 mN/m), and transition to immobilized amorphous patches when complexed with formin partners at high stoichiometry in vivo (PubMed:34210966).
Functional Summary: XopR condensates hijack the actin cytoskeleton during bacterial infection by biphasically regulating formin-mediated actin nucleation: enhancing nucleation at low XopR:formin stoichiometry (early infection) and inhibiting it at high stoichiometry (late infection) (PubMed:34210966). They bundle F-actin through multivalent crosslinking and compete with actin-depolymerizing factor (ADF) to stabilize filaments, progressively remodeling actin dynamics to facilitate Xanthomonas campestris virulence (PubMed:34210966).
Intrinsic Determinants & Regulations: Phase separation is intrinsically driven by the N-terminal intrinsically disordered region (IDR, aa 1–267) through electrostatic-mediated multivalent interactions (PubMed:34210966). Oligomerization state depends on ionic strength: monomers form at 300 mM NaCl, trimers at 150 mM, and oligomers at 50 mM (PubMed:34210966). Deletion of the C-terminal region (XopR-Cter) abolishes phase separation, while deletion of the WH2-like domain (XopRΔHH) impairs actin bundling without affecting LLPS (PubMed:34210966).
Extrinsic Partners & Regulations: XopR co-phase separates with host formin proteins AtFH1 and AtFH6, forming electrostatic-dependent complex coacervates that modulate actin nucleation and clustering (PubMed:34210966). RNA promotes LLPS by lowering the critical concentration for droplet formation and altering viscosity (PubMed:34210966). Anionic partners like supercharged GFP (scGFP(-30)) enhance coacervation through electrostatic interactions, while increased ionic strength (>100 mM NaCl) dissolves condensates (PubMed:34210966).

Overall Phase Separation Overview: NS2 (A0A142DXV5) undergoes self-driven liquid-liquid phase separation (LLPS) dependent on phosphorylation and specific viral RNA binding, forming dynamic liquid-like condensates in vitro and viral inclusion bodies (VIBs) in the cytoplasm of infected cells (PubMed:36259663). These liquid condensates exhibit rapid fluorescence recovery, fusion capability, spherical morphology, and sensitivity to 1,6-hexanediol, confirming their liquid-like material state (PubMed:36259663).
Functional Summary: NS2 phase separation is essential for forming viral inclusion bodies (VIBs) that serve as functional hubs for viral RNA recruitment, subviral particle assembly, and virus maturation (PubMed:36259663). Disruption of LLPS through R6A/R7A mutations abolishes VIB formation and completely prevents viral replication, demonstrating the critical role of phase separation in the Bluetongue virus life cycle (PubMed:36259663).
Intrinsic Determinants & Regulations: The phase separation of NS2 is intrinsically regulated by its N-terminal arginine residues (R6 and R7), which are critical for specific viral RNA binding and LLPS initiation, and phosphorylation at residues S249 and S259 (PubMed:36259663). Mutations at R6/R7 (R6A+R7A) abolish RNA binding and LLPS, while mutations at S249/S259 (S249A+S259A) prevent phosphorylation-mediated LLPS enhancement (PubMed:36259663). Mutations in lysine-rich regions (K160A+K162A, K281A+K283A) show minimal impact on phase separation (PubMed:36259663).
Extrinsic Partners & Regulations: NS2 phase separation is extrinsically modulated by BTV segment 10 (S10) RNA, which acts as an essential scaffold that lowers the saturation concentration for LLPS and enables robust droplet formation (PubMed:36259663). Additionally, phosphorylation by the kinase CK2α significantly enhances LLPS in a dose-dependent manner (PubMed:36259663).

Overall Phase Separation Overview: TDRD1 undergoes phase separation (classified as PS-other) to form cytoplasmic droplets in HeLa cells as observed in vivo. The protein localizes to the cytoplasm, though specific membrane-less organelles and material states remain unspecified in the study (PubMed:39029469).
Functional Summary: The functional implications of TDRD1 phase separation were not specified in the provided data (PubMed:39029469).
Intrinsic Determinants & Regulations: The phase separation of TDRD1 is driven by its full-length protein construct, as no specific domains, mutations, post-translational modifications, or other intrinsic regulatory features were identified in the provided data (PubMed:39029469).
Extrinsic Partners & Regulations: No extrinsic regulators, binding partners, or co-phase separating molecules were reported for TDRD1 in the provided study (PubMed:39029469).

Overall Phase Separation Overview: GRP7 undergoes self-driven, reversible, temperature-dependent liquid-liquid phase separation (LLPS) in vivo and in vitro, forming condensates in the cytoplasm and nucleus (PubMed:38327052). These liquid-like condensates associate with stress granules and exhibit droplet fusion and rapid FRAP recovery, though structural analyses reveal a dense core and porous outer layer described as gel-like puncta in vitro (PubMed:38327052). No explicit material state transitions are reported (PubMed:38327052).
Functional Summary: GRP7 phase separation confers temperature resilience by forming stress granules that sequester eIF4E1, CSP1, and CSP3 to reversibly inhibit mRNA translation during thermal stress, enabling growth arrest adaptation (PubMed:38327052). Natural variation in LLPS capacity at Ser-132 correlates with Arabidopsis accessions' adaptation to wider temperature ranges, while mutants with impaired phase separation exhibit reduced root growth and survival under temperature fluctuations (PubMed:38327052).
Intrinsic Determinants & Regulations: Phase separation is intrinsically driven by the C-terminal glycine-rich intrinsically disordered region (IDR; residues 87-175) containing low-complexity polyglycine repeats, while the N-terminal domain (residues 1-86) enhances LLPS (PubMed:38327052). Phosphorylation by FERONIA at Ser-132 within the IDR robustly promotes LLPS, whereas natural variants (e.g., S132A, Y131C/S132G) impair phase separation capacity (PubMed:38327052).
Extrinsic Partners & Regulations: GRP7 condensates recruit extrinsic partners CSP1, CSP3, and eIF4E1 as clients, sequestering them to inhibit translation without being essential for LLPS initiation (PubMed:38327052). RNA—particularly poly(A) RNA and cellular RNA—lowers the critical concentration for phase separation and promotes droplet formation independently of GRP7's canonical RNA-binding domain (PubMed:38327052).

Overall Phase Separation Overview: The P protein (A0A193AUW9) does not undergo self-driven phase separation but requires the N protein (A0A2H4H6B8) to form cytoplasmic inclusion bodies (IBs) via liquid-liquid phase separation (LLPS) (PubMed:32878896). These IBs initially exhibit liquid-like properties (spherical, fusion-capable) but mature into gel-like states with reduced dynamics, particularly in larger structures (>10 µm²), undergoing a liquid-to-hydrogel transition over time (PubMed:32878896).
Functional Summary: P-N phase separation forms functional IBs that compartmentalize viral RNA replication machinery and sequester host immune factors (e.g., NF-κB p65), thereby blocking nuclear translocation of p65 and inhibiting antiviral signaling to enable immune evasion (PubMed:32878896). This LLPS-mediated assembly is essential for viral replication and represents a key immune evasion strategy in Bovine orthopneumovirus infection.
Intrinsic Determinants & Regulations: Phase separation of P is intrinsically regulated by its intrinsically disordered regions (IDRs) that enable multivalent interactions with N, and through oligomerization where P forms essential complexes with N to drive LLPS (PubMed:32878896). No specific mutations, PTMs, or splicing events were identified as regulators.
Extrinsic Partners & Regulations: P critically depends on the N protein (A0A2H4H6B8) as an extrinsic partner for phase separation, with direct N-P interactions serving as the scaffold for IB formation (PubMed:32878896). No ions, chemicals, or additional protein partners beyond N were reported to modulate P's phase separation behavior.

Overall Phase Separation Overview: DDX5 undergoes self-driven phase separation, forming dynamic liquid-like condensates in vitro that mature into solid aggregates over time (PubMed:38810650). It localizes to both the nucleus and cytoplasm, associating with nuclear speckles through its physiological role in RNA splicing (PubMed:38810650). The protein exhibits a characteristic liquid-to-solid material state transition during prolonged incubation in vitro and during aging in vivo (PubMed:38810650).
Functional Summary: Liquid condensates enhance DDX5's ATP-dependent RNA helicase activity by ~2-fold, potentially facilitating RNA splicing functions (PubMed:38810650). Pathological liquid-to-solid transitions cause complete loss of enzymatic activity and correlate with disorganized puncta formation in aged brains, implicating this maturation process in age-related cognitive decline and neurodegeneration (PubMed:38810650).
Intrinsic Determinants & Regulations: Phase separation is intrinsically driven by the C-terminal intrinsically disordered region (IDR; residues 536–634) containing a prion-like domain (PrD) (PubMed:38810650). Truncation of the IDR (ΔIDR) abolishes phase separation entirely, while deletion of the PrD (ΔPrD) severely impairs physiological condensate formation (PubMed:38810650).
Extrinsic Partners & Regulations: Phase separation is modulated by ionic conditions, with physiological salt concentrations (150 mM NaCl) promoting droplet formation while elevated salt levels (500 mM NaCl) dissolve condensates (PubMed:38810650). No protein interaction partners or chemical regulators were identified in the provided data.

Overall Phase Separation Overview: CAHS8 (A0A1D1UQN2) undergoes stress-induced phase separation, forming reversible granule-like condensates primarily in the nucleus and cytoplasm under hyperosmotic stress, exhibiting partial liquid-like properties and hydrogel formation (PubMed:36067153). The condensates show hexanediol sensitivity in vivo and form small gels in vitro, though material state transitions were not specified (PubMed:36067153).
Functional Summary: Functional implications of CAHS8 phase separation were not specified in the study; experimental conclusions solely noted stress-dependent reversible condensation and cooperative behavior with CAHS12 (PubMed:36067153).
Intrinsic Determinants & Regulations: No specific intrinsic domains, mutations, or features driving CAHS8 phase separation were identified; experiments utilized the full-length protein without characterization of regulatory elements (PubMed:36067153).
Extrinsic Partners & Regulations: CAHS8 phase separation is extrinsically regulated by hyperosmotic stress and co-assembly with partner protein CAHS12, with which it forms cooperative condensates and co-localizes into filaments in HEp-2 cells (PubMed:36067153).

Overall Phase Separation Overview: CAHS12 (A0A1D1VNN8) forms solid-like filaments in the cytosol and nucleus or granules in the nucleus under hyperosmotic stress, exhibiting reversible condensation in both cellular compartments (PubMed:36067153). Its material state transitions between hydrogel and solid phases, with in vitro studies confirming reversible gel formation (PubMed:36067153).
Functional Summary: The reversible solid-like condensates formed by CAHS12 under hyperosmotic stress are implicated in the tardigrade's stress response mechanism (PubMed:36067153). Cooperative assembly with CAHS8 suggests a synergistic role in forming protective structures during cellular stress (PubMed:36067153).
Intrinsic Determinants & Regulations: Phase separation and filament formation are intrinsically driven by the C-terminal CR1 and CR2 helices, which constitute the minimum filament-forming region (motif H2-motif H3-CR1-CR2) (PubMed:36067153). Substitutions L204P and L241P within these domains disrupt filament assembly (PubMed:36067153).
Extrinsic Partners & Regulations: CAHS12 co-assembles into filaments with the partner protein CAHS8, demonstrated through co-localization in HEp-2 cells under stress conditions (PubMed:36067153).

Overall Phase Separation Overview: Ptc2 (A0A1D8PRZ8) undergoes self-driven phase separation to form reversible liquid-like condensates at elevated CO₂ (5%) both in vivo and in vitro (PubMed:39908105). This behavior occurs in Candida albicans cells, enabling selective recruitment of partner proteins. No membrane-less organelle associations or material state transitions were reported.
Functional Summary: Ptc2 condensates enable selective recruitment and dephosphorylation of Hsp90 at S376 under high CO₂, reducing calcineurin levels and enhancing caspofungin susceptibility. This mechanism potentiates echinocandin efficacy during invasive candidiasis therapy in vitro and in murine models (PubMed:39908105).
Intrinsic Determinants & Regulations: The phase separation of Ptc2 is intrinsically driven by its Intrinsically Disordered Region (IDR), which is essential for CO₂ sensing and condensate formation (PubMed:39908105). No mutations, post-translational modifications, or oligomerization features were identified as regulators.
Extrinsic Partners & Regulations: Ptc2 phase separation is modulated by environmental CO₂ (5%) and protein partners: Hsp90 enhances condensate formation by reducing Ptc2 saturation concentration (Csat) by 50% and is recruited into droplets, while Ssb1 inhibits phase separation by increasing Csat and is excluded from condensates (PubMed:39908105).

Overall Phase Separation Overview: The N protein undergoes robust LLPS in vitro, forming liquid droplets. In cells, it forms condensates that colocalize with viral genomic RNA and other viral proteins (M, nsp3). Droplets exhibit liquid-like properties initially but can mature into gel-like/solid states under certain conditions or with specific mutations(PubMed: 37735952).
Functional Summary: N protein forms viral replication factories via phase separation, potentially packages viral genomic RNA, and modulates host stress granule responses(PubMed: 37735952).
Intrinsic Determinants & Regulations: The C-terminal dimerization domain (CTD) is essential for its phase separation; the SR-rich linker region enhances droplet formation; phosphorylation in the SR region (mimicked by S176E/S180E/S183E mutations) inhibits phase separation; the ΔSR truncation mutant reduces droplet quantity and size(PubMed: 37735952).
Extrinsic Partners & Regulations: N protein requires viral genomic RNA as an essential scaffold; it cooperates with the P protein to enhance heterotypic condensation; its condensates are modulated by the M protein; the host protein G3BP1 is recruited into its condensates(PubMed: 37735952).

Overall Phase Separation Overview: P protein resides in the cytoplasm and co-assembles with the N protein and RNA into viral replication factories; it maintains liquid material properties(PubMed: 37735952).
Functional Summary: P protein serves as a core component of viral replication factories and facilitates L polymerase complex recruitment through interaction with the N protein(PubMed: 37735952).
Intrinsic Determinants & Regulations: Its N-terminal domain (NTD) cannot independently form droplets; the C-terminal disordered region is critical for phase separation; identified phosphorylation sites show no confirmed functional effect on phase separation(PubMed: 37735952).
Extrinsic Partners & Regulations: P protein requires the N protein for efficient heterotypic condensate formation; viral genomic RNA modulates its phase separation process(PubMed: 37735952).

Overall Phase Separation Overview: CNF1 (A0A1W5T566) undergoes self-driven liquid-liquid phase separation (LLPS) to form dynamic, reversible liquid-like condensates in the cytoplasm, both in vitro and in host cells (PubMed:35766380). These condensates—described as a 'CNF1-JAK1/2 membraneless complex'—exhibit spherical morphology, rapid fluorescence recovery after photobleaching (FRAP), and sensitivity to 1,6-hexanediol, confirming their liquid material state (PubMed:35766380). No material state transitions were observed under tested conditions (PubMed:35766380).
Functional Summary: CNF1 phase separation enables the formation of a condensate-mediated complex with JAK1/2, facilitating their transphosphorylation and subsequent STAT1 activation (PubMed:35766380). This mechanism drives M1 macrophage polarization, exacerbating kidney inflammation during urinary tract infections (PubMed:35766380).
Intrinsic Determinants & Regulations: Phase separation of CNF1 is intrinsically driven by intrinsically disordered regions (IDRs) within its membrane translocation domain (amino acids 190-720), which enable multivalent interactions (PubMed:35766380). Deletion of these IDRs (in the mutant CNF1<sup>190-720, IDRs</sup>) abolishes droplet formation without disrupting JAK1/2 binding, confirming their essential role in LLPS (PubMed:35766380).
Extrinsic Partners & Regulations: CNF1 condensates recruit and concentrate the scaffold proteins JAK1 and JAK2, forming a functional tripartite complex (PubMed:35766380). High ionic strength (e.g., 500 mM NaCl) dissolves droplets, indicating salt sensitivity (PubMed:35766380).

Overall Phase Separation Overview: FUS-ERG undergoes self-driven phase separation (PS-self), forming liquid-like condensates both in vitro at submicromolar concentrations and in vivo within the nucleus (PubMed:37400539). Its condensates exhibit irregular morphology due to chromatin association (wetting behavior), though DNA binding maintains liquidity while altering droplet shape (PubMed:37400539).
Functional Summary: FUS-ERG phase separation drives aberrant gene expression via chromatin association and transcriptional activation, linking it to pathogenesis in acute myeloid leukemia (AML) and Ewing sarcoma through phase separation-dependent mechanisms (PubMed:37400539).
Intrinsic Determinants & Regulations: Phase separation is intrinsically driven by the N-terminal intrinsically disordered region (IDR) from FUS (PubMed:37400539). The C-terminal DNA-binding domain from ERG modulates morphology, with DNA-binding mutations (R367D/R370D) enabling spherical droplet formation in cells by disrupting chromatin interactions (PubMed:37400539).
Extrinsic Partners & Regulations: DNA, specifically dsDNA with GGAA repeats, acts as a key extrinsic regulator by altering condensate morphology from spherical to irregular shapes upon recruitment while preserving liquid properties (PubMed:37400539).

Overall Phase Separation Overview: FabG (A0A290MWV4) undergoes RNA-dependent phase separation to form condensates in vitro and is enriched in BR-bodies, though its subcellular location and material state remain unspecified with no reported state transitions (PubMed:37815915).
Functional Summary: As a metabolic enzyme with moonlighting RNA-binding activity, FabG's phase separation may organize metabolic pathways by serving as an RNA-dependent scaffold in condensates (PubMed:37815915).
Intrinsic Determinants & Regulations: No intrinsic domains, mutations, or features driving phase separation were identified; the full-length protein lacking intrinsically disordered regions (IDRs) was studied, with condensation strictly dependent on extrinsic RNA binding (PubMed:37815915).
Extrinsic Partners & Regulations: Phase separation of FabG is critically regulated by RNA, which is essential for condensation, as evidenced by dissolution of condensates upon RNase A treatment or high-salt exposure (PubMed:37815915).

Overall Phase Separation Overview: RhlE (A0A290MZ23) from Caulobacter crescentus undergoes RNA-dependent phase separation, forming condensates in vitro and assembling RNase E-independent foci in vivo (PubMed:37815915). It associates with BR-bodies via heterogeneous colocalization and forms independent foci, exhibiting a solid-like material state (hydrogel) with minimal dynamics as evidenced by low fluorescence recovery in FRAP assays (PubMed:37815915).
Functional Summary: RhlE forms distinct ribonucleoprotein (RNP) condensates that likely coordinate RNA processing functions (PubMed:37815915).
Intrinsic Determinants & Regulations: Phase separation of RhlE does not require its intrinsically disordered region (IDR), as deletion of the IDR (ΔIDR mutant) shows no defect in condensation, indicating the IDR is dispensable for phase separation (PubMed:37815915).
Extrinsic Partners & Regulations: RhlE phase separation is critically dependent on RNA, with no condensation occurring in the absence of RNA (PubMed:37815915). Additionally, RhlE is strongly recruited into RNase E condensates (partition coefficient = 11) (PubMed:37815915).

Overall Phase Separation Overview: The CCDC6-RET fusion protein undergoes liquid-liquid phase separation (LLPS) in the cytoplasm, forming dynamic liquid-like condensates that require the CCDC6-101aa fragment and are enhanced by intact kinase activity (PubMed:38805286). Kinase-inactive mutants (K147M) and deletion mutants (Δ21-27, Δ70-77) undergo a liquid-to-solid transition, forming solid-like aggregates (PubMed:38805286).
Functional Summary: Phase separation constitutively activates Ras/MAPK oncogenic signaling through the GRB2/SHC1 ternary niche, driving tumorigenesis in RET fusion-positive cancers (PubMed:38805286). Kinase inhibitors (LOXO292, BLU667) disrupt niche formation by blocking RET activity, while pathological liquid-to-solid transitions in mutants promote cytotoxic aggregation (PubMed:38805286).
Intrinsic Determinants & Regulations: Phase separation is intrinsically driven by the CCDC6-101aa intrinsically disordered region (IDR1), with the RET kinase domain maintaining liquid-like dynamics (PubMed:38805286). Autophosphorylation at tyrosine residues Y451 and Y485 stabilizes condensates, while mutations disrupting kinase activity (Y294F) or structure (K147M, Δ21-27, Δ70-77) impair LLPS or trigger pathological solidification (PubMed:38805286).
Extrinsic Partners & Regulations: CCDC6-RET recruits adaptor protein GRB2 and effector SHC1 via direct binding to form a ternary signaling niche within condensates (PubMed:38805286). GRB2 recruitment depends on its SH2 domain (ΔSH2 mutant abolishes condensates), while SHC1 requires its CH1 domain for cooperative niche assembly (ΔCH1 mutant disrupts complex formation) (PubMed:38805286).

Overall Phase Separation Overview: The N protein (A0A2H4H6B8) forms cytoplasmic viral inclusion bodies (IBs) via liquid-liquid phase separation (LLPS) in cooperation with the P protein, exhibiting initial liquid-like properties (spherical, fusion-capable) that mature into gel-like/hydrogel states with reduced dynamics over time, particularly in larger IBs (>10 µm²). This phase transition is central to its association with viral IBs (PubMed:32878896).
Functional Summary: N-mediated phase separation compartmentalizes viral replication machinery within IBs, concentrating viral RNA to serve as functional sites for RNA synthesis. Critically, IBs sequester host immune factors like NF-κB p65, inhibiting nuclear translocation and suppressing innate immune responses, representing a key immune evasion strategy during viral infection (PubMed:32878896).
Intrinsic Determinants & Regulations: Phase separation is intrinsically driven by multivalent interactions mediated by intrinsically disordered regions (IDRs) in the N protein, with oligomerization via N-P interactions being essential for condensate formation. Neither N nor P alone forms condensates, highlighting the cooperative role of their IDRs in driving LLPS (PubMed:32878896).
Extrinsic Partners & Regulations: N requires the P protein as a scaffold partner for IB formation, confirmed through co-immunoprecipitation and ectopic co-expression studies. The M protein acts as a client within IBs, while viral genomic/mRNA is concentrated in IB sub-compartments (IBAGs) and essential for replication. Host immune factor NF-κB p65 is sequestered into IBs through direct interaction with N/P (PubMed:32878896).

Overall Phase Separation Overview: Tet3 (A0A2R8Q4R6) does not undergo autonomous phase separation but co-phase separates with Sall4 on DNA to form liquid-like transcriptional condensates exclusively in the nucleus. These condensates assemble on the bmp4 promoter, with no observed material state transitions (PubMed:38427557).
Functional Summary: Tet3-Sall4-DNA condensates facilitate Tet3-mediated oxidation of 5-methylcytosine on the bmp4 promoter, activating bmp4 expression to enable BMP signaling. This process is critical for chondrocyte differentiation and craniofacial cartilage development in zebrafish, as evidenced by genetic and biochemical studies (PubMed:38427557).
Intrinsic Determinants & Regulations: Tet3 lacks intrinsic drivers for autonomous phase separation, as its catalytic domain (CD) requires extrinsic partners. Mutations in catalytic residues (H1353Y, D1355A) impair function but were not directly tested for phase separation behavior (PubMed:38427557).
Extrinsic Partners & Regulations: Tet3 co-phase separates strictly through interaction with the scaffold protein Sall4, which is essential for condensate formation. DNA probes from the bmp4 promoter further stabilize these ternary condensates, as demonstrated by in vitro reconstitution and co-localization assays (PubMed:38427557).

Overall Phase Separation Overview: Ddx21 undergoes self-driven liquid-liquid phase separation (LLPS) in vitro, forming dynamic liquid-like droplets that exhibit rapid fluorescence recovery (~80% recovery, t½ 10s) in FRAP assays. In vivo, it localizes specifically to nucleoli within the nucleus of developing zebrafish embryos, confirming its association with this membrane-less organelle (PubMed:37979585).
Functional Summary: Ddx21 phase separation is functionally implicated in ribosome assembly during embryonic development, as evidenced by its nucleolar localization where it co-localizes with markers like fibrillarin. This spatial organization supports its role in ribosome biogenesis within membrane-less organelles in zebrafish embryos (PubMed:37979585).
Intrinsic Determinants & Regulations: The phase separation of full-length Ddx21 was studied, but no specific domains, post-translational modifications, mutations, or oligomerization features were identified as intrinsic regulators in this investigation (PubMed:37979585).
Extrinsic Partners & Regulations: No extrinsic regulators, binding partners, or co-phase separating molecules were reported for Ddx21 in the provided study (PubMed:37979585).

Overall Phase Separation Overview: AfrLEA6 undergoes self-driven phase separation (class: PS-self) in vitro and in vivo, forming dynamic liquid-like droplets in the cytoplasm that transition to gel-like hydrogel states during desiccation (PubMed:33077592). It associates with stress granules, as evidenced by sensitivity to 1,6-hexanediol, puromycin, and cycloheximide treatments (PubMed:33077592).
Functional Summary: AfrLEA6 condensates protect against desiccation by sequestering sensitive proteins and increasing cytoplasmic viscosity to maintain structural integrity during water loss (PubMed:33077592). Ectopic expression in Drosophila Kc167 cells enhances desiccation and osmotic stress tolerance, confirming its protective role (PubMed:33077592).
Intrinsic Determinants & Regulations: Phase separation is intrinsically driven by the SMP domain, as truncation (ΔSMP) abolishes LLPS, while a protein-binding domain (PBD) regulates condensate size—its deletion (ΔPBD) results in small non-fusing droplets (PubMed:33077592).
Extrinsic Partners & Regulations: LLPS requires an ionic/crowded environment (osmosome solution) and is absent in pure water (PubMed:33077592). Condensates selectively partition proteins based on net surface charge, enriching supercharged GFP variant pGFP+36 (+36 charge) while excluding negatively charged variants, which enhances droplet formation (PubMed:33077592).

Overall Phase Separation Overview: CP undergoes liquid-liquid phase separation (LLPS) to form spherical granules in the nucleus and cytoplasm through self-assembly, exhibiting liquid-like properties including rapid movement, fusion, and partial fluorescence recovery after photobleaching (PubMed:36613855). No material state transitions were reported under tested conditions.
Functional Summary: No experimentally supported functional roles or pathological implications of CP phase separation were discussed in the article (PubMed:36613855).
Intrinsic Determinants & Regulations: The phase separation of CP is intrinsically driven by intrinsically disordered regions (IDRs) comprising 45.03% of the protein, including a disordered region at the 5′-terminal, as predicted by PONDR VL-XT disorder analysis (PubMed:36613855).
Extrinsic Partners & Regulations: No extrinsic regulators, partners, or modulators of CP phase separation were reported in the provided data.

Overall Phase Separation Overview: NSP2 (A0A3G1DN32) does not undergo autonomous phase separation but co-phase separates with the scaffold protein NSP5 to form liquid-like viroplasms in the cytoplasm during rotavirus infection (PubMed:34524703). These virus-induced condensates serve as replication factories and exhibit early liquid-like properties including spherical morphology and fusion capability, but mature into solid-like structures with reduced dynamics as infection progresses, undergoing a liquid-to-solid transition between 4-12 hours post-infection (PubMed:34524703).
Functional Summary: As an essential component of viroplasms, NSP2 facilitates viral RNA chaperoning and packaging within these biomolecular condensates, directly enabling genome replication and virion assembly (PubMed:34524703). The liquid-to-solid transition during infection progression correlates with functional maturation of these replication factories, with early liquid condensates being reversibly disruptible by aliphatic diols while late solid-like structures support particle assembly (PubMed:34524703).
Intrinsic Determinants & Regulations: The co-phase separation capability of NSP2 is intrinsically regulated by its stable octameric oligomerization state, which provides multivalency for heterotypic interactions with NSP5 (PubMed:34524703). No specific domains, post-translational modifications, or mutations were identified as direct drivers of its phase behavior in the studied contexts (PubMed:34524703).
Extrinsic Partners & Regulations: NSP2 strictly requires the scaffold protein NSP5 for phase separation, exhibiting no autonomous condensation but efficiently partitioning into NSP5-driven condensates both in vitro and in vivo (PubMed:34524703). It independently binds rotavirus transcripts, which become enriched within the co-condensates and contribute to viroplasm maturation, though RNA binding persists even when condensates are chemically dissolved (PubMed:34524703).

Overall Phase Separation Overview: Nup158 (UniProt ID: A0A3L6KVB1) from Trypanosoma brucei undergoes self-driven phase separation (class: PS-self), forming an FG phase with LCST-type phase separation in vitro. The subcellular location and association with membrane-less organelles were not specified. Material state properties and transitions were not described in the provided data (PubMed:36257947).
Functional Summary: Functional implications of phase separation for Nup158 were not specified in the study. Authors' conclusions focused solely on biophysical properties (conserved cohesive potential and LCST behavior) without describing physiological or pathological roles (PubMed:36257947).
Intrinsic Determinants & Regulations: Phase separation is intrinsically driven by the full-length FG domain, as demonstrated in purified in vitro systems. No specific domains, mutations, PTMs, or oligomerization features regulating this behavior were identified in the study (PubMed:36257947).
Extrinsic Partners & Regulations: No extrinsic regulators, partner proteins, ions, or chemicals modulating phase separation were reported in the provided data (PubMed:36257947).

Overall Phase Separation Overview: NOP1 (A0A3L6L1M3) in Trypanosoma brucei associates with the nucleolus through phase separation-mediated partitioning, primarily occurring in the nucleus (PubMed:36052646). Its nucleolar localization strength correlates directly with RG-repeat abundance, implicating RG motifs in phase separation behavior, though the specific material state (e.g., liquid/solid) and transitions remain unspecified (PubMed:36052646).
Functional Summary: RG-mediated phase separation of NOP1 is essential for ribosome biogenesis, serving as a conserved targeting mechanism for nucleolar localization (PubMed:36052646). This process underpins its critical role in cellular function, though pathological implications or state transitions were not reported (PubMed:36052646).
Intrinsic Determinants & Regulations: Phase separation of NOP1 is intrinsically driven by RG repeats within its N-terminal domain, with reduced repeat abundance weakening nucleolar partitioning (PubMed:36052646). This mechanism is conserved and aligns with LLPS principles observed in systems like LAF-1 and DDX4 (PubMed:36052646).
Extrinsic Partners & Regulations: No extrinsic regulators, partners, or environmental modulators (e.g., ions, chemicals) were identified for NOP1 phase separation in the provided data (PubMed:36052646).

Overall Phase Separation Overview: NBR1 (A0A3Q9VF17) undergoes partner-dependent phase separation (class: PS-other) within the cytoplasm of Nicotiana benthamiana, specifically associating with viral replication organelles (VROs) to form heterogeneous punctate condensates (PubMed:38484009). These VRO-associated condensates exhibit liquid-like material properties, evidenced by partial fluorescence recovery in FRAP assays, with no observed material state transitions reported (PubMed:38484009).
Functional Summary: NBR1 phase separation in VROs plays a critical pro-viral role by facilitating phosphatidylethanolamine (PE) and phosphatidylinositol 3-phosphate (PI3P) lipid enrichment to support viral replication (PubMed:38484009). Concurrently, NBR1 sequestration within these condensates inhibits autophagic flux, enabling viral immune evasion, as knockdown of NBR1 significantly reduces TBSV/CIRV replication (PubMed:38484009).
Intrinsic Determinants & Regulations: No intrinsic domains, mutations, post-translational modifications, or oligomerization features driving NBR1 phase separation were identified in the study (PubMed:38484009).
Extrinsic Partners & Regulations: NBR1 phase separation is extrinsically regulated by viral proteins p33 and p36, which recruit NBR1 to VROs and scaffold condensate formation, as demonstrated through bimolecular fluorescence complementation (BiFC) and proximity labeling (PubMed:38484009). Additionally, NBR1 co-phase separates with ATG8f to form larger dynamic condensates, validated by BiFC and co-localization studies (PubMed:38484009).

Overall Phase Separation Overview: TaHRC (A0A4P9CZP9) undergoes self-driven phase separation (PS-self) forming liquid-like condensates primarily in the nucleus, specifically associated with nuclear speckles (PubMed:38657607). The protein exhibits allele-dependent behavior: TaHRC-S displays robust liquid-liquid phase separation (LLPS) with dynamic droplet fusion and rapid fluorescence recovery, while TaHRC-R shows weaker LLPS propensity with reduced fluidity and slower fusion kinetics (PubMed:38657607). The mycotoxin deoxynivalenol (DON) induces a diffuse-to-condensed transition specifically in TaHRC-S without altering its liquid state, whereas no material state transitions (e.g., liquid-to-solid) were observed (PubMed:38657607).
Functional Summary: Phase separation of TaHRC alleles directly determines Fusarium head blight (FHB) resistance in wheat (PubMed:38657607). TaHRC-S condensation promotes DON-induced cell death in rachial nodes, facilitating Fusarium graminearum spread and FHB susceptibility (PubMed:38657607). Conversely, TaHRC-R suppresses condensation and cell death, conferring FHB resistance (PubMed:38657607). The condensate state of the TaHRC-TaSR45a module regulates alternative splicing of immune-related genes (e.g., spliceosome components and kinases), mechanistically linking LLPS to disease outcomes (PubMed:38657607).
Intrinsic Determinants & Regulations: Phase separation is intrinsically regulated by the coiled-coil (CC) domain, essential for condensation, and modulated by intrinsic disordered regions (IDRs), particularly IDR1 (PubMed:38657607). Allelic differences are critical: TaHRC-S naturally lacks inhibitory cysteines, enabling strong LLPS, whereas TaHRC-R contains N-terminal cysteines (positions 2 and 8) that suppress condensation (PubMed:38657607). Mutations replacing these cysteines with glycines (C2G/C8G) in TaHRC-R restore LLPS to TaHRC-S levels, confirming their inhibitory role (PubMed:38657607).
Extrinsic Partners & Regulations: TaHRC co-assembles into shared condensates with partner proteins including TaZFC10, TaCXIP4, TaSR45a, TaLUC7L, TaPPIase63, TaPPIase95, and TaSRP2 (PubMed:38657607). TaHRC-S promotes partner recruitment and co-phase separation, while TaHRC-R suppresses partner condensation (PubMed:38657607). The mycotoxin deoxynivalenol (DON) acts as an extrinsic enhancer, specifically intensifying TaHRC-S condensation without affecting TaHRC-R (PubMed:38657607). LLPS is salt-sensitive, with droplet formation decreasing at higher NaCl concentrations (PubMed:38657607).

Overall Phase Separation Overview: Nup98 (A0A6I8SCP2) undergoes self-driven phase separation (class: PS-self), forming FG phase with LCST-type phase separation in vitro. This behavior is conserved across evolutionarily distant species (PubMed:36257947).
Functional Summary: Functional implications of Nup98 phase separation were not specified in the provided study (PubMed:36257947).
Intrinsic Determinants & Regulations: The phase separation of Nup98 is intrinsically driven by its Full-length FG domain, as demonstrated by in vitro studies showing conserved cohesive potential (PubMed:36257947).
Extrinsic Partners & Regulations: No extrinsic regulators or partners were reported for Nup98 phase separation in the provided study (PubMed:36257947).

Overall Phase Separation Overview: HNRNPAB (A0A7M4CIF6) undergoes self-driven phase separation (class: PS-self) to form biomolecular condensates in the cytoplasm of Xenopus laevis oocytes, specifically localizing to L-bodies (PubMed:39537752). The full-length protein forms liquid-like condensates both in vivo (within L-bodies) and in vitro, exhibiting high dynamics with a mobile fraction of 96% in FRAP assays, though with static clustering and no fusion in vitro (PubMed:39537752). Its RBD domain forms liquid-like condensates (showing fusion and wetting) in vitro and enriches in L-bodies in vivo, while the IDR domain forms static-like condensates (no fusion) in vitro but enriches dynamically in L-bodies in vivo (PubMed:39537752). No material state transitions were observed (PubMed:39537752).
Functional Summary: HNRNPAB enrichment in L-bodies facilitates mRNA localization during Xenopus oogenesis, with its dynamic association suggesting a role in organizing the protein layer of biomolecular condensates (PubMed:39537752). The RBD domain contributes to RNA-protein interactions within L-bodies, while the IDR domain stabilizes protein interactions by modulating dynamics, as evidenced by reduced mobility when fused to PTBP3 (PubMed:39537752).
Intrinsic Determinants & Regulations: Phase separation of HNRNPAB is intrinsically driven by synergistic contributions from its two RNA-binding domains (RBDs) and intrinsically disordered region (IDR) (PubMed:39537752). Both domains independently undergo phase separation in vitro and mediate enrichment into L-bodies in vivo, but neither fully recapitulates the localization efficiency or dynamic behavior of the full-length protein, indicating cooperative regulation between RBDs and IDR for optimal condensate partitioning (PubMed:39537752).
Extrinsic Partners & Regulations: RNA, specifically Xenopus β-globin RNA, modulates HNRNPAB phase separation: for the full-length protein, it lowers the saturation concentration for condensate formation; for the RBD domain, it increases condensate size at low concentrations; and for the IDR domain, it increases condensate number while reducing size (PubMed:39537752).

Overall Phase Separation Overview: FtsZ (A0A7Y4IHA3) does not undergo autonomous phase separation but functions as a client protein enriched within PomY biomolecular condensates in both in vitro and in vivo systems (PubMed:37380708). It associates with the Z-ring division machinery (classified as 'Other' membrane-less organelle) where it undergoes GTP-dependent polymerization and bundling (PubMed:37380708). No material state transitions were observed for FtsZ within these condensates (PubMed:37380708).
Functional Summary: Enrichment within PomY condensates enables precise spatial regulation of FtsZ polymerization into Z-rings, directly linking biomolecular condensate-mediated localization to cell division machinery assembly in Myxococcus xanthus (PubMed:37380708). This client-partner relationship establishes a mechanistic pathway for division site specification without autonomous phase separation behavior (PubMed:37380708).
Intrinsic Determinants & Regulations: FtsZ lacks intrinsic phase separation drivers, as full-length constructs (untagged or A488-labeled) show no domain, mutation, or structural features enabling self-assembly; it exclusively operates as a client within partner-induced condensates (PubMed:37380708).
Extrinsic Partners & Regulations: FtsZ partitioning and function are extrinsically regulated by PomY, which forms condensates that selectively enrich FtsZ (~3.5±0.5 enrichment factor) and nucleate its GTP-dependent polymerization and filament bundling, as demonstrated through co-localization and in vitro reconstitution assays (PubMed:37380708).

Overall Phase Separation Overview: Ccc1 undergoes self-driven phase separation to form reversible, salt-dependent liquid-like condensates in vitro that fuse and grow, while forming distinct subnuclear foci in vivo within the nucleus (PubMed:37217653). It associates with heterochromatin, specifically concentrating PRC2 and H3K27me3 at subtelomeric regions (PubMed:37217653). The material state is typically liquid-like but exhibits slow dynamics with no FRAP recovery, and transitions to a gel-like hydrogel state occur in the 4KRA mutant at high concentrations (23 µM) (PubMed:37217653).
Functional Summary: Ccc1 phase separation concentrates PRC2 at subtelomeric regions to prevent ectopic H3K27me3 deposition at centromeric HP1 domains, maintaining heterochromatin fidelity (PubMed:37217653). Mutations altering phase separation (e.g., 6KRA, 10KRA, Ccc1-CCΔ) or promoting pathological gelation (4KRA) cause H3K27me3 redistribution and loss of heterochromatin integrity, directly linking condensate dynamics to epigenetic regulation (PubMed:37217653).
Intrinsic Determinants & Regulations: Phase separation is intrinsically driven by the coiled-coil domain (essential for dimerization) and basic clusters within the intrinsically disordered region (IDR, aa 82-402) (PubMed:37217653). Mutations critically regulate this behavior: 6KRA and 10KRA inhibit phase separation, 4KRA promotes gelation, and coiled-coil deletion (Ccc1-CCΔ) abolishes it, while acidic cluster mutants (4DEA, 5DEA, 9DEA) show no effect (PubMed:37217653).
Extrinsic Partners & Regulations: Ccc1 condensates selectively partition the PRC2 complex, which is essential for heterochromatin targeting, as demonstrated by fluorescence microscopy and in vitro reconstitution (PubMed:37217653). Phase separation is reversibly modulated by salt concentration—promoted at low NaCl (250 mM) and dissolved at high NaCl (500 mM)—validated through salt-shift experiments (PubMed:37217653).

Overall Phase Separation Overview: Afadin (UniProt A0A8C0MIV5) forms condensate-like structures at cell junctions in the cytoplasm upon disruption of the actin cytoskeleton by Latrunculin B (LatB) treatment, exhibiting liquid-like properties inferred from morphology though not directly measured (PubMed:40015268). These endogenous condensates are distinct from ZO-1-containing structures and occur without observed material state transitions.
Functional Summary: Afadin condensate formation contributes to adherens junction organization and segregation from tight junctions, maintaining distinct compartmentalization from ZO-1 condensates within the junctional complex (PubMed:40015268). This phase separation behavior is implicated in structural reorganization of cell junctions following cytoskeletal disruption.
Intrinsic Determinants & Regulations: No specific intrinsic domains, mutations, or molecular features driving phase separation were identified in the study. Phase separation was observed for full-length endogenous Afadin, with region involvement inferred from homology to rat Afadin and behavioral analysis (PubMed:40015268).
Extrinsic Partners & Regulations: Phase separation is extrinsically regulated by F-actin integrity, where cytoskeleton disruption via LatB treatment triggers condensate formation (PubMed:40015268). Additionally, junctional localization is sensitive to 1,6-Hexanediol (HD), indicating dependence on weak hydrophobic interactions consistent with liquid-liquid phase separation mechanisms (PubMed:40015268).

Overall Phase Separation Overview: Sec16A undergoes self-driven phase separation to form reversible, liquid-like Sec bodies in the cytoplasm under stress conditions such as 200mM NaCl exposure or amino acid starvation (PubMed:36325988). These membraneless organelles exhibit liquid properties demonstrated by fusion events, rapid reversibility upon stress relief, and sensitivity to 1,6-hexanediol, with no observed material state transitions under tested conditions (PubMed:36325988). Sec bodies feature a distinct shell-core organization where Sec16A surrounds COPII protein cores (PubMed:36325988).
Functional Summary: Sec16A-mediated phase separation serves as a pro-survival mechanism by sequestering ER exit site (ERES) components into Sec bodies, thereby inhibiting protein transport from the ER during cellular stress (PubMed:36325988). The rapid dissolution of these condensates upon stress restoration reactivates secretory pathways, demonstrating their dynamic role in regulating cellular secretion (PubMed:36325988).
Intrinsic Determinants & Regulations: The phase separation of Sec16A is intrinsically driven by its disordered regions and the conserved serum responsive domain (SRDC) at the C-terminus, as inferred from homology to Drosophila Sec16 (PubMed:36325988). While specific domains were not experimentally verified in this study, full-length Sec16A (including endogenous and tagged constructs) was identified as the primary driver for Sec body formation (PubMed:36325988).
Extrinsic Partners & Regulations: Sec16A co-phase separates with multiple COPII subunits including Sec16B, Sec13, Sec24A, and Sec24D, forming organized condensates where Sec16A localizes to the shell surrounding Sec13 cores (PubMed:36325988). This co-assembly occurs simultaneously during stress-induced formation in both INS-1 cells and primary rat neurons, with Sec16A acting as the essential scaffold for partner recruitment (PubMed:36325988).

Overall Phase Separation Overview: Ataxin-2 (Atxn2) undergoes partner-dependent phase separation (class: PS-other) to form ribonucleoprotein (RNP) condensates in the cytoplasm of neurons, as demonstrated through in vivo droplet formation and FRAP experiments (PubMed:39419034). These condensates exhibit liquid-like properties and intrinsic motility along neuronal axons. However, polyglutamine (polyQ) expansions in Ataxin-2 disrupt the liquid-like dynamics of these condensates, indicating a pathological material state transition (PubMed:39419034).
Functional Summary: Ataxin-2 governs mRNA localization and translation through phase-separated RNP condensates in neurons, facilitating axonal transport and local protein synthesis. Pathological polyQ expansions disrupt condensate motility, mislocalize mRNA, and suppress translation, implicating this mechanism in neurodegenerative disease progression (PubMed:39419034).
Intrinsic Determinants & Regulations: The phase separation behavior of Ataxin-2 is intrinsically regulated by its polyglutamine (polyQ) repeat region. Expansions in this repeat domain drive aberrant sequestration of partner proteins and disrupt the liquid-like properties of RNP condensates, as observed in neuronal models (PubMed:39419034).
Extrinsic Partners & Regulations: Ataxin-2 requires co-phase separation with TDP-43 (Tardbp) to form functional RNP condensates. This partnership is critical for condensate motility and mRNA regulation. PolyQ expansions in Ataxin-2 pathologically enhance sequestration of TDP-43 within these condensates, altering their dynamics (PubMed:39419034).

Overall Phase Separation Overview: Tardbp (A0A8I6GLU8) undergoes partner-dependent phase separation (class: PS-other) in the cytoplasm, associating with ribonucleoprotein condensates (PubMed:39419034). It exhibits liquid-like properties in vivo, but these properties can be disrupted under specific conditions (PubMed:39419034).
Functional Summary: Tardbp phase separation in ribonucleoprotein condensates regulates mRNA dynamics and translation in neuronal axons (PubMed:39419034). Disruption of its liquid-like properties by Atxn2 polyQ expansions perturbs mRNA localization and suppresses local translation, indicating a role in neurodegenerative pathology (PubMed:39419034).
Intrinsic Determinants & Regulations: No intrinsic regulators for Tardbp phase separation were reported in the provided data (PubMed:39419034).
Extrinsic Partners & Regulations: Tardbp co-phase separates with Atxn2 (A0A8I6ATU9), where polyQ expansions in Atxn2 aberrantly sequester Tardbp within condensates, disrupting its motility and liquid-like properties (PubMed:39419034).

Overall Phase Separation Overview: TDRD1 (A0A8J0T993) from Xenopus laevis undergoes liquid-liquid phase separation (LLPS), forming cytoplasmic droplets in HeLa cells as observed in vivo (PubMed:39029469). This behavior is driven by the full-length protein and occurs exclusively in the cytoplasm, though the specific material state (e.g., liquid/solid) and associations with membrane-less organelles were not characterized (PubMed:39029469).
Functional Summary: The functional implications of TDRD1 phase separation, including physiological roles or pathological links, were not specified in the provided data (PubMed:39029469).
Intrinsic Determinants & Regulations: Phase separation of TDRD1 is mediated by its full-length structure, as studied in vivo (PubMed:39029469). No specific domains, mutations, post-translational modifications, or oligomerization states were identified as key drivers in the provided data (PubMed:39029469).
Extrinsic Partners & Regulations: No extrinsic regulators, binding partners, or environmental modulators (e.g., ions, chemicals) of TDRD1 phase separation were reported in the provided study (PubMed:39029469).

Overall Phase Separation Overview: PTBP3 (A0A8J0TV93) localizes to L-bodies in the cytoplasm, exhibiting moderate dynamics governed by RNA binding (PubMed:39537752). While not explicitly classified as self-driven phase separation, its localization behavior and tunable dynamics in condensates indicate phase separation properties. The protein associates specifically with L-bodies, with material state properties inferred through FRAP measurements showing partial mobility (~40-50% mobile fraction in wild-type) (PubMed:39537752).
Functional Summary: PTBP3 facilitates mRNA localization through L-body association, where its RNA-binding-dependent dynamics reflect functional RNA interactions (PubMed:39537752). The tunable dynamics via domain architecture (demonstrated by IDR fusion reducing mobility) illustrate how protein-RNA versus protein-protein interaction balances can regulate mRNA localization efficiency and condensate stability (PubMed:39537752).
Intrinsic Determinants & Regulations: Phase separation behavior is intrinsically regulated by PTBP3's RNA-binding domains (RBDs), which mediate RNA interactions and confer moderate dynamics in condensates (PubMed:39537752). Fusion of an intrinsically disordered region (IDR) from hnRNPAB to PTBP3's C-terminus significantly reduces mobility (mobile fraction ~20%), demonstrating how IDR-mediated protein-protein interactions can stabilize incorporation into condensates and alter material properties (PubMed:39537752).
Extrinsic Partners & Regulations: LE RNA (vg1 localization element) serves as an essential extrinsic regulator, required for both L-body localization and dynamic behavior of PTBP3 (PubMed:39537752). RNA binding directly governs the moderate diffusion dynamics observed in wild-type PTBP3 condensates (PubMed:39537752).

Overall Phase Separation Overview: PTBP3 undergoes RNA-dependent phase separation in vivo within cytoplasmic Localization bodies (L-bodies), forming irregularly shaped biomolecular condensates enriched for localized RNAs (PubMed:35982794). In vivo, PTBP3 exhibits moderate liquid-like dynamics within L-bodies, while in vitro it forms non-spherical condensates with solid- or gel-like properties characterized by non-dynamic RNA and slow PTBP3 recovery, suggesting arrested fusion (PubMed:35982794).
Functional Summary: PTBP3 phase separation enables RNA localization to L-bodies for germ layer patterning in Xenopus embryos, where the non-dynamic RNA component provides long-term storage of translationally silenced mRNAs (PubMed:35982794). Dysregulation could disrupt embryonic development due to impaired RNA localization and storage mechanisms (PubMed:35982794).
Intrinsic Determinants & Regulations: Phase separation is intrinsically driven by multivalent RNA binding through four RNA Recognition Motifs (RRMs), with RRM3 and RRM4 being essential for specific LE RNA binding and localization to L-bodies (PubMed:35982794). Multivalent interactions via multiple RRMs regulate PTBP3 dynamics within condensates, where single RRM binding suffices for localization but not full dynamic behavior (PubMed:35982794).
Extrinsic Partners & Regulations: PTBP3 strictly requires RNA scaffolds—specifically LE RNA (vg1-derived), mut PTB LE RNA, or XBM RNA—for condensate formation and maintenance (PubMed:35982794). These RNAs become non-dynamic within condensates, with LE RNA enhancing partitioning and RNA sequence influencing condensate morphology (irregular vs. spherical) and PTBP3 mobility (PubMed:35982794). Phase separation dissolves upon RNase treatment and is salt-/concentration-dependent, inhibited by high RNA concentrations (PubMed:35982794).

Overall Phase Separation Overview: Nup58 (A0A8J1M527) undergoes self-driven phase separation to form hydrogels in vitro, specifically through its FG and FG-like domains. This behavior is associated with the nuclear pore complex (central channel) subcellular location. The material state is characterized as a hydrogel, though no material state transitions were reported (PubMed:23202855).
Functional Summary: Nup58 hydrogel formation contributes to the nuclear pore complex's permeability barrier. However, FG domain hydrogels exhibit non-specific binding to inert probes and poor intrinsic selectivity, indicating that partner domains are required to achieve physiological NPC-like barrier properties (PubMed:23202855).
Intrinsic Determinants & Regulations: The phase separation of Nup58 is intrinsically driven by its FG domain and FG-like domain. Experimental studies of constructs spanning residues 2-72, 511-598, and 2-259 confirmed these regions as key drivers of hydrogel formation (PubMed:23202855).
Extrinsic Partners & Regulations: No extrinsic regulators, partner proteins, or environmental modulators of Nup58 phase separation were identified in the provided data (PubMed:23202855).

Overall Phase Separation Overview: CPEB4 undergoes self-driven phase separation to form cytoplasmic, liquid-like granules distinct from P-bodies and stress granules, as evidenced by spherical droplet morphology, fusion events, and rapid fluorescence recovery after photobleaching (FRAP) (PubMed:27802129). These droplets undergo reversible dissolution into monomers upon hyperphosphorylation by ERK2 and Cdk1, representing a liquid-to-monomer transition (PubMed:27802129).
Functional Summary: Phase separation enables translational regulation by sequestering target mRNAs into translationally inactive cytoplasmic condensates during interphase (PubMed:27802129). Hyperphosphorylation-triggered dissolution during M-phase releases mRNAs for cytoplasmic polyadenylation and activation, which is essential for meiotic progression (PubMed:27802129). This reversible condensation cycle serves as a phosphorylation-regulated switch for mRNA storage and activation during oocyte maturation (PubMed:27802129).
Intrinsic Determinants & Regulations: Phase separation is intrinsically driven by the N-terminal intrinsically disordered region (IDR; amino acids 1-409), which facilitates self-assembly through multivalent interactions (PubMed:27802129). Phosphorylation at 12 specific residues (S18/S38/S40/S97/S250/S253/T324/S328/S330/S351/S357/S362) by ERK2 and Cdk1 disrupts phase separation, as demonstrated by phospho-null mutants (12A) forming persistent droplets while phospho-mimetic mutants (12D) remain diffuse (PubMed:27802129).
Extrinsic Partners & Regulations: CPEB4 selectively sequesters CPE-containing mRNAs into cytoplasmic droplets, as confirmed by filter-binding assays showing specific retention of target RNAs (PubMed:27802129). This RNA partitioning requires the C-terminal RNA-binding domain, which recruits mRNAs to pre-formed condensates without independently driving phase separation (PubMed:27802129).

Overall Phase Separation Overview: Cirbpb (A0A8M1P6M4) undergoes phase separation and forms spontaneous cytoplasmic granules in vivo, associating with the Balbiani body (Bb) in the cytoplasm and nucleus of zebrafish oocytes (PubMed:35065906). The condensates exhibit hydrogel-like, solid-state properties without reported material-state transitions (PubMed:35065906).
Functional Summary: Phase separation enables Cirbpb to integrate maternal mRNAs into the Balbiani body hydrogel for germline-specific mRNA storage and embryonic patterning in zebrafish, serving essential roles in early development (PubMed:35065906).
Intrinsic Determinants & Regulations: Phase separation of Cirbpb is intrinsically driven by its RNA Recognition Motif (RRM) domain and C-terminal Prion-like Domain (PrLD), with the PrLD containing eight [S/G]Y[S/G] repeats critical for its behavior (PubMed:35065906).
Extrinsic Partners & Regulations: Cirbpb interacts with maternal mRNAs through RRM domain-mediated cargo crosslinking and co-phase separates with the Balbiani body scaffold protein Buc, evidenced by proteomic co-identification and shared subcellular localization (PubMed:35065906).

Overall Phase Separation Overview: Ddx3xb undergoes self-driven phase separation (class: PS-self) via its N-terminal intrinsically disordered region (IDR), forming dynamic liquid-like droplets in the cytoplasm both in vitro and in vivo within HEK293 cells and zebrafish embryos (PubMed:35661831). These condensates specifically form during maternal-to-zygotic transition (MZT) and require RNA, with ATP further promoting their assembly. No material state transitions (e.g., liquid-to-solid) were observed under tested conditions (PubMed:35661831).
Functional Summary: Phase separation enhances Ddx3xb's RNA helicase activity within condensates, facilitating unwinding of structured 5' UTRs in maternal mRNAs to boost translation efficiency during MZT, which is essential for timely maternal mRNA clearance, zygotic genome activation, and normal zebrafish embryogenesis (PubMed:35661831). Loss of phase separation ability (via N-terminal IDR deletion or non-functional IDR replacement) disrupts MZT, impairs mRNA translation, and causes developmental defects (PubMed:35661831).
Intrinsic Determinants & Regulations: Phase separation is intrinsically driven by the N-terminal IDR, as its deletion (Ddx3xb△N) abolishes condensate formation, while deletion of the C-terminal IDR (Ddx3xb△C) does not prevent LLPS (PubMed:35661831). The N-terminal IDR can be functionally replaced by IDRs from human FUS or hnRNPA1 to restore phase separation capacity, but not by the YAP IDR (PubMed:35661831).
Extrinsic Partners & Regulations: RNA (including maternal mRNAs like cnot6a and lin28a) is essential for droplet formation, promotes phase separation by lowering the saturation concentration, and is enriched within condensates (PubMed:35661831). ATP promotes phase separation only in the presence of RNA and is enriched in droplets; this effect does not require hydrolysis, as the non-hydrolyzable analog AMP-PNP also enhances condensation (PubMed:35661831). Increased ATP levels during MZT critically promote in vivo droplet assembly (PubMed:35661831).

Overall Phase Separation Overview: The protein ZO-3 (UniProt: A0A8M2BHQ8) does not undergo phase separation, as no experimental evidence of this behavior was observed (PubMed:31675500). It functions cooperatively in tight junction assembly and mechanosensitive actomyosin regulation without forming phase-separated condensates (PubMed:31675500).
Functional Summary: ZO-3 supports tight junction mechanosensitivity through actomyosin regulation but does not utilize phase separation for its function; its role in zebrafish epiboly movements and tension generation occurs without condensate formation (PubMed:31675500).
Intrinsic Determinants & Regulations: No intrinsic regulators of phase separation were identified for ZO-3, as no domains, mutations, or structural features driving phase separation were reported (PubMed:31675500).
Extrinsic Partners & Regulations: ZO-3 functionally interacts with ZO-1b (UniProt: A0A8M3AP85) during tight junction assembly, but no evidence of co-phase separation or modulation by external partners was observed (PubMed:31675500).

Overall Phase Separation Overview: ZO-1b undergoes liquid-liquid phase separation (LLPS) to form dynamic clusters in the cytoplasm of zebrafish embryos, specifically within the yolk syncytial layer (PubMed:31675500). These non-junctional clusters exhibit concentration-dependent formation, fusion, and retrograde flow toward tight junctions (TJs), with material properties transitioning from liquid-like (fast fusion, high mobility) to gel-like/solid-like states over time (PubMed:31675500). ZO-1b associates with TJs as a core structural component, and this phase separation is classified as PS-other (PubMed:31675500).
Functional Summary: ZO-1b phase separation confers tension-dependent mechanosensitivity to tight junctions by enabling actomyosin-driven transport of clusters to TJ sites, which scales TJ assembly with cellular tension during embryonic epiboly (PubMed:31675500). Disruption via ΔC (abolishing LLPS) or ΔABR (impairing actin anchoring) delays tissue spreading by uncoupling TJ formation from actomyosin forces, highlighting its essential role in force transmission during zebrafish development (PubMed:31675500).
Intrinsic Determinants & Regulations: The phase separation of ZO-1b is intrinsically driven by its C-terminal intrinsically disordered region (IDR; residues 1097–1748), which facilitates multivalent interactions (PubMed:31675500). Deletion of the entire C-terminal region (ZO-1bΔC) abolishes LLPS, while deletion of the actin-binding region (ABR) within the IDR (ZO-1bΔABR) permits phase separation but disrupts actin anchoring and increases cluster circularity (PubMed:31675500).
Extrinsic Partners & Regulations: ZO-1b clusters co-localize with Cingulin-like 1 (Pearson’s R = 0.8), suggesting potential co-scaffolding roles (PubMed:31675500). Actin filaments critically regulate cluster morphology and dynamics by confining clusters to cortical surfaces, inducing elongation, and enabling junctional integration; disruption with Latrunculin B increases cluster size and circularity (PubMed:31675500).

Overall Phase Separation Overview: Cirbpa (A0A8M6Z3G7) undergoes self-driven phase separation, forming solid, hydrogel-like condensates primarily within the Balbiani body of stage I oocytes, exhibiting stage-specific cytoplasmic localization distinct from its nuclear localization in somatic cells (PubMed:35065906).
Functional Summary: Phase separation enables mRNA cargo integration into the Balbiani body hydrogel via RRM-PrLD multivalency, supporting germline-specific mRNA storage essential for embryonic patterning (PubMed:35065906). It further contributes to regulatory mechanisms governing Balbiani body disassembly (PubMed:35065906).
Intrinsic Determinants & Regulations: Phase separation is intrinsically driven by multivalent interactions mediated by its RNA recognition motif (RRM) and prion-like domain (PrLD), with the PrLD containing five [S/G]Y[S/G] repeats that promote aggregation (PubMed:35065906). Both domains independently enable localization to the Balbiani body, as demonstrated by truncation constructs CirbpaΔ84−185 (RRM-only) and CirbpaΔ1−83 (PrLD-only) (PubMed:35065906).
Extrinsic Partners & Regulations: Cirbpa interacts with maternal mRNAs via its RRM domain to facilitate cargo integration into the Balbiani body hydrogel (PubMed:35065906). It structurally integrates with the protein Buc within the condensate, evidenced by proteomic co-identification and shared localization, despite lacking common [S/G]Y[S/G] motifs (PubMed:35065906).

Overall Phase Separation Overview: Rbm14 (UniProt: A0A8M9Q1B8) undergoes RNA-driven phase separation to form cytoplasmic condensates termed 'Rbm14-maternal mRNA condensates' in zebrafish blastomeres (PubMed:36477743). These liquid-like condensates exhibit fusion dynamics and associate with centrosomes/spindle poles while concentrating m6A-modified maternal mRNAs and deadenylase Parn (PubMed:36477743). Phase separation occurs in both cytoplasm and nucleus, with formation dose-dependently promoted by m6A-modified RNA and inhibited by m5C-modified RNA (PubMed:36477743). No material state transitions were reported.
Functional Summary: Rbm14 condensates are essential for vertebrate embryogenesis, facilitating deadenylation, protection, and mitotic allocation of maternal mRNAs during maternal-to-zygotic transition (PubMed:36477743). They enable asymmetric/symmetric segregation of mRNAs during cell division and are critical for cell cycle progression and differentiation (PubMed:36477743). Depletion causes blastula arrest, demonstrating their necessity for early development (PubMed:36477743). The co-phase separation with Parn markedly enhances mRNA deadenylation efficiency, directly linking condensate formation to biochemical function (PubMed:36477743).
Intrinsic Determinants & Regulations: Phase separation is intrinsically driven by Rbm14's C-terminal intrinsically disordered region (IDR; aa 766–1668), which is essential for condensation, and N-terminal RNA-recognition motifs (RRMs; aa 1–765) that mediate RNA binding (PubMed:36477743). The critical role of the IDR is demonstrated by the LLPS-defective mutant zRbm14b18S, where 18 tyrosine-to-serine substitutions abolish phase separation capacity (PubMed:36477743).
Extrinsic Partners & Regulations: Extrinsic regulation is dominated by RNA modifications: m6A-modified maternal mRNAs act as essential scaffolds that promote phase separation, while m5C-modified RNA inhibits condensation and dissolves pre-formed droplets (PubMed:36477743). The deadenylase Parn (UniProt: Q7ZU92) serves as a co-scaffold, co-phase separating with Rbm14 and potentiating its condensation (PubMed:36477743). Functionally, Parn recruitment enhances deadenylation efficiency >10-fold within condensates (PubMed:36477743).

Overall Phase Separation Overview: Bucky ball (A0A8V0Z3J5) undergoes phase separation (class: PS-other) to form condensates in vitro in chicken cell lines and exhibits dynamic aggregation patterns in vivo within the cytoplasm and nucleus during early embryonic development, consistent with liquid-liquid phase separation properties (PubMed:36207377). It associates with the germ plasm (Balbiani body equivalent) (PubMed:36207377). Material state and transitions were not specified.
Functional Summary: The phase separation of Bucky ball organizes germ plasm to enable germline specification by concentrating maternal determinants. This dynamic condensation and translocation during embryonic stages (EGK I-X) facilitate germ plasm assembly, positioning Bucky ball as a critical germ plasm organizer (PubMed:36207377).
Intrinsic Determinants & Regulations: The phase separation of Bucky ball is intrinsically driven by its intrinsically disordered protein (IDP) nature, as demonstrated through studies of the full-length protein (PubMed:36207377). No specific domains, mutations, or post-translational modifications regulating this behavior were reported.
Extrinsic Partners & Regulations: Bucky ball co-localizes with Chicken vasa homolog (CVH) in condensates, a partnership essential for germ plasm assembly. This co-localization is observed in cleavage furrows and nuclei during embryonic development (PubMed:36207377). No other extrinsic regulators (e.g., ions, chemicals) were identified.

Overall Phase Separation Overview: TDRD1 undergoes phase separation, forming cytoplasmic droplets in HeLa cells as demonstrated through in vivo experiments (PubMed:39029469). The specific material state (liquid/solid) and transitions were not characterized, and no association with membrane-less organelles was reported.
