Functional Summary: No functional or pathological roles for TDRD1 phase separation were specified in the experimental data; the authors solely concluded that chicken TDRD1 undergoes LLPS without linking it to cellular processes or disease (PubMed:39029469).
Intrinsic Determinants & Regulations: No intrinsic regulatory domains, mutations, or features were identified; phase separation was observed using the full-length protein construct without further mechanistic dissection (PubMed:39029469).
Extrinsic Partners & Regulations: No extrinsic regulators, binding partners, or environmental modulators (ions, chemicals) were reported for TDRD1 phase separation in the provided study (PubMed:39029469).

Overall Phase Separation Overview: NF-κB p65 (A0AAA9SLR3) undergoes phase separation as a client protein, sequestered into bovine respiratory syncytial virus (bRSV) inclusion bodies (IBs) in the cytoplasm. This recruitment inhibits its nuclear translocation and NF-κB activation. The protein associates exclusively with viral IBs, though its material state remains unspecified with no observed transitions (PubMed:32878896).
Functional Summary: Sequestration into viral IBs suppresses NF-κB-mediated immune signaling, representing a viral immune evasion strategy. This inhibition occurs through cytoplasmic retention of p65, preventing nuclear translocation and activation of host defense pathways (PubMed:32878896).
Intrinsic Determinants & Regulations: No intrinsic domains, mutations, or sequence features driving phase separation were identified; experiments utilized the full-length endogenous protein without specified regulatory elements (PubMed:32878896).
Extrinsic Partners & Regulations: Phase separation is extrinsically regulated through recruitment into condensates formed by viral proteins N (Uniprot: A0A2H4H6B8) and P (Uniprot: A0A193AUW9), confirmed by co-localization in IBs and co-immunoprecipitation (PubMed:32878896).

Overall Phase Separation Overview: Whi3 undergoes heterotypically driven phase separation primarily through interactions with RNA molecules, forming ribonucleoprotein condensates in both the nucleus and cytoplasm (PubMed:36798397). These condensates exhibit viscoelastic material properties with partial protein mobility and RNA immobilization, and demonstrate dynamical demixing into compositionally distinct phases due to asynchronous crosslink timescales in ternary systems (PubMed:36798397).
Functional Summary: Whi3 phase separation serves critical physiological functions: Whi3-CLN3 condensates regulate nuclear division, while Whi3-BNI1/SPA2 condensates control actin-mediated cell polarity (PubMed:36798397). The demixing into compositionally distinct condensates enables spatial segregation of these functions within the cell (PubMed:36798397).
Intrinsic Determinants & Regulations: The phase separation of Whi3 is intrinsically regulated by its Glutamine-rich region and RNA recognition motif (RRM), both identified as essential domains for driving condensate formation (PubMed:36798397).
Extrinsic Partners & Regulations: Whi3 phase separation is extrinsically modulated by specific RNA partners: CLN3 RNA acts as an essential scaffold that drives condensate formation and demixing through cognate sites; BNI1 and SPA2 RNAs enable phase separation via enriched non-cognate sites at high concentrations; while BNI1mut RNA weakens phase separation at low concentrations but preserves it at high concentrations (PubMed:36798397).

Gene Names: cpeb1b cepb1b cpeb1 fd15c06 wu:fd15c06 ZOR-1 zorba
Overall Phase Separation Overview: Cpeb1b (A0AB32TRZ9) does not undergo autonomous phase separation but localizes into Pabpc1b-induced liquid-like condensates in the cytoplasm (PubMed:36745802). These condensates exhibit liquid properties, including dynamic molecular exchange via FRAP and fusion capabilities, with no observed material state transitions.
Functional Summary: Condensate localization enables Cpeb1b to mediate cytoplasmic polyadenylation and translation of shha mRNA, upregulating Shha protein to activate Hedgehog–Vegf–Notch signaling pathways essential for definitive hematopoiesis during development (PubMed:36745802).
Intrinsic Determinants & Regulations: No intrinsic domains or features driving phase separation were identified; Cpeb1b lacks prion-like domains and shows no autonomous condensation capacity in vitro or in vivo (PubMed:36745802).
Extrinsic Partners & Regulations: Cpeb1b recruitment requires extrinsic partners: it partitions into Pabpc1b scaffolds whose condensate formation is enhanced by Cpeb1b co-expression (PubMed:36745802). Within these condensates, Cpeb1b interacts with shha mRNA via CPE motifs and colocalizes with Tent2, forming a ternary regulatory complex.

Protein Name: Mediator of RNA polymerase II transcription subunit 19
Overall Phase Separation Overview: Med19 undergoes phase separation in the nucleus of mammalian cells, forming condensates observed in vivo. While specific material states and MLO associations are not defined, the condensates exhibit regulated dynamics: their lifetimes increase significantly upon transcription elongation inhibition by DRB and revert to baseline upon inhibitor removal (PubMed:33333019).
Functional Summary: Med19 condensate lifetime is functionally coupled to transcription elongation. Prolonged condensate persistence during elongation inhibition suggests a role in transcriptional regulation, with dynamics normalizing upon restored transcriptional activity (PubMed:33333019).
Intrinsic Determinants & Regulations: No intrinsic domains, mutations, or protein features driving Med19 phase separation were identified in the provided study (PubMed:33333019).
Extrinsic Partners & Regulations: Med19 condensate dynamics are extrinsically regulated by transcription elongation status. Inhibition via DRB treatment prolongs condensate lifetime, while reversal occurs upon DRB washout, indicating transcriptional activity directly modulates phase separation behavior (PubMed:33333019).

Gene Names: sall4 cb372 cb614 ik:tdsubc_2c1 sb:cb372 sb:cb614 wu:fa01g03 xx:tdsubc_2c1
Overall Phase Separation Overview: Sall4 (A0MWC1) undergoes self-driven phase separation to form liquid-like nuclear condensates via self-assembly and directs co-phase separation with Tet2/3 catalytic domains on DNA probes to form transcriptional condensates on the bmp4 promoter (PubMed:38427557).
Functional Summary: Sall4-mediated phase separation facilitates targeted 5-methylcytosine oxidation on the bmp4 promoter through Tet2/3 recruitment, activating BMP signaling essential for chondrocyte differentiation and pharyngeal cartilage development in zebrafish (PubMed:38427557). This TET-BMP-Sall4 regulatory axis represents a critical mechanism for craniofacial morphogenesis (PubMed:38427557).
Intrinsic Determinants & Regulations: The phase separation of Sall4 is intrinsically driven by its low-complexity (LC) domains and DNA-binding zinc finger domains, which enable self-assembly through multivalent interactions (PubMed:38427557). Deletion mutations in these domains (ΔZFC1-3, ΔZFC1, ZFC1) disrupt condensate formation both in vivo and in vitro, confirming their essential role in phase separation (PubMed:38427557).
Extrinsic Partners & Regulations: Sall4 requires co-phase separation partners for functional condensates: it recruits Tet2 and Tet3 catalytic domains into transcriptional condensates, with neither protein phase separating independently (PubMed:38427557). DNA probes from the bmp4 promoter enhance Sall4 phase separation and are required for efficient condensate assembly (PubMed:38427557).

Overall Phase Separation Overview: MSMEG_1642 (A0QSY1) undergoes self-driven phase separation (PS-self) in vitro (PubMed:31366629). Phosphorylation by PknF reduces its saturation concentration for condensate formation, with orthologous behavior to Rv1747 indicating evolutionary conservation (PubMed:31366629).
Functional Summary: Evolutionary conservation suggests phase separation regulates ABC transporter clustering or activity in Mycolicibacterium smegmatis, though specific functional details remain unspecified (PubMed:31366629).
Intrinsic Determinants & Regulations: Phase separation is intrinsically driven by residues 1-340, which encompass essential FHA domains and an intrinsically disordered linker region (PubMed:31366629). Phosphorylation serves as a critical post-translational regulator, lowering the concentration threshold for condensation (PubMed:31366629).
Extrinsic Partners & Regulations: The kinase PknF acts as an extrinsic regulator by phosphorylating MSMEG_1642, experimentally shown to enhance phase separation through reduced saturation concentration in vitro (PubMed:31366629).

Overall Phase Separation Overview: MEX3A undergoes self-driven liquid-liquid phase separation (LLPS) in the cytoplasm, forming dynamic liquid-like condensates both in vitro and in vivo (PubMed:38565536). It associates with processing bodies (P-bodies), where its phase separation facilitates the assembly of these membrane-less organelles by recruiting RNA and protein components (PubMed:38565536). The condensates exhibit liquid-like material properties, characterized by rapid fluorescence recovery after photobleaching (FRAP), droplet fusion, and dynamic exchange, with no reported transitions to solid or gel states (PubMed:38565536).
Functional Summary: MEX3A phase separation enables assembly of functional processing bodies (P-bodies) that degrade PDE5A mRNA via UPF1, leading to suppression of autophagy and enhanced proliferation, migration, and tumorigenesis in colorectal cancer (CRC) cells (PubMed:38565536). This pathological axis correlates with poor patient survival in CRC (PubMed:38565536).
Intrinsic Determinants & Regulations: Phase separation of MEX3A is intrinsically driven by its intrinsically disordered regions (IDRs), as truncation of these regions abolishes droplet formation (PubMed:38565536). While the KH2 domain is essential for binding the RNA partner circMPP6 and subsequent recruitment to P-bodies, it does not directly drive phase separation (PubMed:38565536).
Extrinsic Partners & Regulations: MEX3A phase separation is modulated by the RNA scaffold circMPP6, which enhances MEX3A-P-body protein interactions and promotes P-body aggregation (PubMed:38565536). Key protein partners recruited into MEX3A/circMPP6 condensates include MOV10, UPF1, and PABP1, all essential for P-body-mediated mRNA decay (PubMed:38565536). Droplet formation is sensitive to environmental conditions, including temperature, protein concentration, and ionic strength (PubMed:38565536).

Gene Names: Pcf11 anon-WO0118547.146 Dmel\CG10228 dPcf11 Inr-a l(2)k08015 PCF11 pcf11 Pcf11-RA
Overall Phase Separation Overview: Pcf11 undergoes phase separation mediated by protein partners, forming liquid-like condensates in the nucleus (PubMed:40015272). It forms nuclear puncta partially co-localizing with RNA Pol II, with no observed material state transitions reported (PubMed:40015272).
Functional Summary: Phase separation is essential for RNA Pol II stalling during transcription termination, facilitating piRNA-guided heterochromatin formation and transposon silencing (PubMed:40015272). Loss of α-helical-mediated condensation abrogates RNA Pol II stalling, confirming the mechanistic requirement (PubMed:40015272).
Intrinsic Determinants & Regulations: Phase separation is intrinsically driven by Pcf11's α-helical region (aa 186-255), with a charge-reversal mutation (K/R-to-D/E) in this region abolishing condensation capability (PubMed:40015272).
Extrinsic Partners & Regulations: Pcf11 co-condenses with RNA Pol II, which scaffolds droplet formation at physiological concentrations, and is enhanced by unphosphorylated Spt5-CTR (PubMed:40015272). Spt5 phosphorylation by CDK9 inhibits condensation, while PNUTS/PP1-mediated dephosphorylation enables cellular recruitment (PubMed:40015272).

Overall Phase Separation Overview: ZMYND8 undergoes self-driven phase separation to form dynamic liquid-like condensates in the nucleus, both in vitro and in vivo (PubMed:34764296). These condensates associate with nuclear speckles and translocate to latent super-enhancers upon LPS stimulation (PubMed:34764296). While typically exhibiting liquid properties (rapid FRAP recovery, fusion capability), a D/E-to-A mutation induces an irreversible liquid-to-solid transition, forming solid aggregates (PubMed:34764296).
Functional Summary: Phase separation enables ZMYND8 translocation to latent super-enhancers, where it recruits KDM1A to demethylate H3K4 and suppress pro-inflammatory genes (e.g., Ccl2, Il1b) during immune responses (PubMed:34764296). Loss of liquidity via D/E-to-A mutation prevents chromatin translocation and gene suppression, exacerbating inflammation in colitis/obesity models, while Zmynd8 knockout yields similar pathological outcomes (PubMed:34764296).
Intrinsic Determinants & Regulations: Phase separation is intrinsically driven by ZMYND8's C-terminal Intrinsically Disordered Region (IDR; aa 388-899), whereas the N-terminal PBP domain (aa 1-387) cannot form condensates (PubMed:34764296). A D/E-to-A mutation within the IDR (acidic residues mutated to alanine) abolishes liquidity, causing solidification and loss of dynamic properties (PubMed:34764296).
Extrinsic Partners & Regulations: ZMYND8 co-phase separates with RelA (p65), which scaffolds droplet coalescence and enhances fusion; this interaction requires LPS stimulation and is potentiated by RelA acetylation at K122 (PubMed:34764296). KDM1A (LSD1) is recruited into condensates via RelA-dependent mechanisms, reducing droplet fluidity upon incorporation (PubMed:34764296). Condensate formation is salt-sensitive, dissolving at high NaCl concentrations (250 mM) (PubMed:34764296).

Protein Name: Mediator of RNA polymerase II transcription subunit 12
Overall Phase Separation Overview: MED12 undergoes phase separation to form liquid-like nuclear puncta associated with transcriptional condensates (PubMed:34605568). This behavior is classified as PS-other, indicating involvement beyond self-driven assembly. Puncta formation is reduced upon SRSF3 depletion, suggesting regulatory dependencies, though no material state transitions are reported (PubMed:34605568).
Functional Summary: MED12 phase separation is essential for mediator complex function in transcription, directly linking condensate formation to transcriptional regulation (PubMed:34605568). The dependence on SRSF3 establishes a mechanistic connection between splicing factors and transcriptional condensate dynamics, though pathological implications remain unspecified (PubMed:34605568).
Intrinsic Determinants & Regulations: Phase separation is intrinsically regulated by an intrinsically disordered region (IDR) encoded by exon 3 (S3-LCE), which serves as the primary molecular driver (PubMed:34605568). No mutations, PTMs, or oligomerization features were identified as modulators in the studied context (PubMed:34605568).
Extrinsic Partners & Regulations: SRSF3 critically promotes MED12 condensate formation, as evidenced by reduced nuclear puncta upon SRSF3 depletion in C2C12 cells (PubMed:34605568). Co-silencing of Hnrnpk partially restores puncta formation, indicating an antagonistic regulatory relationship between SRSF3 and Hnrnpk (PubMed:34605568). No other extrinsic partners or chemical modulators were reported.

Overall Phase Separation Overview: Cep152 does not undergo self-driven phase separation but partitions into pre-existing condensates in the cytoplasm (PubMed:33658185). It associates with deuterosomes - non-membranous organelles for centriole amplification - and resides in gel-like/solid condensates exhibiting minimal molecular mobility, as evidenced by low FRAP recovery (PubMed:33658185).
Functional Summary: Compartmentalization within Deup1 condensates enables Cep152's essential role in centriole biogenesis during multiciliogenesis by spatially regulating assembly machinery alongside Plk4 in deuterosomes, with gel-like/solid properties providing structural stability during organelle biogenesis (PubMed:33658185).
Intrinsic Determinants & Regulations: No intrinsic phase separation capability was observed for Cep152; it lacks self-assembly domains, mutations, or structural features enabling autonomous condensate formation (PubMed:33658185).
Extrinsic Partners & Regulations: Cep152 partitions into condensates formed by Deup1 (Q7M6Y5) through direct binding to Deup1's C-terminal region, as demonstrated by optogenetic recruitment showing 4.5-fold enrichment (PubMed:33658185).

Overall Phase Separation Overview: ARID1A undergoes self-driven phase separation to form liquid-like nuclear puncta as part of the BAF complex condensates (PubMed:34605568).
Functional Summary: The phase separation of ARID1A is essential for BAF complex assembly and chromatin remodeling, and disruption of condensate formation through SRSF3 depletion impairs this function (PubMed:34605568).
Intrinsic Determinants & Regulations: The phase separation of ARID1A is intrinsically driven by its intrinsically disordered region (IDR) encoded by exon 3, with splicing regulation by SRSF3 being essential for exon inclusion; depletion of SRSF3 causes exon skipping and deletion of the IDR, disrupting condensate formation (PubMed:34605568).
Extrinsic Partners & Regulations: No extrinsic regulators or partners modulating ARID1A phase separation were reported in the provided data (PubMed:34605568).

Overall Phase Separation Overview: NSP2 (A2T3P0) undergoes heterotypic phase separation as a co-scaffold with NSP5 to form liquid-like viroplasm condensates in the cytoplasm (PubMed:36700549). These dynamic, RNA-enriched compartments exhibit liquid-like properties and serve as functional viral ribonucleoprotein condensates, with no observed material state transitions reported.
Functional Summary: NSP2 phase separation facilitates inter-segment RNA interactions for viral genome assortment and packaging by confining transcripts within phase-separated compartments, preventing non-cognate interactions (PubMed:36700549). This process is indispensable for viroplasm assembly and selective transcript enrichment, as demonstrated by NSP2 knockdown abolishing RNA clustering and condensate formation (PubMed:36700549).
Intrinsic Determinants & Regulations: The phase separation of NSP2 is intrinsically driven by its capacity to self-assemble into octamers and its RNA-binding surfaces, which are essential for condensate formation and function (PubMed:36700549).
Extrinsic Partners & Regulations: NSP2 requires the extrinsic partner NSP5 for co-phase separation, forming heterotypic condensates through mutual dependency (PubMed:36700549). Additionally, Rotavirus transcripts act as essential clients that are selectively enriched within the condensates, with RNA clustering abolished upon NSP2 depletion (PubMed:36700549).

Overall Phase Separation Overview: NSP5 (A3DSG0) undergoes self-driven liquid-liquid phase separation (LLPS) in the cytoplasm to form viroplasms, which serve as rotavirus replication factories (PubMed:34524703). These condensates exhibit liquid-like properties during early infection—characterized by spherical morphology, fusion capability, rapid component exchange, and sensitivity to aliphatic diols—but transition to a viscoelastic/solid-like state during late infection, as evidenced by reduced dynamics and altered morphology (PubMed:34524703).
Functional Summary: NSP5 LLPS establishes viroplasms that concentrate viral RNAs and proteins for genome replication and packaging (PubMed:34524703). Disrupting liquid-phase condensates (e.g., with 1,6-hexanediol) during early infection reduces viral replication and NSP5 phosphorylation (PubMed:34524703). The liquid-to-solid transition during late infection facilitates virion assembly, with mature solid-like structures resistant to dissolution (PubMed:34524703).
Intrinsic Determinants & Regulations: Phase separation is intrinsically driven by the C-terminal region (CTR; residues ~188-197), which is essential for LLPS initiation and oligomerization (PubMed:34524703). A ΔCTR mutant (residues 1-188) fails to form droplets but partitions into preformed condensates, confirming the CTR's role in nucleation (PubMed:34524703). Phosphorylation dynamically regulates material state transitions during infection progression, while polyvalent electrostatic interactions promote condensation (PubMed:34524703).
Extrinsic Partners & Regulations: NSP5 requires the RNA chaperone NSP2 as an essential co-scaffold for efficient phase separation at physiological concentrations, forming heterotypic condensates (PubMed:34524703). Rotavirus transcripts enrich within these condensates and contribute to maturation (PubMed:34524703). Poly-arginine (but not shorter Arg-9 peptides) induces LLPS at high concentrations via electrostatic interactions, while molecular crowding agents like PEG-20K promote droplet formation at elevated concentrations (PubMed:34524703).

Overall Phase Separation Overview: ORF112 undergoes self-driven phase separation (class: PS-self) primarily in the nucleus, forming dynamic ribonucleoprotein (RNP) condensates that initially exhibit liquid-like properties but transition to hydrogel-like networks over time (PubMed:36130731). It associates with Stress Granules (particularly upon arsenite treatment) and RNP condensates, with full-length protein recruitment occurring in 98% of transfected cells under stress conditions (PubMed:36130731).
Functional Summary: Phase separation enables viral immune evasion by sequestering dsRNA within RNP condensates to avoid host sensors like PKZ and RIG-I, while pathological aggregation occurs through aberrant phase transitions (PubMed:36130731). The Zα domain is essential for viral replication through A-to-Z RNA conversion and condensate formation, with its dysfunction proving lethal, while the N-terminal IDR provides redundant condensate-forming capacity but remains dispensable for replication (PubMed:36130731).
Intrinsic Determinants & Regulations: Phase separation is intrinsically driven by two key domains: the N-terminal intrinsically disordered region (IDR) containing Q-rich and H-rich low-complexity domains (LCDs), and the C-terminal Zα domain (aa189-280) (PubMed:36130731). Both domains independently enable homotypic phase separation, though the Zα domain's function is impaired by the N255A-Y259A mutation, which abolishes Z-RNA-dependent droplet formation and reduces stress granule recruitment by 12% while retaining PEG-induced phase separation capability (PubMed:36130731).
Extrinsic Partners & Regulations: Z-RNA serves as an essential extrinsic nucleation factor for phase separation, with droplet formation strictly dependent on its presence for both full-length ORF112 and the isolated Zα domain (PubMed:36130731). The absence of functional Z-RNA binding prevents condensate formation despite retained homotypic interaction capacity (PubMed:36130731).

Overall Phase Separation Overview: GSAP undergoes self-driven liquid-liquid phase separation (LLPS) in vitro, forming dynamic liquid droplets whose formation depends on protein concentration and ionic strength, and in cells it forms cytoplasmic puncta-like condensates (PubMed:35298330). The condensates exhibit liquid-like properties with slower dynamics (55% FRAP recovery in vitro; 33% in cells), indicating a viscous liquid state, but no material state transitions were reported (PubMed:35298330).
Functional Summary: Phase separation regulates γ-secretase-mediated cleavage of APP-C99: dilute-phase GSAP enhances production of amyloidogenic Aβ42 (implicated in Alzheimer’s disease), while condensates sequester APP-C99 to suppress cleavage (PubMed:35298330). Elevated GSAP concentrations increase the Aβ42/Aβ40 ratio, a key Alzheimer’s disease risk factor (PubMed:35298330).
Intrinsic Determinants & Regulations: Phase separation is disrupted by a deletion mutation (Δ734-758) in GSAP-16K, which abolishes interaction and colocalization with its key partner APP-C99 (PubMed:35298330).
Extrinsic Partners & Regulations: GSAP co-phase separates with APP, which acts as an essential co-scaffold that enhances droplet formation, evidenced by colocalization and centrifugation assays (PubMed:35298330). LLPS is strongly inhibited by high NaCl concentrations (≥300 mM), demonstrating ionic strength sensitivity (PubMed:35298330).

Overall Phase Separation Overview: ENO (A4W2T1) does not undergo autonomous phase separation but requires partners for heterotypic co-condensation (PubMed:38331785). Located in the cytoplasm, it co-localizes with RPSA/VIM membrane-associated condensates and promotes ternary complex formation (PubMed:38331785). The co-condensates exhibit liquid-like properties, evidenced by 1,6-Hexanediol sensitivity, but no autonomous material state transitions were reported (PubMed:38331785).
Functional Summary: ENO-mediated co-condensation with RPSA and VIM concentrates pathogen-receptor complexes on host cell surfaces during Streptococcus suis infection (PubMed:38331785). This triggers intracellular Ca²⁺ influx, mitochondrial damage, and apoptosis in brain endothelial cells, contributing to bacterial meningitis pathogenesis (PubMed:38331785).
Intrinsic Determinants & Regulations: No intrinsic domains, repeats, or mutations driving phase separation were identified for ENO (PubMed:38331785). Its ability to form condensates relies entirely on binding to the internally disordered region (IDR) of RPSA, as truncation studies confirm ENO requires RPSA's IDR2/3 for co-condensation (PubMed:38331785).
Extrinsic Partners & Regulations: ENO forms heterotypic co-condensates with human RPSA and vimentin (VIM) (PubMed:38331785). It scaffolds RPSA-VIM interactions, enhancing their co-localization in membrane puncta by 3.5-fold in a 1,6-Hexanediol-sensitive manner (PubMed:38331785). No ions, chemicals, or additional extrinsic modulators were reported for ENO-specific regulation (PubMed:38331785).

Overall Phase Separation Overview: Myosin II (A6HFI0) undergoes self-driven phase separation (PubMed:38889317) in the cytoplasm, exhibiting a reentrant phase transition behavior (PubMed:38889317). At low Vitamin C (Vc) concentrations (10 µM), it forms amorphous condensates, while dissociating into a soluble state at high Vc concentrations (100 µM), observed both in vitro and in primary cortical neurons (PubMed:38889317). This transition involves reversible structural changes between aggregated and soluble states (PubMed:38889317).
Functional Summary: The reentrant phase transitions regulate actomyosin assemblies and F-actin bundle dynamics (PubMed:38889317). This directly impacts neurotransmitter exocytosis kinetics in primary cortical neurons, where Vc concentration modulates myosin II aggregation states and cytoskeletal organization (PubMed:38889317).
Intrinsic Determinants & Regulations: Phase separation is intrinsically regulated by reversible α-helix to β-sheet conversion in the actin-binding domain of the heavy chain (PubMed:38889317). This structural transition occurs in the full-length protein and is directly mediated by Vc binding (PubMed:38889317).
Extrinsic Partners & Regulations: Vitamin C (Vc) acts as a direct extrinsic modulator of phase behavior (PubMed:38889317). At 10 µM Vc, it induces myosin II aggregation into amorphous condensates, while 100 µM Vc promotes complete dissociation into soluble monomers, as demonstrated through TEM, DLS, and cellular imaging (PubMed:38889317). The transition follows concentration-dependent kinetics observed in purified systems and neurons (PubMed:38889317).

Overall Phase Separation Overview: MaSpI8 (A7M8K7) does not undergo self-driven phase separation but is recruited as a cargo protein into synthetic liquid condensates in the cytoplasm of Escherichia coli via an engineered light-responsive system (PubMed:38665676).
Functional Summary: The phase separation behavior serves as a synthetic tool for light-controlled protein recruitment in Escherichia coli, demonstrating rapid reversibility for potential applications in cellular engineering (PubMed:38665676).
Intrinsic Determinants & Regulations: No intrinsic domains, mutations, or features driving phase separation of MaSpI8 were reported in the provided data (PubMed:38665676).
Extrinsic Partners & Regulations: MaSpI8 recruitment into condensates is extrinsically regulated by the heterodimerization pair iLID (P9WEU0) and SspB (P0AFZ3), which form a blue light-responsive system enabling rapid, light-dependent recruitment and release of cargo proteins within seconds (PubMed:38665676).

Overall Phase Separation Overview: SINTBAD (TBKBP1) undergoes stress-induced phase separation to form liquid-like cytosolic and nuclear speckles, termed SINT-speckles, in response to cellular stressors such as heat shock, arsenite, and sorbitol (PubMed:31442668). These dynamic, reversible condensates do not colocalize with known membrane-less organelles like stress granules or P-bodies, and their formation is antagonized by HSP chaperone activity and ULK1/2 kinase activity (PubMed:31442668).
Functional Summary: SINT-speckles act as signaling hubs for TBK1 regulation, with loss of SINTBAD or AZI2 impairing TBK1 phosphorylation (PubMed:31442668). ULK1/2 knockdown specifically inhibits heat shock-induced TBK1 activation, revealing pathway-specific control of immune responses (PubMed:31442668). These condensates dynamically assemble during cellular stress to coordinate kinase signaling pathways (PubMed:31442668).
Intrinsic Determinants & Regulations: Phase separation is intrinsically regulated by SINTBAD's N-terminal region (amino acids 1-165), which is critical for partner interactions (PubMed:31442668). Phosphorylation events, particularly during mitosis, contribute to speckle disassembly (PubMed:31442668). Truncation mutants (∆N1:106-615, ∆N2:165-615, ∆C:1-520) confirm the functional importance of these domains (PubMed:31442668).
Extrinsic Partners & Regulations: SINTBAD co-phase separates with constitutive partners AZI2 and ABIN2, which induce speckle formation even in unstressed cells, and inducible partner PTPN23 that colocalizes under stress (PubMed:31442668). Extrinsic modulation includes: 1) Positive regulation by acetyltransferase KAT2A (induces speckles) and HSP70/HSP90 inhibitors (trigger formation in unstressed conditions), 2) Negative regulation by ULK1 kinase activity (inhibits speckles; kinase-inactive K46I mutant promotes them) (PubMed:31442668).

Overall Phase Separation Overview: BuGZ undergoes self-driven liquid-liquid phase separation (LLPS) in vitro and forms reversible, liquid-like nuclear puncta in intestinal stem cells during aging and after injury (PubMed:37872148). These condensates partially colocalize with H3K27me3-marked chromatin but do not associate with predefined membrane-less organelles like nucleoli or PML bodies (PubMed:37872148). No material state transitions (e.g., liquid-to-solid) were reported.
Functional Summary: BuGZ phase separation promotes intestinal stem cell proliferation, enabling gut repair after injury and driving age-associated hyperproliferation that regulates intestinal homeostasis and lifespan (PubMed:37872148). Disruption of phase separation (via BuGZ13S mutation or BuGZC inhibitory peptide) rescues aging phenotypes, suppresses pathological proliferation, and extends longevity (PubMed:37872148).
Intrinsic Determinants & Regulations: BuGZ phase separation is intrinsically driven by its intrinsically disordered region (IDR, residues 1-121) and zinc finger domain (PubMed:37872148). Disease-relevant mutations, including BuGZ13S (tyrosine/phenylalanine-to-serine substitutions) that disrupt phase separation and BuGZΔzinc (zinc finger deletion) that impairs DNA binding and reduces condensation, demonstrate the critical role of these domains (PubMed:37872148).
Extrinsic Partners & Regulations: BuGZ phase separation is enhanced by DNA (specifically the P8 promoter of YT521-B) via zinc finger-mediated binding, which accelerates droplet formation and reduces dynamics (PubMed:37872148). Conversely, it is inhibited by the proteins Ime4 and Mettl14, which bind BuGZ and suppress droplet formation in vitro and puncta formation in vivo (PubMed:37872148).

Overall Phase Separation Overview: Gtpbp4 (A8E612) is classified as a phase separation-associated protein (class: PS-other) and localizes to the nucleus, specifically associating with the nucleolus (granular component) in Xenopus laevis (PubMed:35607824). It co-localizes with Npm1 in the granular component, indicating involvement in ribosomal subunit maturation, though its material state and transitions remain unspecified (PubMed:35607824).
Functional Summary: The phase separation-related association of Gtpbp4 with the nucleolar granular component is functionally implicated in facilitating the late maturation of 60S ribosomal subunits (PubMed:35607824).
Intrinsic Determinants & Regulations: The phase separation behavior of Gtpbp4 is potentially driven by intrinsic features including predicted intrinsically disordered regions (IDR), a nuclear localization signal (NLS), and a nucleolar localization signal (NoLS) (PubMed:35607824).
Extrinsic Partners & Regulations: Gtpbp4 co-localizes with Npm1 in the granular component of the nucleolus, suggesting functional partnership in ribosomal assembly; however, no additional extrinsic regulators, partners, or chemical modulators were identified (PubMed:35607824).

Overall Phase Separation Overview: AfLEA1 (B1PM75) undergoes self-driven liquid-liquid phase separation (LLPS) both in vitro and in vivo, forming spherical liquid-like condensates primarily in the cytoplasm and nucleus (PubMed:35327618). During desiccation, LLPS occurs in vitro when RNA is present, while in vivo it forms cytoplasmic biomolecular condensates without association with predefined membrane-less organelles. No material state transitions were observed (PubMed:35327618).
Functional Summary: AfLEA1 phase separation promotes desiccation tolerance through 'hydration buffering'—reorganizing water within condensates to protect biomolecules, sequestering RNA/proteins, and increasing cytoplasmic viscosity during dehydration. It independently protects lactate dehydrogenase via molecular shielding, suggesting dual protective mechanisms for extreme stress survival (PubMed:35327618).
Intrinsic Determinants & Regulations: The phase separation of AfLEA1 is intrinsically regulated by eight repeats of the Group 1 motif, which provide multivalency for molecular interactions driving condensate formation (PubMed:35327618).
Extrinsic Partners & Regulations: RNA is essential for AfLEA1 phase separation, significantly lowering the hydration threshold required for LLPS during desiccation in vitro. Without RNA, phase separation occurs only under extreme dehydration conditions and may represent non-physiological salt-induced precipitation (PubMed:35327618).

Overall Phase Separation Overview: TRIM5α undergoes phase separation to form liquid-like cytoplasmic bodies (CBs) in cells, located exclusively in the cytoplasm (PubMed:35930602). These condensates exhibit liquid material properties demonstrated by fluorescence recovery after photobleaching (FRAP), fusion capability, and hexanediol sensitivity (PubMed:35930602).
Functional Summary: TRIM5α condensates sequester overexpressed protein and may function as storage compartments or aggresome precursors, suggesting roles in protein homeostasis management (PubMed:35930602).
Intrinsic Determinants & Regulations: Phase separation is intrinsically regulated by the RING domain, essential for E3 ligase activity, as its impairment via C30S mutation disrupts CB formation (PubMed:35930602).
Extrinsic Partners & Regulations: Ubiquitin acts as an essential extrinsic partner that promotes CB assembly, evidenced by co-localization within condensates and increased CB size/number upon overexpression (PubMed:35930602).

Overall Phase Separation Overview: NS80 (B2BNE2) undergoes self-driven liquid-liquid phase separation to form dynamic, liquid-like viroplasm-like structures (VLSs) in the cytoplasm of transfected cells and authentic viroplasms during Grass carp reovirus infection (PubMed:39194247). These condensates initially exhibit liquid properties—including fusion, fission, rapid fluorescence recovery, and sensitivity to 1,6-hexanediol—but undergo maturation to a less dynamic, hydrogel-like state over time, demonstrating a clear liquid-to-gel transition (PubMed:39194247).
Functional Summary: NS80 phase separation forms viroplasms that serve as viral factories for genome replication (via VP2/RdRp recruitment) and virion assembly (via VP1/VP3/VP4 recruitment) (PubMed:39194247). Pathologically, condensates sequester host antiviral sensors (RLR pathway components), suppressing interferon activation to enable immune evasion (PubMed:39194247). Mutations disrupting LLPS impair viral replication and immune evasion, confirming its critical role in viral pathogenesis (PubMed:39194247).
Intrinsic Determinants & Regulations: The phase separation of NS80 is intrinsically driven by a conserved intercoil region, with residues Y565, H569, C571, N573, and E576 being essential for LLPS (PubMed:39194247). Mutations in these residues (e.g., Y565A/H569A/C571A/N573A/E576A) abolish phase separation and disrupt the recruitment of viral and host factors (PubMed:39194247).
Extrinsic Partners & Regulations: NS80 recruits viral proteins VP2, VP1, VP3, and VP4 as clients into condensates, essential for replication and virion assembly (PubMed:39194247). It co-phase separates with viral dsRNA and sequesters host immune factors (IRF3, IRF7, RIG-I, MDA5, LGP2, MAVS, TRAF3, TBK1) to enable immune evasion (PubMed:39194247). Condensate coalescence is microtubule-dependent, evidenced by nocodazole treatment fragmenting structures into smaller puncta (PubMed:39194247).

Overall Phase Separation Overview: Dnd1 (B2GPX0) exhibits phase separation behavior classified as PS-other, forming discontinuous clusters specifically enriched at the periphery of germ granules in the cytoplasm of zebrafish germ cells. This in vivo behavior is essential for nanos3 mRNA localization to the granule periphery, though its material state and transitions remain unspecified (PubMed:37463577).
Functional Summary: Dnd1 phase separation enables nanos3 mRNA translation at germ granule peripheries, critically preserving germ cell fate. Loss of this function triggers somatic transdifferentiation, highlighting its essential role in zebrafish germline development (PubMed:37463577).
Intrinsic Determinants & Regulations: No intrinsic regulators (domains, PTMs, mutations, or structural features) driving Dnd1 phase separation were identified in the provided study (PubMed:37463577).
Extrinsic Partners & Regulations: Dnd1 interacts with nanos3 mRNA as an extrinsic partner, scaffolding its localization to germ granule peripheries. Experimental evidence from live imaging confirms proximity in clusters, and Dnd1 knockdown disrupts nanos3 mRNA positioning (PubMed:37463577).

Overall Phase Separation Overview: p300 (B2RWS6) undergoes phase separation forming dynamic, liquid-like clusters in the nucleus of mouse embryonic stem cells (mESCs) (PubMed:33651988). These clusters exhibit rapid component exchange, spatial correlation with transcription factor foci (e.g., Sox2, NF-κB p65), and stress-dependent regulation, with potential maturation into solid-like states under specific conditions (PubMed:33651988). The protein associates with transcription factor condensates rather than predefined membrane-less organelles (PubMed:33651988).
Functional Summary: p300 condensates facilitate transactivation of its histone acetyltransferase activity, promoting recruitment of coactivators (e.g., Brd4) to genomic loci, enhancing promoter histone acetylation (H3K27ac), and activating target genes (PubMed:33651988). They critically modulate transcriptional bursting kinetics by increasing burst initiation rate and duration, linking phase separation to dynamic gene regulation (PubMed:33651988).
Intrinsic Determinants & Regulations: Phase separation is intrinsically driven by the intrinsically disordered regions (IDRs), specifically the C-terminal region (CTR) and N-terminal region 1 (NTR1), as validated through optoDroplet assays and in vitro reconstitution (PubMed:33651988). A Q-to-A (Q2A) mutation in the CTR IDR completely abolishes condensation capacity, confirming the critical role of these domains (PubMed:33651988).
Extrinsic Partners & Regulations: Phase separation is modulated by partner proteins including Sox2, which scaffolds co-condensate formation and enhances cluster stability (increasing half-life by ~50%), and CBP, with which p300 co-assembles into shared condensates showing colocalization and similar FRAP dynamics (PubMed:33651988). Cluster formation relies on hydrophobic interactions, as demonstrated by 1,6-hexanediol sensitivity, and is regulated by cytokine stress (e.g., TNF-α) (PubMed:33651988).

Overall Phase Separation Overview: Rhn1 (B6JVN3) does not undergo self-driven phase separation but co-phase separates with the protein Seb1, incorporating into liquid-like condensates that form at specific chromosomal loci (e.g., sme2 locus) during meiosis (PubMed:39520300). These RNA-protein condensates exhibit dynamic properties including fusion and molecular mobility modulation by RNA.
Functional Summary: Rhn1 cooperates with Seb1 in RNA-dependent condensates proposed to mediate homologous chromosome pairing during meiosis through RNA-specific droplet fusion at chromosomal loci like sme2, facilitating recognition of homologous genomic regions (PubMed:39520300).
Intrinsic Determinants & Regulations: No intrinsic domains, motifs, or mutations driving phase separation were identified for Rhn1; studies focused exclusively on full-length constructs without identifying specific phase-separation drivers (PubMed:39520300).
Extrinsic Partners & Regulations: Rhn1 requires Seb1 for incorporation into condensates, as it cannot phase separate alone and only localizes to condensates when Seb1 is present (PubMed:39520300). These condensates are RNA-dependent, forming cooperatively with noncoding RNAs (e.g., sme2 lncRNA) that stabilize the assemblies and modulate their dynamics.

Overall Phase Separation Overview: Pab2 undergoes self-driven liquid-liquid phase separation to form dynamic, liquid-like nuclear condensates in Schizosaccharomyces japonicus (PubMed:40163528). These condensates localize specifically in the nucleus and associate with centromeric heterochromatin domains, forming distinct structures referred to as Pab2 nuclear condensates (PubMed:40163528). The condensates exhibit liquid material properties characterized by fusion capability, rapid dissolution with 1,6-hexanediol treatment, and reformation after removal, with no observed material state transitions reported (PubMed:40163528).
Functional Summary: Pab2 nuclear condensates recruit heterochromatin assembly factors Clr4 (H3K9 methyltransferase) and Mit1 (chromatin remodeler) to centromeres, enabling H3K9me2/me3 deposition and constitutive heterochromatin formation (PubMed:40163528). Disruption of phase separation through RRM or IDR mutations impairs heterochromatin assembly, resulting in elevated centromeric transcripts, defective chromosome segregation (evidenced by thiabendazole sensitivity), and failure in selective mRNA decay of meiotic genes (PubMed:40163528).
Intrinsic Determinants & Regulations: Phase separation of Pab2 is intrinsically driven by its RNA recognition motif (RRM) and intrinsically disordered region (IDR), both essential for condensate formation (PubMed:40163528). Arginine residues within the IDR are critical for efficient phase separation, as demonstrated by the Pab2RA mutation (arginine-to-alanine substitution), which severely impairs condensate formation both in vivo and in vitro (PubMed:40163528). RNA binding capability, mediated primarily by the RRM with partial contribution from the IDR, serves as a fundamental requirement for phase separation (PubMed:40163528).
Extrinsic Partners & Regulations: Pab2 phase separation is scaffolded by centromeric non-coding RNAs, whose binding is essential for condensate formation (PubMed:40163528). Pab2 co-assembles with protein partners Red5, Rmn1, and Ppn1 into nuclear condensates, with these interactions mediated through Pab2's N-terminal region (PubMed:40163528). Disruption of these protein-protein interactions (e.g., via Pab2ΔN mutation) abolishes condensate formation and compromises heterochromatin functionality (PubMed:40163528).

Overall Phase Separation Overview: Tir (B7UM99) undergoes ligand-dependent phase separation to form dynamic, liquid-like nanoclusters (≈200 nm diameter) in the plasma membrane when bound to intimin on supported lipid bilayers (PubMed:37649226). These clusters exhibit fluid properties with subsecond molecular exchange and are spaced ≈500 nm apart. Tyrosine phosphorylation stabilizes clusters and enables downstream signaling, with no observed material state transitions reported (PubMed:37649226).
Functional Summary: Tir nanoclusters serve as signaling platforms that recruit Nck/N-WASP to initiate Arp2/3-mediated actin polymerization, enabling enteropathogenic E. coli (EPEC) pedestal formation and host cell attachment (PubMed:37649226). Disruption of clustering—through tyrosine mutations (Tir-4YF) or intimin depletion—prevents actin assembly, demonstrating the critical role of phase separation in bacterial pathogenesis (PubMed:37649226).
Intrinsic Determinants & Regulations: Phase separation is intrinsically driven by Tir's beta-barrel membrane-anchoring domain, which enables self-association and cluster formation (PubMed:37649226). Tyrosine phosphorylation at residues Y454, Y474, Y483, and Y511 critically stabilizes clusters by doubling dwell times and reducing dissociation rates. Disease-relevant mutations (Tir-4YF: Y454F/Y474F/Y483F/Y511F) disrupt this regulation, reducing cluster size by 22%, increasing dissociation rates, and abolishing signaling (PubMed:37649226).
Extrinsic Partners & Regulations: Phase separation requires the bacterial adhesion protein intimin as an essential scaffold, with reconstitution experiments confirming cluster formation only occurs when intimin is present (PubMed:37649226). Phosphorylated Tir clusters recruit the adaptor protein Nck via SH2-phosphotyrosine interactions, forming co-localized dynamic condensates (83% spatial overlap) that bridge to downstream effectors like N-WASP (PubMed:37649226).

Overall Phase Separation Overview: Npm3 (B7ZP66) undergoes phase separation within the nucleus, specifically associating with the nucleolus granular component (GC), where it co-localizes with Npm1 and functions as a negative regulator of Npm1 (PubMed:35607824).
Functional Summary: The phase separation of Npm3 in the nucleolus granular component regulates Npm1 activity during ribosome export, implicating its role in ribosome biogenesis pathways (PubMed:35607824).
Intrinsic Determinants & Regulations: The phase separation of Npm3 is intrinsically associated with its predicted intrinsically disordered region (IDR) and nuclear localization signal (NLS), as identified through bioinformatic analysis (PubMed:35607824).
Extrinsic Partners & Regulations: Npm3 co-localizes with and is modulated by the protein partner Npm1, which acts as a negative regulator of its phase separation behavior in the nucleolus granular component (PubMed:35607824).

Overall Phase Separation Overview: ParB undergoes self-driven phase separation to form liquid-like, spherical droplets in vitro, as evidenced by in vitro reconstitution experiments. This behavior is stabilized by the nucleotide CTP. The subcellular location and membrane-less organelle associations were not specified in the study (PubMed:34902429).
Functional Summary: No functional implications or disease associations of ParB phase separation were reported in the provided study. The experimental focus was limited to in vitro characterization of condensate formation without physiological or pathological context (PubMed:34902429).
Intrinsic Determinants & Regulations: No specific intrinsic domains, mutations, or protein features driving phase separation were reported for ParB. The full-length protein was studied, but no key regulatory domains or modifications were identified in the provided data (PubMed:34902429).
Extrinsic Partners & Regulations: The nucleotide CTP acts as a key extrinsic regulator, stabilizing ParB condensates by increasing turbidity and lowering the saturation concentration required for droplet formation. No protein partners or additional chemical modulators were reported (PubMed:34902429).

Overall Phase Separation Overview: Hfq undergoes RNA-dependent phase separation in vitro and forms heterogeneous foci in the cytoplasm in vivo (PubMed:37815915). It associates with BR-bodies through heterogeneous colocalization and can form independent foci, though its material state and transitions remain unspecified (PubMed:37815915).
Functional Summary: Hfq phase separation facilitates small RNA (sRNA)-mRNA annealing and mRNA decay within condensates, occurring in association with BR-bodies (PubMed:37815915).
Intrinsic Determinants & Regulations: The C-terminal intrinsically disordered region (IDR) of Hfq promotes phase separation, as deletion of this domain (ΔIDR) reduces but does not abolish condensate formation (PubMed:37815915).
Extrinsic Partners & Regulations: RNA is essential for Hfq phase separation, with condensates dissolving upon RNase A treatment or high-salt conditions (PubMed:37815915). Hfq also partitions into RNase E droplets with a partition coefficient of 7.5 (PubMed:37815915).

Overall Phase Separation Overview: PNPase (B8GWZ0) does not undergo autonomous phase separation but is recruited as a client protein into liquid-like Bacterial Ribonucleoprotein bodies (BR-bodies) within the cytoplasm through specific protein-protein interactions with RNase E (PubMed:37558691).
Functional Summary: Recruitment into BR-bodies enhances PNPase's ribonuclease activity 3.4-fold, accelerates poly(A) degradation rates 5.4× compared to poly(U), and improves substrate selectivity, providing kinetic advantages for mRNA decay during phosphate limitation (PubMed:37558691). This compartmentalization optimizes enzymatic efficiency in nutrient-stress responses.
Intrinsic Determinants & Regulations: Recruitment into condensates is regulated by intrinsic structural features, including specific residues at positions V104/E224/F233 that form a binding interface with RNase E; mutations at these sites (V104A/E224A/F233A) disrupt condensate recruitment (PubMed:37558691). While KH and S1 RNA-binding domains are present, their direct role in phase separation remains untested.
Extrinsic Partners & Regulations: Extrinsic recruitment requires the scaffold protein RNase E, which forms BR-bodies via phase separation (PubMed:37558691). Activity is modulated by poly(A) RNA substrate enrichment (partitioning ratio=1.6) within condensates and dissolved by phosphate ions (>10 mM), which disrupt RNase E condensates and abolish functional enhancement (PubMed:37558691).

Overall Phase Separation Overview: PodJ undergoes self-driven phase separation (LLPS) to form liquid-like biomolecular condensates in vitro and in living cells, primarily localized in the cytoplasm at cell poles where it forms a polarity scaffold-signaling hub (PubMed:36418326). These condensates exhibit liquid properties including fusion and rapid FRAP recovery (~85% recovery in ~15 seconds) but transition to amorphous/solid-like states under low-salt conditions or with aging (PubMed:36418326).
Functional Summary: Phase separation assembles the PodJ-centered signaling hub at new cell poles to recruit client proteins (PleC, CpaE, FliG) for asymmetric cell division (PubMed:36418326). Dysregulation by SpmX-mediated inhibition facilitates hub disassembly during cell identity transitions (swarmer-to-stalked), enabling cell-pole remodeling (PubMed:36418326).
Intrinsic Determinants & Regulations: Phase separation is intrinsically driven by the coiled-coil 4–6 (CC4–6) and intrinsically disordered region (IDR) domains, with CC4–6 containing three tandem repeats (AE#R#A#AI) enabling multivalent interactions (PubMed:36418326). Oligomerization into ~8-mer complexes (≥480 kDa) is critical for self-assembly, while the CC1–3 domain enhances fluidity but promotes aggregation at high concentrations (PubMed:36418326).
Extrinsic Partners & Regulations: PodJ recruits client proteins PleC and CpaE into its condensates, evidenced by co-localization in vitro and in E. coli (PubMed:36418326). The protein SpmX acts as a potent inhibitor, binding to condensate interfaces to suppress fusion, reduce diffusion coefficients (from 0.28 µm²/s to 0.04 µm²/s), promote disassembly, and diminish polar accumulation in vivo (PubMed:36418326).

Overall Phase Separation Overview: CTTNBP2 undergoes self-driven phase separation to form dynamic liquid-like condensates via its C-terminal intrinsically disordered region (IDR), primarily in the cytoplasm where it associates with the postsynaptic density (PubMed:35562389). These condensates exhibit reversible liquid-to-gel transitions upon zinc binding to the N-terminal domain, resulting in reduced mobility and enhanced synaptic retention (PubMed:35562389).
Functional Summary: Phase separation enables synaptic enrichment of CTTNBP2, facilitating dendritic spine formation and maintenance through recruitment of synaptic proteins like SHANK3 (PubMed:35562389). Zinc-induced phase transitions promote synaptic retention and structural stabilization, while ASD-linked mutations disrupt condensate dynamics, reducing spine density and causing autism-like behaviors in mice; these deficits are rescued by zinc supplementation (PubMed:35562389).
Intrinsic Determinants & Regulations: Phase separation is intrinsically driven by the C-terminal IDR (amino acids 200-630), while the N-terminal coiled-coil domain (amino acids 1-271) mediates zinc-induced oligomerization that regulates phase transitions (PubMed:35562389). Autism spectrum disorder (ASD)-linked mutations significantly alter condensate dynamics: D570Y enhances microtubule binding and forms larger condensates, R533* truncation eliminates C-terminal function resulting in smaller condensates without synaptic localization, and M120I disrupts domain interactions causing increased mobility and heightened sensitivity to hexanediol (PubMed:35562389).
Extrinsic Partners & Regulations: CTTNBP2 co-phase separates with the synaptic scaffold protein SHANK3, forming co-condensates that enhance synaptic clustering, as demonstrated through in vitro co-condensation assays and neuronal co-localization (PubMed:35562389). Zinc ions act as critical extrinsic regulators by binding the N-terminal domain to induce reversible liquid-to-gel transitions that immobilize condensates at synapses (PubMed:35562389).

Overall Phase Separation Overview: LL-III (C0HK44) does not undergo autonomous liquid-liquid phase separation but partitions into α-synuclein (α-Syn) droplets in vitro, where it stabilizes the condensates and inhibits fibril maturation (PubMed:34165838).
Functional Summary: Partitioning of LL-III into α-Syn condensates inhibits pathological α-Syn fibril formation, suggesting a therapeutic strategy for Parkinson's disease by modulating aggregation pathways (PubMed:34165838).
Intrinsic Determinants & Regulations: No intrinsic domains or sequence features driving phase separation were identified; the full-length 15-residue peptide was studied without specifying regulatory elements (PubMed:34165838).
Extrinsic Partners & Regulations: LL-III requires α-synuclein (α-Syn) as a scaffold for co-partitioning, with fluorescence microscopy confirming co-localization in droplets. This interaction stabilizes α-Syn condensates without altering its conformation, as demonstrated by CD spectroscopy (PubMed:34165838).

Overall Phase Separation Overview: EGC-1 undergoes partner-dependent phase separation to scaffold E granules, a novel subcompartment of germ granules in Caenorhabditis elegans germ cells (PubMed:38987544). It localizes exclusively to the cytoplasm and forms perinuclear foci through interdependent assembly with ELLI-1, recruiting the EGO module components (EGO-1, DRH-3, EKL-1) to these condensates (PubMed:38987544). The material state remains unspecified, with no observed transitions reported (PubMed:38987544).
Functional Summary: EGC-1 phase separation enables E granule assembly, which is essential for synthesizing 5′-derived E-class 22G RNAs (siRNAs) in Caenorhabditis elegans germ cells (PubMed:38987544). Disruption of condensate formation through EGC-1 loss causes defective siRNA biogenesis, impaired RNA interference (RNAi) response, and significantly reduced fertility due to disordered endogenous siRNA production (PubMed:38987544).
Intrinsic Determinants & Regulations: Phase separation of EGC-1 is intrinsically driven by its intrinsically disordered regions (IDRs) (PubMed:38987544). Its scaffold function is strictly interdependent with ELLI-1, as loss of ELLI-1 prevents EGC-1 foci formation, leading to diffuse cytoplasmic localization (PubMed:38987544).
Extrinsic Partners & Regulations: EGC-1 exclusively co-scaffolds E granules with ELLI-1, exhibiting mutual dependence for condensate formation (PubMed:38987544). It recruits EGO module partners (EGO-1, DRH-3, EKL-1) to E granules, with loss of EGC-1 abolishing their localization (PubMed:38987544). RNA (22G RNAs) production machinery associates with these condensates but does not directly regulate EGC-1 phase separation (PubMed:38987544).

Overall Phase Separation Overview: The Nyamanini virus P protein (C4NFL9) forms nuclear puncta when expressed alone and associates with nuclear speckles, but requires co-expression with the viral N protein (C4NFM0) to co-assemble into viral inclusion bodies (IBs) with condensate and puncta morphologies in the nucleus (PubMed:37047525). These IBs serve as viral replication factories and recruit host nuclear speckles, though the material state (liquid/solid) remains unspecified.
Functional Summary: The co-phase separation of P with N forms viral inclusion bodies that function as replication factories, facilitating Nyamanini virus replication. Association with nuclear speckles suggests roles in host-virus interactions, though phase separation is not directly linked to P's polymerase co-factor activity (PubMed:37047525).
Intrinsic Determinants & Regulations: Phase separation of P is intrinsically regulated by its C-terminal region (residues 356–382), which is essential for recruitment to N condensates, and its N-terminal region (residues 1–85), which contributes to IB formation when co-assembled with N (PubMed:37047525). No mutations, PTMs, or oligomerization effects were reported.
Extrinsic Partners & Regulations: P exclusively co-phase separates with the viral N protein (C4NFM0), which acts as a scaffold for reconstructing viral inclusion bodies. Experimental evidence confirms that N enables IB formation through co-expression and colocalization, a behavior absent when P is expressed alone (PubMed:37047525).

Overall Phase Separation Overview: The N protein (C4NFM0) of Nyamanini virus undergoes phase separation, forming nuclear condensates when expressed alone and co-assembling with the P protein (C4NFL9) to form viral inclusion bodies (IBs) with diverse morphologies (condensates and puncta) in the nucleus (PubMed:37047525). It associates with host nuclear speckles during co-expression with P, but its material state and transitions remain unspecified (PubMed:37047525).
Functional Summary: Phase separation enables formation of viral replication factories (IBs) and association with nuclear speckles, suggesting roles in viral replication and host-pathogen interactions (PubMed:37047525). This process reconstructs IB-like structures morphologically similar to those in infected cells, implicating condensate formation in viral lifecycle coordination (PubMed:37047525).
Intrinsic Determinants & Regulations: No specific intrinsic domains, mutations, or modifications driving phase separation were identified; studies exclusively utilized the full-length N protein without characterizing domain contributions (PubMed:37047525).
Extrinsic Partners & Regulations: Phase separation is extrinsically regulated by the P protein (C4NFL9), which is essential for reconstructing viral inclusion body (IB)-like structures through co-phase separation (PubMed:37047525). Co-expression induces condensate and puncta formation absent in N-alone expression, with P recruitment dependent on its C-terminal residues (PubMed:37047525).

Overall Phase Separation Overview: ELLI-1 undergoes partner-dependent phase separation to form E granules in the cytoplasm of Caenorhabditis elegans germ cells (PubMed:38987544). These membrane-less organelles exhibit developmental regulation, forming in adult germlines but absent in early embryos. ELLI-1 requires mutual dependency with EGC-1 for scaffold integrity and granule assembly, though the specific material state remains uncharacterized (PubMed:38987544).
Functional Summary: ELLI-1 phase separation in E granules coordinates 5′-derived siRNA production critical for RNA interference pathways. Loss of granule assembly disrupts endogenous siRNA profiles, impairs germline RNAi response, and causes severe fertility defects with brood size reductions up to 87.6% at elevated temperatures (PubMed:38987544).
Intrinsic Determinants & Regulations: The phase separation of ELLI-1 is intrinsically regulated by its intrinsically disordered regions (IDRs), which facilitate scaffold assembly within E granules (PubMed:38987544).
Extrinsic Partners & Regulations: ELLI-1 phase separation is extrinsically regulated by the partner protein EGC-1, with whom it exhibits mutual scaffold dependency essential for E granule formation (PubMed:38987544).

Overall Phase Separation Overview: SAFB (D3YXK2) undergoes self-driven phase separation to form liquid-like condensates in the nucleus, specifically associated with pericentromeric heterochromatin foci (PubMed:31677973). Its phase separation is RNA-dependent and dynamically regulates chromatin architecture, exhibiting properties such as fusion/fission events and partial fluorescence recovery (~60-80%) in FRAP assays (PubMed:31677973). These condensates dissolve rapidly upon 1,6-hexanediol treatment, confirming reliance on weak hydrophobic interactions (PubMed:31677973).
Functional Summary: SAFB phase separation stabilizes pericentromeric heterochromatin architecture by maintaining H3K9me3/HP1α foci and 3D genome organization (PubMed:31677973). Depletion of SAFB leads to heterochromatin decondensation, increased chromatin accessibility, and remodeling of topologically associating domain (TAD) boundaries and compartments, directly linking its condensate dynamics to genome integrity (PubMed:31677973).
Intrinsic Determinants & Regulations: Phase separation of SAFB is intrinsically driven by its R/G-rich domain, which mediates RNA binding and is essential for condensate formation (PubMed:31677973). Deletion of this domain (ΔR/G-rich mutation) abolishes phase separation both in vitro and in vivo, confirming its critical role (PubMed:31677973).
Extrinsic Partners & Regulations: SAFB's phase separation is extrinsically regulated by MajSAT RNAs, which act as essential co-factors that promote and enlarge droplet clusters in a concentration-dependent manner (PubMed:31677973). Knockdown of MajSAT RNAs disperses SAFB foci and disrupts heterochromatin stability (PubMed:31677973). SAFB also binds MinSAT and LINE-1 RNAs, though their functional role in phase separation remains untested (PubMed:31677973).

Overall Phase Separation Overview: Sec24A associates with Sec bodies, stress-induced membraneless organelles in the cytoplasm, through redistribution from ER exit sites under salt stress (200mM NaCl) or amino acid starvation conditions (PubMed:36325988). It does not self-assemble but is recruited into these condensates primarily driven by Sec16A, exhibiting liquid-like properties including reversibility and hexanediol sensitivity (PubMed:36325988). No material state transitions were reported.
Functional Summary: Sequestration of Sec24A into Sec bodies depletes ER exit sites of COPII components, inhibiting ER-to-Golgi protein transport during cellular stress (PubMed:36325988). This serves as a pro-survival mechanism; rapid dissolution upon stress relief restores secretory capacity (PubMed:36325988).
Intrinsic Determinants & Regulations: No intrinsic drivers or regulatory features (domains, mutations, PTMs) were identified for Sec24A phase separation in the provided study; experiments focused solely on full-length endogenous protein behavior without domain-specific analysis (PubMed:36325988).
Extrinsic Partners & Regulations: Sec24A recruitment to Sec bodies requires extrinsic partners including Sec16A (primary driver) and Sec16B, with colocalization confirmed experimentally (PubMed:36325988). Stress conditions—high salt or amino acid starvation—trigger redistribution, while stress relief rapidly dissolves condensates (PubMed:36325988).

Overall Phase Separation Overview: GvpU undergoes self-driven phase separation (class: PS-self) both in vitro and in cells, forming liquid-like condensates via an upper critical solution temperature (UCST) mechanism (PubMed:38553608). This concentration-dependent and salt-sensitive phase transition mediates gas vesicle clustering through multivalent interactions (PubMed:38553608). The condensates exhibit liquid-like properties including spherical morphology, fusion capability, and reversible dissolution upon temperature or salt changes, with no observed solid-state transitions (PubMed:38553608).
Functional Summary: GvpU phase separation organizes gas vesicles into honeycomb clusters that minimize cytosolic space occupancy and optimize bacterial buoyancy (PubMed:38553608). This clustering directly enhances bacterial fitness by improving growth recovery in E. coli (PubMed:38553608). Engineered GvpU variants enable programmable clustering for applications in biosensing and biomedical imaging, including MRI contrast enhancement (PubMed:38553608).
Intrinsic Determinants & Regulations: Phase separation is intrinsically driven by GvpU's central region featuring hydrophobic residues (F57, F71) that promote condensation and an acidic residue (E74) that antagonizes it (PubMed:38553608). Predicted pentamer-heptamer oligomeric assemblies enable essential multivalency (PubMed:38553608). Mutations critically modulate behavior: F57S and F71S impair clustering, E74S/E74G enhance clustering, while combined F/E→S/G mutations disrupt phase separation (PubMed:38553608).
Extrinsic Partners & Regulations: GvpU binds the scaffold protein GvpA2_Mega via its α2-C-terminal region, which is essential for gas vesicle clustering (PubMed:38553608). ATP acts as a potent inhibitor, dissolving condensates and reducing cluster size at 12 mM concentration (PubMed:38553608). Phase separation is salt-sensitive, requiring intermediate ionic strength (25 mM NaCl) for optimal droplet formation (PubMed:38553608).

Overall Phase Separation Overview: The N protein (D5LWW7) does not autonomously undergo phase separation in vitro, forming aggregates rather than liquid droplets (PubMed:39642233). It is recruited into liquid-like Mumps virus Inclusion Bodies (IBs) in the cytoplasm, scaffolded by the P protein, where it localizes peripherally and contributes to a cage-like structural organization (PubMed:39642233). No material state transitions were reported.
Functional Summary: Recruitment of N into P condensates is essential for forming functional viral IBs, where N creates a cage-like structure that shelters viral RNA and replication machinery while evading host immune detection (PubMed:39642233). This compartmentalization facilitates efficient viral replication within the liquid organelle environment (PubMed:39642233).
Intrinsic Determinants & Regulations: No intrinsic drivers (domains, mutations, PTMs, or oligomerization features) regulating phase separation were identified for the N protein in the provided study (PubMed:39642233).
Extrinsic Partners & Regulations: The N protein is recruited into condensates exclusively by the P protein (UniProt:P60166), which serves as the scaffold for IBs (PubMed:39642233). Within these condensates, N interacts with host G4-RNAs (e.g., MRPS34 mRNA, BBC3 mRNA) that enhance molecular condensation and with viral genomic RNA, which it encapsidates (PubMed:39642233).

Overall Phase Separation Overview: PATJ (E2QYC9) does not undergo autonomous phase separation but partitions into ZO-1 condensates at epithelial cell-cell contacts, forming the tight junction belt—a continuous supramolecular adhesion complex sealing epithelial tissues (PubMed:39112699). It localizes to the apical interface of this structure as part of the apical polarity complex. While PATJ itself lacks a specified material state, it integrates into liquid-like ZO-1 condensates that exhibit rapid dynamics and fusion, with no observed material state transitions for PATJ (PubMed:39112699).
Functional Summary: PATJ-mediated partitioning into ZO-1 condensates is critical for epithelial barrier integrity, facilitating tight-junction belt formation that regulates transepithelial electrical resistance and macromolecule exclusion (PubMed:39112699). Disruption of PATJ function—particularly through loss of its L27 membrane-binding or PDZ1/PDZ6 interaction domains—causes fragmented junctions, permeability defects, and compromised barrier strength, directly linking its condensate activity to epithelial homeostasis (PubMed:39112699).
Intrinsic Determinants & Regulations: The partitioning of PATJ into condensates is intrinsically regulated by its PDZ1 and PDZ6 domains, which mediate direct interaction with ZO-1 (PubMed:39112699). Additionally, its L27 domain enables apical membrane binding, creating a scaffold that anchors ZO-1 condensates to the cellular interface (PubMed:39112699). No mutations, PTMs, or oligomerization features were identified as regulators.
Extrinsic Partners & Regulations: PATJ strictly requires the extrinsic partner ZO-1 for condensate integration, co-partitioning via PDZ domain interactions (PubMed:39112699). This partnership enables ZO-1 condensate wetting and elongation along the apical membrane, forming functional tight junctions. Loss of PATJ disrupts ZO-1 condensate dynamics and junction continuity, confirming its essential scaffolding role (PubMed:39112699).

Overall Phase Separation Overview: Tet2 (E7F958) does not undergo self-driven phase separation but requires partners for condensate formation, classified as PS-other (PubMed:38427557). It exclusively localizes to the nucleus where it co-phase separates with Sall4 on DNA to form liquid-like transcriptional condensates on the bmp4 promoter (PubMed:38427557). These condensates exhibit multi-step maturation from intermediate droplets to mature liquid condensates (PubMed:38427557).
Functional Summary: Tet2-Sall4-DNA condensates enable targeted 5mC oxidation on the bmp4 promoter, activating BMP signaling essential for pharyngeal cartilage development in zebrafish (PubMed:38427557). Loss of Tet2/3 disrupts this pathway, impairing chondrocyte differentiation due to insufficient BMP signaling, establishing the TET-BMP-Sall4 axis as critical for skeletal development (PubMed:38427557).
Intrinsic Determinants & Regulations: Tet2 lacks intrinsic phase separation drivers and requires extrinsic partners for condensation (PubMed:38427557). Its catalytic domain (CD) participates in condensate formation but is insufficient alone, as catalytic mutants (H1137Y, D1139A) retain phase separation capacity though their functional impact on chondrogenesis is impaired (PubMed:38427557).
Extrinsic Partners & Regulations: Tet2's phase separation is entirely dependent on the scaffold protein Sall4, which enables co-condensation through weak multivalent interactions validated by co-immunoprecipitation and droplet reconstitution assays (PubMed:38427557). DNA probes from the bmp4 promoter further stabilize condensates, with in vitro systems demonstrating ternary complex formation (Sall4-Tet2-DNA) is essential for droplet assembly (PubMed:38427557).

Overall Phase Separation Overview: The Laf1 protein undergoes phase separation as part of a fusion construct (Laf1-NOX) in vitro, forming liquid-like micron-sized condensates and nanoclusters (PubMed:38637545). This behavior is driven by heterotypic interactions rather than self-assembly, classified as PS-other. No specific subcellular locations or membrane-less organelle associations were reported, and no material state transitions were observed in the study.
Functional Summary: Phase separation concentrates the Laf1-NOX fusion enzyme but does not enhance its specific catalytic activity (kcat) compared to homogeneous solutions (PubMed:38637545). The local microenvironment within Laf1 LCD-driven condensates fails to modulate enzymatic reactions, indicating no functional advantage under tested conditions.
Intrinsic Determinants & Regulations: Phase separation is primarily driven by Laf1's N-terminal low-complexity domain (LCD; residues 1-168), which features a net charge of +4 and mediates multivalent electrostatic interactions involving arginine/aromatic residues (PubMed:38637545). The dimeric state of the fused NOX moiety further promotes multivalent interactions, enhancing condensate formation.
Extrinsic Partners & Regulations: Laf1-NOX condensates recruit NADH (partition coefficient Kp=5.8±0.7) and FAD (Kp=3.2±0.7), though less effectively than other LCD fusions (PubMed:38637545). Phase separation is inhibited by NaCl at concentrations >300 mM, which dissolves condensates and nanoclusters as confirmed by microscopy and dynamic light scattering.

Overall Phase Separation Overview: Rubisco (E9PAI6) undergoes heterotypic phase separation exclusively through partner-mediated assembly (class: PS-other), forming biomolecular condensates in the Rubiscondensation organelle (PubMed:39326491). While its material state is not explicitly characterized, it integrates into liquid-like condensates nucleated by PYCO1, with no observed state transitions reported (PubMed:39326491).
Functional Summary: Phase separation sequesters Rubisco into the pyrenoid condensate, enabling efficient CO₂ fixation essential for photosynthesis in Phaeodactylum tricornutum (PubMed:39326491). This heterotypic condensation represents an adaptive mechanism for carbon concentration, with no pathological implications discussed in the available data (PubMed:39326491).
Intrinsic Determinants & Regulations: Phase separation is intrinsically regulated by the KWSPR motif in Rubisco's small subunit, where tryptophan residues act as stickers for heterotypic interactions (PubMed:39326491). However, flanking positively charged residues weaken the interaction network rather than driving condensation (PubMed:39326491).
Extrinsic Partners & Regulations: Rubisco strictly requires the extrinsic partner PYCO1 for phase separation (PubMed:39326491). PYCO1 undergoes homotypic liquid-liquid phase separation to nucleate heterotypic condensates that incorporate Rubisco, forming the functional Rubiscondensate (PubMed:39326491). No ions, chemicals, or additional partners are reported for Rubisco's phase separation in the provided data.

Overall Phase Separation Overview: Ccdc85c does not undergo self-driven phase separation alone but acts as a critical regulator of Par3 phase separation by relieving its auto-inhibited conformation, forming dynamic liquid-like condensates in the cytoplasm of radial glial cells (PubMed:37352102). These condensates specifically localize to apical junctions and exhibit rapid fluorescence recovery after photobleaching (FRAP), confirming their liquid material state, with no observed state transitions reported.
Functional Summary: Ccdc85c-Par3 condensates recruit Numb to regulate Notch signaling, maintaining radial glial cell (RGC) proliferation. Disruption of condensate formation through loss of Ccdc85c or mutagenesis triggers premature RGC differentiation, directly linking phase separation to neurodevelopmental processes (PubMed:37352102).
Intrinsic Determinants & Regulations: The coiled-coil domain (residues 50–160) of Ccdc85c is essential for driving its functional interaction with Par3, as point mutations (D79A, D92A, D152A) within this domain disrupt Par3 binding and abolish condensate formation (PubMed:37352102).
Extrinsic Partners & Regulations: Ccdc85c strictly requires the scaffold protein Par3 for phase separation, forming heterotypic condensates only upon co-expression. Biochemical binding between Ccdc85c and Par3 is necessary for puncta formation, evidenced by disrupted condensates when Par3 carries the R1137A mutation that impairs this interaction (PubMed:37352102).

Overall Phase Separation Overview: NuMA (E9Q7G0) undergoes self-driven phase separation via its C-terminal intrinsically disordered region (IDR) to form dynamic, liquid-like condensates in the nucleus (PubMed:39218187). This autonomous, concentration-dependent process produces droplets exhibiting fusion, rapid fluorescence recovery after photobleaching (FRAP), and sensitivity to 1,6-hexanediol. LGN binding enhances phase separation and enables recruitment of mInsc as a client protein (PubMed:39218187).
Functional Summary: NuMA condensates coordinate asymmetric cell division by forming spindle-orientation complexes with LGN and mInsc, overcoming competitive binding constraints to enable coexistence of these partners (PubMed:39218187). They coacervate with Par3 condensates to integrate polarity and spindle-orientation pathways, essential for assembling the Par3/Par6β/mInsc/LGN/NuMA signalosome (PubMed:39218187).
Intrinsic Determinants & Regulations: Phase separation is intrinsically driven by hydrophobic clusters (I2052/L2053, L2059/L2063/L2064) and charged patches (D1953/E1954/E1955/D1960, R2065/R2066/K2070/K2071, R2081/R2085/R2086) within the C-terminal IDR (aa 1826-2115) (PubMed:39218187). Mutations disrupting these residues (e.g., MUT1-5, del-tail) abolish phase separation in vitro and reduce puncta formation in cells (PubMed:39218187).
Extrinsic Partners & Regulations: LGN significantly enhances NuMA phase separation by lowering its critical concentration (90% LLPS at 1 µM with LGN vs. 20% without) and increasing droplet size (PubMed:39218187). This enables recruitment of mInsc as a ternary client despite competitive binding to LGN, with all three proteins colocalizing in condensates (PubMed:39218187).

Overall Phase Separation Overview: Prox1a (F1QAE1) undergoes phase separation, forming distinct liquid-like puncta specifically in the nucleus of differentiating photoreceptors during zebrafish retinal regeneration. This behavior occurs without requiring partner molecules and is classified as phase separation of undetermined class (PS-other). The puncta exhibit liquid material properties, with no observed state transitions reported (PubMed:37930995).
Functional Summary: Prox1a phase separation is functionally essential for photoreceptor differentiation during retinal regeneration in zebrafish. Disruption of condensates via 1,6-HD treatment significantly reduces Prox1a expression in photoreceptors and impairs regeneration, demonstrating that liquid-liquid phase separation mediates compartmentalization critical for photoreceptor maturation following injury (PubMed:37930995).
