Overall Phase Separation Overview: MLL1 (Q03164) does not undergo autonomous phase separation but partitions into pre-existing biomolecular condensates formed by partner proteins (PubMed:37945831, 38777743, 39922194). It localizes primarily to nuclear condensates, including the chromosome passenger complex (CPC) in the inner centromere (PubMed:37945831), nuclear bodies formed by SET::NUP214 and NUP98 fusions (PubMed:37516964), and SPIN1-formed condensates (PubMed:38777743). These condensates exhibit liquid-like material properties, characterized by dynamic behavior and reversibility (PubMed:38777743, 39922194), with no observed state transitions directly involving MLL1.
Functional Summary: MLL1 condensate partitioning regulates genome stability and drives oncogenesis. Physiological CPC enrichment ensures accurate chromosome segregation (PubMed:37945831). Pathologically, recruitment into fusion protein condensates (SET::NUP214, NUP98-PHF23) or SPIN1 droplets aberrantly activates oncogenes (HOX clusters, MAPK pathway) by concentrating methyltransferase activity at target loci, altering chromatin architecture and promoting leukemogenesis (PubMed:37516964, 38777743, 39922194). This mislocalization enables tumorigenic gene expression programs in hepatocellular carcinoma and leukemia.
Intrinsic Determinants & Regulations: MLL1 lacks intrinsic phase separation drivers but regulates condensate dynamics through its methyltransferase activity. Its SET domain mediates non-canonical methylation of Borealin K143, which modulates CPC phase separation (PubMed:37945831). No intrinsic domains or mutations directly enabling MLL1 self-assembly were identified across studies.
Extrinsic Partners & Regulations: MLL1 partitioning is extrinsically regulated by scaffold proteins forming nuclear condensates. It is recruited to CPC condensates via Borealin methylation (PubMed:37945831), to SET::NUP214/CRM1 nuclear bodies in leukemia cells (PubMed:37516964), to NUP98-fusion condensates through FG-repeat-mediated partitioning (PubMed:37516964, 39922194), and to SPIN1 condensates via IDR-dependent interactions (PubMed:38777743). These scaffolds (CPC, CRM1, NUP98-fusions, SPIN1) spatially concentrate MLL1 to enable targeted histone methylation.

Overall Phase Separation Overview: CSB (Q03468) exhibits phase separation-related behavior classified as PS-other, localizing to nuclear nucleoli – phase-separated condensates – through selective binding to multimolecular G-quadruplexes (mG4s) (PubMed:39555660). It partitions into these condensates without undergoing self-driven phase separation, though material state properties and transitions remain unspecified (PubMed:39555660).
Functional Summary: CSB-mG4 interactions within nucleolar condensates facilitate chromatin remodeling, nucleolar assembly, and transcriptional activation (PubMed:39555660). Dysregulation of this process is linked to Cockayne syndrome pathology through impaired DNA repair mechanisms and aberrant epigenetic rewiring (PubMed:39555660).
Intrinsic Determinants & Regulations: The phase separation-associated behavior of CSB is intrinsically regulated by its Helicase domain (CSB-HD), which is essential for high-affinity binding to mG4 structures and mediates resolvase activity critical for condensate engagement (PubMed:39555660).
Extrinsic Partners & Regulations: CSB recruitment to nucleolar condensates is extrinsically regulated by multimolecular G-quadruplexes (mG4s), which serve as essential nucleic acid scaffolds that stabilize mG4 networks (PubMed:39555660). This interaction is evidenced by electrophoretic mobility shift assays confirming picomolar affinity binding and cellular colocalization studies (PubMed:39555660).

Overall Phase Separation Overview: Secretogranin II (SgII) undergoes self-driven liquid-liquid phase separation (LLPS) dependent on Ca²⁺ at neutral pH, forming liquid-like droplets in vitro and in the cytoplasm (PubMed:35896896). It associates with the intravesicular matrix of Large Dense-Core Vesicles (LDCVs), exhibiting spherical droplet formation, fusion, and full fluorescence recovery after photobleaching without observed material state transitions under tested conditions (PubMed:35896896).
Functional Summary: SgII phase separation scaffolds LDCV biogenesis by recruiting lipids, directly determining vesicle size and quantal neurotransmitter release in adrenal chromaffin cells (PubMed:35896896). Dysregulation may underlie secretory disorders, as evidenced by reduced LDCV diameter and quantal size in knockdown models that are only rescued by phase separation-competent constructs (PubMed:35896896).
Intrinsic Determinants & Regulations: Phase separation is intrinsically regulated by protein length and intrinsically disordered regions (IDRs), with ≥325 residues required for droplet formation (residues 1-479 showing full activity) and the N-terminal signal peptide (1-30) identified as a key region (PubMed:35896896). No mutations, PTMs, or oligomerization effects were reported (PubMed:35896896).
Extrinsic Partners & Regulations: Extrinsic regulation involves Ca²⁺ as essential for droplet formation (minimal threshold: 20 mM without crowding agents), with Mg²⁺ also supporting condensation while monovalent ions fail to induce phase separation (PubMed:35896896). SgIII (UniProt:P47867) inhibits phase separation by dissolving SgII droplets in vitro and reducing vesicle size in cells, and the process demonstrates pH-dependency with droplet formation at pH 7.5 but not at pH 5.5 (PubMed:35896896).

Overall Phase Separation Overview: Gephyrin (Q03555) does not undergo self-driven phase separation alone but requires partners to form dynamic, liquid-like condensates in the cytoplasm, specifically at inhibitory postsynaptic densities (iPSDs) (PubMed:33139925). These condensates exhibit rapid fluorescence recovery and fusion events, maintaining a liquid material state without observed transitions under tested conditions (PubMed:33139925).
Functional Summary: Gephyrin-mediated phase separation clusters glycine and GABA_A receptors at inhibitory synapses to form functional iPSDs, essential for synaptic inhibition (PubMed:33139925). Dysregulation of this process—through mutations, altered phosphorylation, or ionic imbalance—is linked to neurological disorders including autism, epilepsy, and schizophrenia (PubMed:33139925).
Intrinsic Determinants & Regulations: Phase separation is intrinsically regulated by gephyrin's E-domain (residues 318-736), which drives condensate formation, while its C-domain autoinhibits this process (PubMed:33139925). G-domain-mediated trimerization increases valency to promote phase separation, and phosphorylation at residues S268/S270 (or phosphomimetic mutations p.S268E/p.S270E) weakens phase separation by modulating autoinhibition (PubMed:33139925).
Extrinsic Partners & Regulations: Phase separation is extrinsically triggered by multivalent interactions with glycine receptor β subunit (GlyR-β) or GABA_A receptor subunits (notably α3), which act as essential scaffold-client partners (PubMed:33139925). Dynein light chain 1 (DLC1) enhances condensate formation by increasing complex valency, while high NaCl concentrations (≥200 mM) inhibit phase separation by disrupting charge-charge interactions (PubMed:33139925).

Overall Phase Separation Overview: Clu1 (Q03690) undergoes phase separation classified as PS-other, forming hydrogel-state condensates in the cytoplasm of Saccharomyces cerevisiae during hyperosmotic stress (PubMed:31285266). It associates with Osmotic Shock Foci (OSF), which dynamically appear and disappear within seconds in response to osmotic changes, correlating with cell volume fluctuations. The assembled state of Clu1 is a prerequisite for its incorporation into these foci (PubMed:31285266).
Functional Summary: Clu1-containing Osmotic Shock Foci represent a rapid cellular response to hyperosmotic stress, facilitating immediate adaptation through dynamic condensate formation. This process correlates with cell volume changes and involves proteins with assembly-prone properties, though explicit physiological or pathological roles are not elaborated in the provided study (PubMed:31285266).
Intrinsic Determinants & Regulations: Specific intrinsic domains or mutations regulating Clu1 phase separation are not detailed in the provided data. However, the protein's ability to form large assemblies is identified as essential for its participation in Osmotic Shock Foci formation (PubMed:31285266).
Extrinsic Partners & Regulations: No direct extrinsic regulators or partners for Clu1 are specified. However, Osmotic Shock Foci contain diverse proteins including chaperones, metabolic enzymes, P-body components, and amyloidogenic proteins, suggesting potential co-phase separation within a heterogeneous condensate environment (PubMed:31285266).

Overall Phase Separation Overview: Scc2 (Q04002) undergoes phase separation as part of the cohesin holocomplex (with Smc1, Smc3, Scc1, Scc3, and Scc4) on DNA, forming liquid-like condensates in vitro that exhibit fusion, rapid fluorescence recovery after photobleaching, and molecular exchange; this clustering is DNA length-dependent, occurring only on DNA exceeding 3 kilo-base pairs (PubMed:33568486).
Functional Summary: No functional implications of phase separation for Scc2 were reported in the study (PubMed:33568486).
Intrinsic Determinants & Regulations: No specific intrinsic regulators of Scc2 driving phase separation were identified in the study; the phase separation is driven by cohesin holocomplex formation and its ATP-independent interactions with DNA (PubMed:33568486).
Extrinsic Partners & Regulations: The phase separation of Scc2 is regulated by DNA, specifically requiring double-tethered λDNA segments exceeding 3 kilo-base pairs, and occurs through cooperative interactions within the cohesin holocomplex (PubMed:33568486).

Overall Phase Separation Overview: RelA (p65) undergoes self-driven phase separation, forming liquid-like droplets in vitro (PubMed:34764296). It co-phase separates with ZMYND8, with acetylation at K122 enhancing coalescence and droplet fusion (PubMed:34764296).
Functional Summary: RelA guides ZMYND8 condensates to NF-κB-associated latent super-enhancers, enabling suppression of pro-inflammatory genes (e.g., Ccl2, Il1b) (PubMed:34764296). Impairment of this process via the K122R mutation disrupts ZMYND8 translocation and exacerbates inflammation in disease models (PubMed:34764296).
Intrinsic Determinants & Regulations: The phase separation behavior of RelA is intrinsically regulated by post-translational modification, specifically acetylation at K122, which significantly enhances co-phase separation with ZMYND8 (PubMed:34764296). The K122R mutation abolishes this enhancement, impairing coalescence (PubMed:34764296).
Extrinsic Partners & Regulations: RelA co-phase separates with ZMYND8, forming coalescent droplets in vitro and exhibiting LPS-dependent cellular co-localization (PubMed:34764296). This partnership functions as a co-scaffold mechanism, with droplet fusion efficiency modulated by RelA's acetylation state (PubMed:34764296).

Overall Phase Separation Overview: Grh1 undergoes self-driven liquid-liquid phase separation (LLPS) forming liquid-like coacervates in vitro, with enhanced formation under starvation-like low-pH conditions (PubMed:38923199). These condensates exhibit reversible liquid-to-solid transitions into amyloid-like structures over time under prolonged starvation, as evidenced by ThT fluorescence and autofluorescence (PubMed:38923199). While specific subcellular locations aren't explicitly stated, the condensates are functionally associated with the Compartment for Unconventional Protein Secretion (CUPS) (PubMed:38923199).
Functional Summary: Grh1 phase separation facilitates cellular adaptation by recruiting UPS cargo (e.g., ACBP) into condensates for unconventional secretion via CUPS during stress (PubMed:38923199). While LLPS protects against fibrillation under normal conditions, prolonged starvation triggers pathological liquid-to-solid transitions that accelerate amyloid formation and may underpin CUPS irreversibility (PubMed:38923199). These state transitions create ThT-positive amyloid signatures and are functionally linked to packaging efficiency for unconventional protein secretion (PubMed:38923199).
Intrinsic Determinants & Regulations: Phase separation of Grh1 is intrinsically driven by multivalent interactions within its full-length structure (PubMed:38923199). The disordered SPR domain serves as a critical regulator that prevents amyloid formation under normal conditions and crowded environments, acting as a fibrillation suppressor (PubMed:38923199). N-terminal acetylation by the NatC complex shows no significant impact on either LLPS or aggregation behavior (PubMed:38923199).
Extrinsic Partners & Regulations: Grh1 condensate behavior is modulated by multiple extrinsic factors: low pH promotes LLPS initiation and cargo recruitment (PubMed:38923199); heparin accelerates amyloidogenesis by reducing the lag phase in fibrillation kinetics (PubMed:38923199); and ions (Mg²⁺, NH₄⁺) significantly modulate aggregation kinetics (PubMed:38923199). These condensates selectively recruit client proteins like ACBP under starvation conditions, with recruitment efficiency increasing alongside condensate aging (PubMed:38923199). Crowding agents (PEG) suppress fibrillation at neutral pH while lipid membranes show no protective effect against aggregation (PubMed:38923199).

Overall Phase Separation Overview: The Phosphoprotein (Q04671) undergoes self-driven phase separation to form liquid-like cytoplasmic condensates, including viral replication factories (PubMed:37116470) and viral inclusion bodies (PubMed:39194235). These condensates exhibit rapid internal rearrangement and fusion kinetics consistent with liquid properties, with no material state transitions observed under tested conditions (PubMed:37116470).
Functional Summary: Q04671 condensates form viral replication factories that concentrate viral RNA, N, and L components while shielding them from host immune defenses like JAK1/STAT2 signaling (PubMed:37116470). By recruiting WDR5, these condensates suppress PKR-mediated integrated stress response, preventing translational shutdown and enhancing viral replication (PubMed:39194235). Stress-induced phosphorylation further stabilizes the replication complex to upregulate viral transcription (PubMed:37116470).
Intrinsic Determinants & Regulations: Phase separation of Q04671 is intrinsically driven by its intrinsically disordered regions (IDRs) and oligomerization domain (P-OD) (PubMed:37116470). Phosphorylation at residues S292, S294, T298, and S301 within the IDR enhances binding to the viral polymerase (L) and stabilizes the replication complex under cellular stress (PubMed:37116470).
Extrinsic Partners & Regulations: Q04671 recruits viral genomic RNA (modulating condensate properties) and viral components including nucleocapsid protein (N) and polymerase (L) into its condensates (PubMed:37116470). It also scaffolds recruitment of host protein WDR5 to viral inclusion bodies via direct interaction, with the WDR5 WBM site residue L240 being critical for this localization (PubMed:39194235).

Overall Phase Separation Overview: NAP-22 (BASP1) undergoes concentration-dependent oligomerization in vitro, forming higher-order annular oligomers and filaments that participate in liquid-liquid phase separation (LLPS) on membrane rafts (PubMed:32750402). This behavior is regulated by ions, pH, lipids, and fatty acids, with observed structures exhibiting solid-like material properties and no reported liquid-state dynamics or phase transitions (PubMed:32750402).
Functional Summary: NAP-22 LLPS-driven oligomerization is proposed to regulate membrane dynamics in presynaptic rafts, potentially organizing synaptic components through phase separation mechanisms (PubMed:32750402). Pathological implications were not explored, though the solid-like oligomeric structures suggest possible aggregation relevance in neurological contexts (PubMed:32750402).
Intrinsic Determinants & Regulations: The oligomerization and LLPS of NAP-22 are intrinsically driven by its intrinsically disordered nature and self-association properties, regulated by ionic strength thresholds (>20 mM NaCl or >1 mM MgCl₂) and pH sensitivity (optimal at pH 7.5, reduced at pH 6.0) (PubMed:32750402). While myristoylation is present, its direct role in phase separation remains untested (PubMed:32750402).
Extrinsic Partners & Regulations: Extrinsic regulators include fatty acids (DHA, AA, EPA) and acidic phospholipids (PS, PG, CL) that promote large oligomer formation, while lysophosphatidylserine reduces oligomerization (PubMed:32750402). Ions (Na⁺, Mg²⁺) are essential for oligomerization, and Ca²⁺/calmodulin inhibits the process by forming a 1:1 complex with NAP-22 (PubMed:32750402).

Overall Phase Separation Overview: The L protein (Q05318) of Zaire ebolavirus undergoes phase separation within cytoplasmic viral factories, exhibiting both liquid and solid material states without observed transitions (PubMed:37443171). It clusters into foci with spatial organization linked to replication activity, classified as PS-other behavior where it associates with viral factories but requires partners for condensate formation (PubMed:37443171).
Functional Summary: Phase-separated L protein foci serve as active sites for viral RNA synthesis within viral factories, with their spatial arrangement directly facilitating genome encapsidation during Ebola virus replication (PubMed:37443171). This condensate-mediated organization is critical for coordinating viral RNA synthesis and nucleocapsid assembly processes (PubMed:37443171).
Intrinsic Determinants & Regulations: No intrinsic regulators (domains, PTMs, mutations, or specific protein regions) driving L protein phase separation were identified in the study (PubMed:37443171). Full-length constructs including FLAG-L and L-sEX were examined but yielded no domain-specific drivers (PubMed:37443171).
Extrinsic Partners & Regulations: L protein recruitment to viral factories is strictly dependent on the extrinsic partner VP35 (Q05127), with co-localization confirming their essential interaction within condensates (PubMed:37443171). This partnership facilitates L's spatial organization in ternary condensates and modulates VP35 mobility through direct binding (PubMed:37443171).

Overall Phase Separation Overview: VP24 (Q05322) is recruited to droplet-like viral factories in the cytoplasm but does not undergo autonomous phase separation (PubMed:37443171). It exclusively associates with replication-active viral factories and drives morphological transitions in partner condensates, transforming VP35 droplets into network-like structures (PubMed:37443171). Material properties remain unspecified, with no observed state transitions reported.
Functional Summary: VP24 is essential for nucleocapsid assembly and serves as a marker of functional viral replication compartments, being exclusively recruited to replication-active droplet-like viral factories while excluded from inactive network-like factories (PubMed:37443171). Its partnership with VP35 alters condensate morphology to facilitate spatial coordination of viral processes (PubMed:37443171).
Intrinsic Determinants & Regulations: No intrinsic molecular features (domains, mutations, PTMs, or oligomerization states) driving or regulating VP24's phase separation behavior were specified in the study (PubMed:37443171).
Extrinsic Partners & Regulations: VP24 acts as an extrinsic modulator of VP35 condensates, increasing interaction valence to transform liquid droplet morphology into network-like structures through direct partnership (PubMed:37443171).

Overall Phase Separation Overview: Ent2 requires its prion-like domain (PLD) for partitioning into endocytic condensates in the cytoplasm of Saccharomyces cerevisiae, where it co-assembles with partner proteins into viscoelastic hydrogel structures (PubMed:34887356). These condensates exhibit reversible thermoresponsive behavior and can be dissolved by 1,6-hexanediol, indicating regulation through weak hydrophobic interactions (PubMed:34887356).
Functional Summary: Ent2 contributes to the organization of endocytic condensates that facilitate actin-independent membrane invagination and vesicle formation in Saccharomyces cerevisiae (PubMed:34887356). While its prion-like domain is essential for condensate localization, Ent2 is not required for endocytosis itself, suggesting specialized roles in regulating endocytic machinery assembly (PubMed:34887356).
Intrinsic Determinants & Regulations: The phase separation of Ent2 is intrinsically regulated by its prion-like domain (residues 255-615), which features a glutamine-to-asparagine ratio of approximately 4:1 (PubMed:34887356). Deletion of this domain abolishes condensate localization, demonstrating its essential role in partitioning behavior (PubMed:34887356).
Extrinsic Partners & Regulations: Ent2 co-assembles with partner proteins including Sla1, Sla2, Ent1, Yap1801, and Yap1802 into shared endocytic condensates (PubMed:34887356). Condensate formation is modulated by temperature sensitivity and disrupted by 1,6-hexanediol treatment, indicating regulation through weak hydrophobic interactions (PubMed:34887356).

Overall Phase Separation Overview: Deup1 undergoes self-assembly to form highly stable macromolecular condensates in the cytoplasm, both in vitro and in vivo, as demonstrated by in vivo droplet formation assays (PubMed:33658185). This phase separation behavior is concentration-dependent and facilitated by molecular crowding, with the N-terminal region (residues 469-604) containing multiple coiled-coil domains identified as critical for self-assembly (PubMed:33658185).
Functional Summary: Deup1 phase separation plays a critical role in multiciliogenesis by forming deuterosomes that compartmentalize centriole biogenesis components, thereby facilitating centriole amplification during cellular differentiation (PubMed:33658185). This conserved mechanism in human cells enables spatial organization of key regulators like Plk4 and Cep152 in the cytoplasm (PubMed:33658185).
Intrinsic Determinants & Regulations: The phase separation of Deup1 is intrinsically driven by its N-terminal coiled-coil domains, which mediate self-assembly and confer stability to the condensates, as evidenced by low protein turnover rates (PubMed:33658185).
Extrinsic Partners & Regulations: Deup1 condensates recruit and compartmentalize the centrosomal proteins Cep152 and Plk4 – master regulators of centriole biogenesis – through interactions mediated by its C-terminal region, as demonstrated via optogenetic approaches (PubMed:33658185).

Overall Phase Separation Overview: Kap95 (Q06142) does not undergo self-driven phase separation (class: PS-other) but co-phase separates with partners to form liquid-like condensates in the cytoplasm, specifically within daughter-specific cytosolic condensates during yeast cell division (PubMed:39356635). It associates with the nuclear pore complex and non-canonical daughter-specific condensates (PubMed:39356635). No material state transitions were observed for Kap95 itself.
Functional Summary: Kap95 functions as part of a surveillance system that maintains FG-nucleoporins in assembly-competent liquid-like states for nuclear pore complex biogenesis in daughter cells, preventing pathological aggregation (PubMed:39356635). Concurrently, it enables selective nuclear transport by facilitating receptor-mediated cargo import into phase-separated FG-Nup barriers that mimic nuclear pore functionality (PubMed:31723007).
Intrinsic Determinants & Regulations: No intrinsic features (domains, mutations, PTMs, or other protein-specific attributes) driving or regulating Kap95 phase separation were reported in the provided studies (PubMed:31723007, 39356635).
Extrinsic Partners & Regulations: Kap95's phase separation is extrinsically regulated through partnerships: it co-scaffolds daughter-specific condensates with Nsp1, evidenced by 79% co-localization in foci (PubMed:39356635). It also modulates FG-nucleoporin phase behavior, promoting liquid-like states in Nup116 (increasing circularity from ~0.6 to ~0.8 and reducing partition coefficients) and Nup100 while suppressing their aggregation (PubMed:39356635). As a nuclear transport receptor, it enables facilitated import of cargo complexes into FG-Nup49 droplets without co-phase separating (PubMed:31723007).

Overall Phase Separation Overview: Atg17 (Q06410) undergoes heterotypic phase separation as a core scaffold component within the autophagy-initiating complex, requiring partners Atg13, Atg29, and Atg31 for condensate formation in the cytoplasm (PubMed:32025038). It associates with the Pre-autophagosomal structure (PAS), exhibiting liquid-like properties in vivo with rapid fluorescence recovery after photobleaching (FRAP) and dynamic droplet fusion (PubMed:32025038). These condensates can undergo environmentally dependent liquid-to-solid transitions, as observed through high-speed atomic force microscopy on modified surfaces (PubMed:32025038).
Functional Summary: Atg17 serves as the organizational scaffold for PAS assembly, enabling autophagosome biogenesis through phase separation-mediated concentration of autophagy machinery (PubMed:32025038). Pathological disruption occurs via mutations (D247A/P393A) that impair phase separation, leading to failed PAS formation and compromised autophagy (PubMed:32025038). These condensates provide the structural foundation for spatial coordination of autophagic initiation (PubMed:32025038).
Intrinsic Determinants & Regulations: Phase separation of Atg17 is intrinsically driven by its dimeric oligomerization state, which provides essential scaffolding capacity, and through specific binding interfaces (17BR and 17LR) that mediate multivalent interactions with Atg13 (PubMed:32025038). Mutations D247A and P393A within these interaction domains disrupt phase separation by impairing Atg13 binding (PubMed:32025038).
Extrinsic Partners & Regulations: Atg17 forms an obligate ternary complex with Atg29 and Atg31, which are always co-purified and function as integral scaffold components (PubMed:32025038). It exhibits mutual dependence on Atg13 for droplet formation, with co-localization confirming their partnership in condensates (PubMed:32025038). Environmental conditions significantly modulate material properties, as surfaces can trigger liquid-to-solid state transitions (PubMed:32025038).

Overall Phase Separation Overview: Atg13 (Q06628) undergoes partner-dependent phase separation, requiring the Atg17-Atg29-Atg31 complex to form liquid-like condensates in the cytoplasm known as Pre-autophagosomal structures (PAS) (PubMed:32025038). These condensates exhibit rapid fluorescence recovery after photobleaching (FRAP), droplet fusion, and spherical morphology, characteristic of liquid states. A liquid-to-solid transition occurs on charged surfaces in vitro, as observed by high-speed atomic force microscopy (PubMed:32025038).
Functional Summary: Atg13 phase separation scaffolds PAS assembly, enabling autophagosome biogenesis and autophagy initiation (PubMed:32025038). Phosphorylation status at Ser428/Ser429 links nutrient sensing (via TORC1) to autophagy regulation, with dephosphorylation promoting PAS formation during starvation (PubMed:32025038). Impairment of phase separation—through mutations, persistent phosphorylation, or partner deficiencies—disrupts PAS formation and causes autophagic defects (PubMed:32025038).
Intrinsic Determinants & Regulations: Phase separation of Atg13 is intrinsically driven by its Atg17-binding region (17BR) and Atg17-linking region (17LR), which facilitate multivalent interactions with Atg17 (PubMed:32025038). Phosphorylation at Ser428/Ser429 by TORC1 inhibits phase separation, while dephosphorylation promotes it (PubMed:32025038). Disease-associated mutations F375A and F430A impair droplet formation by disrupting critical interactions (PubMed:32025038).
Extrinsic Partners & Regulations: Atg13 requires scaffold partners Atg17, Atg29, and Atg31 for condensate formation, with mutations in these partners (e.g., D247A/P393A in Atg17) abolishing phase separation (PubMed:32025038). It tethers to membranes via Vac8, whose absence causes PAS mislocalization (PubMed:32025038). ATP dissolves condensates through Atg1 kinase-mediated phosphorylation of Atg13, while the phosphatase Ptc2 reverses this effect (PubMed:32025038).

Overall Phase Separation Overview: CKAP4 undergoes self-driven liquid-liquid phase separation (LLPS) specifically in response to solid stress (≥2.0 nN force magnitude and ≥338 kPa elasticity), forming dynamic liquid-like condensates in the cytoplasm both in vitro and in vivo (PubMed:39528501). These condensates exhibit fusion events and partial FRAP recovery (~60-80%), confirming their liquid-like material state, with smaller droplets (<1 µm) showing increased viscosity (PubMed:39528501). No association with predefined membraneless organelles or material state transitions was reported (PubMed:39528501).
Functional Summary: CKAP4 condensates mechanically remodel microtubule networks to induce branching and lamellipodia formation, enhancing cancer cell motility and metastasis in vivo (PubMed:39528501). Solid stress-induced condensates promote distant metastasis (e.g., liver colonization), reversible by losartan (stress-reducing drug) or CKAP4 depletion (PubMed:39528501). Pathologically, this mechanosensing mechanism bridges solid stress in tumor microenvironments to metastatic progression in cancers like bladder carcinoma (BLCA) and lung adenocarcinoma (LUAD) (PubMed:39528501).
Intrinsic Determinants & Regulations: Phase separation of CKAP4 is intrinsically driven by its intrinsically disordered regions (IDRs), with IDR2 serving as the primary driver of condensation while IDR1 supports structural efficiency (PubMed:39528501). Truncation of IDR1 (CKAP4-ΔIDR1) reduced phase separation efficiency, requiring higher crowding agents, whereas deletion of IDR2 (CKAP4-ΔIDR2) abolished phase separation entirely even under optimal conditions (PubMed:39528501). Phosphorylation and palmitoylation mutations showed no effect on phase separation behavior (PubMed:39528501).
Extrinsic Partners & Regulations: CKAP4 phase separation is extrinsically regulated by calcium ions (Ca²⁺) influx through Cav1.2 channels, where calcium depletion abolishes condensation while agonists induce it independently of mechanical stress (PubMed:39528501). The protein Tubulin serves as a structural scaffold, with CKAP4 condensates binding to microtubules to induce branching and curvature remodeling; this adhesion requires intact IDR1 for microtubule binding and IDR2 for phase separation competency (PubMed:39528501).

Overall Phase Separation Overview: TIS11B (Q07352) undergoes phase separation to form mesh-like condensates called TIS granules in the cytoplasm, exhibiting liquid-like material properties despite their irregular morphology as evidenced by rapid fluorescence recovery after photobleaching (FRAP) (PubMed:33650968). These condensates are intrinsically intertwined with the endoplasmic reticulum (ER) and require RNA binding for their characteristic mesh formation (PubMed:33650968).
Functional Summary: TIS11B condensates create the TIGER domain at the ER interface, facilitating membrane protein trafficking and translation regulation (PubMed:33650968). The RNA-dependent mesh architecture enables dynamic protein exchange while maintaining structural integrity, positioning these granules as functional hubs for post-transcriptional regulation (PubMed:33650968).
Intrinsic Determinants & Regulations: The RNA-binding domain (RBD) of TIS11B is the primary intrinsic driver of phase separation and mesh morphology (PubMed:33650968). Mutations in the RBD (e.g., C135H/C173H) disrupt RNA binding and result in sphere-like condensates lacking ER association, while fusion of the RBD to heterologous multivalent domains like FUS-IDR or SUMO-SIM preserves mesh formation capabilities (PubMed:33650968).
Extrinsic Partners & Regulations: TIS11B phase separation is extrinsically regulated by specific target mRNAs (e.g., CD47, CD274, ELAVL1 3'UTRs) that serve as essential scaffolds for mesh formation (PubMed:33650968). These mRNAs with large disordered regions recruit TIS11B to form condensates, and their absence disrupts both the filamentous structure and ER intertwining (PubMed:33650968).

Overall Phase Separation Overview: The protein Ex (Q07436) undergoes phase separation, forming apical puncta under endogenous conditions and inducing micron-scale cytoplasmic condensates upon overexpression, which recruit Hpo and phosphorylated Wts (pWts) (PubMed:36807601). These spherical condensates occur exclusively in the cytoplasm, with no specified membrane-less organelle associations. The material state remains unspecified, and no material state transitions were reported (PubMed:36807601).
Functional Summary: Ex nucleates active signaling condensates that activate the Hpo signaling pathway, demonstrated by the presence of phosphorylated Wts (pWts) within condensates and their role in growth regulation (PubMed:36807601).
Intrinsic Determinants & Regulations: Phase separation of Ex is intrinsically driven by its long intrinsically disordered region (IDR) and PPXY motifs, which enable condensate formation (PubMed:36807601).
Extrinsic Partners & Regulations: Ex recruits Hpo as a client protein into its cytoplasmic condensates, evidenced by co-localization in Ex-induced condensates (PubMed:36807601).

Overall Phase Separation Overview: Bre1 (Q07457) does not undergo self-driven phase separation but integrates into liquid-like Lge1 condensates as a catalytic shell within the nucleus (PubMed:32214243). This integration enables the formation of core-shell condensates where Bre1 recruits essential partners to facilitate spatially organized biochemical reactions.
Functional Summary: As part of core-shell condensates, Bre1 catalyzes spatially augmented H2B ubiquitination, enabling genome-wide H2BK123ub deposition essential for chromatin regulation (PubMed:32214243). Disruption of condensate integrity through Lge1 deletion or mutation impairs nucleosome ubiquitination and compromises cellular viability (PubMed:32214243).
Intrinsic Determinants & Regulations: The integration of Bre1 into condensates is driven by its ligand-binding domain (LBD, amino acids 308-632), which is necessary and sufficient for shell formation around Lge1 cores (PubMed:32214243). No mutations, post-translational modifications, or oligomerization features were identified as intrinsic regulators.
Extrinsic Partners & Regulations: Bre1's phase separation behavior is extrinsically dependent on the scaffold protein Lge1, whose coiled-coil domain enables core-shell architecture formation (PubMed:32214243). Within these condensates, Bre1 recruits the E2 enzyme Rad6 and nucleosomal substrates, facilitating targeted biochemical activity (PubMed:32214243).

Overall Phase Separation Overview: Sub2 (Q07478) regulates phase separation by preventing aberrant nuclear foci formation in Saccharomyces cerevisiae, as evidenced by 1,6-hexanediol sensitivity indicating phase-separated behavior (PubMed:31435012). Its depletion induces nuclear foci that accumulate mRNA, implicating its role in RNA release from transcription sites (PubMed:31435012).
Functional Summary: Sub2 prevents aberrant RNA accumulation at transcription sites through phase separation regulation, ensuring efficient mRNA export and maintaining transcriptional fidelity (PubMed:31435012).
Intrinsic Determinants & Regulations: No specific domains, mutations, or intrinsic drivers of phase separation were identified; the full-length protein without detectable low-complexity domains is essential for its regulatory function in preventing aberrant phase separation at transcription sites (PubMed:31435012).
Extrinsic Partners & Regulations: No extrinsic partners or regulatory molecules modulating Sub2's phase separation behavior were reported in the provided data (PubMed:31435012).

Overall Phase Separation Overview: EBF1 undergoes self-driven phase separation (class: PS-self) to form liquid-like condensates in vitro and dynamic nuclear foci in vivo, primarily within the nucleus (PubMed:33159853). These reversible, salt-sensitive condensates exhibit rapid FRAP recovery and spherical morphology but do not associate with predefined membraneless organelles. Instead, they colocalize with FUS and Brg1 in nuclear foci (PubMed:33159853).
Functional Summary: EBF1 phase separation enables Brg1 recruitment for chromatin remodeling at CTD-dependent sites, stabilizing chromatin binding and activating B-lineage genes (PubMed:33159853). This process coordinates chromatin accessibility and developmental progression from progenitors to pro-B cells, underpinning B-cell programming (PubMed:33159853).
Intrinsic Determinants & Regulations: The phase separation of EBF1 is intrinsically driven by its C-terminal domain (CTD), which contains a prion-like domain (PLD) enabling liquid-liquid phase separation through weak protein-protein interactions (PubMed:33159853). This domain confers salt-responsive condensate formation and is essential for efficient partitioning into heterotypic condensates (PubMed:33159853).
Extrinsic Partners & Regulations: EBF1 co-phase separates with the RNA-binding protein FUS, which scaffolds EBF1 recruitment into condensates, with the CTD enhancing partitioning efficiency (PubMed:33159853). The chromatin remodeler Brg1 partitions into these condensates as a client protein, and this recruitment is facilitated by EBF1-FUS interactions (PubMed:33159853).

Overall Phase Separation Overview: Golgin160 (Q08378) undergoes phase separation driven by coiled-coil domain interactions, forming large irregular cytoplasmic condensates that encircle the nucleus and are associated with Golgin condensates (PubMed:32668013). These structures exhibit an initial liquid-like state with coalescence capabilities but undergo a time-dependent transition to a solid-like material state with reduced dynamics and protein-dense organization lacking aqueous channels (PubMed:32668013).
Functional Summary: Golgin160 condensates contribute to Golgi matrix formation and exhibit potential roles in Golgi apparatus reassembly during cell cycle progression (PubMed:32668013). The hardening transition observed in these structures may reflect functional maturation in Golgi organization processes.
Intrinsic Determinants & Regulations: Phase separation is intrinsically regulated by the coiled-coil domains, with condensation occurring through inter-domain interactions (PubMed:32668013). No mutations, post-translational modifications, or other intrinsic features were identified as regulators in the available data.
Extrinsic Partners & Regulations: The motor protein Dynein (Q8NCM8) serves as a key extrinsic regulator, mediating condensate movement along microtubules and facilitating coalescence and convergence to the pericentrosomal region (PubMed:32668013).

Overall Phase Separation Overview: Vts1 undergoes self-driven phase separation to form reversible, non-amyloid, gel-like condensates via its intrinsically disordered region in the cytoplasm (PubMed:31757755). These hydrogel-like condensates exhibit minimal fluorescence recovery after photobleaching and can undergo state transitions: reversibility upon crowder removal under normal conditions, but irreversible aggregation under heat stress at 55°C (PubMed:31757755).
Functional Summary: Vts1 condensates function as infectious particles that template the prion state [$SMAUG⁺], which hyperactivates mRNA decay (2.1-fold faster degradation of SRE⁺ targets; p<0.0001), rewires the transcriptome by downregulating carbohydrate metabolism genes, and serves as a heritable epigenetic element enhancing growth under glucose limitation (PubMed:31757755). Under heat stress, irreversible aggregation occurs, compromising this regulatory function, while protein transformation assays confirm transmission of the [$SMAUG⁺] phenotype to 80% of naive cells (p<0.0001 versus controls) (PubMed:31757755).
Intrinsic Determinants & Regulations: Phase separation is intrinsically driven by Vts1's intrinsically disordered region (IDR), which is both necessary and sufficient for self-assembly into condensates and promotes oligomerization (PubMed:31757755). This IDR-mediated assembly enables the formation of gel-like states without amyloid fibril formation, as confirmed by protease sensitivity assays, negative stain EM, and Thioflavin-T staining (PubMed:31757755).
Extrinsic Partners & Regulations: RNA molecules significantly modulate Vts1 phase separation, with both poly(A) RNA and specific SRE⁺ RNA lowering the saturation concentration required for condensate formation (1 µM Vts1 with 10 ng/µL RNA versus >10 µM without RNA) (PubMed:31757755). The condensates retain sequence-specific RNA binding capability, showing >5-fold stronger co-localization with SRE⁺ RNA compared to control RNAs (p<0.0001), and recruit deadenylase machinery components CCR4/POP2 from yeast lysates (PubMed:31757755).

Overall Phase Separation Overview: Nrd1 undergoes phase separation under stress conditions, forming cytoplasmic granules that co-localize with Hsp90 aggregates under arsenite stress (distinct from conventional stress granules) while associating with stress granules under heat stress (PubMed:39040524). These granules exhibit reversible liquid-like properties that transition to an irreversible state under intense or prolonged arsenite exposure (2.0 mM, 180 min) (PubMed:39040524).
Functional Summary: While functional implications specific to Nrd1 were not detailed, its recruitment to Hsp90 granules—which are required for arsenite tolerance and proposed as protective aggregation centers—suggests a role in cellular stress response mechanisms (PubMed:39040524).
Intrinsic Determinants & Regulations: No intrinsic molecular features (domains, mutations, PTMs, etc.) driving Nrd1 phase separation were identified in the study (PubMed:39040524).
Extrinsic Partners & Regulations: Nrd1 phase separation is extrinsically regulated by Hsp90, which serves as a scaffold for recruitment, evidenced by co-localization and reduced granule formation upon Hsp90 inhibition with geldanamycin (PubMed:39040524). Arsenite is essential for inducing granule formation, and ongoing translation is required, as inhibition by cycloheximide reduces granule count by >80% (PubMed:39040524).

Overall Phase Separation Overview: Sad1 undergoes self-driven phase separation to form dynamic liquid-like condensates both in vitro and in vivo, primarily localized in the nucleus at nuclear envelope-associated puncta and spindle pole bodies (PubMed:38773107). These condensates exhibit liquid properties including droplet fusion and rapid fluorescence recovery. H2A-H2B significantly enhances phase separation by increasing droplet size, lowering critical concentration, and improving salt tolerance, though no material state transitions were observed under tested conditions (PubMed:38773107).
Functional Summary: Sad1 phase separation facilitates the recruitment of histone deacetylases (Clr3/Sir2) to the nuclear periphery to maintain heterochromatin identity and silencing (PubMed:38773107). This process is essential for tethering telomeres and mating-type loci to the nuclear envelope, with condensate formation enabling spatial organization of heterochromatin factors at the nuclear envelope (PubMed:38773107).
Intrinsic Determinants & Regulations: The phase separation of Sad1 is intrinsically driven by its N-terminal 80 amino acid region, which functions independently of its histone-binding motif (residues 110-140) (PubMed:38773107). A Sad1-5R mutant (D114R/E117R/F118R/E121R/E122R) retains intrinsic phase separation capability but loses responsiveness to H2A-H2B enhancement due to disrupted histone binding (PubMed:38773107).
Extrinsic Partners & Regulations: H2A-H2B acts as a critical co-phase separation partner that enhances Sad1 condensate formation, increasing droplet size by 300% and enabling phase separation at lower critical concentrations with improved salt tolerance (up to 300 mM NaCl) (PubMed:38773107). Additionally, the heterochromatin factor Clr3 is recruited into Sad1 condensates with significantly increased binding affinity (from 42.9 µM to 10.3 µM) when H2A-H2B is present (PubMed:38773107).

Overall Phase Separation Overview: The protein Fcho2 (Q0JRZ9) does not undergo self-driven phase separation alone but forms solid-like aggregates in vitro. However, it co-assembles with Eps15 to form liquid-like droplets in the cytoplasm. This partner-dependent behavior results in a transition from solid to liquid material states (PubMed:33820972).
Functional Summary: The phase separation of Fcho2 with Eps15 is functionally implicated in endocytosis, where they cooperatively catalyze processes. Their co-assembly into condensates facilitates membrane domain organization and scaffolding activities essential for cellular function (PubMed:33820972).
Intrinsic Determinants & Regulations: Phase separation of Fcho2 is intrinsically regulated by its F-BAR domain, which mediates dimerization, and its μ-homology domain that specifically binds DPF motifs in Eps15. These domains enable cooperative assembly essential for condensate formation (PubMed:33820972).
Extrinsic Partners & Regulations: Fcho2 requires the extrinsic partner Eps15 (P42567) for liquid-like phase separation. Eps15 acts as an essential co-scaffold, driving co-localization in both 3D droplets and 2D membrane domains. This interaction is critical for condensate formation and material state transition (PubMed:33820972).

Protein Name: Transcription factor FER-LIKE IRON DEFICIENCY-INDUCED TRANSCRIPTION FACTOR
Overall Phase Separation Overview: FIT undergoes self-driven, blue light-inducible liquid-liquid phase separation (LLPS) to form reversible, liquid-like nuclear bodies (FIT NBs) in the nucleus (PubMed:38393070). It associates with nuclear speckles and photobodies, forming homodimeric and heterodimeric complexes preferentially within condensates (PubMed:38393070). The mutant FITmSS271AA exhibits impaired phase separation with fewer/smaller NBs and delayed kinetics, indicating the critical role of intrinsic structural features (PubMed:38393070).
Functional Summary: Phase separation concentrates active transcription complexes in nuclear bodies, enhancing iron acquisition gene expression (e.g., FRO2, IRT1) in response to light signals (PubMed:38393070). This process integrates environmental light cues with iron nutrition, where impaired phase separation in the FITmSS271AA mutant directly correlates with reduced iron uptake activity (PubMed:38393070).
Intrinsic Determinants & Regulations: Phase separation is intrinsically driven by the C-terminal intrinsically disordered region (IDR) containing Ser271/272, with phosphorylation at these residues inferred as a key regulatory mechanism (PubMed:38393070). The FITmSS271AA mutation disrupts homodimerization and heterodimerization within condensates, confirming this IDR's essential role in normal phase separation dynamics (PubMed:38393070).
Extrinsic Partners & Regulations: FIT co-phase separates with its essential heterodimerization partner bHLH039, which alone cannot undergo phase separation (PubMed:38393070). It is recruited to pre-existing nuclear speckles by SR45 and partially by SRm102, while recruiting PININ to FIT NBs (PubMed:38393070). Photobody association occurs via recruitment by PIF3 and PIF4, demonstrating light-dependent extrinsic regulation (PubMed:38393070).

Overall Phase Separation Overview: YTHDF2 undergoes liquid-liquid phase separation (LLPS) in the cytoplasm of myoblasts, forming dynamic, liquid-like condensates that co-localize with P-bodies (PubMed:39778834). This phase separation is enhanced by heat shock stress and critically depends on m⁶A-modified RNA, with no observed material state transitions under tested conditions (PubMed:39778834).
Functional Summary: The phase separation of YTHDF2 facilitates degradation of m⁶A-modified mRNAs, specifically TM4SF1 mRNA, within P-bodies, regulating myoblast proliferation and differentiation to control muscle development (PubMed:39778834). Disruption of this pathway via METTL3 knockdown impairs muscle development (PubMed:39778834).
Intrinsic Determinants & Regulations: The phase separation of YTHDF2 is intrinsically driven by its multiple intrinsically disordered regions (IDRs), identified as decisive factors for condensate formation (PubMed:39778834).
Extrinsic Partners & Regulations: YTHDF2 phase separation is extrinsically regulated by m⁶A-modified RNA, which is essential for condensate formation as evidenced by reduced LLPS in METTL3-deficient cells (PubMed:39778834). Additionally, heat shock stress significantly enhances condensate formation (PubMed:39778834).

Overall Phase Separation Overview: Rbp47b (Q0WW84) associates with stress granules in the cytoplasm of Arabidopsis thaliana during heat stress (PubMed:37401663, 25736060). As a core stress granule component, it forms cytoplasmic foci that exhibit partial dynamics in FRAP experiments, with a 60% immobile fraction in wild-type plants, though no explicit material state (e.g., liquid/solid) is defined (PubMed:25736060). No material state transitions have been reported under tested conditions (PubMed:37401663, 25736060).
Functional Summary: Rbp47b functions as a core stress granule component involved in mRNA storage and processing during heat stress in Arabidopsis thaliana (PubMed:25736060). Its TSN1/2-dependent stabilization in granules is crucial for mRNA catabolism and heat tolerance (PubMed:25736060). Furthermore, MC1-mediated regulation of Rbp47b dynamics facilitates the clearance of pathological protein aggregates (e.g., polyQ, TTR), thereby delaying senescence and mitigating proteotoxicity during stress (PubMed:37401663).
Intrinsic Determinants & Regulations: No intrinsic domains, mutations, or features driving Rbp47b phase separation are reported in the provided studies (PubMed:37401663, 25736060).
Extrinsic Partners & Regulations: Rbp47b's phase separation and dynamics are regulated by extrinsic partners. It is stabilized in stress granules by TUDOR-SN proteins TSN1 and TSN2, which reduce its mobility and increase its immobile fraction (PubMed:25736060). Additionally, the metacaspase MC1 modulates Rbp47b dynamics, enhancing its mobility and promoting stress granule disassembly, as evidenced by accelerated FRAP recovery in MC1-deficient plants (PubMed:37401663).

Overall Phase Separation Overview: RING1B (Q0WX00) does not undergo self-driven phase separation but acts as a client protein that partitions into nuclear condensates, specifically those formed by CBX2 in nuclear bodies (PubMed:37756159). No material state or state transitions were reported for RING1B itself.
Functional Summary: The functional implications of RING1B's phase separation behavior were not specified in the study (PubMed:37756159).
Intrinsic Determinants & Regulations: No intrinsic features driving phase separation of RING1B were identified in the study; the full-length protein was examined but no specific domains, mutations, or regulatory elements were reported (PubMed:37756159).
Extrinsic Partners & Regulations: RING1B's phase separation behavior is extrinsically regulated through heterotypic interactions with CBX2, acting as a client protein that induces re-entrant phase transitions in CBX2 condensates – promoting condensation at low concentrations but dissolving droplets at high concentrations (PubMed:37756159).

Overall Phase Separation Overview: The H2A-H2B heterodimer undergoes partner-dependent phase separation (class: PS-other), forming liquid-like droplets in vitro as demonstrated by spherical droplet formation and co-localization experiments. This behavior enhances and occurs jointly with Sad1, though subcellular locations and membrane-less organelle associations are not specified in the available data. The material state is consistently liquid, with no observed state transitions reported (PubMed:38773107).
Functional Summary: The phase separation of H2A-H2B modulates Sad1 condensate properties to facilitate HDAC recruitment, contributing to heterochromatin maintenance. This regulatory role underscores the functional significance of heterodimer-driven condensate formation in epigenetic processes (PubMed:38773107).
Intrinsic Determinants & Regulations: No intrinsic regulators (domains, PTMs, mutations, or specific protein regions) are identified as drivers of phase separation in the provided data. Phase separation is studied using full-length heterodimeric constructs, either as single-chain H2AB fusions or co-expressed subunits, but no specific molecular features are attributed to regulating this behavior (PubMed:38773107).
Extrinsic Partners & Regulations: Phase separation is extrinsically regulated through co-phase separation with Sad1, with which H2A-H2B forms mixed condensates. Experimental evidence confirms H2A-H2B enhances Sad1's phase separation capability, as observed in vitro through co-localization in mixed droplets (PubMed:38773107).

Overall Phase Separation Overview: The Ricin B-like lectin R40C1 (Q10M12) undergoes phase separation classified as PS-other in the cytoplasm of Oryza sativa, associating with septum-like structures (SLS) (PubMed:35630784). It was identified in the distal proteome of dispersion-prepared granules and hypothesized to serve as a cementitious component of SLS, though its material state and transitions remain unspecified (PubMed:35630784).
Functional Summary: Phase separation reinforces SLS integrity through lectin-mediated interactions, enabling stable agglomeration of polyhedral granules into compound starch grains for efficient storage (PubMed:35630784). The lectin acts as a structural 'cement' facilitating granule adhesion via carbohydrate interactions, critical for starch grain formation in mature rice kernels (PubMed:35630784).
Intrinsic Determinants & Regulations: Phase separation is intrinsically driven by the Ricin B-type lectin domain, with studies conducted on the full-length protein (PubMed:35630784). No mutations, PTMs, splicing variants, oligomerization states, or repeat features were identified as regulatory elements.
Extrinsic Partners & Regulations: The lectin co-localizes and interacts with the protein partner BT1 (Q6F380) in SLS, as co-detected in the distal proteome, indicating cooperative roles in phase separation (PubMed:35630784).

Overall Phase Separation Overview: Atg29 undergoes phase separation as an essential scaffold component of the Atg13-Atg17-Atg29-Atg31 complex, forming liquid-like droplets in vitro and in vivo within the cytoplasm, specifically associating with the Pre-autophagosomal structure (PAS) (PubMed:32025038). These condensates exhibit dynamic liquid properties including rapid fluorescence recovery and coalescence, though they can undergo liquid-to-solid transitions under specific environmental conditions such as on charged surfaces (PubMed:32025038).
Functional Summary: The phase-separated Atg13-Atg17-Atg29-Atg31 complex scaffolds assembly of the Pre-autophagosomal structure (PAS), enabling autophagosome biogenesis and initiation of autophagy (PubMed:32025038). Disruption of this process—via mutations in complex components or impaired phase separation—abrogates PAS formation and compromises cellular autophagy, highlighting its critical role in nutrient stress response (PubMed:32025038).
Intrinsic Determinants & Regulations: No specific intrinsic domains, post-translational modifications, or mutations regulating Atg29's phase separation were identified in the provided data; its role is defined through its integration into the ternary Atg17-Atg29-Atg31 complex, where it functions as an essential structural scaffold (PubMed:32025038).
Extrinsic Partners & Regulations: Atg29's phase separation is extrinsically regulated through obligate interactions with partner proteins: it forms a core scaffold complex with Atg13, Atg17, and Atg31, where mutations disrupting these interactions (e.g., in Atg17) impair condensate formation (PubMed:32025038). Atg29 also associates with the client protein Atg1, whose kinase activity triggers ATP-dependent dissolution of the condensates (PubMed:32025038).

Overall Phase Separation Overview: Scc1 (Q12158) undergoes phase separation as part of the cohesin holocomplex (comprising Smc1, Smc3, Scc1, Scc3, and the loader complex Scc2-Scc4) on DNA substrates, forming liquid-like condensates in vitro that exhibit fusion, rapid fluorescence recovery after photobleaching (FRAP), and environmental exchange (PubMed:33568486). This DNA-dependent clustering occurs exclusively on DNA exceeding 3 kilo-base pairs in length, demonstrating biomolecular condensation hallmarks (PubMed:33568486).
Functional Summary: No explicit functional implications of Scc1 phase separation were discussed in the provided study (PubMed:33568486).
Intrinsic Determinants & Regulations: No specific intrinsic domains, mutations, or regulatory features of Scc1 driving phase separation were identified in the provided data; its condensation behavior is fundamentally dependent on incorporation into the cohesin holocomplex (PubMed:33568486).
Extrinsic Partners & Regulations: Scc1 phase separation requires extrinsic partners including cohesin subunits Smc1, Smc3, Scc3, Scc2, and Scc4, with cluster formation driven by ATP-independent interactions between the holocomplex and long DNA molecules (>3 kbp) such as double-tethered λDNA (PubMed:33568486).

Overall Phase Separation Overview: The Smc4 protein undergoes DNA-dependent liquid-liquid phase separation (LLPS) via its intrinsically disordered region (IDR), forming dynamic liquid-like droplets in vitro that exhibit rapid fusion and high mobility. This behavior is strictly scaffolded by DNA substrates and is sensitive to ionic conditions, with droplet formation inhibited by high salt concentrations (PubMed:38985672).
Functional Summary: Smc4 phase separation is proposed to facilitate initial chromatin recruitment of the condensin complex for chromosome condensation during early mitosis. Functional evidence shows that deletion of DNA-binding motifs (N/B) – which disrupts phase separation – causes severe defects in chromosome condensation/segregation, dysregulated condensin turnover on chromatin, and cell death, though direct cellular demonstration of LLPS remains unconfirmed (PubMed:38985672).
Intrinsic Determinants & Regulations: Phase separation is intrinsically driven by the N-terminal IDR (residues 1-153), which contains clusters of charged amino acids and conserved motifs including Arg-Gly, Pro-Thr-Ser, and Ser-Arg repeats that facilitate electrostatic interactions. Deletion of specific DNA-binding motifs (N and B) within the IDR abolishes phase separation capacity and causes functional defects. Phosphorylation by Cdk1/Cdc28 is suggested to regulate DNA affinity, though its direct impact on LLPS remains untested (PubMed:38985672).
Extrinsic Partners & Regulations: DNA acts as an essential extrinsic scaffold, with both double-stranded (dsDNA; FX174 RF I) and single-stranded (ssDNA; FX174 virion) substrates enabling droplet formation at low concentrations (20 μM protein with 30 nM DNA). Phase separation is electrostatically regulated and inhibited by high ionic strength (100 mM NaCl), demonstrating salt-sensitive behavior (PubMed:38985672).

Overall Phase Separation Overview: Mam3 (Q12296) partitions exclusively to the liquid-disordered (Ld) phase of the phase-separated vacuole membrane in stationary-stage Saccharomyces cerevisiae, as observed in vivo (PubMed:36635960). In the log stage, it distributes uniformly on the vacuole membrane without phase partitioning (PubMed:36635960). This behavior classifies as PS-other, indicating phase separation mediated by membrane properties rather than self-assembly.
Functional Summary: Mam3 functions as a reliable marker for the liquid-disordered (Ld) phase in stationary-stage vacuole membranes and outperforms other proteins for immuno-isolation of vacuole membranes in both growth stages (PubMed:36635960). Its phase-specific partitioning enables precise spatial mapping of membrane microdomains.
Intrinsic Determinants & Regulations: No specific domains, mutations, post-translational modifications, or structural features driving Mam3 partitioning were identified (PubMed:36635960). Experiments utilized full-length Mam3 with C-terminal tags (myc-3C-3xFLAG or GFP), but no intrinsic regulatory elements were characterized (PubMed:36635960).
Extrinsic Partners & Regulations: No extrinsic regulatory partners, ions, or chemicals modulating Mam3 partitioning were reported (PubMed:36635960). The vacuole membrane phase separation itself serves as the sole external context for its localization behavior.

Overall Phase Separation Overview: Hsp42 undergoes self-driven phase separation (class: PS-other) to form hydrogel-based condensates in the cytoplasm (PubMed:31285266). It associates with Osmotic Shock Foci during hyperosmotic stress and co-localizes with Stress Granules under severe stress conditions (PubMed:31285266, 26238190). No material state transitions were reported in the provided data.
Functional Summary: Hsp42-containing Osmotic Shock Foci facilitate rapid cellular response to hyperosmosis, organizing chaperones and metabolic enzymes for stress adaptation (PubMed:31285266). Its co-localization with stress granule components suggests a role in mRNA/protein storage during severe stress, though direct functional evidence remains unspecified (PubMed:26238190).
Intrinsic Determinants & Regulations: No specific domains, mutations, or intrinsic features regulating Hsp42 phase separation are detailed in the provided data. However, an assembled state is noted as a prerequisite for its participation in stress-induced foci (PubMed:31285266).
Extrinsic Partners & Regulations: Hsp42 phase separation is extrinsically triggered by hyperosmotic stress, leading to Osmotic Shock Foci formation (PubMed:31285266). Under severe stress (heat shock/glucose depletion), it co-localizes with the stress granule protein Nrp1, indicating cooperative assembly (PubMed:26238190).

Overall Phase Separation Overview: Atg31 undergoes heteromeric phase separation as part of the Atg1 complex scaffold, forming liquid-like condensates specifically localized to cytoplasmic pre-autophagosomal structures (PAS) (PubMed:32025038). It functions as an essential scaffold component within Atg13-Atg17-Atg29-Atg31 droplets, with no observed material state transitions reported (PubMed:32025038).
Functional Summary: The phase-separated Atg31-containing scaffold complex enables formation of the pre-autophagosomal structure (PAS), serving as the organizational center for autophagosome biogenesis and autophagy initiation (PubMed:32025038). Impairment of this phase separation mechanism disrupts PAS formation and compromises autophagy function (PubMed:32025038).
Intrinsic Determinants & Regulations: No intrinsic regulators (domains, PTMs, mutations, or structural features) specifically driving Atg31 phase separation were reported in the provided data (PubMed:32025038).
Extrinsic Partners & Regulations: Atg31 phase separation is extrinsically regulated through essential partnerships with Atg13, Atg17, and Atg29, forming the core scaffold complex required for droplet formation (PubMed:32025038). Mutations disrupting Atg13-Atg17 interactions (e.g., Atg13 F430A/F375A or Atg17 D247A/P393A) impair complex assembly and phase separation (PubMed:32025038).

Overall Phase Separation Overview: Nop56 (Q12460) undergoes phase separation as a component of the C/D snoRNP complex, forming homogeneous, liquid-like condensates in the nucleolus of Saccharomyces cerevisiae (PubMed:33836082). This behavior manifests as LLPS droplets that demix from rDNA-binding proteins upon transcriptional repression, with no observed material state transitions reported (PubMed:33836082).
Functional Summary: Phase separation of Nop56 facilitates rRNA processing within the nucleolus as an essential component of the C/D snoRNP complex, enabling efficient ribonucleoprotein assembly during ribosomal biogenesis (PubMed:33836082).
Intrinsic Determinants & Regulations: The provided study did not specify any intrinsic domains, mutations, or structural features driving Nop56 phase separation; experiments utilized full-length protein constructs without identified regulatory elements (PubMed:33836082).
Extrinsic Partners & Regulations: rRNA serves as a critical scaffold for Nop56 phase separation, promoting cohesive droplet formation during transcriptional repression (PubMed:33836082).

Overall Phase Separation Overview: Ent1 requires partner proteins for phase separation and associates with endocytic condensates in the cytoplasm (PubMed:34887356, 35412456). These condensates exhibit viscoelastic hydrogel properties and undergo reversible, temperature-sensitive phase transitions (PubMed:34887356). Ent1 partitions into these structures through its prion-like domain and is recruited to Ede1 liquid-like condensates at endocytic sites (PubMed:34887356, 35412456).
Functional Summary: Phase separation of Ent1 is essential for organizing endocytic machinery and enabling actin-independent endocytosis, with PLD deletion impairing both condensate localization and endocytic function (PubMed:34887356). In Ede1 condensates, Ent1 recruitment contributes to initiating endocytosis by clustering early components (PubMed:35412456).
Intrinsic Determinants & Regulations: Phase separation of Ent1 is intrinsically regulated by its prion-like domain (PLD, residues 214-455) with a Gln:Asn ratio of approximately 3:1 (PubMed:34887356). Deletion of this domain (ΔPLD) abolishes condensate localization and impairs endocytic function (PubMed:34887356).
Extrinsic Partners & Regulations: Ent1 co-assembles with multiple endocytic proteins including Sla1, Sla2, Ent2, Yap1801, and Yap1802 to form shared condensates (PubMed:34887356). It is also recruited to Ede1 condensates that cluster early endocytic machinery (PubMed:35412456).

Overall Phase Separation Overview: Atg11 undergoes self-driven phase separation to form liquid-like 'initiation hubs' on cargo surfaces in the cytoplasm (PubMed:39774270). It associates with Ede1-dependent endocytic protein deposits (ENDs) at the plasma membrane (PubMed:34334089). These condensates exhibit liquid-like properties, evidenced by rapid molecular exchange in FRAP and reversible dissolution by hexanediol (PubMed:34334089, 39774270).
Functional Summary: Atg11 phase separation forms initiation hubs that recruit autophagy machinery (Atg1, Atg9) and coalesce at vacuolar contact sites to trigger phagophore nucleation for selective autophagy (PubMed:39774270). On ENDs, Atg11 scaffolds phagophore formation, enabling autophagic clearance of aberrant endocytic assemblies—a process strictly dependent on Ede1's phase separation capability (PubMed:34334089, 39774270).
Intrinsic Determinants & Regulations: The phase separation of Atg11 is intrinsically driven by its coiled-coil regions 2-3 (amino acids 454–873), which are essential for condensation (PubMed:39774270).
Extrinsic Partners & Regulations: Atg11 interacts with Atg19, which recruits it to cargo and enables condensation (PubMed:39774270). It also binds Vac8 to anchor condensates to the vacuolar membrane (PubMed:39774270). Additionally, Atg11 acts as a scaffold for phagophore formation on Ede1-dependent endocytic protein deposits (ENDs), with its recruitment dependent on co-immunoprecipitation with Ede1 (PubMed:34334089).

Overall Phase Separation Overview: KIF1A (Q12756) undergoes phase separation classified as PS-other, forming liquid-like condensates in the cytoplasm (PubMed:37724036). This behavior occurs via microtubule-directed transport and local nucleation, recruiting nonfunctionalized 5Fm scaffolds as clients. No membrane-less organelle associations or material state transitions were reported.
Functional Summary: KIF1A-mediated condensates enable asymmetric positioning of RNAs when combined with MCP scaffolds, facilitating targeted cellular localization (PubMed:37724036). No disease associations or pathological transitions were observed.
Intrinsic Determinants & Regulations: Phase separation is driven by the multivalency of the engineered 5Fm scaffold fused to the KIF1A motor domain (residues 1–383), which enables peripheral localization but does not intrinsically drive condensation (PubMed:37724036). No mutations, PTMs, or splicing variants influencing phase separation were identified.
Extrinsic Partners & Regulations: The client protein 5Fm is recruited into preformed KIF1A condensates, with Fm-Fm dimerization essential for integrity, as evidenced by rapid dissolution upon FK506 treatment (PubMed:37724036). No other protein partners, ions, or chemical regulators were reported.

Protein Name: SWI/SNF-related matrix-associated actin-dependent regulator of chromatin subfamily B member 1
Overall Phase Separation Overview: SMARCB1 does not undergo autonomous phase separation but partitions into ARID1A-containing transcriptional condensates in the nucleus (PubMed:39095374). Its association with transcriptional condensates occurs through recruitment by ARID1A, though the material state of these condensates remains unspecified.
Functional Summary: Functional implications of SMARCB1's partitioning behavior were not specified in the provided study (PubMed:39095374).
Intrinsic Determinants & Regulations: No intrinsic drivers (domains, mutations, PTMs, or structural features) enabling autonomous phase separation were identified for SMARCB1 in the studied context; experiments utilized the full-length protein but observed no self-assembly capacity (PubMed:39095374).
Extrinsic Partners & Regulations: SMARCB1 partitioning into condensates is extrinsically regulated by ARID1A, requiring ARID1A's Pfam domain for recruitment. SMARCB1 co-localizes with wild-type ARID1A and PrLD2 variants but remains diffuse when ARID1A lacks its disordered domain (ΔDD), PrLD tyrosine/serine residues (PrLD(Y/S)), or Pfam domain (ΔPfam) (PubMed:39095374).

Overall Phase Separation Overview: BPTF (Q12830) does not undergo self-driven phase separation (class: PS-other) but partitions into liquid-like nuclear condensates formed by the NUP98-NSD1 fusion protein, which are sensitive to 1,6-hexanediol and exhibit rapid dynamics with ~90% fluorescence recovery within 50 seconds in FRAP assays (PubMed:35073946). These condensates are localized exclusively in the nucleus and are classified as nuclear bodies (PubMed:35073946). No material state transitions were reported for BPTF under studied conditions (PubMed:35073946).
Functional Summary: The recruitment of BPTF into NUP98-NSD1 nuclear condensates regulates transcription of stem cell differentiation genes (e.g., HoxA9, Meis1) and is critical for maintaining the transformed phenotype in acute myeloid leukemia, though condensate formation alone is insufficient for leukemogenesis (PubMed:35073946).
Intrinsic Determinants & Regulations: No intrinsic domains, mutations, or features driving the phase separation behavior of BPTF were specified in the study (PubMed:35073946).
Extrinsic Partners & Regulations: BPTF partitions into nuclear condensates formed by the NUP98-NSD1 fusion protein, which are strictly dependent on the phenylalanine-glycine (FG) repeat domains of NUP98 (PubMed:35073946). BPTF co-localizes with NUP98 and NSD1 in these condensates, as confirmed by proximity ligation assays in NUP98-NSD1/FLT3-ITD cells (PubMed:35073946).

Overall Phase Separation Overview: GluN2A (Q12879) does not undergo self-driven phase separation but co-phase separates with Rph3A in liquid-like condensates within the cytoplasm (PubMed:36693856). It is recruited into Rph3A droplets via its C-terminal domain and forms ternary complexes with Rph3A and PSD95 that enhance Rph3A phase separation (PubMed:36693856).
Functional Summary: Rph3A-mediated phase separation stabilizes GluN2A surface clusters, reduces GluN2A mobility, and sustains synaptic function through ternary complex formation with PSD95 (PubMed:36693856).
Intrinsic Determinants & Regulations: The co-phase separation of GluN2A is intrinsically regulated by its C-terminal domain (CTD; residues 1244–1464), which is essential for recruitment into Rph3A condensates (PubMed:36693856).
Extrinsic Partners & Regulations: GluN2A requires Rph3A for co-phase separation, with experimental evidence showing recruitment into Rph3A droplets in vitro and HEK293 cells (PubMed:36693856). Ternary complex formation with PSD95 further enhances Rph3A phase separation and promotes GluN2A clustering (PubMed:36693856).

Overall Phase Separation Overview: ILF3 undergoes self-driven phase separation (class_ PS-self), forming dynamic liquid-like droplets in vitro and in the cytoplasm (PubMed:40011431). Its phase separation is enhanced by ZNF252P RNA, and it critically stabilizes c-Myc mRNA through condensate formation (PubMed:40011431).
Functional Summary: ILF3 phase separation stabilizes c-Myc mRNA via 3'UTR binding, forming a ZNF252P/ILF3/c-Myc feedback loop that promotes tumorigenesis (PubMed:40011431). This process occurs through concentration-dependent enhancement by ZNF252P in cytoplasmic condensates, directly linking phase separation to mRNA regulation and cancer progression (PubMed:40011431).
Intrinsic Determinants & Regulations: Phase separation of ILF3 is intrinsically driven by its intrinsically disordered region (IDR; aa 342-898), as deletion or mutation of this domain abolishes droplet formation (PubMed:40011431). Specifically, glycine-to-threonine mutations within the IDR (ILF3-IDRMUT) impair phase separation capability (PubMed:40011431).
Extrinsic Partners & Regulations: ILF3 phase separation is extrinsically regulated by RNA partners: ZNF252P RNA acts as a scaffold that enhances droplet formation, while c-Myc mRNA (3'UTR) is recruited as a client into condensates (PubMed:40011431). Experimental evidence from RNA pull-down and droplet assays confirms these interactions (PubMed:40011431).

Overall Phase Separation Overview: TRAF2 (Q12933) does not undergo self-driven phase separation but is recruited into biomolecular condensates formed by partner proteins. It associates with Nur77 condensates in both the nucleus and cytoplasm (PubMed:34645818) and with PrPC condensates in the cytoplasm (PubMed:39333690). These host condensates exhibit liquid-like material states, with TRAF2 functioning as a scaffold component within them without undergoing state transitions itself.
Functional Summary: Within Nur77 condensates, TRAF2-mediated ubiquitination enables p62 body formation and mitophagy, mitigating inflammation and mitochondrial dysfunction (PubMed:34645818). In PrPC condensates, TRAF2 recruitment activates NF-κB signaling, promoting IL-8 upregulation and driving hepatocellular carcinoma progression through enhanced proliferation, migration, and metastasis (PubMed:39333690).
Intrinsic Determinants & Regulations: No intrinsic drivers for TRAF2 phase separation were identified in the provided studies, as TRAF2 itself does not undergo phase separation (PubMed:34645818, 39333690).
Extrinsic Partners & Regulations: TRAF2 is recruited to biomolecular condensates formed by partner proteins: It serves as an E3 ligase mediating Nur77 ubiquitination within Nur77-p62 condensates (PubMed:34645818), and forms scaffold ring structures around PrPC condensates where it facilitates K63-linked ubiquitination essential for NF-κB pathway activation (PubMed:39333690).

Overall Phase Separation Overview: DLG1 (SAP97/hDLG) undergoes self-driven phase separation, forming nanoscale condensates in the cytoplasm of cells that follow first-order phase transition kinetics, and micron-scale liquid droplets in vitro (PubMed:35869063). These condensates exhibit liquid-like properties with concentration-dependent formation and differential fluorescence recovery kinetics, primarily localized near cell-cell junctions and postsynaptic densities (PubMed:35869063). No explicit material state transitions (e.g., liquid-to-solid) were reported under tested conditions (PubMed:35869063).
Functional Summary: DLG1 condensates organize nanoscale signaling complexes at plasma membranes, scaffolding transmembrane receptors/channels to regulate synaptic function and cell-cell junction integrity (PubMed:35869063). Activity-dependent modulation occurs via Ca²⁺/Calmodulin sensitivity and isoform compositionality, controlling molecular exchange kinetics and condensate organization during cellular signaling (PubMed:35869063).
Intrinsic Determinants & Regulations: Phase separation is intrinsically driven by the disordered HOOK region, specifically the I2 and I3 splice isoforms within HOOK, along with the C-terminal SH3-HOOK-GUK fragment (PubMed:35869063). The I3 isoform exhibits higher phase separation propensity (lower critical concentration in vitro) and distinct exchange kinetics compared to I2, indicating splicing-dependent regulation (PubMed:35869063).
Extrinsic Partners & Regulations: Calcium ions and Calmodulin critically regulate DLG1 phase separation: Calmodulin co-condenses with DLG1 in a strictly Ca²⁺-dependent manner, with higher affinity for the I3 isoform (PubMed:35869063). Elevated Ca²⁺ increases cluster density, while Calmodulin inhibition (w7) or Ca²⁺ chelation (Bapta) alters nucleation barriers, critical cluster radii, and molecular packing—differentially modulating I2/I3 mobility and recovery kinetics (PubMed:35869063).

Overall Phase Separation Overview: MALL associates with PML nuclear bodies (PML NBs), exhibiting liquid-like behavior in interphase nuclei and transitioning to solid-like condensates during mitosis (PubMed:35399121). Its incorporation into these biomolecular condensates requires PML expression and is conformation-dependent, with localization observed in both nucleus and cytoplasm (PubMed:35399121). The material state undergoes reversible liquid-to-solid transitions synchronized with the cell cycle (PubMed:35399121).
Functional Summary: MALL condensates stabilize PML NB integrity by reducing surface tension, but their dysregulation has pathological consequences (PubMed:35399121). Overexpression disrupts nuclear envelope reassembly during mitosis via mislocalization of emerin, LAP2β, and BAF proteins, leading to aberrant nuclei formation linked to cancer malignancy—a correlation validated in pancreatic cancer prognosis data (PubMed:35399121).
Intrinsic Determinants & Regulations: No specific intrinsic domains, mutations, or modifications driving phase separation were identified (PubMed:35399121). However, phase separation behavior is conformation-dependent and requires the full-length membrane-tetraspanning structure of MALL, as evidenced by studies of intact protein and GFP-fusion constructs (LOOP1-GFP, LOOP2-GFP, LOOP3-GFP) (PubMed:35399121).
Extrinsic Partners & Regulations: MALL absolutely requires the scaffold protein PML for condensate formation, as PML enables nuclear localization and confers a condensate-compatible conformation (PubMed:35399121). This dependence is demonstrated by the absence of MALL condensates in PML-knockout cells and rescue upon PML re-expression (PubMed:35399121). No other regulatory partners, ions, or chemicals were reported.
