Extrinsic Partners & Regulations: HMGA co-phase separates with ADCP1, forming a complex essential for heterochromatin condensation, and this interaction unlocks ADCP1's autoinhibited state (PubMed:39014153). Additionally, HMGA's phase separation is scaffolded by multivalent binding to AT-rich DNA regions, which targets it to chromatin borders and enables heterochromatin compaction (PubMed:39014153).

Overall Phase Separation Overview: Idi (Q46822) does not undergo self-driven phase separation but is enriched in condensates via RIAD-RIDD interaction, requiring partners for assembly (class_=PS-other). It co-assembles with IspA to enhance catalytic activity in vitro, though subcellular locations and material states remain unspecified (PubMed:32343131).
Functional Summary: Condensate co-assembly of Idi with IspA accelerates terpene biosynthesis, increasing farnesyl pyrophosphate (FPP) production by 54% compared to untagged systems. This catalytic enhancement underscores the role of engineered phase separation in metabolic pathway optimization (PubMed:32343131).
Intrinsic Determinants & Regulations: The phase separation enrichment of Idi is intrinsically regulated by an engineered C-terminal RIDD tag, which enables strong recruitment into condensates. No natural domains, mutations, or post-translational modifications are reported as drivers (PubMed:32343131).
Extrinsic Partners & Regulations: Idi recruitment into condensates is extrinsically mediated by scaffolding proteins Shank and Homer, achieving 56-fold fluorescence enrichment. Its co-assembly with enzymatic partner IspA (P22939) in condensates enhances catalytic efficiency, demonstrating partner-dependent functional modulation (PubMed:32343131).

Overall Phase Separation Overview: USH1G (Q495M9) undergoes partner-dependent phase separation, requiring MYO7A and USH1C to form liquid-like condensates in the cytoplasm, associated with receptor clusters (PubMed:31644917). When expressed alone, it localizes predominantly to the nucleus and forms puncta at high expression levels, but does not undergo self-driven phase separation (PubMed:31644917). No material state transitions were reported.
Functional Summary: Phase separation of the MYO7A/USH1C/USH1G complex enables assembly of stereocilia tip-link densities, providing mechanical stability for hearing and balance (PubMed:31644917). Defects in this process are linked to Usher syndrome, though no specific USH1G mutations affecting phase separation were reported (PubMed:31644917).
Intrinsic Determinants & Regulations: Phase separation of USH1G is intrinsically regulated by its binding domains that interact with MYO7A's N-terminal MyTH4-FERM domain and USH1C, enabling multivalent interactions essential for tripartite complex condensation (PubMed:31644917).
Extrinsic Partners & Regulations: USH1G exclusively co-phase separates with extrinsic partners MYO7A and USH1C to form membraneless condensates in cells, as demonstrated by co-localization in puncta (PubMed:31644917). Condensate formation requires both partners, with MYO7A serving as a critical scaffold for complex assembly (PubMed:31644917).

Overall Phase Separation Overview: VPS26B (Q4G0F5) undergoes phase separation behavior classified as PS-other, forming cytoplasmic puncta that co-localize with P-bodies in vivo, as observed in HeLa cells. The primary subcellular location is the cytoplasm, with specific association to P-body membrane-less organelles. Material state and state transitions were not specified in the study (PubMed:38459060).
Functional Summary: VPS26B phase separation is implicated in P-body assembly, with cytoplasmic puncta formation co-localizing with the P-body marker EDC4, suggesting a role in cellular organization through this membrane-less organelle (PubMed:38459060).
Intrinsic Determinants & Regulations: No intrinsic domains, modifications, mutations, or specific protein regions driving phase separation were identified; experiments studied the full-length endogenous protein without characterizing specific drivers (PubMed:38459060).
Extrinsic Partners & Regulations: No extrinsic regulators, partner proteins, or environmental modulators of VPS26B phase separation were reported in the study (PubMed:38459060).

Overall Phase Separation Overview: Abl2 undergoes self-driven liquid-liquid phase separation both in vitro and in vivo within the cytoplasm and nucleus, forming dynamic, liquid-like condensates (PubMed:37858340). This behavior is concentration-dependent, salt-sensitive, and enhanced by molecular crowding agents like dextran. No specific membrane-less organelle associations or material state transitions were reported (PubMed:37858340).
Functional Summary: Abl2:tubulin co-condensates promote microtubule nucleation by reducing the critical concentration 11-fold (from 5.5 µM to 0.5 µM) and facilitate microtubule lattice repair at damage sites (PubMed:37858340). In cells, Abl2 phase separation accelerates microtubule reassembly following nocodazole treatment, establishing its role in microtubule rescue and cellular morphogenesis (PubMed:37858340).
Intrinsic Determinants & Regulations: Phase separation is intrinsically driven by Abl2's C-terminal half (residues 557-1182), an intrinsically disordered region containing tubulin-binding Site I (aa 688-924) and Site II (aa 1024-1090) (PubMed:37858340). The C-terminal half alone is sufficient for phase separation, while the N-terminal half lacks this capability. Deletion of Site I (Abl2Δ688-790 mutant) maintains phase separation but abolishes tubulin recruitment (PubMed:37858340).
Extrinsic Partners & Regulations: Abl2 co-condenses with tubulin dimers, which partition into its condensates with high efficiency (partition coefficient >3) (PubMed:37858340). Phase separation is attenuated by increased KCl concentrations but enhanced by molecular crowding (dextran) (PubMed:37858340). No other extrinsic partners or chemical regulators were identified.

Overall Phase Separation Overview: AMOT undergoes self-driven phase separation to form liquid-like condensates in the cytoplasm in response to cell-cell contact or osmotic stress (PubMed:36318920). These condensates, termed 'Hippo-activating condensates', enrich core Hippo pathway components including MST/SAV, LATS/MOB, and YAP, exhibiting liquid material properties with fusion and rapid FRAP recovery without reported state transitions (PubMed:36318920).
Functional Summary: AMOT condensates facilitate Hippo pathway activation by enriching core components (MST/SAV, LATS/MOB, YAP) during cellular stress, enabling phosphorylation cascades that regulate YAP activity (PubMed:36318920). Phase separation deficiency (e.g., via ΔCC mutation) impairs YAP phosphorylation and target gene repression, demonstrating its critical role in Hippo-mediated signaling and cellular homeostasis (PubMed:36318920).
Intrinsic Determinants & Regulations: The phase separation of AMOT is intrinsically driven by its coiled-coil domains (CC, residues 430-751), which are essential for droplet formation (PubMed:36318920). Conversely, the actin-binding domain (AB, residues 157-191) suppresses phase separation by sequestering AMOT to F-actin; mutations disrupting this domain (ΔAB or S175E) enable phase separation even in non-permissive conditions (PubMed:36318920).
Extrinsic Partners & Regulations: AMOT phase separation is extrinsically regulated by F-actin binding, which suppresses condensate formation in sparse cultures but is relieved during cell-cell contact (PubMed:36318920). AMOT co-phase separates with KIBRA (Q8IX03) via PY-WW domain interactions to form bi-scaffold condensates, and further coalesces with SLMAP (Q14BN4) into tri-scaffold condensates, where AMOT enhances KIBRA-SLMAP interactions (PubMed:36318920).

Overall Phase Separation Overview: The protein zRbm14a (UniProt: Q503D7) undergoes phase separation, forming cytoplasmic and nuclear puncta in zebrafish embryonic cells that associate with unspecified RNP compartments (PubMed:31636951). This behavior is classified as PS-other, with the protein localizing to both cytoplasm and nucleus. The material state is not explicitly specified, and no material state transitions were reported.
Functional Summary: zRbm14a phase separation is essential for dorsoventral patterning in zebrafish embryos, as depletion causes dorsalization phenotypes through attenuation of BMP signaling (PubMed:31636951). This function is redundant with paralog Rbm14b, and overexpression of BMP-related proteins rescues developmental defects caused by zRbm14a depletion.
Intrinsic Determinants & Regulations: Phase separation of zRbm14a is intrinsically driven by its Intrinsically Disordered Region (IDR), which demixes into liquid droplets in vitro despite poor sequence conservation with mammalian homologs (PubMed:31636951). No specific domains, mutations, or post-translational modifications regulating this behavior were identified in the provided data.
Extrinsic Partners & Regulations: No extrinsic regulators, molecular partners, or environmental conditions modulating zRbm14a phase separation were reported in the provided context (PubMed:31636951).

Overall Phase Separation Overview: SRRM1 undergoes phase separation, forming nuclear puncta at active genes in vivo within the nucleus, and is associated with nuclear speckles (PubMed:31391587).
Functional Summary: The functional implications of SRRM1 phase separation were not explicitly detailed, but its formation of nuclear puncta at active genes and colocalization with Nanog foci in mouse embryonic stem cells suggests a potential role in gene regulation (PubMed:31391587).
Intrinsic Determinants & Regulations: No intrinsic regulators of phase separation were specified for SRRM1 in the provided study (PubMed:31391587).
Extrinsic Partners & Regulations: No extrinsic regulators or partners modulating SRRM1 phase separation were reported in the provided study (PubMed:31391587).

Overall Phase Separation Overview: CRTC2 undergoes self-driven, cAMP-induced liquid-liquid phase separation (LLPS) both in vitro and in vivo, forming dynamic liquid-like condensates exclusively in the nucleus (PubMed:35037420). These condensates associate with transcriptional condensates and exhibit properties including rapid FRAP recovery, droplet fusion, and dissolution by 1,6-hexanediol or high salt concentrations. No material state transitions were reported (PubMed:35037420).
Functional Summary: CRTC2 nuclear condensates recruit and concentrate P-TEFb, facilitating its extraction from the inhibitory 7SK snRNP complex to activate transcription elongation of cystogenesis-associated genes (PubMed:35037420). This mechanism is pathologically elevated in autosomal dominant polycystic kidney disease (ADPKD), where aberrant condensates drive cyst formation in renal epithelial cells. Genetic depletion of CRTC2 suppresses cyst growth, confirming its causal role in disease pathogenesis (PubMed:35037420).
Intrinsic Determinants & Regulations: Phase separation is intrinsically driven by the C-terminal intrinsically disordered region (IDR), where arginine residues play a critical role (PubMed:35037420). Arginine-to-alanine (R>A) substitutions within this IDR completely abolish phase separation capacity, as demonstrated through mutagenesis studies and optogenetic assays (PubMed:35037420).
Extrinsic Partners & Regulations: CRTC2 phase separation is induced by cAMP signaling and modulated by external factors (PubMed:35037420). It co-assembles with the P-TEFb protein complex into condensates, which is essential for functional activation and confirmed through co-localization and co-immunoprecipitation (PubMed:35037420). Formation is inhibited by high salt concentrations and 1,6-hexanediol, indicating sensitivity to ionic conditions and aliphatic alcohols (PubMed:35037420). HEXIM1 indirectly influences CRTC2 condensates by dissolving P-TEFb droplets, which CRTC2 can counteract to restore phase separation (PubMed:35037420).

Overall Phase Separation Overview: GLE1 associates with stress granules as a recruited client component in the cytoplasm, co-localizing within dynamic, liquid-like OptoGranules scaffolded by G3BP1. These granules exhibit fusion behavior and rapid fluorescence recovery after photobleaching (FRAP), characteristic of liquid condensates (PubMed:30893049).
Functional Summary: As a component of stress granules, GLE1 participates in cellular stress response mechanisms. Chronic persistence of G3BP1-scaffolded granules leads to their evolution into pathological, cytotoxic inclusions containing ubiquitinated proteins and phosphorylated TDP-43, recapitulating features of amyotrophic lateral sclerosis (ALS) and frontotemporal dementia (FTD) pathology (PubMed:30893049).
Intrinsic Determinants & Regulations: No intrinsic drivers or regulators of GLE1 phase separation were identified in the provided study, as no specific domains, mutations, or modifications were investigated for their role in its condensate behavior (PubMed:30893049).
Extrinsic Partners & Regulations: GLE1 recruitment into condensates is extrinsically regulated by the scaffold protein G3BP1, which drives stress granule assembly. GLE1 co-partitions with multiple stress granule components including PABP, TDP-43, TIA1, TIAR, eIF4G, eIF3η, ataxin 2, FUS, and polyadenylated mRNAs within the G3BP1-formed OptoGranules (PubMed:30893049).

Overall Phase Separation Overview: USP39 undergoes self-driven liquid-liquid phase separation to form dynamic, liquid-like condensates exclusively in the nucleolus, specifically within all subcompartments (fibrillar center, dense fibrillar component, granular component) (PubMed:39885503). This behavior is driven by its N-terminal intrinsically disordered region (IDR; residues 1-103) and occurs both in vitro under macromolecular crowding/salt conditions and in vivo within the nucleus (PubMed:39885503). The condensates exhibit rapid fluorescence recovery after photobleaching, fusion events, spherical morphology, and sensitivity to 1,6-hexanediol, confirming their liquid material state; no material state transitions were observed under tested conditions (PubMed:39885503).
Functional Summary: USP39 phase separation in the nucleolus promotes lung adenocarcinoma progression by upregulating the oncogenic transcription factor GLI1 (PubMed:39885503). Knockdown of USP39 suppresses GLI1 expression, inhibits cancer cell growth/migration in vitro, and reduces tumor xenograft growth in vivo; these effects are rescued by exogenous USP39 complementation only when both the N-terminal IDR (for phase separation) and C-terminal domains (for catalytic activity) are intact (PubMed:39885503). This establishes USP39 condensates as functional drivers of tumorigenesis, suggesting therapeutic targeting of its phase separation may suppress lung cancer progression (PubMed:39885503).
Intrinsic Determinants & Regulations: The phase separation of USP39 is intrinsically regulated by its N-terminal intrinsically disordered region (IDR; residues 1-103), which is necessary and sufficient for condensate formation (PubMed:39885503). Deletion of the IDR (in constructs USP39-ΔN and USP39-(184–565)) abolishes phase separation and nucleolar localization, resulting in diffuse cellular distribution, while constructs retaining the IDR (full-length USP39, USP39-N(1-103), USP39-ΔC, USP39-ΔUBP) form condensates (PubMed:39885503). No mutations, post-translational modifications, splicing variants, oligomerization domains, or repeat features were identified as regulators (PubMed:39885503).
Extrinsic Partners & Regulations: USP39 phase separation is modulated by extrinsic physicochemical conditions but no protein partners or co-condensers were reported (PubMed:39885503). In vitro droplet formation requires macromolecular crowding agents (e.g., PEG 4000) and intermediate NaCl concentrations (150–300 mM), with size and frequency increasing at higher protein concentrations (≥3 µM) (PubMed:39885503). Condensate dissolution occurs upon treatment with the aliphatic alcohol 1,6-hexanediol, confirming hypersensitivity to hydrophobic disruptors (PubMed:39885503).

Overall Phase Separation Overview: Nup98 undergoes self-driven phase separation, spontaneously forming solid 'FG particles' in the nucleus as part of the nuclear pore complex. This behavior occurs without requiring sophisticated experimental conditions or auxiliary eukaryotic factors (PubMed:25562883).
Functional Summary: The phase separation of Nup98 FG domains is fundamental to nuclear pore complex structure and function, directly accounting for the permeability properties of the nuclear pore (PubMed:25562883).
Intrinsic Determinants & Regulations: Phase separation is intrinsically driven by the FG domain, which forms in authentic nuclear pore complexes and accounts for their permeability properties. The region spanning residues 1-719 was experimentally confirmed to mediate this behavior (PubMed:25562883).
Extrinsic Partners & Regulations: No extrinsic regulators or partner molecules were reported to modulate Nup98 phase separation in the provided study (PubMed:25562883).

Overall Phase Separation Overview: CrhR (Q55804) undergoes RNA-dependent liquid-liquid phase separation to form dynamic membraneless organelles described as 'aggresomes' and 'crescents' in the cytoplasm of Synechocystis sp., specifically localized between the cytoplasmic and thylakoid membranes (PubMed:36920190). These liquid condensates form in response to diverse abiotic stresses (cold, osmotic, light), transitioning from dispersed cytoplasmic foci under normal conditions to organized crescent structures during stress, and rapidly dissipate upon stress alleviation or hexanediol treatment (PubMed:36920190). No transitions to solid/gel states were reported under studied conditions.
Functional Summary: CrhR phase separation compartmentalizes RNA helicase activity and ribonucleoprotein complexes to facilitate rapid adaptation to abiotic stresses (PubMed:36920190). This process maintains thylakoid membrane integrity and enables photosynthetic apparatus adaptation during environmental challenges, serving as a spatial-temporal regulatory mechanism for stress response (PubMed:36920190).
Intrinsic Determinants & Regulations: Phase separation is intrinsically driven by the C-terminal extension (CTE), particularly a low-complexity domain (LCD) within residues 456-489 enriched in arginine-glycine (RGG) motifs and asparagine/glutamine residues (PubMed:36920190). Dimerization contributes to condensate formation, while truncation of the CTE (CrhR_TR mutant) ablates stress-induced crescent assembly, confirming the domain's essential role (PubMed:36920190).
Extrinsic Partners & Regulations: RNA acts as a critical extrinsic regulator, essential for condensate formation both in vivo and in vitro (PubMed:36920190). RNA binding lowers the saturation concentration for phase separation, promotes droplet formation, increases droplet size, and exhibits specificity for RNA over DNA (PubMed:36920190). Phase separation is sensitive to ionic conditions, being disrupted by high salt concentrations (PubMed:36920190).

Overall Phase Separation Overview: In Trypanosoma brucei, ATXN2 (Q57UZ7) is a cytoplasmic protein that exhibits diffuse localization in its wildtype form but undergoes spontaneous condensation upon deletion of the PAM2 motif, forming cytoplasmic condensates. No material state specification, state transitions, or association with membrane-less organelles were reported (PubMed:37295429).
Functional Summary: No functional implications or disease associations related to ATXN2 phase separation were specified in the provided context (PubMed:37295429).
Intrinsic Determinants & Regulations: The phase separation behavior of ATXN2 is intrinsically regulated by its PAM2 motif, which prevents spontaneous condensation. Deletion of this motif (ΔPAM2 mutant) drives cytoplasmic condensate formation, as demonstrated in GFP-tagged constructs studied in vivo (PubMed:37295429).
Extrinsic Partners & Regulations: No extrinsic regulators, partner proteins, ions, or chemicals modulating ATXN2 phase separation were identified in the provided context (PubMed:37295429).

Overall Phase Separation Overview: Q57VP6 (TbCenA) undergoes self-driven phase separation to form calcium-dependent liquid-like droplets in vitro, as evidenced by turbidity assays and droplet fusion behavior (PubMed:38150475). The material state is consistently liquid, with no observed state transitions reported.
Functional Summary: No functional implications of phase separation for Q57VP6 are reported in the provided context (PubMed:38150475).
Intrinsic Determinants & Regulations: Phase separation of Q57VP6 is intrinsically driven by its predicted N-terminal intrinsically disordered region (IDR), which facilitates liquid droplet formation (PubMed:38150475).
Extrinsic Partners & Regulations: Calcium ions (Ca²⁺) serve as essential extrinsic inducers of Q57VP6 phase separation, with droplet formation occurring exclusively in the presence of Ca²⁺ and dissolution upon EDTA treatment (PubMed:38150475).

Overall Phase Separation Overview: PABPC (Q58A45) does not undergo autonomous phase separation (class: PS-other) but acts as an RNA-dependent chaperone regulating phase separation of partner proteins like ATXN2 (PubMed:37295429). Located in the cytoplasm, it associates with stress granules under arsenite or heat shock stress. Its regulatory role involves modulating condensate wetting and mixing without forming autonomous condensates, and no material state transitions are observed for PABPC itself.
Functional Summary: PABPC's chaperone activity prevents irreversible ATXN2 condensation, enabling adaptive stress granule assembly during cellular stress (PubMed:37295429). Dysregulation—such as loss of PABPC function or RNA-binding capacity—contributes to neurodegeneration via pathological aggregation and sequestration of PABPC in cytotoxic aggregates. This evolutionarily conserved mechanism maintains proteostasis, with RNA-dependent wetting of condensate phases being critical for cellular viability.
Intrinsic Determinants & Regulations: The RNA recognition motif (RRM) domains of PABPC are intrinsically essential for its chaperone function, with RNA binding licensing its holdase activity (PubMed:37295429). Mutations in RRM domains—such as the F-PABPC* variant where aromatic residues are replaced by leucine—abolish this regulatory capability, confirming that specific RNA-binding residues govern PABPC's phase separation modulation.
Extrinsic Partners & Regulations: PABPC interacts with ATXN2 to prevent its aberrant condensation and enable stress granule mixing, with disruption of this interaction (e.g., via ATXN2 ΔPAM2 mutation) leading to pathological aggregation (PubMed:37295429). Cellular mRNA licenses PABPC's holdase activity, as RNA-binding-deficient mutants lose function, while engineered RNA recruitment (e.g., via hnRNPI-PopTag chimera) prevents condensate coalescence. PABPC also bridges immiscible condensate phases, promoting wetting between stress granules and other compartments.

Overall Phase Separation Overview: TDRD1 undergoes phase separation classified as PS-other, forming cytoplasmic droplets in HeLa cells during in vivo experiments (PubMed:39029469). The subcellular location is cytoplasmic, but no specific membrane-less organelles (MLOs) were associated. Material state properties and state transitions were not specified in the study.
Functional Summary: Functional implications of TDRD1 phase separation were not specified in the study; authors solely concluded that zebrafish TDRD1 undergoes liquid-liquid phase separation based on cytoplasmic droplet formation (PubMed:39029469).
Intrinsic Determinants & Regulations: No intrinsic regulators (domains, mutations, PTMs, or structural features) driving phase separation were identified; the full-length protein construct was studied without further characterization of specific regions (PubMed:39029469).
Extrinsic Partners & Regulations: No extrinsic regulators, partners, or co-phase separating molecules were reported in the study (PubMed:39029469).

Overall Phase Separation Overview: Brg1 (Q59LY1) undergoes phase separation to form liquid-like nuclear condensates in mammalian cells, driven by its intrinsic domains (PubMed:38091321). These condensates are essential for biofilm formation and filamentation in Candida albicans, with mutations disrupting phase separation impairing cellular functions in vitro and in vivo (PubMed:38091321).
Functional Summary: Brg1 phase separation is essential for biofilm formation, filamentation, and murine gastrointestinal colonization in Candida albicans (PubMed:38091321). It regulates hyphal-specific genes (e.g., ALS3), with YF-to-S mutations abolishing condensate formation, reducing biofilm/hyphal gene expression, and blocking filamentation during host colonization (PubMed:38091321).
Intrinsic Determinants & Regulations: Phase separation is intrinsically regulated by Brg1's N-terminal and C-terminal prion-like domains (PrLDs), with deletion of both domains (ΔNC) abolishing function (PubMed:38091321). PolyQ tracts further modulate this behavior, as their deletion reduces filamentation while YF-to-S mutations in PrLDs eliminate phase separation and impair biofilm formation (PubMed:38091321).
Extrinsic Partners & Regulations: No extrinsic regulators or interacting partners were reported for Brg1 phase separation in the study (PubMed:38091321).

Protein Name: Transcriptional regulator of filamentous growth FLO8
Overall Phase Separation Overview: Flo8 undergoes self-driven phase separation, forming liquid-like condensates in vitro and in the nucleus of mammalian cells (PubMed:38091321). These condensates exhibit liquid properties including fusion and dissolution by 1,6-hexanediol, with no reported material state transitions (PubMed:38091321).
Functional Summary: Flo8 phase separation is essential for biofilm formation, filamentation, and regulation of hyphal genes in Candida albicans (PubMed:38091321). Mutations abolishing phase separation (PrLD deletion, YF-to-S) concurrently impair biofilm formation and filamentation, establishing a direct mechanistic link (PubMed:38091321). The polyQG mutation reveals functional uncoupling where filamentation persists despite biofilm defects (PubMed:38091321).
Intrinsic Determinants & Regulations: Phase separation is intrinsically driven by the N-terminal Prion-Like Domain (PrLD, aa 100-400) and polyQ repeat tracts (PubMed:38091321). The YF-to-S mutation (tyrosine/phenylalanine to serine) abolishes phase separation, while deletion of polyQ tracts (ΔpolyQ) eliminates function; notably, a polyQ-to-polyglycine mutation (polyQG) uncouples filamentation from biofilm defects (PubMed:38091321).
Extrinsic Partners & Regulations: Genomic DNA enhances droplet formation and increases droplet size in vitro (PubMed:38091321). Additionally, RNA Polymerase II C-terminal domain (CTD) partitions into Flo8 condensates with an enrichment ratio >2 (PubMed:38091321).

Overall Phase Separation Overview: Bcr1 exhibits low intrinsic phase separation capacity and is classified as requiring partners for phase separation (PS-other) (PubMed:38091321). In U2OS cell nuclei, it forms only limited foci at LacO arrays without forming enlarged condensates or additional puncta, yet retains heterotypic interaction capability (PubMed:38091321).
Functional Summary: Bcr1's PrLD-mediated interactions are critical for biofilm adherence in Candida albicans, as deletions of N-terminal, C-terminal, or both PrLDs and YF-to-S mutations significantly reduced biofilm mass (PubMed:38091321). Filamentation remained largely unaffected except by ΔN/ΔNC deletions (PubMed:38091321). Pathological implications were not discussed (PubMed:38091321).
Intrinsic Determinants & Regulations: The functional interactions of Bcr1 are regulated by its N- and C-terminal Prion-Like Domains (PrLDs), which are essential for biofilm formation (PubMed:38091321). PolyQ tracts (6 tracts) were dispensable for function, as their deletion or mutation did not affect biofilm formation, whereas tyrosine/phenylalanine-to-serine (YF-to-S) mutations in PrLDs reduced biofilm formation, highlighting the importance of aromatic residues (PubMed:38091321).
Extrinsic Partners & Regulations: Bcr1 engages in heterotypic interactions with the transcription factor Efg1, evidenced by recruitment of Efg1 to Bcr1 foci in U2OS cell nuclei (PubMed:38091321).

Overall Phase Separation Overview: NRP1 (Q5A791) from Candida albicans associates with stress granules in the cytoplasm, forming cytoplasmic foci in both unstressed and stressed cellular conditions (PubMed:26238190). The stress granules exhibit properties of solid protein aggregates, distinct from typical liquid condensates, and their material state is regulated by protein disaggregases (PubMed:26238190).
Functional Summary: NRP1-containing stress granules in yeast adopt a solid aggregate-like state controlled by protein disaggregases, indicating a role in stress response mechanisms distinct from conventional liquid condensates (PubMed:26238190).
Intrinsic Determinants & Regulations: No intrinsic domains, mutations, or protein features regulating NRP1 phase separation were reported in the provided context (PubMed:26238190).
Extrinsic Partners & Regulations: NRP1 co-localizes with proteins Pab1 and Pub1 as co-components within stress granules, as demonstrated by co-localization microscopy (PubMed:26238190).

Overall Phase Separation Overview: Pom121 undergoes self-driven phase separation to form a hydrogel in vitro (PubMed:23202855). It is localized in the nucleus and associates with the Nuclear Pore Complex (PubMed:23202855). The hydrogel state exhibits high permeability to inert probes.
Functional Summary: The hydrogel formed by Pom121's FG domain demonstrates high permeability to mCherry and tCherry, suggesting a physiological role in establishing the selective permeability barrier of the Nuclear Pore Complex (PubMed:23202855).
Intrinsic Determinants & Regulations: The phase separation of Pom121 is intrinsically driven by its FG domain (residues 571-1050), which forms hydrogels consistent with the permeability properties of the Nuclear Pore Complex (PubMed:23202855).
Extrinsic Partners & Regulations: No extrinsic regulators or partners modulating Pom121 phase separation were reported in the provided data (PubMed:23202855).

Overall Phase Separation Overview: Sgo1 (Q5FBB7) does not undergo self-driven phase separation but partitions into liquid-like condensates formed by the Chromosomal Passenger Complex (CPC) in the nucleus (PubMed:31481798). It modulates the phosphorylation-driven phase separation of HP1α in heterochromatin bodies, which are membrane-less organelles (PubMed:36537242, 28636604).
Functional Summary: Sgo1's enrichment in CPC condensates is essential for proper inner-centromere localization and chromosome segregation during mitosis (PubMed:31481798). By enhancing HP1α phase separation, Sgo1 contributes to heterochromatin domain formation, gene silencing, and chromatin compartmentalization (PubMed:36537242, 28636604).
Intrinsic Determinants & Regulations: No intrinsic features driving Sgo1 phase separation are reported in the provided studies (PubMed:36537242, 28636604, 31481798).
Extrinsic Partners & Regulations: Sgo1 partitions into CPC condensates formed by Survivin, Borealin, and INCENP (PubMed:31481798). It also enhances the phosphorylation-driven liquid-liquid phase separation of HP1α, lowering its saturation concentration (PubMed:36537242, 28636604).

Overall Phase Separation Overview: TIP150 (Q5JR59) undergoes self-driven phase separation under crowding conditions but primarily forms liquid-like biomolecular condensates through co-phase separation with EB1 in the cytoplasm (PubMed:38323478, 36536176). It localizes to the spindle apparatus and centrosome, where it organizes microtubule plus-end machinery. While its condensates exhibit liquid-like properties including fusion and dynamic recovery when complexed with EB1, no material state transitions were reported for TIP150 itself (PubMed:38323478).
Functional Summary: Co-phase separation of TIP150 with EB1 and MCAK creates biochemical hubs that ensure accurate kinetochore-microtubule attachments and chromosome segregation during mitosis (PubMed:38323478, 36536176). These condensates concentrate tubulin dimers and plus-end tracking proteins (+TIPs), regulating microtubule dynamics including growth rate and catastrophe frequency. Disruption of co-phase separation causes severe mitotic defects: chromosome misalignment, delayed anaphase onset, reduced kinetochore tension, and impaired MCAK localization (PubMed:38323478). The evolutionary conservation of this mechanism is demonstrated by functional studies in Drosophila embryos (PubMed:38323478).
Intrinsic Determinants & Regulations: Phase separation of TIP150 is intrinsically driven by its C-terminal region (aa 800–1368), which contains an intrinsically disordered EB1-binding domain (EBD) and a coiled-coil MCAK-binding domain essential for co-phase separation (PubMed:38323478). The full-length protein is intrinsically disordered, contributing to its phase separation propensity. These domains enable synergistic interactions that lower the phase separation threshold when complexed with EB1 and MCAK (PubMed:38323478, 36536176).
Extrinsic Partners & Regulations: TIP150 requires EB1 for functional co-phase separation, forming dynamic condensates that serve as scaffolds for microtubule regulators (PubMed:38323478, 36536176). This co-condensation enhances droplet size and dynamics, with faster fluorescence recovery after photobleaching (FRAP) observed in complexes. Without EB1, TIP150 only forms droplets in the presence of crowding agents like 5% PEG-8000 (PubMed:38323478). TIP150 also interacts with MCAK in the EB1 complex, though MCAK alone cannot induce TIP150 phase separation (PubMed:38323478).

Overall Phase Separation Overview: The N protein (Q5MQC6) of Human coronavirus HKU1 forms cytoplasmic condensates integrated into stress granules, exhibiting the highest responsiveness to hyperosmotic stress among human coronaviruses (PubMed:39684875). These condensates are observed in >10% of cells under basal conditions and increase significantly to 32.9% under osmotic stress, with ultrastructural analysis revealing fibrillar, membrane-less architectures consistent with stress granules (PubMed:39684875).
Functional Summary: Condensate formation induces cellular stress that triggers stress granule-mediated translation arrest, disrupting cellular protein synthesis (PubMed:39684875). The unique osmotic stress sensitivity suggests concentration-dependent regulation during infection, potentially influencing viral pathogenesis through stress granule hijacking (PubMed:39684875).
Intrinsic Determinants & Regulations: No intrinsic molecular drivers (domains, mutations, PTMs, or oligomerization states) regulating phase separation were specified in the study (PubMed:39684875).
Extrinsic Partners & Regulations: Phase separation is modulated by hyperosmotic stress, which significantly enhances condensate formation (PubMed:39684875). The protein co-localizes with the stress granule marker G3BP1 and recruits RNA partners including poly-A RNA and 18S rRNA into condensates, as demonstrated by FISH and co-localization assays (PubMed:39684875).

Overall Phase Separation Overview: Cobl (Q5NBX1) undergoes self-driven phase separation (PS-self) in vitro and within the cytoplasm of epithelial cells, forming dynamic liquid-like condensates that associate with the apical junctional complex (AJC) but do not colocalize with predefined membrane-less organelles like stress granules or P-bodies (PubMed:36791197). These condensates exhibit liquid material properties, with no observed transitions to solid/gel states under tested conditions (PubMed:36791197).
Functional Summary: Phase separation concentrates Cobl on microtubules at the apical junctional complex, enhancing actin nucleation for circumferential actin ring assembly critical for epithelial morphogenesis and barrier function (PubMed:36791197). This process regulates apical constriction and paracellular barrier integrity, with loss of function (in Cobl-KO or Δ84 mutants) causing reduced transepithelial resistance and gastric barrier defects. LLPS also suppresses Cobl's actin-severing activity, biasing functionality toward actin assembly (PubMed:36791197).
Intrinsic Determinants & Regulations: Phase separation is intrinsically driven by Cobl's microtubule-binding domains (D1, D3, D4) which enable multivalent interactions (PubMed:36791197). The actin-binding D5 domain is dispensable for LLPS but required for actin nucleation. The 84-bp deletion mutant (CoblΔ84) disrupts microtubule-facilitated phase separation while retaining basal phase separation capability (PubMed:36791197).
Extrinsic Partners & Regulations: Microtubules (composed of α/β-tubulin) act as essential scaffolds that significantly lower the concentration threshold for phase separation and provide spatial organization (PubMed:36791197). Depolymerization of microtubules with nocodazole dissolves cellular condensates, while the CoblΔ84 mutant fails to form condensates in cells despite intact microtubule binding (PubMed:36791197).

Overall Phase Separation Overview: JMJD3 (Q5NCY0) undergoes phase separation, forming nuclear puncta in neural stem cells (NSCs) and associating with transcriptional condensates at enhancer clusters. This behavior occurs in the nucleus and is classified as PS-other, indicating involvement in phase separation through mechanisms beyond self-assembly. The material state and transitions were not specified (PubMed:35672304).
Functional Summary: JMJD3 phase separation is essential for TGFβ-driven assembly of enhancer clusters at the Chst8 locus, facilitating gene activation and maintaining 3D chromatin architecture in neural stem cells. Depletion disrupts chromatin contacts, directly linking its condensate formation to transcriptional regulation and genome organization (PubMed:35672304).
Intrinsic Determinants & Regulations: No specific intrinsic domains, mutations, or features driving JMJD3 phase separation were identified; experiments exclusively studied the endogenous full-length protein without characterizing regulatory domains or modifications (PubMed:35672304).
Extrinsic Partners & Regulations: No extrinsic regulators, partners, or environmental modulators (e.g., ions, chemicals, or binding proteins) of JMJD3 phase separation were reported in the study (PubMed:35672304).

Overall Phase Separation Overview: IE180 (Q5PP75) does not undergo phase separation itself (class: PS-other) but disrupts cytoplasmic stress granule formation by hijacking G3BP scaffold proteins into the nucleus, forming unclassified nuclear foci (PubMed:40145738). It localizes to both the nucleus and cytoplasm (PubMed:40145738). This inhibition prevents the assembly of liquid-like stress granules without involving material state transitions in IE180 itself (PubMed:40145738).
Functional Summary: By suppressing stress granule formation through nuclear sequestration of G3BPs, IE180 facilitates immune evasion for Pseudorabies virus, enhancing viral replication (PubMed:40145738). This disruption of the antiviral stress granule defense mechanism represents a key viral strategy to overcome cellular host defenses (PubMed:40145738).
Intrinsic Determinants & Regulations: The inhibitory function of IE180 is intrinsically regulated by its ICP4L-N domain (amino acids 1-490), which is essential for binding G3BP1 and G3BP2 (PubMed:40145738). Nuclear localization sequences (NLS) are critical for its nuclear translocation, enhancing the sequestration efficiency that underlies stress granule suppression (PubMed:40145738).
Extrinsic Partners & Regulations: IE180 extrinsically regulates phase separation by interacting with and sequestering the stress granule scaffold proteins G3BP1 and G3BP2 into the nucleus (PubMed:40145738). This hijacking disrupts their cytoplasmic phase separation capacity, directly inhibiting stress granule assembly as confirmed by co-immunoprecipitation and nuclear colocalization evidence (PubMed:40145738).

Overall Phase Separation Overview: CEP112 undergoes liquid-liquid phase separation (LLPS) to form dynamic liquid-like condensates in vitro and in vivo, exhibiting self-assembly behavior as indicated by its classification as PS-other (PubMed:39349455). These condensates localize to both the cytoplasm and nucleus, where they associate with RNA granules during spermiogenesis – specifically described as cytoplasmic foci functioning as biomolecular condensates for mRNA regulation (PubMed:39349455). The condensates consistently display liquid material properties characterized by rapid fusion/fission, complete FRAP recovery, spherical morphology, and sensitivity to 1,6-hexanediol, with no observed material state transitions reported (PubMed:39349455).
Functional Summary: CEP112 condensates serve as translationally active hubs that recruit target mRNAs (Fsip2, Cfap61, Cfap74) and translation machinery to regulate localized gene expression during spermiogenesis, as observed in mouse germ cell lines (PubMed:39349455). Disruption of this phase separation – particularly through patient-derived mutations – impairs translation efficiency of fertility-related genes, directly leading to sperm defects and male infertility (PubMed:39349455).
Intrinsic Determinants & Regulations: Phase separation of CEP112 is intrinsically driven by its predicted intrinsically disordered regions (IDRs), as identified through computational PONDR analysis (PubMed:39349455). The full-length protein was predominantly studied, with no reported regulatory effects from mutations, post-translational modifications, splicing variants, oligomerization states, or repeat features in the available data (PubMed:39349455).
Extrinsic Partners & Regulations: CEP112 phase separation is modulated by multiple extrinsic partners: it co-assembles with proteins hnRNPA2B1, EEF1A1, and EIF4A1 into condensates where they influence droplet size, as demonstrated by co-localization experiments in vitro (PubMed:39349455). RNA significantly enhances phase separation, with total testicular RNA increasing droplet formation concentration-dependently, while specific transcripts like Fsip2-CDS both lower the saturation concentration and are selectively recruited into condensates (PubMed:39349455).

Protein Name: Mediator of DNA damage checkpoint protein 1
Overall Phase Separation Overview: MDC1 (Q5PSV9) undergoes partner-driven phase separation mediated by pre-rRNA interactions, forming liquid-like condensates in vitro and in vivo (PubMed:34980897). This behavior occurs exclusively in the nucleus, where it associates with DNA damage foci (IRIF) and the XY body (PubMed:34980897). No material state transitions were reported.
Functional Summary: MDC1 phase separation is critical for DNA double-strand break (DSB) repair, serving as the molecular basis for foci formation that recruits repair factors (e.g., BRCA1, TopBP1) to lesions (PubMed:34980897). Disruption of this process impairs DSB response efficiency in cellular systems (PubMed:34980897).
Intrinsic Determinants & Regulations: Phase separation is intrinsically regulated by MDC1's forkhead-associated (FHA) domain and proline-serine-threonine-rich (PST) repeats, which directly bind pre-rRNA to scaffold condensate formation (PubMed:34980897). Deletion of either the FHA domain (ΔFHA) or PST repeats (ΔPST) abolishes phase separation and disrupts DNA damage foci assembly (PubMed:34980897).
Extrinsic Partners & Regulations: Pre-rRNA acts as an essential extrinsic scaffold for MDC1 phase separation, demonstrated through co-immunoprecipitation, in vitro LLPS assays, and IRIF rescue experiments (PubMed:34980897). This RNA-dependent mechanism enables recruitment of DNA repair factors to nuclear condensates.

Overall Phase Separation Overview: NSP2 (Q5Q1N6) undergoes partner-dependent phase separation with NSP5 to form liquid-like viroplasms (viral factories) in the cytoplasm of rotavirus-infected cells (PubMed:36749077). These condensates exhibit liquid material properties, including fusion competence, and are essential sites for viral replication. The K294E mutation impairs phase separation efficiency and viroplasm maturation without inducing material state transitions.
Functional Summary: Phase separation enables viroplasm biogenesis, concentrating viral components for RNA synthesis and virion assembly (PubMed:36749077). Impairment of this process via the K294E mutation disrupts viroplasm fusion kinetics and perinuclear localization, significantly reducing viral replication efficiency without affecting phosphorylation-dependent functions.
Intrinsic Determinants & Regulations: Phase separation is intrinsically regulated by the flexibility of the C-terminal region (CTR; residues 291-317), with molecular dynamics simulations confirming reduced CTR flexibility in the K294E mutant impairs interoctamer interactions and condensation capacity (PubMed:36749077). This mutation specifically diminishes droplet formation kinetics and reduces condensate size both in vitro and in vivo.
Extrinsic Partners & Regulations: NSP2 strictly requires the extrinsic partner NSP5 for phase separation, as NSP5 serves as an essential scaffold for co-condensation in both cellular and purified protein systems (PubMed:36749077). Mutations in NSP2 (e.g., K294E) directly reduce co-condensation efficiency with NSP5, demonstrating partner-dependent modulation of phase behavior.

Protein Name: Mediator of RNA polymerase II transcription subunit 13
Overall Phase Separation Overview: MED13 undergoes self-driven phase separation (class: PS-self) to form liquid droplets in vitro, as demonstrated by droplet formation assays and fluorescence recovery after photobleaching (FRAP) experiments. This behavior is mediated by its exon20-coding intrinsically disordered region (IDR), which forms spherical droplets under molecular crowding conditions when fused to mCherry (PubMed:34605568). No specific subcellular locations, membrane-less organelle associations, or material state transitions were reported.
Functional Summary: No functional implications or disease associations of MED13 phase separation were specified in the provided study (PubMed:34605568).
Intrinsic Determinants & Regulations: The phase separation of MED13 is intrinsically driven by its exon20-coding intrinsically disordered region (IDR). Recombinant expression of this IDR fused to mCherry confirmed its capacity to form spherical droplets under crowding conditions, establishing it as the primary molecular driver. No mutations, post-translational modifications, oligomerization domains, or repeat features were identified as regulators in the provided data (PubMed:34605568).
Extrinsic Partners & Regulations: No extrinsic regulators, binding partners, ions, or chemicals modulating MED13 phase separation were identified in the provided study (PubMed:34605568).

Overall Phase Separation Overview: The protein Q5T1M5 (FKBP/Fm) does not undergo self-driven phase separation in its native state but participates in engineered phase separation systems. In the cytoplasm, it forms synthetic liquid-like condensates (ArtiG) through concentration-dependent phase separation, exhibiting spherical morphology, fusion, coalescence, and rapid component exchange (PubMed:31324804). Alternatively, it compartmentalizes into SUMO5-FRB/SIM6 synthetic condensates as a client protein upon rapamycin-induced binding, displaying liquid-like properties and mobility confirmed by FRAP (PubMed:36396954). No material state transitions were reported in either system.
Functional Summary: Engineered phase separation systems serve functional roles: ArtiG condensates act as protein reservoirs buffering cytosolic concentration fluctuations and can recruit specific RNA targets when functionalized (PubMed:31324804). Rapamycin-inducible recruitment validates controllable protein clustering tools for synthetic biology applications (PubMed:36396954).
Intrinsic Determinants & Regulations: Phase separation behavior is intrinsically regulated by engineered domains: The F36M-FKBP domain enables homodimerization (Kd ~µM), creating multivalent interactions essential for ArtiG condensate formation, where wild-type FKBP fails to phase separate (PubMed:31324804). The FKBP domain facilitates binding to the FRB-rapamycin complex, enabling recruitment into synthetic condensates (PubMed:36396954).
Extrinsic Partners & Regulations: Condensate formation requires extrinsic regulators: Rapamycin induces FKBP recruitment into SUMO5-FRB/SIM6 condensates by mediating FRB binding (PubMed:36396954). ArtiG formation is concentration-dependent, with nucleation occurring at critical cytosolic concentrations (PubMed:31324804).

Overall Phase Separation Overview: Wild-type RBM20 localizes to nuclear speckles without cytoplasmic granule formation, while the R636S mutation causes mislocalization from the nucleus to sarcoplasm, forming liquid-like RNP granules (R3Gs) that exhibit fusion events, wetting behavior, and partial FRAP recovery (t½ ~100s) with core-shell substructure (PubMed:33188278). These granules associate with cytoskeletal elements, recruit mRNA, and fuse with stress granules, classified as PS-other behavior (PubMed:33188278).
Functional Summary: Pathological R3G formation disrupts actin cytoskeleton organization, reducing cardiomyocyte striation by 41% and impairing sarcomere biogenesis, leading to dilated cardiomyopathy and heart failure (PubMed:33188278). These granules sequester cell cycle regulators to arrest cardiomyocyte proliferation and fuse with stress granules, disrupting mRNA metabolism (PubMed:33188278).
Intrinsic Determinants & Regulations: Phase separation is intrinsically driven by the N-terminal low-complexity domain (LCD), with deletion of this domain (ΔN mutant) abolishing granule formation (PubMed:33188278). The pathogenic R636S mutation enables cytoplasmic mislocalization and granule assembly, while deletion constructs (del1-658, del658-1227) confirm the requirement of the N-terminal region containing the LCD for phase separation (PubMed:33188278).
Extrinsic Partners & Regulations: R3Gs recruit poly-A+ mRNA and partition ACTC1 to their phase boundary, demonstrated through FISH co-localization and co-staining (PubMed:33188278). They fuse with stress granules containing TIA1, TIAR, and G3BP1 upon sodium arsenite-induced stress, with complete absorption of G3BP1 observed (PubMed:33188278).

Overall Phase Separation Overview: UBAP2 (Q5T6F2) does not undergo self-driven phase separation but is recruited by K6-polyubiquitinated PAICS to drive liquid-liquid phase separation (LLPS), forming purinosome condensates in the cytoplasm (PubMed:37848033). These condensates exhibit liquid-like properties, including dynamic fusion events and rapid fluorescence recovery after photobleaching (FRAP) both in vivo and in vitro (PubMed:37848033). No material state transitions (e.g., liquid-to-solid) were reported.
Functional Summary: UBAP2-mediated phase separation drives purinosome assembly, enhancing de novo purine synthesis (DNPS) flux to support cellular proliferation and tumorigenesis in melanoma (PubMed:37848033). Depletion of UBAP2 impairs cell growth and purinosome formation, which is rescued by wild-type UBAP2 but not ΔUBA or ΔIDR mutants, linking phase separation directly to oncogenic metabolism (PubMed:37848033).
Intrinsic Determinants & Regulations: UBAP2's phase separation is intrinsically regulated by two critical features: its ubiquitin-associated (UBA) domain (aa 46-94) that binds polyubiquitin chains, and multiple intrinsically disordered regions (IDRs: IV:aa 622-736, V-VI:aa 853-966, VII-VIII:aa 982-1119) that provide multivalency (PubMed:37848033). Deletion of either the UBA domain (ΔUBA) or IDRs (ΔIDR) abolishes phase separation in vivo and in vitro, confirming their essential synergistic roles (PubMed:37848033).
Extrinsic Partners & Regulations: UBAP2's phase separation is extrinsically regulated by K6-polyubiquitinated PAICS, which provides multivalent binding sites for UBAP2's UBA domain to initiate condensate assembly (PubMed:37848033). Additionally, K6-linked tetra-ubiquitin chains (K6-Ub₄) directly induce UBAP2 phase separation in vitro, with specificity over other chain types (e.g., K48-Ub₄ shows no activity) (PubMed:37848033).

Overall Phase Separation Overview: NCOA4 (Q5U4H9) undergoes phase separation classified as PS-other, forming detergent-insoluble cytoplasmic condensates in iron-replete cells (PubMed:35318808). These condensates are not associated with known membrane-less organelles (MLOs) and exhibit an unspecified material state, with no observed state transitions reported.
Functional Summary: NCOA4 condensates regulate ferritin accumulation during early iron repletion and facilitate ferritin degradation via lysosomal delivery during prolonged iron repletion, directly linking phase separation to cellular iron homeostasis (PubMed:35318808).
Intrinsic Determinants & Regulations: Phase separation is intrinsically driven by multivalent interactions generated through iron binding, though no specific domains, mutations, or protein regions were identified as regulators in the study (PubMed:35318808).
Extrinsic Partners & Regulations: Iron acts as a critical extrinsic regulator, inducing condensate formation and subsequent insolubility in cellular environments (PubMed:35318808). No protein partners or additional chemical modulators were reported.

Overall Phase Separation Overview: EB1 undergoes self-driven phase separation to form liquid-like condensates in the cytoplasm, primarily associated with spindle apparatus and centrosomes (PubMed:38323478, 36536176). These dynamic condensates serve as scaffolds for microtubule regulators and exhibit reversible fusion and rapid fluorescence recovery. In engineered systems, EB1 forms fiber-like synthetic organelles along microtubules (PubMed:35033560). While wild-type condensates maintain liquid properties, specific mutations (e.g., EB1-hnRNPA1D262V) undergo pathological liquid-to-gel transitions (PubMed:36536176).
Functional Summary: EB1 condensates organize microtubule plus-end machinery by concentrating tubulin, TIP150, and MCAK to regulate microtubule dynamics (growth rate, catastrophe frequency) and ensure accurate chromosome segregation during mitosis (PubMed:38323478, 36536176). Disruption (e.g., via IDR mutations) causes spindle defects, lagging chromosomes, and impaired kinetochore attachments (PubMed:36536176). In synthetic biology, EB1 enables orthogonal translation within engineered organelles (PubMed:35033560). EB1-tau co-condensates facilitate microtubule regulation, while EB1 inhibits pathological tau phase separation and aggregation, suggesting neuroprotective roles (PubMed:32997736, 38445984).
Intrinsic Determinants & Regulations: Phase separation is driven by multivalent interactions among EB1's calponin homology (CH) domain, C-terminal coiled-coil (EBH) dimerization domain, C-terminal tail (CTT), and intrinsically disordered region (IDR, residues 126-183) (PubMed:36536176). Charged lysine/arginine residues within the IDR constitute critical 'molecular grammar', as mutations (e.g., KR6Q: K174Q/R176Q/K178Q/K180Q/K182Q/R183Q) attenuate phase separation by disrupting electrostatic interactions (PubMed:36536176). Acetylation at Lys220 promotes self-phase separation but disrupts co-condensation with partners; the K220Q mutation mimics this effect (PubMed:38323478).
Extrinsic Partners & Regulations: EB1 co-phase separates with microtubule regulators TIP150 and MCAK, which synergistically lower phase separation thresholds and enhance condensate dynamics (PubMed:38323478, 36536176). In engineered systems, RNA-binding proteins FUS and EWSR1 enhance EB1's phase separation efficiency within synthetic organelles (PubMed:35033560). Tubulin dimers are enriched within condensates, forming reservoirs for microtubule growth (PubMed:36536176). EB1 also co-phase separates with tau's proline-rich domain to form heterotypic microtubule-associated condensates (PubMed:32997736).

Overall Phase Separation Overview: RIF1 (Q5UIP0) undergoes partner-driven phase separation through incorporation into Mitotic Stress Bodies (MSBs) in the nucleus of colon cancer cells during prolonged mitotic arrest or spontaneously in normally dividing cancer cells (PubMed:36606487). These MSBs exhibit liquid-like properties including spherical morphology, sensitivity to 1,6-hexanediol, salt, and osmotic stress, and reformation after washout. RIF1 does not independently form condensates but co-localizes with TP53BP1 within these dynamic structures adjacent to centromeres (PubMed:36606487).
Functional Summary: RIF1 incorporation into MSBs contributes to the sequestration of DNA repair machinery components during mitosis, which in cancer cells suppresses aberrant nonhomologous end joining (NHEJ) activation, prevents telomere fusion and lethal chromosome breakage, reduces DNA damage (γH2AX foci), and promotes survival following mitotic stress (PubMed:36606487). This mechanism facilitates cancer cell viability after aberrant mitoses but specific pathological implications of RIF1's phase separation were not detailed independently.
Intrinsic Determinants & Regulations: No intrinsic domains, mutations, or features regulating RIF1's phase separation were identified in the provided study (PubMed:36606487). The key_drivers section explicitly states no specifications for domains, PTMs, oligomerization, repeat features, or mutations related to RIF1's condensate behavior.
Extrinsic Partners & Regulations: RIF1 requires TP53BP1 for incorporation into Mitotic Stress Bodies, co-localizing exclusively with this partner within MSBs (PubMed:36606487). No other extrinsic regulators (ions, chemicals, or additional protein partners) influencing RIF1's phase separation were reported in the provided data.

Overall Phase Separation Overview: Sec13 (Q5XFW8) undergoes partner-dependent phase separation (class PS-other) to form liquid-like Sec bodies in the cytoplasm under stress conditions (PubMed:36325988). It redistributes from ER exit sites (ERES) to form the core of Sec bodies, which exhibit liquid-like material properties and are surrounded by a Sec16A shell. No material state transitions were reported.
Functional Summary: Sequestration of Sec13 into Sec bodies depletes COPII components from ER exit sites, inhibiting ER export function. These membraneless structures serve as stress-responsive compartments that modulate cellular trafficking pathways (PubMed:36325988).
Intrinsic Determinants & Regulations: No intrinsic drivers (domains, PTMs, mutations, or oligomerization states) regulating Sec13 phase separation were identified in the study of endogenous full-length protein (PubMed:36325988).
Extrinsic Partners & Regulations: Sec13 co-phase separates with Sec16A, forming the core of condensates surrounded by a Sec16A shell, and associates with Sec16B as a co-component, as demonstrated by colocalization and super-resolution microscopy (PubMed:36325988).

Overall Phase Separation Overview: Snu13 (Q5XH16) undergoes phase separation as part of the box C/D snoRNP complex, associating primarily with the dense fibrillar component (DFC) of the nucleolus in the nucleus (PubMed:35607824). While self-assembly capability isn't explicitly demonstrated, its classification as 'PS-other' indicates phase separation occurs through complex formation rather than autonomous behavior. The material state isn't specified, but co-localization with canonical DFC markers suggests integration into biomolecular condensates (PubMed:35607824).
Functional Summary: The phase-separated state of Snu13 enables its role in rRNA methylation during ribosome biogenesis within the nucleolar DFC compartment (PubMed:35607824). As an essential component of the box C/D snoRNP complex, its condensate integration facilitates precise spatial organization for ribosomal RNA processing, though disease associations or stress-induced transitions weren't reported (PubMed:35607824).
Intrinsic Determinants & Regulations: Phase separation of Snu13 may be influenced by a minor intrinsically disordered region (IDR) predicted in its sequence, though this feature remains experimentally unverified (PubMed:35607824). No specific domains, post-translational modifications, oligomerization states, or mutations were identified as key drivers in the studied contexts (PubMed:35607824).
Extrinsic Partners & Regulations: Snu13 co-phase separates with protein partners Fbl and Nop56 within the box C/D snoRNP complex, evidenced by their co-localization in the dense fibrillar component of the nucleolus (PubMed:35607824). This cooperative assembly occurs in Xenopus laevis oocytes, indicating rRNA likely serves as a scaffold for complex formation though direct experimental validation is absent (PubMed:35607824).

Overall Phase Separation Overview: nsP3 (Q5XXP4) forms cytoplasmic foci distinct from stress granules through recruitment of G3BP, inhibiting stress granule assembly. This behavior occurs exclusively in the cytoplasm and is classified as PS-other, indicating phase separation-like properties not driven by self-assembly. The material state of these foci remains unspecified with no observed state transitions (PubMed:22837213).
Functional Summary: nsP3/G3BP foci sequester G3BP to block stress granule assembly, countering antiviral responses and enabling viral RNA replication. These foci are functionally distinct from stress granules by morphology, absence of eIF3 marker, resistance to cycloheximide-induced disassembly, and inability to form bona fide stress granules under arsenite stress (PubMed:22837213).
Intrinsic Determinants & Regulations: The formation of cytoplasmic foci is intrinsically regulated by nsP3's C-terminal domain, particularly the SH3 domain-binding motif (residues 398-406). Deletion of the SH3 motif (del398-406) abolishes foci formation, resulting in diffuse cytoplasmic and nuclear distribution. Additionally, deletion of the variable domain within the C-terminal region alters morphology to filamentous structures instead of foci (PubMed:22837213).
Extrinsic Partners & Regulations: nsP3 exclusively co-phase separates with the cellular protein G3BP (Q13283), forming cytoplasmic foci in Vero and HEK293T cells. This interaction occurs independently of viral RNA replication or other viral proteins and is mediated through the SH3 domain-binding motif of nsP3 (PubMed:22837213).

Overall Phase Separation Overview: NOX (Q60049) does not undergo self-driven phase separation (class: PS-other) but is modulated by partner-induced condensates (PubMed:38637545). It localizes to the nucleus and associates with biomolecular condensates that exhibit liquid material properties (PubMed:38637545). No material state transitions were reported.
Functional Summary: Biomolecular condensates formed by partner LCDs regulate NOX enzymatic activity, with cationic Dbp1 condensates significantly enhancing activity, demonstrating how condensate microenvironments can optimize biochemical reactions (PubMed:38637545).
Intrinsic Determinants & Regulations: No intrinsic domains, mutations, or features driving NOX phase separation were identified in this study (PubMed:38637545).
Extrinsic Partners & Regulations: NOX enzymatic activity is modulated by condensates formed by partner proteins Dbp1, Laf1, and Ddx4 (PubMed:38637545). Activity enhancement is most pronounced in cationic condensates formed by Dbp1's low-complexity domain, indicating microenvironment-dependent regulation (PubMed:38637545).

Protein Name: Rho guanine nucleotide exchange factor TIAM1
Overall Phase Separation Overview: Tiam1 (Q60610) does not undergo self-driven phase separation but partitions into pre-existing Ca²⁺-dependent liquid-like condensates formed by CaMKII and GluN2B in vitro. This partitioning occurs via its specific CaMKII-binding domain and persists even after Ca²⁺ removal (PubMed:33927400).
Functional Summary: The incorporation of Tiam1 into CaMKII/GluN2Bc condensates enables activity-dependent trapping of synaptic proteins, suggesting a role in synaptic reorganization during plasticity. This mechanism facilitates spatial organization of signaling complexes at postsynaptic sites (PubMed:33927400).
Intrinsic Determinants & Regulations: The partitioning of Tiam1 is intrinsically regulated by its CaMKII-binding domain (residues 1544-1565), which mediates specific interaction with the T-site of CaMKII within condensates (PubMed:33927400).
Extrinsic Partners & Regulations: Tiam1 partitioning is extrinsically dependent on CaMKII/GluN2B condensates triggered by Ca²⁺. It co-localizes with GluN2B and CaMKII in these assemblies, with Ca²⁺ acting as an essential initiator for condensate formation. The persistence of Tiam1 within condensates after Ca²⁺ chelation relies on CaMKII T286 autophosphorylation (PubMed:33927400).

Overall Phase Separation Overview: SATB1 undergoes phase separation with distinct isoform-specific behaviors (class: PS-other). The short isoform forms reversible liquid-like droplets in vitro through self-assembly, exhibiting droplet fusion and partial FRAP recovery (43% immobile fraction), while the long isoform displays higher phase separation propensity, forming hexanediol-sensitive nuclear speckles that transition to irreversible cytoplasmic aggregates. Both isoforms localize to the nucleus and cytoplasm, associating with transcriptional condensates and nucleoli. The long isoform additionally forms stress granule-like structures when mislocalized. Material states range from liquid (nuclear) to solid/hydrogel (aggregated cytoplasmic), with concentration-dependent liquid-to-gel transitions in the short isoform and pathological liquid-to-solid transitions in the cytoplasm for the long isoform (PubMed:37635874).
Functional Summary: SATB1 phase separation forms transcriptional condensates that regulate immune gene expression during T-cell development, with nuclear speckles co-localizing with active transcription sites. Dysregulation causes pathological consequences: cytoplasmic aggregation of the long isoform and aberrant EP splicing correlate with cancer progression and poor prognosis. Irreversible liquid-to-solid transitions in the cytoplasm generate cytotoxic aggregates, while hexanediol-sensitive phase-separated bonds identified via Raman spectroscopy are essential for native transcriptional organization (PubMed:37635874).
Intrinsic Determinants & Regulations: Phase separation is intrinsically driven by the N-terminal ULD and CUTL domains that mediate multivalent self-oligomerization. The long isoform's C-terminal extra peptide (EP) – a low-complexity domain – significantly enhances phase separation propensity (catGRANULE score: 0.390) and promotes aggregation when adjacent to the poly-Q repeat domain. Phosphorylation at S635 (short isoform) or S666 (long isoform) maintains solubility, while hypo-phosphorylation or the S635A mutation triggers aggregation. The inherent properties of IDR regions also contribute to phase behavior (PubMed:37635874).
Extrinsic Partners & Regulations: Nuclear RNA (including Xist lncRNA) serves as a critical extrinsic regulator, maintaining SATB1 nuclear solubility through direct binding confirmed by RNA immunoprecipitation. RNA depletion via RNase A treatment triggers mislocalization and aggregation, indicating RNA is essential for proper phase behavior regulation (PubMed:37635874).

Overall Phase Separation Overview: Adora1 (Q60612) undergoes self-oligomerization to form clusters with a monotonically decreasing size distribution in HL-1 cells in vivo, classified as a phase separation-related phenomenon (PS-other) (PubMed:39739811).
Functional Summary: The functional implications of Adora1 cluster formation are not specified in the provided study (PubMed:39739811).
Intrinsic Determinants & Regulations: The cluster formation of Adora1 is intrinsically driven by weak interactions facilitating self-oligomerization, observed for the full-length protein (PubMed:39739811).
Extrinsic Partners & Regulations: No extrinsic regulators or partners were reported for Adora1 cluster formation in the provided study (PubMed:39739811).

Overall Phase Separation Overview: Grb2 (Q60631) does not undergo autonomous phase separation but is recruited to and co-assembles within liquid-like LAT condensates at the plasma membrane interface in the cytoplasm, specifically within TCR signaling microclusters (PubMed:36460640). These condensates form abruptly after TCR binding events, exhibit dynamic molecular exchange and centripetal transport, and serve as discrete signaling quanta.
Functional Summary: Co-assembly within LAT condensates enables Grb2 to facilitate downstream signaling – particularly SOS recruitment for Ras activation – thereby amplifying TCR signals while enabling kinetic proofreading for antigen discrimination (PubMed:36460640). This mechanism filters noise and correlates with NFAT translocation activation thresholds (45-75 condensates/12min).
Intrinsic Determinants & Regulations: Recruitment of Grb2 to condensates is intrinsically mediated by its SH2 domains, which bind phosphorylated tyrosine residues (Y175, Y195, Y235) on LAT (PubMed:36460640). No autonomous phase separation drivers were identified for Grb2 itself.
Extrinsic Partners & Regulations: Grb2 partitioning is extrinsically regulated by phosphorylated LAT, which scaffolds the condensates (PubMed:36460640). Enrichment occurs simultaneously with LAT condensation (<2s resolution) without pre-accumulation, and is abolished when LAT tyrosine phosphorylation sites are mutated (LAT(4F) mutant).

Overall Phase Separation Overview: RIPK1 (Q60855) does not undergo self-driven phase separation but is recruited into condensates formed by extrinsic partners in the cytoplasm (PubMed:38272024). It associates with RIPK1 aggregates and exhibits a solid material state, with no observed state transitions reported (PubMed:38272024).
Functional Summary: Phase separation enables PARylation-dependent ubiquitination of RIPK1 at lysine 376, promoting proteasomal degradation of activated RIPK1 to restrain necroptosis, establishing a phase separation-dependent cell death checkpoint (PubMed:38272024).
Intrinsic Determinants & Regulations: No intrinsic regulators (domains, mutations, or structural features) driving RIPK1 phase separation were identified in the provided data (PubMed:38272024).
Extrinsic Partners & Regulations: RIPK1 phase separation is extrinsically regulated through recruitment into condensates formed by PARP5A and RNF146 via multivalent interactions, facilitated by the adaptor protein TAX1BP1 (PubMed:38272024). Within these condensates, RIPK1 undergoes poly ADP-ribosylation (PARylation) and PARylation-dependent ubiquitination (PubMed:38272024).

Overall Phase Separation Overview: PML undergoes phase separation to form nuclear bodies (NBs) via liquid-liquid phase separation in response to oxidative stress, such as arsenic exposure, exclusively within the nucleus (PubMed:36175410). As a structural scaffold of PML NBs, it recruits partner proteins and enhances SUMO2/3 conjugation, with assembly and dissolution dynamics regulated by stress conditions (PubMed:36175410).
Functional Summary: PML NBs coordinate SUMO2-dependent ubiquitination and degradation of targets like the KAP1 complex and repress transposable elements in mouse embryonic stem cells by sumoylating DPPA2/KAP1, preventing 2-cell-like state transition (PubMed:36175410). Loss of PML causes transposable element derepression and aberrant cellular transitions, while the condensates create a reduced microenvironment that protects sumoylation enzymes from ROS inhibition (PubMed:36175410).
Intrinsic Determinants & Regulations: PML phase separation is intrinsically driven by its cysteine-rich domains, which are essential for multimerization and NB formation (PubMed:36175410). Sumoylation at K160 (or equivalent residue) is required for partner recruitment, as demonstrated by the Pmlᴱᴵ¹⁶⁷ᴿ mutation that impairs both NB assembly and partner sumoylation (PubMed:36175410).
Extrinsic Partners & Regulations: PML co-phase separates with partner proteins including KAP1, DPPA2, SP100, DAXX, and the sumoylation enzyme UBC9, which becomes concentrated within NBs and is essential for PML-driven hyper-sumoylation (PubMed:36175410). Assembly is triggered by oxidative stressors like arsenic, while prolonged stress induces dissolution (PubMed:36175410).

Overall Phase Separation Overview: Cas (Q61140) undergoes liquid-liquid phase separation in vitro under physiologic conditions and associates with Integrin adhesion complexes (IACs) in mouse embryonic fibroblasts. These condensates exhibit liquid-like properties and demonstrate sensitivity to environmental perturbations including temperature and pH (PubMed:35049497).
Functional Summary: Cas phase separation is sufficient to reconstitute kindlin-dependent integrin clustering in vitro and directly contributes to Integrin adhesion complex formation. Environmental perturbations (temperature/pH) similarly affect in vitro condensates and cellular IACs, with phase separation modulations directly impacting IAC numbers in cells (PubMed:35049497).
Intrinsic Determinants & Regulations: No intrinsic regulators for Cas were described in the provided data (PubMed:35049497).
Extrinsic Partners & Regulations: Cas phase separation is promoted by interactions with Nck and N-WASP, requiring multiply-phosphorylated Cas for cooperative phase separation. Additionally, Cas undergoes synergistic phase separation with FAK, where mutual interactions enhance condensate formation (PubMed:35049497).

Overall Phase Separation Overview: DDX4 (Q61496) undergoes self-driven phase separation (class: PS-self) to form liquid-like nuage granules in the cytoplasm of living cells, which are partitioned from chromatin, and also undergoes liquid-liquid phase separation (LLPS) in vitro when mixed with polyethylene glycol (PEG) (PubMed:36526633). The material state is liquid, as evidenced by half-FRAP experiments showing fluorescence recovery dynamics (PubMed:36526633). No material state transitions were reported (PubMed:36526633).
Functional Summary: Functional implications of DDX4 phase separation are not discussed in the provided context (PubMed:36526633).
Intrinsic Determinants & Regulations: Phase separation of DDX4 is driven by its full-length sequence, as studied using a YFP-tagged construct (PubMed:36526633). No specific domains, post-translational modifications, splicing variants, oligomerization states, repeat features, or mutations were identified as key drivers in the provided context (PubMed:36526633).
Extrinsic Partners & Regulations: The crowding agent polyethylene glycol (PEG) promotes in vitro phase separation of DDX4 (PubMed:36526633). No protein partners, ions, or other extrinsic regulators were reported (PubMed:36526633).

Overall Phase Separation Overview: EWSR1 undergoes partner-dependent phase separation rather than self-driven assembly, primarily forming liquid-like condensates within the nucleus (PubMed:36754961, PubMed:37098348). It associates with NONO bodies (non-paraspeckle condensates) through incorporation into NONO scaffolds and co-assembles into stress granules, with no observed material state transitions reported (PubMed:36754961, PubMed:37098348).
Functional Summary: EWSR1 phase separation enables functional complexes for miR-29b suppression within NONO condensates, promoting collagen production and cardiac fibrosis pathogenesis (PubMed:36754961). Its co-assembly with FUS in stress granules suggests additional roles in stress response mechanisms, though explicit pathological implications were not detailed (PubMed:37098348).
Intrinsic Determinants & Regulations: No intrinsic domains, mutations, or molecular features driving EWSR1 phase separation were identified in the provided studies; all observed phase separation behavior occurred through partner-dependent mechanisms without reported regulatory domains or mutations (PubMed:36754961, PubMed:37098348).
Extrinsic Partners & Regulations: EWSR1 requires protein partners for phase separation: it co-phase separates with VGLL3 within NONO condensates dependent on architectural RNA integrity (PubMed:36754961), and co-assembles with FUS into shared condensates including stress granules (PubMed:37098348). Additional partners include NONO, which scaffolds the condensates (PubMed:36754961).

Overall Phase Separation Overview: Gli3 (Q61602) forms distinct liquid-like bodies in the nucleus when co-expressed with SPOP, exhibiting co-localization in dynamic puncta with fusion events and rapid fluorescence recovery after photobleaching (FRAP) (PubMed:27220849). These structures, referred to as Gli3^{1-455}/SPOP-positive bodies, represent a non-canonical membrane-less organelle and display liquid material properties without observed state transitions (PubMed:27220849).
Functional Summary: Co-phase separation of Gli3 with SPOP facilitates CRL3<sup>SPOP</sup>-mediated ubiquitination and degradation of Gli3 within nuclear bodies, enhancing substrate turnover efficiency (PubMed:27220849). Cancer-associated mutations disrupting SPOP oligomerization may impair this regulatory mechanism, potentially contributing to disease pathology (PubMed:27220849).
Intrinsic Determinants & Regulations: The N-terminal fragment (residues 1-455) of Gli3 is sufficient for co-phase separation with SPOP, though specific intrinsic domains or motifs within Gli3 driving this behavior are not detailed in the provided data (PubMed:27220849).
Extrinsic Partners & Regulations: Gli3's phase separation is strictly dependent on SPOP, which forms higher-order oligomers via its BTB domain (dimerization) and BACK domain (dimerization-mediated oligomerization) (PubMed:27220849). Disruption of SPOP oligomerization through mutations (e.g., Y353E in BACK or L186D/L190D/L193D/I217K in BTB) abolishes condensate formation (PubMed:27220849).

Protein Name: Protein kinase C and casein kinase substrate in neurons protein 1
Overall Phase Separation Overview: Syndapin 1 (Q61644) does not undergo self-driven phase separation but requires partners to form condensates (class: PS-other) (PubMed:35809574). It localizes to the cytoplasm and associates with endocytic condensates described as liquid droplets at endocytic sites (PubMed:35809574). These condensates exhibit liquid-like properties based on co-condensation behavior, with no observed material state transitions under tested conditions (PubMed:35809574).
Functional Summary: Syndapin 1-mediated phase separation enables ultrafast endocytosis by concentrating Dynamin 1 at endocytic sites, reducing endocytosis time from ~257 ms to 28–39 ms (PubMed:35809574). Disruption via domain mutations (I122D/M123E or P434L) or Syndapin 1 knockdown slows endocytosis by 100-fold, demonstrating its essential role in membrane trafficking kinetics (PubMed:35809574).
Intrinsic Determinants & Regulations: Phase separation is intrinsically regulated by Syndapin 1's F-BAR domain for membrane binding and SH3 domain for partner interaction (PubMed:35809574). Mutations disrupting these domains—I122D/M123E in F-BAR (impairing membrane binding) and P434L in SH3 (abolishing Dynamin 1 interaction)—prevent condensate formation (PubMed:35809574).
Extrinsic Partners & Regulations: Syndapin 1 strictly requires Dynamin 1 as an extrinsic partner for condensate formation, acting as an adaptor between the plasma membrane and Dynamin 1 (PubMed:35809574).
